Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season and will be the largest storm system to make landfall in the region since Hurricane Helene in September 2024. Hurricane Isaias’s forecasted path toward the Gulf Coast has already impacted crude oil and natural gas production in the region. The Marine Minerals Administration reports that as of Thursday, October 8, 130 production platforms and rigs have been evacuated or moved resulting in production shut-ins of about 1.3 million barrels per day of crude oil and 1.1 billion million cubic feet per day of natural gas. The U.S. Gulf Coast is home to a large portion of the U.S. refining fleet, and the impacts from Hurricane Isaias could affect refinery operations . events.title: The humble chickpea has just boomed in value
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Chickpea prices hit $1,000 per tonne as importers rush to lock in supply Aussie chickpea prices are on the up. ( ABC Everyday: Heidi Sze ) Chickpea prices have skyrocketed to $1,000 per tonne. Several countries are rushing to lock in supply ahead of Ramadan. Australia's chickpea production is forecast to be down more than 50 per cent this season. Australian chickpeas are in hot demand, with delivered prices surging this month towards $1,000 per tonne in some regions. It is a significant jump from earlier in the year, when the market was trading closer to $600 per tonne. Grains Australia Pulse Council chair Peter Wilson said it was a great result for growers. "We haven't seen $1,000 per tonne since 2024 , so it's significant. It's a great price," he said. Chickpea prices have gone up considerably this month. ( ABC Landline ) So what is driving the sudden price surge for Australian chickpeas? Mr Wilson said it was due to a combination of factors. "There's a lot of volatility globally right now, which is creating enormous turbulence in logistics and supply chains, which is keeping buyers on edge," he said. "We're also seeing the impacts of El Niño, which looks to have left parts of India with lower-than-average rainfall from the monsoon, which has caused their local chickpea prices to rise, which is pushing everything along." The season's first delivery of chickpeas to the Mt McLaren receival site in Queensland. ( Supplied: Marc Johnston/GrainCorp ) Mr Wilson said there were several nations wanting to lock in supply ahead of Ramadan, which starts in early February. "Ramadan creates peak demand for a lot of our pulse crops [like chickpeas], and we see buyers wanting to have product pre-positioned at least one month ahead of Ramadan," he said. "So we're seeing some urgency from buyers trying to get product onboard vessels for key destination markets such as Pakistan, Bangladesh and the UAE, so it's in the market and ready for that Ramadan demand." In its most recent crop forecast, the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences (ABARES) predicted Australian chickpea production would fall by 52 per cent "to just over 1 million tonnes in 2026–27" due to significant cuts to area planted and expected lower yields in the major growing regions of northern New South Wales and Queensland. ABC Landline has been told that forecast may be "optimistic" and the overall crop might be even lower, which is another reason why there is some buyer urgency at the moment. Prices are expected to ease as harvest supply increases. New season chickpeas arrive at the receival site at Yamala, Queensland. ( Supplied: Fred Smith/GrainCorp ) North West Queensland chickpea grower Lucas Findley said he was pleased with his harvest, yielding about 1.2 tonnes per hectare. Although he had already forward-sold most of his chickpeas at a lower price, he said it was still exciting to see the market rally. "High prices are always good for any commodity and I'm happy for anyone who can take full advantage of these prices," Mr Findley said. "We'd sold around 75 per cent of our chickpea crop prior to this recent price rise at a good price that we were happy with. "But we still have around 25 per cent of the crop available to take advantage of the stronger prices, which will be a very nice finish to the season." Hummus is made from cooked, mashed chickpeas. ( ABC News: Wesley Mitton ) Mr Findley grows about 1,300 hectares of chickpeas as part of his grain and cotton rotation in Julia Creek. His chickpeas will be exported out of the Townsville Port, which is gearing up for its second-ever dry bulk shipment of the pulse. Last October, more than 38,000 tonnes of chickpeas were sent to India and Pakistan in a first-of-its-kind shipment from north Queensland, sourced from growing regions including Richmond, Julia Creek, Maxwelton and Marathon. This year, the port will also export sorghum for the first time, which Mr Findley said was "fantastic". "It just shows that people are supporting the expansion of North West Queensland farming more and more," he said. Watch ABC TV's Landline at 12:30pm on Sunday or on ABC iview .

events.title: US coastguard rescues 16 after boat sinks off Mexico’s Baja coast
events.summary: At least 11 people believed to still be missing, with rescue operations underway. The US coastguard has said it rescued 16 people from the Pacific Ocean after a boat sank off Mexico’s Baja coast. The coastguard said on Friday it responded to a Mayday call reporting that a boat was sinking. The search is ongoing for 11 people believed to be still missing. list 1 of 3 Two deaths reported as Hurricane Simon, storm Rachel batter Mexico’s coast list 2 of 3 Mexican court closes case against official over 2023 detention centre fire list 3 of 3 ICE tactics spark debate before pivotal US midterm elections The boat went down about 225km (140 miles) west of Ensenada, Mexico. A rescue helicopter reached the site about two hours after someone on the boat transmitted the Mayday call at about 1am (08:00 GMT) on Friday, said coastguard Lieutenant Santiago Tamburini. It took about 90 minutes for the coastguard crew, which included a rescue swimmer, to pull the 16 people from the water, Tamburini said. The people rescued were Mexican nationals, according to the Mexican consulate. One survivor was being treated for a suspected shark bite and two were in critical condition, authorities said. The rescued were flown by helicopter to San Diego, California, and transported to hospitals. The Mexican consulate in San Diego said it offered consular assistance. The coastguard and US Navy are continuing to search the area with two helicopters, a fixed-wing plane, a cutter and a navy combat ship. The boat sank in an area frequented by smugglers transporting migrants to the US. It is also popular with fishing and leisure boats. Details about the boat’s origin, destination and what it was doing are not clear. No vessel, only debris, was found, and it was unclear what type of boat was involved, the coastguard said. “Boats in that area can be for fishing, leisure, personal recreation. We just don’t know what they were doing out there. We all know it’s a suspected smuggling route,” Tamburini said.

events.title: Travel booking platform Klook Technology files to withdraw US listing
events.summary: Klook joins smart-ring maker Oura and nuclear services company Holtec among a growing list of companies that have deferred IPO plans in 2026. Klook Technology has filed to withdraw its US IPO plans on Oct 16, saying “this is not the right time to proceed with an IPO” because of market conditions. Reuters said US IPO activity has slowed as higher bond yields, a restrictive policy outlook and geopolitical uncertainty have made investors cautious. The Hong Kong-based travel platform, founded in 2014, said revenue rose 24% to US$417.1 million in 2024 and bookings are on track to exceed 80 million in 2026. Travel booking platform Klook Technology on Oct 16 filed to withdraw its US initial public offering plans amid market volatility. “Given current market conditions, Klook has decided this is not the right time to proceed with an IPO,” a company spokesperson told Reuters. “We will continue to evaluate the right time for a listing.” IPO activity in the US market has softened in recent weeks as higher bond yields, a prolonged restrictive policy outlook and geopolitical uncertainty have made investors more cautious. Klook joins smart-ring maker Oura and nuclear services company Holtec among a growing list of companies that have deferred IPO plans in 2026 as volatile markets continue to curb investor appetite for new listings. The Hong Kong-based company had filed for a US IPO in November 2025 , and at the time disclosed a 24% jump in 2024 revenue to US$417.1 million (S$534.8 million). Founded in 2014, Klook offers bookings for tours, attractions, transport and other travel experiences across a wide range of locations globally. It competes with global platforms such as Booking.com, TripAdvisor, China’s Trip.com and South Korea’s Yanolja. “Our business continues to grow, with total experiences booked on track to exceed 80 million this year,” the spokesperson said. Klook was aiming to list its shares on NYSE under the symbol “KLK”. REUTERS

events.title: Katie Zacharia ousted as White House press secretary
events.summary: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia was ousted Friday after just five days on the job, according to two senior Trump administration officials. Why it matters: Zacharia will be the shortest-tenured press secretary in modern history, with her first and only week in the White House marked by speculation about her legal credentials and criticism of her first press briefing. Trump told reporters Friday that he had urged Zacharia to "reconsider" the job, saying: "The news has been so nasty to her. I've never seen anything like it actually. And I said to her, 'honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider. You think about it, but I would reconsider." "POTUS is a big fan of Katie's, and what POTUS said to the reporters is exactly what he said in private," a senior White House official said. Driving the news: Zacharia was seen as a surprise pick when Trump announced her hiring on Oct. 9. She started work the following Monday, Oct. 12, and gave her first — and likely only — press briefing the following day. In that press conference, she was visibly shaky and nervous and left the president unimpressed, a White House official told Axios. Trump was also "blindsided" when he learned she wasn't an "attorney" as he had posted on Truth Social when he announced her hire. Zacharia tried to do damage control after a Wall Street Journal report that she wasn't licensed to practice law in any U.S. state. She told Fox News that she failed the exam and never retook it, since she was moving to China But her interview explanations weren't seen as up to snuff by Trump, the source said. Background: Zacharia's hiring was solely a Trump decision, one furthered along with the strong input of his personal assistant Natalie Harp. Zacharia flew out Thursday to Washington, slipped quietly into the White House without seeing any friends in the media or administration and had a good meeting with Trump. On Friday, Trump offered her the job on the spot. Contrary to other reports, Trump told Chief of Staff Susie Wiles his decision. Wiles, who did not know Zacharia before, raised no objections because she knew the press secretary job is a personal one for the president, another administration source said. Before hiring Zacharia , Trump wanted to hire former Fox News host Maria Bartiromo, two administration sources said, but she signaled she was not going to take the job. Conservative commentator Scott Jennings was in contention but wasn't offered the job. Behind the scenes: Zacharia's arrival concerned some staffers who feared she wanted to replace them. Zacharia denied this and tried to put their minds at ease. A White House official told Axios that Zacharia and her family are having dinner tonight with Vice President Vance and Vance's family at the VP's residence at the Naval Observatory. "The warmth for Katie goes well beyond the president," the official said. What we're watching: Fox News correspondent Peter Doocy said he spoke with Trump on Friday and that the president is in "no rush" to name a replacement for the press secretary. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information throughout. Go deeper: Trump press secretary explains failed bar exam Barak Ravid contributed to this story.

events.title: Work starts on Bundaberg's first hotel development in 20 years
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Topic: Regional Development and Planning The 4.5-star hotel will offer almost 100 rooms. ( Supplied: Bundaberg Regional Council ) Work has started on Bundaberg's first hotel development in 20 years. A recent report into the region's accommodation needs showed it was 800 beds short every night. Construction on the new hotel on Airport Drive is due to finish by the middle of next year. It has taken two decades, but Bundaberg's next hotel development is underway. Four hours north of Brisbane, the city is a key tourism destination for the southern Great Barrier Reef but has not attracted significant short-term accommodation development in 20 years, according to Bundaberg Regional Council. The 4.5-star, three-storey hotel, situated across the road from the Bundaberg Airport, will offer 97 rooms. Mayor Helen Blackburn said the demand for accommodation was constantly growing. "The hotel demand study showed us that we were 800 beds short every night in our region," she said. "This is just one step towards bridging that gap." Cr Blackburn said it had been difficult to attract hotel developers to the region due to the current stock of aging motels. "Those older motels sell their rooms at a cheaper rate, which then doesn't give investors the confidence to think that if they build a new hotel, they can get the price for the rooms that they need," she said. Developer MVP said the new hotel would refresh the hospitality offering in Bundaberg. "We hope that it will be a destination of choice for travellers to the region and will bring more travellers to the region," a spokesperson said. Construction is due to finish by the middle of next year. ( Supplied: Bundaberg Regional Council ) The hotel has been funded by investor MyState Limited, with chief executive Brett Morgan saying the demand was clear. "Every time you go down the street in Bundaberg, there's no-vacancy signs everywhere," he said. Mr Morgan said the hotel would also create about 50 ongoing jobs. Bundaberg Tourism chief executive Duncan Littler said the development would cater to leisure and business travellers. "Already, there's more than 750,000 people that choose to visit the beautiful Bundaberg region each year and they stay for more than 2 million nights," he said. "We hope that investments like this will also encourage other [tourism] operators, potentially even airlines, to consider investing in the region." Brett Morgan, Helen Blackburn and Duncan Littler have welcomed the project. ( ABC Wide Bay: Grace Whiteside ) Cr Blackburn said other accommodation applications were in the pipeline but did not elaborate. "We have definitely been encouraging accommodation providers in terms of hotels, student accommodation and even aged care accommodation to set up in our region because we know that we need that here," she said. Construction on the Airport Drive hotel is due to finish by mid-2027, with the first guests expected later next year. events.title: Oregon school shooter was former special needs student, police say
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections A teacher fought the teenage shooter and a parent shot him dead, police say on Friday, a day after four people were killed. The 16-year-old who killed three children and a teacher at an elementary school in the US state of Oregon was a former special-needs student at the school, police and school officials have said. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz identified the attacker on Friday, a day after the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School, as Griffin J. John II. list 1 of 3 Minneapolis shooting kills two, wounds three police officers list 2 of 3 US arrests suspect in connection with Tumbler Ridge school shooting list 3 of 3 Nine killed in shooting in US state of Pennsylvania, including two children He said the teenager attacked a classroom of special-needs students, where all the victims were shot. Steven Cook, superintendent of Bend-La Pine Schools, said John was not enrolled in the local public school system at the time. “That classroom was a special needs classroom, and the suspect was a special needs student in that school,” Cook told a news conference. Krantz said John shot his way through locked doors with a 12-gauge shotgun, firing as many as 15 shots, and had about 44 rounds left when he was killed. Police are still trying to determine how he obtained the gun. Under Oregon law, a minor may possess a shotgun if provided by a parent or with a parent’s consent. The shooter’s mother, Shauntai Nickerson, separately told reporters outside her apartment: “I’m so sorry, I wish I could have done something.” A teacher threw her phone at the gunman, then tackled and fought him, likely saving lives, Krantz said, calling her actions “heroic”. She was not injured. A 36-year-old father, Kaylub Giamanco, who has two children at the school, then followed the gunman inside and shot him dead minutes after the first 911 call. US President Donald Trump called Giamanco a “great hero”. “It’s a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it,” Trump said. The children killed were aged five, eight and 11, and the teacher was Meghan Lambert, 25, police said. A seven-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were taken to hospital in critical condition. The shooting is the 28th mass killing in the US this year, according to a database by The Associated Press, USA Today and Northeastern University. The Gun Violence Archive in the US has documented 369 mass shootings in 2026, defined as incidents in which four or more people are shot. The Everytown for Gun Safety group has counted at least 100 incidents of gunfire on school grounds this year, with 34 deaths.

events.title: Players are experiencing safety threats from ‘vitriol’ of prediction market users, 11x WNBA All-Star Nneka Ogwumike warns
events.summary: As prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket are increasingly being used for sportsbetting, athletes are warning of the negative and even violent consequences of these platforms on players. At the Fortune Most Powerful Women Summit in Santa Barbara, California on Tuesday, Nneka Ogwumike, former Los Angeles Sparks forward, 2016 MVP, and 11-time All-Star in the league, said prediction markets are having a clear adverse impact on WNBA players. “It’s not a safe place for athletes,” Ogwumike told Most Powerful Women editor Emma Hinchliffe. “I don’t think I ever want to say that something is outrightly bad unless it absolutely is, but players are definitely having a hard time dealing with the vitriol that comes with prediction markets as it relates to our performance.” Prediction markets have emerged as an alternative and supplement to online sportsbooks because they are classified as a financial exchange, rather than gambling platforms, allowing them to bypass regulations and restrictions . Last week, both Kalshi and Polymarket hit new records, according to Dune Analytics data , reaching a combined weekly volume of $22.2 billion as a result of NFL and NCAA-bolstered trading volumes. College athletes are reporting harassment associated with sportsbetting. The 2025 NCAA Growth, Opportunities, Aspirations and Learning of Students in College study found more than have of Division 1 men’s basketball players reported social media abuse based on their on-court performance, and 46% said the highest rate of negative or threatening messages were from someone who placed a bet on a game they played in. On Tuesday, both the NBA and WNBA announced a responsible gaming campaign , partnering with National Council on Problem Gambling (NCPG) to educate fans about sports betting risks. Ogwumike said more efforts are required to mitigate abuse of players related to sports betting. “There’s been a lot of safety issues and concerns that haven’t necessarily been publicly displayed,” she said. “Through the [players association] and through the WNBA, there’s resources that are available to try and mitigate those things, but it doesn’t mean that it stops players from experiencing things that could potentially and have potentially affected their performance.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Katie Zacharia had the shortest tenure as press secretary in history. Here are the others who didn't last long.
events.summary: Katie Zacharia came under scrutiny for her legal credentials shortly after her first press briefing on Tuesday. Win McNamee/Getty Images President Donald Trump chose Katie Zacharia to serve as the new White House press secretary. After five days, a White House official said that she is "transitioning out" of the role. Zacharia is among three other former press secretaries with tenures lasting under two months. Katie Zacharia's first briefing as President Donald Trump's press secretary was on Tuesday. By Friday, the White House confirmed she was out. The record five-day tenure came after days of missteps by Zacharia, and amid two watchdog groups filing complaints with the State Bar of California on Wednesday, asking it to investigate whether she violated California law by calling herself a lawyer. While the longest-serving press secretary was Stephen Early, who held the post for 12 years under Franklin D. Roosevelt, only four press secretaries have lasted under two months. Here's a closer look at White House press secretaries with the shortest tenures. Katie Zacharia Katie Zacharia served as press secretary under Donald Trump for five days. Samuel Corum/Pool/FTWP Katie Zacharia made her White House press briefing debut on Tuesday and quickly came under intense scrutiny over her legal credentials. Shortly after Tuesday's briefing, she was asked which state she passed the bar exam in and replied: " When I moved to China ." On Thursday in an interview with right-wing provocateur Jack Posobiec , Zacharia said she took the bar exam but failed, and never retook it. Zacharia moved to China after earning her law degree in 2011, and told Posobiec she had already preregistered for the bar exam before moving to Beijing, where her husband was working at an American private equity firm. "I didn't want to withdraw from that," Zacharia said of the bar exam. "And we knew we would be moving out to China, and I was obviously incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited for finally being married to someone who I had been long-distance from for at least a year." She served as press secretary between October 12 and October 16. Stephen Early Stephen Early served as Franklin D. Roosevelt's press secretary for 12 years. He briefly served as acting press secretary under Harry S. Truman in December 1950 for 14 days. Original Caption Stephen Early is both the longest-serving press secretary in US history and the press secretary with the second-shortest tenure. He was President Franklin D. Roosevelt's press secretary for 12 years, from 1933 to March 1945. Early then briefly returned as acting press secretary under President Harry S. Truman in December 1950 after the death of press secretary Charles Ross. Early was in the position for 14 days, from December 5 to December 18, 1950. Jerald TerHorst Gerald TerHorst served as press secretary under President Gerald Ford for 31 days. UPI/Bettmann Archive/Getty Images Jerald TerHorst served as President Gerald Ford's press secretary for over one month, from August 9 to September 8, 1974. He resigned in protest of Ford's pardon of former President Richard Nixon following the Watergate scandal. TerHorst said he could not defend Ford's decision in good conscience, despite his long-standing friendship with the president. Jonathan Daniels Jonathan Daniels (far left) served as press secretary under both Franklin D. Roosevelt and Harry S. Truman for 48 days. Keystone-France/Gamma-Keystone via Getty Images Jonathan Daniels served a short tenure as press secretary at the end of Franklin D. Roosevelt's presidency and at the beginning of Harry S. Truman's. That brings his tenure to 48 days, from March 29 to May 15, 1945. He was appointed shortly before Roosevelt's death and stayed on temporarily to help Truman transition into the presidency. Truman then selected Charles Ross as Daniels' replacement. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Albanian PM blames ‘foreign hands’ for unrest as student protests intensify
events.summary: Riot police clash with protesters for fourth day, as young Albanians protest corruption and poor university conditions Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama has blamed “foreign hands” for the increasingly violent student-led protests that are calling on him to resign. Riot police clashed with protesters outside the education ministry for the fourth day in a row, as thousands of young Albanians marched through the capital, Tirana, on Friday to protest government corruption and poor university conditions. list 1 of 3 ‘Each country goes its own way’: How Balkan politics shape ties with Israel list 2 of 3 ‘Boiling point’: Why students are protesting against Albania’s Edi Rama list 3 of 3 Albania’s PM dismisses calls to resign as student protests spread “This is not a student phenomenon,” Rama said in a video address on Friday. He said there were “foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace”. Rama insisted that the protest had “absolutely nothing to do with the hardships, problems or legitimate aspirations of anyone who desires a better life”. Police officers used water cannon and tear gas as demonstrators hurled rocks. The protests have spread beyond the capital to Elbasan, Shkodra and Korca, where demonstrators broke windows and set fire to rubbish bins, local media reported. The ongoing escalation follows months of mostly peaceful demonstrations, originally sparked by the sale of part of Albania’s coastline to a luxury resort development linked to Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law. Days of unrest have increasingly targeted banks and government buildings. Protesters hurled bricks and concrete blocks at the education ministry on Tuesday. They also set fire to several buildings across the city, including the prime minister’s office, the finance and justice ministry buildings and branches of several banks. According to a police statement, 160 people were detained over alleged acts of violence on Thursday evening. Demonstrators are demanding Rama’s resignation, as well as electoral and education reforms. The prime minister, whose government denies corruption, said he would be ready to discuss rising education costs but rejected the calls to resign. He said on Thursday, “My responsibility is to listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward.” His dismissal “would be a betrayal of the Albanians who gave me a strong mandate to complete negotiations on European Union membership”, he added. Corruption scandals have complicated Albania’s efforts to join the EU. Analysts say the country is a hub for gangs seeking to launder money from drugs and weapons trafficking. Rama won a fourth term last year on promises to take Albania into the EU, aiming for membership as early as 2028.

events.title: China’s tourists flock to experience a pretend typhoon as ‘dark tourism’ flourishes
events.summary: The concept of ‘paying to suffer’ soars in popularity, with simulated disasters proving a modern twist on visiting sites of historic tragedies W hen Leon Lv was looking for somewhere to travel last year, she turned to the Chinese social media app RedNote for ideas. The algorithm took her to videos of people struggling to survive typhoon-strength winds and flash floods. “I never experienced a typhoon. I don’t know how it will feel and what will happen. I just have seen it on the news,” says the 28-year-old from Chongqing in south-west China . “So that’s why I want to go there to have a safe place to experience it and learn something.” She travelled more than 1,300km to Hangzhou in the east, and joined a group of 20 to take part in a disaster simulation that featured a typhoon-fuelled flooding scenario. Standing in a simulated flood, her mind momentarily went blank as hundreds of tonnes of water swept people off their feet, and carried them towards a safety barrier. As the surge hit, she forgot she was in a simulation. “One thing I learned is how to stay calm and protect myself during a flood. I learned how to use the right body position to stay safe,” she says. “No book and no school [can] teach me like that.” Across Chinese social platforms phrases like “paying to suffer”, or “paying to buy fear” are trending online as part of a wave of interest in experiences known as “dark tourism”. Lvxing Base, a company in Hangzhou offering simulated disaster experiences has gone viral. The founders spent 10 years making documentaries in some of the world’s most extreme environments. At a 200,000 square metre facility, which opened in 2024, they simulate extreme weather conditions like typhoons and mudslides, giving participants the experience of what it would be like in a disaster. “I don’t deny that many people come because they want excitement,” says general manager Wang Kuanghan. They want to see what this place is like, what a real typhoon and torrential rain feel like, and whether they themselves can withstand it. Most of our individual customers are between 20 and 30 years old.” It plans to open five more centres across China within the next three years. It also plans to create earthquake and fire simulations. The offering are not limited to private companies. At Beijing’s Haidian public safety museum, tourists experience simulated earthquakes, tsunamis and fires using a 4D theatre, equipped with moving platforms and sound effects. Last year the southern Chinese city of Guangzhou opened a five-storey centre to teach visitors how to respond to emergencies and disasters. Its earthquake simulator can recreate ground shaking equivalent to a 7.2 magnitude quake. Extreme weather has become increasingly common in China. In 2025, China recorded its highest number of hot days since records began, and was hit by 10 typhoons, well above the long-term annual average. China’s ministry of emergencies reported that 67 million people were affected by such disasters across the country. In 2024, local governments were instructed to promote immersive disaster education, instructing safety centres, museums and training bases to use simulations to teach people how to respond in a real crisis. “The new generation of Chinese travellers want to experience a place rather than simply see famous attractions,” says Robert Li, director of the School of Hotel and Tourism Management at the Chinese University of Hong Kong. But some travellers have found a way to blend the two approaches; rather than indulging in the white-knuckle ride of a simulated typhoon, they are travelling to real sites of death and destruction. In May 2008 a magnitude 8.0 earthquake devastated towns in China’s Sichuan province, killing more than 70,000 people. Alice*, a 30-year-old writer from Sichuan walked around Beichuan, one of the affected towns, the ruins of which the government had preserved. Metal beams hold collapsed buildings in place for the public to visit. She saw the site where schools collapsed, crushing students inside. In Yingxue close to the epicentre, a broken clock surrounded by the remains of a middle school is frozen at 2.28, the moment the earthquake struck. “I felt scared because of the power of nature and how many children and students could not escape from it,” says Alice, who plans to start a Chinese language Substack account detailing her journeys into tragedy. “Everything was so broken. It became like a ghost town, because nobody lives in the old town any more.” Alice believes dark tourism helps a country reconcile with its past, even if the government decides what can be remembered. In recent years, tour guide Samantha Wang has seen an increase in Chinese tourists attending the Nanjing Massacre Memorial Hall. In 1937 the Japanese Imperial army captured Nanjing, and Chinese official accounts say 300,000 civilians and soldiers were killed over weeks of massacres.

events.title: ServiceNow CFO says leaders working 14 hours and getting 4 hours of sleep set a ‘terrible example’ for their employees
events.summary: Leaders in the corporate world are familiar with a sports metaphor: They want to get a project across the finish line or make sure workplace standards are up to par. But many seemingly fail to carry forward the value athletes have in rest. ServiceNow president and Chief Financial Officer Gina Mastantuono, who has espoused the benefits of fitness in both individual health and leadership, said that while the importance of recovery has broken into culture outside of athletics, it hasn’t fully permeated the vocabulary or habits of business leaders. Speaking at the Fortune Most Powerful Women Summit in Santa Barbara, Calif. on Tuesday, Mastantuono said many senior employees still embody toxic ideas about overworking. “There’s always been this—if you have to work 14-hour days and you get four hours sleep, and that shows that you’re working the hardest and you deserve the most,” she told Alicia Hatch, U.S. Sports chief commercial officer and women’s sports leader at Deloitte. “And in fact, that is such a terrible example for the people around us.” Research has consistently shown the value of boundaries and the establishment of work-life balance. A University of Florida meta-analysis of nearly 200 studies, for example, found recovery from work is associated with better sleep, improved mental health, and increased long-term satisfaction with one’s life. But internalizing that rest is important is a different matter, Mastantuono noted. “Recovery is part of the performance; it’s not secondary,” she said. “Muscle doesn’t grow when we pump out at the gym. It grows when we’re sleeping at night and letting the muscles recover.” Mastantuono has noticed the benefits of recovery in her own life, attributing better work-life balance to a honed ability to listen instead of reaction, and maintain calm under duress and pressure, which has enabled her teams to execute more effectively. “When we do focus on taking care of ourselves, then we are much better bosses, much better colleagues, much better parents,” she said. Janet Evans, a four-time Olympic medalist and swimming and chief athlete officer of LA28, the organizing committee for the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games in Los Angeles, was well-versed in the importance of recovery in the context of competition, but has similarly needed reminders about taking a breather. Evans told Hatch about LA28 CEO Reynold Hoover, a three-star ex-U.S. Army Lieutenant General who frequently incorporates military parlance into in-office conversations. “No one’s guns are drawn. No one is shooting each other,” Evans recalled Hoover saying. “So Janet, you’re gonna figure this out tomorrow.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Boardrooms are no longer rewarded for being right, Lumen CEO says, and it means executive partnerships are more important than ever
events.summary: Amid geopolitical uncertainty and the AI boom, executive leadership has had to become a much less insular affair. Lumen Technologies CEO Kate Johnson, speaking at the Fortune Most Powerful Women Summit in Santa Barbara, Calif. on Tuesday, said that as companies have had to become more nimble in their decision-making, it’s no longer realistic for them to rely only on their respective leaderships to make tough calls and should instead rely on partnerships between, not just within, C-suites. “This notion of the boardroom and the conference room that I grew up in—we were rewarded for being right. We had to know our stuff. We had to be the best. We had to come in with a strong opinion. We had to have all the facts we had to master, and that is just not possible in today’s market,” Johnson told Fortune ’s Diane Brady. Johnson explained that instead, you have to “build a machine” for decision-making, which includes coming up with a hypothesis, but then looking at signals, as well as experts inside and outside a business to inform constant course-correction. “I’m getting signals every day, and we’re pivoting every day,” she added. “My job is to get a grant and to allocate the capital accordingly, and you have to have a bench of partners that you can go to to deliver those outcomes.”   IBM has already begun to measure changes in how CEOs are interacting with one another. More than 80% of chief executives of AI-first companies are engaging partners from external or specialized networks to talk about risk and build off each other’s strengths, according to its 2026 CEO Study . A large part of that shift comes from rapid changes in AI and how workplaces are adopting it, compressing decision-making cycles and forcing companies to break down previously established boundaries in search of cooperation, the report noted. More broadly, Boston Consulting Group similarly observed that as mergers and acquisitions slow , companies are instead looking for alliances, with 60% of surveyed business leaders saying that over the next three to five years, joint ventures and partnerships will be more important to growth than pursuing M&A. Lumen Technologies found one such partner in consultancy EY. In June 2025, EY U.S. and Blue Planet formed a strategic alliance to improve autonomous networking with AI, and Lumen was the project’s first client. Johnson’s initial connection with EY CEO and Global Chair Janet Truncale was a spontaneous one. Johnson approached Truncale at a Business Roundtable breakfast a few years ago and in hopes of improving her day, Johnson said to Truncale, “Will you be my best friend?” “And I was happy to oblige,” Truncale told Brady. The interaction shifted Truncale’s own approach in meeting new leaders. “In the last two years, I’ve frankly tried to pay that forward,” she said, “so when there are new CEOs, I try to reach out and say, ‘Hey, I’ve just been through this.’” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

Who: Leeds United vs Manchester United What: English Premier League Where: Elland Road, Leeds, United Kingdom When: Sunday, October 18, at 2pm local time (13:00 GMT) How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will have all the build-up from 9:00 GMT ahead of our live text commentary stream Manchester United against Leeds United has long been one of the fiercest rivalries in football. list 1 of 4 Real Madrid demand resignation of La Liga chief after Goebbels comparison list 2 of 4 Pro-Nazi chants before Ajax match slammed by Croatia leaders list 3 of 4 Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia still on, organisers say, but golf tour postponed list 4 of 4 FIFA set for rule change after Balogun red card row at the World Cup: reports The former’s closest shot to ending their wait since 1967 for an English top flight title came in 1993 when Sir Alex Ferguson’s side were pipped to the title by the latter. The following year United’s wait was over as Ferguson’s side – buoyed by the arrival of Eric Cantona from Leeds – lifted the inaugural Premier League crown. The rest for United and Ferguson was history, but since the most successful manager in English football retired the Old Trafford club have been in decline. The fortunes of Leeds, who have won three league titles, dipped dramatically after that last piece of domestic silverware. Ten years later, they were relegated and three years were even spent in League One, the third tier of English football. Now the Elland Road club are back in the top flight, having won the Championship two seasons ago, and have an eye on the top four this weekend. Al Jazeera Sport takes a look at the match that for Leeds marks the arrival of their fiercest rivals, who have lurched to a 40-year low. How have Leeds United fared this season? Leeds have lost only one of their six league games this season, a 2-1 reverse at Arsenal in their last match when the Premier League holders were second best for much of the match and were forced to come from behind. Two wins and two draws in their first five league matches saw Leeds holding onto the coat-tails of Arsenal and City. That run culminated with a stunning 4-1 home win against Newcastle United. A disappointing home draw with Crystal Palace sat in between the defeat at Arsenal . A 6-3 defeat at Chelsea ended their League Cup hopes, but the home side needed two goals in the last ten minutes to pull clear in the thrilling encounter. How have Manchester United fared this season? United’s season – and Michael Carrick’s start as permanent manager – couldn’t have got off to a worse start with a 2-0 defeat at newly-promoted Hull City. When the Red Devils fell a goal behind against another promoted side, Ipswich Town, at Old Trafford in their next match, the warning signs were there. Carrick’s side came back to win 5-2 – and that remains United’s only league win of the season. A contentious 1-0 home defeat by Manchester City – in which a controversial VAR decision separated the sides – has been one of United’s better performances with deflating draws against Everton , Fulham and Tottenham surrounding the derby. United were also dumped out of the League Cup by Brighton, who overcame the home side’s early 2-0 first-half lead to the disbelief of Old Trafford. What is the latest on Lisandro Martinez’s Manchester United criticism? Defender Lisandro ‌‌Martinez will be available for Sunday’s game after ⁠⁠United accepted ⁠⁠his apology for criticising its transfer policy, Carrick told reporters on Friday. Martinez met Carrick and senior club officials on Thursday, two days after suggesting United ⁠⁠needed greater investment to compete at the highest level following their 2-0 Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid. The centre back later apologised for his remarks and Carrick ⁠⁠sought to downplay the episode when he spoke to reporters on Friday. “We’ve moved on from that. It was one of those things. It’s really not a drama for the group,” Carrick said. “The squad have trained really well and they are in good spirits. There is ‌‌a freshness about the group… “He’s part of the squad [for Sunday].” What happened the last time Leeds played Manchester United? Leeds were 2-1 winners at Old Trafford when the sides met in the Premier League in April. Noah Okafor scored both goals for Leeds to inflict the only defeat of Carrick’s interim tenure, having replaced Ruben Amorim as manager. Martinez was sent off early in the second half, but Casemiro offered United some hope just after the hour mark. What happened in the corresponding Leeds-Man Utd game last season? The teams shared a 1-1 draw in the Premier League match at Elland Road last season. Leeds’ Brenden Aaronson opened the scoring in the 62nd minute with Matheus Cunha levelling three minutes later. events.title: Italy probes Israel’s Katz over abuse, sexual assault of flotilla activists
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? Rome prosecutors also name 12 senior military, police and prison officials over alleged abuse of detained activists. Italian prosecutors have placed Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz and 12 senior military, police and prison officials under investigation over the treatment of activists detained on Gaza-bound solidarity boats, widening a probe that had centred on far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. The Rome prosecutors’ office said on Friday that the case concerns suspected torture, kidnapping, personal injury, robbery and damage when Israeli forces intercepted small fleets of activist boats heading towards Gaza in 2025 and 2026. list 1 of 3 Gaza flotilla activists allege abuse, sexual assault in Israeli detention list 2 of 3 Italy’s foreign minister slams Israel’s Ben-Gvir over ‘flip-flop’ comments list 3 of 3 ‘Active in BDS’: Document reveals how Israel scrutinised global NGOs It opened the investigation after complaints from 50 Italian citizens who were detained following two Global Sumud Flotilla missions last year and this year. Those named as suspects include Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir. Prosecutors said activists detained after the first mission in 2025 reported beatings , injuries, death threats, insults and accusations of terrorism. Those on the second mission in 2026 reported harsher treatment, including beatings in the dark and the use of tasers and rubber bullets, the statement said. The activists reported at least 15 cases of sexual assault, including rape. Luca Poggi, an Italian economist who was detained, told Reuters news agency in May: “We were stripped, thrown to the ground, kicked.” Ben-Gvir dismissed news of the investigation in June, saying he would “continue to stand proudly alongside” Israeli soldiers. Flotilla organisers say they aim to break Israel’s blockade of Gaza by delivering humanitarian aid. The first Global Sumud Flotilla set sail from Barcelona in September 2025 with 42 boats and 462 activists. Israeli forces intercepted it in international waters in early October that year, with hundreds detained and later deported. The second mission left Barcelona in April 2026. Israeli forces began intercepting its vessels near the southern Greek island of Crete on April 30, and by May 19 had detained about 430 people on some 50 ships in international waters, with the final interceptions taking place off Cyprus. Ben-Gvir later posted a video showing him taunting activists who were cable-tied and kneeling at a makeshift prison at the port of Ashdod while Israel’s national anthem played. Prosecutors said they sent Israel a request for judicial assistance in June, seeking information to reconstruct events and establish individual responsibility, but did not say whether Israel had responded. They also held talks at Eurojust, the EU’s judicial cooperation agency, as other similar investigations are under way in other European countries. Under Italian law, crimes committed abroad against Italian citizens can be prosecuted in Rome. If the investigation finds the charges warranted, prosecutors could formally request a trial.

events.title: Anthropic polled 1,334 of its employees. They're more sure than most of us that AI will take over jobs.
events.summary: Attendees chat at Anthropic's developer conference in May. Don Feria/AP Content Services for Anthropic Anthropic published new surveys comparing its staffers' sentiments to those of US workers. The AI startup's employees expect the tech to change work and the economy far more dramatically. Most Anthropic employees guessed that unemployment would top 12% in 2030. Anthropic employees believe that AI will make their labor obsolete. Most US workers don't see their jobs that way at all. The AI company published research on Friday that compares surveys with US adults against an internal poll of 1,334 Anthropic employees. Most of the Anthropic staffers said AI will handle at least 80% of their jobs by 2030, while only about 5% of the US workers felt the same. The research, titled " The AI expectations gap, " shows the chasm between how the employees at the AI startup feel and how other American adults feel. Anthropic workers are far more optimistic about the progress of AI capabilities, how much it's already saving time, and how fast the economy will grow. The median Anthropic employee said that by the end of 2030, they expect AI to handle 95% of the work of building a new AI model. Peter McCrory, Anthropic's chief economist, wrote on X that the views might help outsiders prepare for more capable AI systems . "We're publishing this research because Anthropic runs roughly a year and a half ahead of the economy on AI adoption, so what happens at Anthropic could be a leading indicator for the broader world," he said. Anthropic workers expect higher unemployment and extreme GDP growth Anthropic's surveys examined how workers already use AI and how they think it will change. "US adults and Anthropic staff largely agree about what AI can do today," the researchers wrote. "However, they disagree about how quickly it will improve, how widely it will be used, and how large the productivity gains measured by time saved will be." There are a few possible explanations for the discrepancies. Anthropic employees have larger budgets for the tools and often get access to unreleased models. US workers, on average, are more likely to work with their hands or in a service industry. The researchers found that workers in manual trades , production, and transport thought AI would handle the least of their work by 2030, compared with Anthropic staffers, tech workers, and respondents in business and finance. Most Anthropic employees surveyed said that they expect the unemployment rate to top 12% in 2030. The majority of the US workers thought it would hover around or under 8%. It's currently 4.2%. So far, researchers have found mixed evidence on AI disrupting the job market — a Yale team recently found it had mainly changed jobs, and had "no connection" to changes in unemployment. The Anthropic researchers also compiled survey responses to estimate predictions on economic growth. Based on their answers, the median US adult's guess for GDP growth in 2030 was 5.4%, compared with 17.1% among Anthropic employees. The country's GDP grew by 2.2% last year. Anthropic's staffers are following their leader Anthropic's CEO, Dario Amodei , has become one of the industry's most closely watched voices on labor upheaval. In March of 2025, he said he expected AI to write 90% of code within 6 months, and "essentially all of the code" within the year. He made more headlines that May, telling Axios that AI could wipe out half of entry-level white-collar jobs within five years and lift unemployment to 10% or 20%. Amodei expanded on that claim in a later essay , writing that he expects AI to be different from prior technological changes. He wrote that he expects an "unprecedented" short-term shock to labor, and that the economy will grow dramatically. "AI isn't a substitute for specific human jobs but rather a general labor substitute for humans," he wrote. Have a tip? events.title: Darwin accountant trades tax for cane toad taxidermy
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts 'More to life': Darwin accountant trades numbers for cane toad taxidermy Mithram Selvaratnam transforms cane toads into souvenirs sold at Darwin's Mindil Markets. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) There are 531 dead cane toads in Mithram Selvaratnam's Darwin backyard freezers. By Christmas, some will be wearing Santa hats. The former accountant runs an unusual souvenir business, which sees him doing everything from sandblasting and whitening crocodile skulls to gutting and stuffing dead toads. Former accountant Mithram Selvaratnam now sells taxidermy cane toads and crocodile products at Darwin's markets. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) It's a far cry from the life he envisioned for himself when he left Malaysia to study accounting in Australia 16 years ago. "When I grew up it was all about the rat race," he said. The decision to leave it all behind came to Mr Selvaratnam after working full time as an accountant in Melbourne. "I was doing that corporate life, 9 to 5, stuck in the office, and I just felt like there was more to life," he said. Christmas-themed cane toads are being prepared for the festive season. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) Word of Mr Selvaratnam's dilemma got out to his Darwin-based aunt, who offered an unexpected solution. For decades she had been selling curries at the iconic Mindil Markets and a neighbouring stall had put his Territory souvenir business up for sale. That was in 2017 and the transition from spreadsheets to stuffed toads hasn't always been smooth sailing. Mr Selvaratnam was initially purchasing the toads from a taxidermist in Queensland, but when the supplier decided to retire, he was left with two choices — give up the business or take matters into his own hands. Grace Ray works on a taxidermy cane toad at Mithram's Leanyer work space. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) "Before I started doing this, I could barely pick a toad up," he said. "But I thought, we have plenty of toads in the Territory, an abundance of supply, so I'll just make them myself. "I went [to Townsville] and put myself through a two-day bootcamp of learning how to do it." It was through gritted teeth and pinched nostrils that Mr Selvaratnam learnt to gut, tan, stuff and dry the warty pests before painting them with varnish to make them "look pretty". Former accountant Mithram Selvaratnam couldn't even touch cane toads until he underwent 'taxidermy bootcamp'. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) Armed with his new-found knowledge, a head torch and gloves, Mr Selvaratnam began scouring golf courses and gardens hunting the pests. Community 'toad busts', like the one held recently at the Territory Wildlife Park , can provide hundreds of dead toads to Mr Selvaratnam in a single night without him having to lift a finger. Territory Wildlife Park ranger Luke Hare says toad busts aim to reduce the numbers of the pests while also educating the community of their dangers. "Cane toads produce significant risk to a lot of our native species," he said. "A lot of our natives can't tolerate the toxins cane toads have, so when they eat the cane toad, or try to eat them, often it will kill them." Mr Hare estimates that there could be hundreds of thousands of cane toads running rampant in the wildlife park on Darwin's outskirts. For Mr Selvaratnam, the park's latest haul of 531 toads has come just in time for his end-of-year Christmas orders. Soon, newly minted santa hat-clad critters will join their rum-drinking, ukulele-playing and occasionally X-rated counterparts. The recent toad bust has filled the freezers at his Leanyer workshop. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) But cane toads aren't the only unwanted creatures finding a second life in Mr Selvaratnam's backyard. Among the tanning equipment and taxidermy tools are chest freezers full of crocodile heads. "I started with the toads and the skulls came about a year after that," he said. Crocodile teeth and skulls are also turned into souvenirs. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) Mr Selvaratnam had initially been buying the skulls from a supplier, but in a case of deja vu, retirement once again threatened his supply chain. "This time I didn't go down to Queensland to learn, I just got him on the phone and he ran me through it, and from then, on experimentation, really," he said. The skulls are a by-product from crocodile farms in the Territory, and along with croc teeth, buffalo heads and other leather goods, they make up the rest of Mr Selvaratnam's unlikely livelihood. He's also recently been experimenting with other forms of taxidermy including the Territory's iconic barramundi.

events.title: The $124 trillion Great Wealth Transfer and women’s earning power has created a ‘perfect storm’ of opportunity, wealth executives say
events.summary: Women already have more money than ever before—and they’ll soon step into even more financial power. They’re not only set to inherit $52 trillion by 2048 as major players in the $124 trillion Great Wealth Transfer, according to Cerulli Associates, but they’re also wielding growing financial mettle in rising to top-level roles. Wealth management professionals are already looking to meet the moment. At Fortune ’s Most Powerful Women Summit this year, financial services execs say women are at the helm of great financial opportunity. Anna Maria Nekoranec, CEO and cofounder of Align Private Capital, noted that women are amassing significant fortunes as they win out in business and take over boardrooms. It’s her “personal mission” to assist women stepping into wealth make smart decisions with their money, because she believes “we can change the world with it.” “We have a perfect storm because it’s not just this wealth transfer,” Nekoranec told leadership editor Claire Zillman during the discussion. “What we’re seeing is this acceleration of super talented women reaching higher levels of organizations, getting higher comp, and getting stock…These windfalls need to be planned for.” Mitra Best, founder and CEO of fintech firm Avvra, added that the rise of AI is turbocharging their net worths. As an investor and AI scientist herself, she’s witnessed how the industry’s wealth is “imbalanced” as decisions are made by a select few at the top, and decided to enter financial services to help women invest in “where the future is going to be.” She wants Avvra to be their eyes and ears on what companies are getting funding, what technologies are drawing money, and what issues are getting solved. “Who writes the checks funds the future,” Best said. But the wealth management leaders collectively urge women to take matters into their own hands. They acknowledge that life can get busy; women are often working full-time jobs while shouldering the majority of housework and family responsibilities. But to build wealth, they need to make time on the books, one Fidelity executive advises. Karla D’Alleva Valas, the head of private wealth management at the financial services giant, urged women to make their financial futures a priority by carving out meetings to actively manage their money. It’s estimated that 53% of women’s assets are currently unmanaged by professional advisors, according to McKinsey & Company, compared to 45% for men. It’s a $10 trillion market opportunity for wealth managers, and a chance for women to take greater control of their financial futures. “All of us need to measure ourselves on our level of engagement. Meeting with your financial advisor—if you have one—one time a year, that’s your choice,” D’Alleva Valas said during the discussion. When they put in the effort and set a financial strategy, they can “optimize their blood, sweat, and tears” to grow paychecks and investments into fortunes.  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Analysis: Why a $2 trillion deficit and 5% Treasury yields are becoming America's biggest economic challenge
events.summary: Treasury yields remain above 5%, pushing mortgage rates toward 7.5%. The deficit was $1.99 trillion for fiscal 2026, up 12% from last year. AI investment is increasing competition for capital. Divided government will likely take meaningful deficit reduction off the table. Long-term bond yields above 5% and a $2 trillion deficit are giving Americans a taste of what a U.S. debt crisis would be like. A true emergency would hurt much more, and isn't baked in. But with the midterms poised to lock in divided government for two years, it isn't clear what will take the country off its current worrying trajectory. Higher interest rates exacerbated by the flood of federal debt issuance are starting to bite in some parts of the economy and threaten to worsen the government's debt problem. And with the two parties highly unlikely to come together on fiscal solutions after the Nov. 3 midterms, any fixes are years off in the future. The housing market is showing signs of slowing as the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage hovers around 7.5%. Pending home sales fell 4% in September, Redfin said Monday, the biggest monthly drop in three years. Mortgage rates track the 10-year Treasury yield . The 10-year has climbed 114 basis points, or hundredths of a percentage point, since the end of February through midday Friday, when the 10-year traded at 5.1%. Trump census plan to cut noncitizens from 2030 count spurs potential legal fight Elon Musk becomes biggest known donor of 2026 midterm election Trump defends Russia diesel deal: 'I made the right choice' Several factors are pushing up the 10-year, including the war with Iran, which kicked off on Feb. 28 and precipitated the rise in long-term yields. Oil and diesel prices are up sharply, and that has bond traders asking for more yield to account for the possibility that central banks such as the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates. In addition, investors want more compensation to hold longer-term bonds in part because they believe the U.S. government will continue to flood the market with them. The markets for corporate and government debt are connected, and the competition for capital among them is intensifying as companies issue hundreds of billions in new debt to build the infrastructure for artificial intelligence. Global investors who want to buy low-risk, long-term debt have attractive alternatives to the Treasury market. If the U.S. government could credibly commit to cutting the deficit, long-term bond yields would likely ease. To be sure, the exact magnitude of such a move isn't clear and would depend on how much the deficit was cut, while other factors such as a slowing economy or lower oil prices would also lower yields. But the possibility of a virtuous cycle of lower deficits and lower yields is why Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has argued that the U.S. ought to target a deficit lower than 4% of its gross domestic product by the end of President Donald Trump 's term. There is almost no way the U.S. will hit that target. The deficit was $1.992 trillion for the 2026 fiscal year, up 12% from last year, data released Friday by the U.S. Treasury showed. That deficit amounts to approximately 6.2% of gross domestic product, based on an estimate of third-quarter GDP. Higher rates make debt reduction tougher. If interest rates stay a half-point above the CBO's expectations, the cumulative deficit over 10 years will come in $1.9 trillion higher, the agency estimates . If rates overshoot by 1.5 points, that adds $6 trillion in deficits. The CBO expects the 10-year Treasury to average 4.3% over that period, compared with 5.1% today. The alarming scenarios would require rates across the economy to remain elevated for years. "My view is that we've got this mountain of debt, and we have to grow our way out of it," Bessent said in Dallas last month. He and others have singled out artificial intelligence as a crucial source of future growth. AI could help but can't fix the problem entirely. It would take a decade of 7.2% growth to balance the budget with growth alone, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget , a research group that advocates for balanced budgets. GDP growth was recently revised up for the second quarter from 1.5% to 2.2% at an annualized rate. The acceleration that quickly would get us to 7.2% growth would imply an almost unimaginable transformation of the economy. Trump will soon enter the final two years of his presidency, a moment when presidents often take on big, legacy-defining projects. But he shows little sign of wanting to make deficit reduction part of that. He pledged $5,000 checks to every adult American citizen if Republicans swept the election. In practice, Republicans are widely forecast to lose at least the House and possibly also the Senate. Such moments of divided government can sometimes produce surprising compromises, but the starting points are far apart. Rep.

events.title: Apple’s $1,999 iPhone Duo puts the company's status-symbol power to the test
events.summary: Apple's iPhone Duo launch-day pickup inventory sold out quickly, with some delivery estimates already slipping into late January online. The price of the first foldable iPhone reaches $3,199 at 2TB, creating a new tier above the Pro and Pro Max. Analysts say the Duo could boost Apple’s average selling prices through trade-ups, Android switchers and a halo effect across the rest of the iPhone lineup. Apple 's iPhone Duo , its most expensive iPhone ever, went up for preorder Friday, with launch-day pickup inventory selling out and some online delivery estimates already slipping into late January. The company said in a statement that the preorder demand was "nothing short of extraordinary." "We are working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers' hands as quickly as possible, and we will continue accepting orders online," Apple said. Apple's first foldable phone starts at $1,999 and passes $3,000 at the 2TB storage tier. It is the biggest change to the physical design of the iPhone in years and establishes an entirely new price point above the Pro and Pro Max. The early rush offers a first glimpse at the demand behind Apple's bet: Whether a dramatic new design can persuade customers to spend more and push the iPhone even further as a status symbol. But analysts who spoke with CNBC said Apple's bet is not that foldables suddenly become a mass-market product. It is that a relatively small group of its highest-spending customers can become significantly more valuable. Foldables are expected to make up just over 2% of global smartphone units this year but nearly 7% of industry revenue, according to IDC. By 2030, IDC expects the category to account for 10% of smartphone revenue while still representing only about 3% of units. That gap between volume and value is central to Apple's opportunity. "Duo is fast becoming an aspirational foldable," IDC's Nabila Popal told CNBC, comparing its appeal with Apple's broader position as an aspirational smartphone brand. Popal, global senior research director for the Consumer Device Team at IDC, said the technology itself is not necessarily the breakthrough. Foldable Android phones have existed for years. What's new is Apple bringing that form factor to the enormous base of consumers already invested in the iPhone ecosystem. Apple itself has been exploring the form factor for more than a decade. In 2011, Ternus and five other Apple engineers filed a patent application for foldable electronic devices, according to a recent Time profile. "It's not that it's a breakthrough or new technology, but it's from Apple," Popal said. The Duo could also prove more accessible than some industry watchers had anticipated. Anshel Sag, an analyst at Moor Insights who attended Apple's launch event, said many expected the foldable iPhone to start between $2,400 and $2,500. Apple coming in at $1,999, Sag said, suggests the company "wants a lot of share." Sag expects the Duo to become "very much a status symbol" during the holiday season and potentially into next year. That status appeal could be reinforced by scarcity. Amazon launches new Bee 'personal AI' devices that listen to conversations Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang urges U.S.-China dialogue on 'potentially dangerous' AI OpenAI sued by 8 states over ChatGPT safety concerns Anthropic's third-quarter revenue is said to hit $16.8 billion ahead of IPO Counterpoint Research Director Tarun Pathak told CNBC the firm expects initial demand to exceed supply. Apple has an installed base of roughly 1.4 billion iPhones, he noted, meaning even a small percentage of early adopters could overwhelm the roughly 6 million or fewer units Counterpoint expects to be available in the near term. IDC also expects supply to be constrained initially because of the complexity of the device and Apple's manufacturing and quality standards. "Exclusivity is part of the current appeal," Popal said. And Apple has made explicit luxury plays before. When the first Apple Watch launched, the company offered the 18-karat gold Edition starting at $10,000. Apple also formed a long-running partnership with Hermès around premium watch bands and designs. That push came during the tenure of Angela Ahrendts, the former Burberry CEO who joined Apple in 2014 to lead retail and online stores, as the company experimented with bringing more of the language and presentation of luxury fashion into its stores and products. The Duo takes that idea into Apple's largest product business. IDC expects Apple to ship roughly 7 million units this year, or roughly 3% of Apple's total shipments in 2026. Popal, the IDC analyst, forecasts Duo shipments could grow another 70% next year. That would give Apple roughly 40% of the global foldable market and would make it the category's largest player, surpassing Samsung and Huawei. According to her forecast, Apple could ship as many Duos in the next six months as the previous category leaders did in all of 2025.

events.title: 10 things that lasted longer than Katie Zacharia’s time as White House press secretary
events.summary: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia held her first conference on Tuesday and left the role three days later. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images Katie Zacharia is out as White House press secretary after five days on the job. That's likely a record for the shortest-serving White House press secretary in history. Here are 10 other things that last longer than Zacharia's time in the White House. Katie Zacharia is out as White House press secretary after five days on the job, officials confirmed on Friday. The lawyer-ish-person-turned-White House spokesperson had a rocky debut at the podium on Tuesday, during which she stumbled over prepared remarks and later raised eyebrows after she told a reporter that she passed the bar in China. President Donald Trump said on Friday that he told Zacharia to reconsider the role. Later that day, a White House official told Business Insider that Zacharia was "transitioning out" of the position. By standards of the Trump White House, which had a notorious revolving door  during the first go-round, that's pretty short. There are a lot of other things that lasted longer than Zacharia's tenure. Here are 10 of them. Anthony Scaramucci as White House comms director: 10 days Anthony Scaramucci at a White House press briefing. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images Scaramucci's firing in July 2017 became a spectacle, not least in part because of his notably short tenure. First came a profanity-laced call to a New Yorker reporter, in which Scaramucci badmouthed some of his colleagues in the White House. Then came John F. Kelly, laying down the law in the West Wing by firing Scaramucci and making an example of him on his first day on the job as chief of staff. Sally Yates as acting attorney general: 10 days Former acting U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images Sally Yates lasted exactly One Mooch. Yates was a holdover from the second Obama Administration, taking on the AG role after Loretta Lynch stepped down at Trump's inauguration in 2017. Her position as attorney general was expected to be short. Still, acting AGs from the previous administration typically held on to their roles until the incoming president picked a new attorney general, who would then be confirmed by the Senate. Yates was fired after she told the Justice Department not to defend Trump's first travel-ban executive order. Jerald TerHorst as WH press secretary: 31 days Jerald terHorst UPI/Bettmann Archive/Getty Images After Zacharia, TerHorst takes the record for the second shortest-serving White House press secretary. TerHorst served under President Gerald Ford from August 9, 1974, to September 8, 1974. He resigned in protest after Ford granted Richard Nixon a full pardon. Liz Truss as Britain's prime minister: 49 days Liz Truss Yui Mok/PA Images via Getty Images An opinion piece in The Economist quipped that Truss' premiership will have the "shelf-life of a lettuce." The comment came after Truss's economic package immediately unnerved investors, sending the pound and government-bond markets spiraling. Thus, the lettuce meme was born. On October 14, 2022, Daily Star, a tabloid newspaper, was inspired by The Economist's comment and set up a livestream of a lettuce wearing a wig: "Will Liz Truss outlast this lettuce ?" She didn't. Truss resigned six days later. She was the PM from September 6 to October 25, 2022. A hard-boiled egg in the fridge: 7 days Hard-boiled eggs Ricardo DeAratanha/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images Keeping in theme with the foods that last longer than political positions: The US Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service says a hard-boiled egg can be stored in the fridge for up to seven days. Lady Jane Grey as Queen of England: 9 days A portrait of Lady Jane Grey The Print Collector/Getty Images Lady Jane Grey was proclaimed queen on July 10, 1553, but her half-sister, Mary — the eldest daughter of Henry VIII — gathered enough political support to overthrow her. Mary would claim the crown on July 19, 1553. Grey became known as the "Nine Days Queen" and was executed by beheading in 1554. Apollo 11: 8 days Astronaut Buzz Aldrin on the moon. NASA/Newsmakers The Apollo 11 crew spent more time in space than Zacharia did as the press secretary: 8 days, 3 hours, 18 minutes, and 35 seconds to be exact. We can dig in more. Zacharia's first press briefing lasted about 14 minutes, according to recordings. Neil Armstrong spent more time walking on the moon: 2 hours, 31 minutes, and 37 seconds, a NASA report said. Buzz Aldrin was on the moon for about 40 minutes less, according to the report. Six-Day War: You can guess A member of the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) raises the brigade flag. Dan Porges/Getty Images The 1967 conflict between Israel and neighboring Arab states was so short that its duration became its namesake. The war lasted from June 5 to June 10, 1967. Apple TV+ free trial: 7 days Apple TV logo Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images You have more time to binge-watch "Severance" or "Ted Lasso" on Apple TV than Zacharia had time in the White House. Maybe we shouldn't point this out unless we want Apple to realize there are shorter things than the company's free-trial policy. Kim Kardashian's marriage to Kris Humphries: 72 days Chris Humphries and Kim Kardashian Paul Drinkwater/NBC/NBCU Photo Bank Reality TV star Kim Kardashian married NBA player Kris Humphries on August 20, 2011. She filed for divorce on October 31, 2011. To be fair, this may still be more of a reflection on Kardashian than on Zacharia. You would hope a marriage lasts longer than five days, right? Then again, this is the longest thing on the list, so you go, Kim! Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: With U.S. debt above $40 trillion, the IMF chief warns that economic growth alone won’t solve the problem
events.summary: The U.S. has a $40 trillion debt problem, and the leader of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) says supercharging the nation’s growth isn’t enough to solve it. Speaking during the IMF’s annual meetings in Bangkok this week, IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva said that while growth can ease the U.S. debt problem, it isn’t a catch-all solution. “Growth, of course, helps, but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustments,” she said, adding that the budget deficit must also come down. The Treasury Department pushed back against Georgieva’s warning by questioning the IMF’s forecasting record in a statement to Fortune . “When we see pieces on the IMF, it’s good to remember how messy their forecasts have been in the past,” said David Zervos, counselor to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who pointed to rosy economic predictions before the 2008 Global Financial Crisis and the 1997 Asian financial crisis as evidence. The IMF did not immediately respond to Fortune ’s request for comment. Georgieva’s comments come at an uncertain time for the U.S. fiscal situation. At $40.3 trillion, according to Treasury data, the national debt is at a record high . It is also the largest in the world. Even more worrying to experts is the U.S. gross debt-to-GDP ratio, which stood at about 126%, according to the Treasury Department . Publicly held debt is lower, at 100% of GDP, but is still the highest since shortly after World War II ended, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. A growing economy can make existing debt easier to manage. But if Washington keeps borrowing faster than the economy expands, the ratio can continue rising even when the economy grows. The mounting debt also means a greater share of the government’s revenue goes toward interest payments instead of other priorities like public services. Net interest payments made up about 15% of federal spending in fiscal 2026 —and about 20% of revenue. And by fiscal 2031, the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget has predicted that the average interest rate on federal debt will exceed the economy’s rate of growth—a predicament that could contribute to a self-reinforcing “ debt spiral ” and eventually require more drastic spending cuts or tax increases to correct, Fortune previously reported. ‘ We can grow our way out of that ’ At the same time, Bessent has argued that consistent U.S. economic growth of 3%, fueled partly by AI, can be enough to deal with the issue. “There’s nothing magic about the $40 trillion number,” he told CNBC in August. “And we can grow our way out of that.” Whether growth alone can actually solve the federal debt is doubtful. An article by the Council on Foreign Relations last month explained that annual 3% economic growth is hard to achieve .  The U.S. has only hit the 3% mark of growth in five calendar years, the most recent being 2019 during President Donald Trump’s first term. U.S. GDP is estimated to grow 2.2% this year, up from 2% GDP growth in 2025. Congressional Budget Office Director Phillip Swagel also recently warned, “ It’s probably not plausible ” that growth will stabilize the U.S. financial trajectory, explaining that real GDP growth would have to hit 5% to 6%. Instead, changes in revenue and spending are necessary, he noted. To be sure, Bessent has said he and White House budget director Russell Vought are working with Trump on a broader deficit-reduction plan, but details have yet to be released. The IMF has previously sounded the alarm about the U.S.’s debt problem. In an annual review of the U.S. economy published in April, the organization acknowledged the strength of the U.S. economy.  Still, in the report, the IMF’s executive directors also said the growing debt could be a problem not just for the U.S., but for the rest of the world. “They emphasized that the fiscal trajectory creates a growing financial stability tail risk for the U.S. and for the global economy, given the importance of the U.S. Treasury market for the global financial system.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com
