events.title: Yemen’s government says Houthis fired two missiles at Aden airport
events.summary: Attack comes as Yemeni gov’t forces claim advances in Marib province and say they ‘neutralised’ 430 Houthi fighters in 24 hours. Yemen’s internationally recognised government says the Houthis have launched missiles at the airport in Aden, a day after carrying out a deadly attack targeting the presidential palace in the port city. Yemeni Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said two missiles landed near the runway at Aden International Airport on Friday, 500 metres (1,640 feet) from an aircraft that was preparing to take off. list 1 of 3 Yemeni families’ search for missing loved ones hindered by new fighting list 2 of 3 Yemeni government launches air strikes on Houthi positions list 3 of 3 Houthis strike Aramco hours after Saudi-led coalition hits Sanaa oil site All passengers and crew were safe, he said on X, thanking “divine providence” for preventing a potential “horrific humanitarian catastrophe” and calling the attacks on the airport “a grave violation of international laws and norms”. The Houthis, in a statement attributed to a military source, said on Friday that they launched an attack on “the Saudi forces’ command headquarters in the Badr camp in Aden province” as well as a weapons depot, the AFP news agency reported. The latest attack in Aden, which is the seat of the internationally recognised government, comes amid continued heavy fighting in Yemen’s reignited civil war between the Saudi-backed government and the Iran-aligned Houthis. Yemeni government forces said earlier on Friday that troops had advanced in Marib province northeast of Sanaa. Military spokesman Majed al-Nazili said Yemeni government forces, with air support, had made significant “territorial gains” in the eastern part of the province, securing “key positions”. He also said Yemeni forces had “neutralised” more than 430 Houthi fighters in 24 hours, while destroying or disabling more than 100 of their vehicles and military assets. Elsewhere, in Taiz governorate, which has emerged as a key battlefront in the war, Yemeni government forces claimed to have fended off several “large-scale” Houthi attacks, inflicting “heavy losses” on the group. Yemeni government forces also claimed to have captured a specialised drone team affiliated with the Houthis in the Taiz area. In recent weeks, Houthi forces have encircled the city of Taiz — Yemen’s third largest urban centre — by ⁠cutting its main road south to Aden, causing widespread ⁠displacement and worsening a humanitarian crisis. Elsewhere on Friday, the Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis said it had downed missiles and drones over Riyadh and other parts of Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia has accused Iran of encouraging Houthi attacks against the kingdom, including by arming and training the group. But Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Friday rejected the accusation, saying Tehran had not played a role in any Houthi operations. The ministry also reiterated a proposal to mediate between the Houthis and Riyadh. The war in Yemen erupted in 2014 when the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), seized the capital, Sanaa, and forced the government to flee. An international military coalition led by Saudi Arabia intervened in support of the internationally recognised government in 2015, leading to years of fighting between the warring sides. A 2022 UN-backed truce halted most fighting, but tensions have been high in Yemen since the Houthis declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabian ports and shipping passing through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait in July. In September, the Houthis carried out a lightning ground offensive on Mocha, pushing back forces loyal to Yemen’s government from the Red Sea port city. The same month, the group’s forces again swept through and seized territory along the western coast and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, including the strategically located Mayyun Island in the strait.

events.title: ‘He can’t run again’: MAGA merch sellers are closing shop and cutting prices. One sold $63 million but now she’s closed three stores
events.summary: Richard Kligman didn’t set out to sell President Donald Trump and “Make America Great Again” merch. But Kligman spotted a business opportunity in 2016, when customers began asking for MAGA hats and flags at the Myrtle Beach, South Carolina kite shop he ran with his brother. The duo opened their Trump Super Store in the empty storefront next door in 2018 to keep up with the demand. “You’d have thought I was selling crack,” Kligman jokingly told Fortune . But now he wants out. “You have to read the writing on the wall that as we go into ‘27, it’s definitely going to fall off, and I’d like to be out of it as much as I could be by the end of ‘27,” he said.  Sales were “going gangbusters,” Kligman said, between the 2020 and 2024 presidential elections, and the brothers were putting in seven days a week just to keep up with demand from both locals and visitors from around the country.  But now, Kligman said sales of Trump-branded merch have since fallen 39% from their 2024 levels.  “A lot of the Trump merchandise stores across the country are closing because they see that things are going to change a bit, and the demand is not what it once was,” Kligman said. “It’s absolutely gone down, but it had to because he can’t run again.” Kligman isn’t alone in thinking this. The “Make America Great Again” slogan helped Trump win the White House in 2016 and has been plastered over hats, shirts, flags and other collectibles for more than a decade. But MAGA merch sellers and suppliers across the country told Fortune their sales have fallen from the heights of the 2024 election. That’s when Amazon sellers reported an estimated $140 million in Trump-themed merch from April through September, according to e-commerce marketing platform Omnisend. Sellers have cut prices, closed stores, branched into other patriotic merchandise or turned to Trump’s rallies for sales. But with Trump barred by the Constitution from another presidential run, the business faces an uncertain future after he leaves office. Steven Slaton, who has run the Trumped Store and Coffee Shop in Show Low, Arizona for a decade with his wife Karen, told Fortune he’s felt the change, saying sales now are “night and day” compared to the 2016 and 2024 election seasons. He estimated that Trump merch sales in September were down 20% to 25% from the same month in 2024. He and Karen have started clearing out older merch, marking hats and shirts that once cost $30 down to $10.  “It’s like everybody took a big, deep breath and then everybody’s looking for a new type of gear,” Slaton said. Slaton attributed part of the decline to customers with less money to spend as food, housing and gas prices strain their budgets. Economic dissatisfaction is also weighing on Trump politically. A Fox News poll from Oct. 14 found that 77% of registered voters disapproved of his handling of inflation, and 70% disapproved of his handling of the economy, and his overall approval rating fell to 36%, the lowest recorded by Fox News during either of Trump’s two presidencies. The sales decline is severe enough for some stores to close. Fortune found that this year alone, at least three independent Trump merch stores have closed—in Connecticut , Pennsylvania , and Tennessee —including one that made 350 sales a day at an average of $60 each. Less demand for MAGA merch also means less business for merch manufacturers. Eric Turney, sales director of custom product manufacturing firm The Monterey Company, told Fortune the company earned about $250,000 in 2024 making MAGA hats, keychains, and buttons for nine wholesalers, but now has only three regular wholesalers for that same merch.  “Once he went into office, [demand] really dropped off the face of the cliff,” Turney said, noting that Monterey used to get an average of 15 merch orders per month in 2024, but only 13 in total from 2025 to this year. Online interest in MAGA hats is also down. After peaking in Google search popularity in December 2018 and November 2024, interest in the search term “MAGA hat” has plummeted by 95% as of October, according to Google Trends data. Ronald Solomon, president of The MAGA Mall, a wholesaler and retailer of Republican and conservative-branded products, told Fortune rallies renewed demand for MAGA and Trump 2028 hats, recalling selling “a tremendous amount” of them at a rally in Vandalia, Ohio last week. The Trump Organization itself began offering $50 “Trump 2028” hats in April 2025.  “During the summer, the MAGA stuff wasn’t selling as much, but now all of a sudden it’s selling a lot again,” Solomon said.  But his MAGA product sales in recent months are down 34% from 2024. He attributes the decline to 2026 being a midterm year. “There’s no way I expected it to be as brisk as a presidential year,” he said. For some sellers, though, the slowdown has pushed them to change strategy. Sany Dash, who said she has sold $63 million in Trump merch over the past nine years, closed all three of her USA Trump Stores this year because revenue fell so far: two in Texas (Gainesville and Arlington) and one in Loveland, Colorado. She might open one in Dallas, but she will focus on selling patriotic-themed jewelry and clothing at rallies and other political events, where she estimates 40% to 50% of attendees buy merch. “The stores are not doing well, but the rallies are doing incredibly good,” Dash said. “We have to look at, logistically, where we’re going to open up our new store, and it may not say Trump—it may just say ‘patriotic merch,’ I don’t know yet.” Dash sells merch only for Trump and doubts the MAGA merch brand will have the same pull after he leaves office. “After Trump is gone, I don’t see MAGA continue because Trump is the face of MAGA,” she said.  Slaton is preparing for that possibility, too. He said the Trumped Store might change its name and offerings to support whoever becomes the new Republican figurehead.  “We’re telling people we’ll probably transition over to JD Vance or Marco [Rubio] or whomever the prospective nominee is going to be,” he said. “We’ll have to figure out how we’re going to do that.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Healey backs pro-growth case for Heathrow third runway after Burnham ducks issue
events.summary: Chancellor says government will study responses to public consultation, with airports being ‘big part of jobs and growth’ John Healey has said there is a pro-growth case for going ahead with a third runway at Heathrow despite the prime minister declining to back it. Healey’s predecessor as chancellor, Rachel Reeves, put approval of the long-planned runway at the heart of her “growth speech” last year, saying it would “make Britain the world’s best-connected place to do business” . However, since arriving in No 10 in July, Andy Burnham has ducked the issue of whether the runway should go ahead, suggesting it should be “a matter for London and Londoners”. A recent Sunday Times report suggested the prime minister had told the transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, that he was “unconvinced” by arguments for the megaproject. Asked for his views in Bangkok this week, Healey said the government would study responses to a public consultation, which recently closed. He appeared to strike a markedly more positive note than Burnham, however. “I think in recent decades, and this is true in Heathrow and airports right across the UK, that they have been a big part of jobs and growth. And the case for a third runway at Heathrow has always been a case for growth,” he said. Healey has insisted economic growth is his and Burnham’s “number one mission” in government. Heathrow’s chief executive, Thomas Woldbye, has warned that investors could reassess their backing for the £33bn infrastructure project if it does not receive the prime minister’s support. “Our shareholders would like to do this,” he said earlier this week. “They do think that things are taking a long time, and so far they have decided to be OK with that … But of course we cannot wait for ever.” The airport’s owners include Qatar’s investment authority; the French private equity firm Ardian; Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund and Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund, GIC. They are expected to decide in the coming months whether to apply for formal planning permission. Healey voted in favour of the third runway when the question was put to the House of Commons in 2018. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The chancellor was in Bangkok to attend the International Monetary Fund annual meetings but has returned to London to put the finishing touches to his 28 October budget. The UK was praised by the IMF this week for taking action to cut its deficit, while other large economies have opted not to do so. The IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, urged Healey to “stay the course” in his budget. On Thursday, official figures showed the UK economy unexpectedly continued to grow in August.

events.title: Katie Zacharia out as Trump's White House press secretary
events.summary: New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving her job just five days after starting it, a White House official told CNBC. Zacharia, who succeeded Karoline Leavitt, faced widespread criticism over her performance and came under mounting scrutiny about her legal background. President Donald Trump said Friday afternoon that he told Zacharia, "You don't have to do this if you don't want." New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving her job after just five days in the face of criticism over her performance , a White House official confirmed to CNBC on Friday. Earlier Friday afternoon, President Donald Trump told reporters that he had just suggested to Zacharia that she quit. "I just spoke to her about it. I said, 'Katie, is this for you?'" Trump said outside the White House. "'If I were you, I'd reconsider,'" the president said he told Zacharia. The White House official, who asked not to be named in order to discuss the staffing shake-up, confirmed Fox News' report that Zacharia is "transitioning" out of the press secretary role. Zacharia's five-day tenure in the Trump administration is shorter than that of Anthony Scaramucci, who in 2017 served as White House communications director for less than 11 days. That length of time became jokingly referred to as a "Scaramucci" and was used to measure the durations of other officials who served briefly. By that metric, Zacharia lasted one-half of one Scaramucci. "Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people's pain," Scaramucci said in an X post later Friday. Zacharia, a conservative commentator who worked at Trump Media & Technology Group , had faced widespread criticism in the days since she led a short and shaky first press briefing. She also came under mounting scrutiny about her legal background. Trump spoke to reporters before heading to Georgia for a political rally as he hopes to boost Republicans' electoral chances with just 18 days until the midterms. But Trump's efforts to sell his agenda have been muddled in part by Zacharia, who ended her first, and only, press briefing on Tuesday after delivering halting remarks and taking questions from just three reporters. In the less than six minutes she spent answering questions, Zacharia revealed that U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle had been asked to step down. That departure, and Zacharia's, follow those of a number of other high-ranking female officials in the Trump administration who have quit or been fired in recent months. Trump census plan to cut noncitizens from 2030 count spurs potential legal fight Elon Musk becomes biggest known donor of 2026 midterm election Trump defends Russia diesel deal: 'I made the right choice' "You know, she's been treated very rough. And she's a nice person," Trump said of Zacharia outside the White House. He accused the media of treating her "very badly" and said that even Fox News TV host Sean Hannity, a supporter of the administration, was "a little bit tough" on Zacharia during her appearance on his show Thursday night. Hannity, after calling Zacharia's debut briefing "widely panned," had asked about her past claims about her legal work in light of reports that she never passed a bar exam. Zacharia has defended identifying herself as a lawyer, drawing a distinction between that label and calling herself an "attorney." Hannity pointed out that Zacharia had called herself an attorney in multiple social media posts. "I think they were retweets, and I corrected the record," she replied. Trump called Zacharia "an attorney" in his Oct. 9 Truth Social post announcing her selection to replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the Trump administration in late August. Zacharia's first day was Columbus Day. White House officials had defended Zacharia earlier this week. "Up and down the White House, everyone has been thoroughly impressed with Katie in just a few short days on the job," White House communications director Steven Cheung said in an X post Wednesday. "At the end of this second term, she'll be remembered as one of the all-time greats," Cheung wrote. CNN chief White House correspondent Kaitlan Collins, however, reported Friday that Trump was "embarrassed by the coverage of Zacharia's briefing and when he polled other aides about her, Zacharia had few allies willing to stand up for her or defend her performance." "She's been treated, I would say, pretty nastily," Trump said of Zacharia in Friday's remarks outside the White House. "And I said to Katie just two minutes ago, I said, 'Katie, you know, you don't have to do this if you don't want.'" Asked if he would keep her in the role, Trump said, "I'm going to let her make that decision."

events.title: Wall Street tumbles as worries about AI trade and high oil prices weigh
events.summary: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange before the closing bell in New York City on Oct 16. Wall Street tumbled on Oct 16, with CoreWeave, Broadcom and other AI-related technology stocks under renewed pressure, while a jump in oil prices spooked traders heading into the weekend. The Nasdaq was on track for a loss of over 4% for the week, hammered by concerns that debt-laden AI infrastructure companies may not turn profits in time to repay debts, particularly with borrowing costs expected to rise. Nvidia-backed CoreWeave slumped 12%, bringing its loss over the past five sessions to about 25%. The data centre operator’s bonds also sold off sharply this week, pushing yields above 15%. Broadcom fell 3.6%, and the PHLX chip index sank 2.5%, on track for its eighth straight day of declines. Investors on Oct 16 were also watching oil prices jump more than 3% due to Middle East supply worries. “There is some fear in the market,” said Rob Haworth, senior investment strategist at US Bank Wealth Management in ​Seattle. “High oil prices, in particular, tend to weigh on the price/earnings multiple of stocks, and so I think you have investors looking to be cautious into the weekend rather than take more risk.” Adding to concerns around AI financing, some current Anthropic investors and prospective investors are weighing a lower valuation for the company in its upcoming IPO, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The S&P 500 was down 1.22% at 7,649.71 points. The Nasdaq declined 2.19% to 26,128.13 points, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 0.55% at 51,891.77 points. Six of the 11 S&P 500 sector indexes declined, led lower by communication services, down 2.52%, followed by a 2.38% loss in information technology. The S&P 500 was set for its steepest weekly loss since January, and the Nasdaq was heading for its sharpest weekly fall since June. Third-quarter earnings season shifts into gear next week with reports from Tesla, Meta Platforms and Procter & Gamble. Analysts on average see quarterly earnings surging over 30%, driven by AI-related megacaps, according to LSEG data. While the S&P 500 remains up about 12% in 2026, most of that gain has come from AI-related tech stocks, and the index’s median component has climbed only about 6%, year to date. About 185 S&P 500 stocks have lost ground in 2026. Hotter-than-expected consumer and producer inflation reports this week showed price pressures were extending beyond energy commodities. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh on Oct 16 voiced optimism about US economic strength and surprise about how well global economies have been “hanging in there” during a lingering energy shock and tighter monetary policy to fight inflation. Markets increasingly expect the Fed to keep interest rates unchanged in October. Barclays now expects 25-basis-point hikes each in December and January. Tesla dropped 2.5% after the electric-vehicle maker unveiled a redesigned Roadster, powered by rocket-style thrusters, developed in collaboration with SpaceX. Netflix appointed former Disney executive Peter Rice as chief content officer on Oct 15. Its shares were down 2.9%. Declining stocks outnumbered rising ones within the S&P 500 by a 1.3-to-one ratio. The S&P 500 posted 19 new highs and one new low; the Nasdaq recorded 49 new highs and 263 new lows. REUTERS

events.title: Replit is no longer working with Anthropic, CEO says
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt . Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer with Anthropic. “I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.” Replit sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser. Under its partnership with Anthropic, Replit used the AI lab’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly. Masad’s comments were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place. There is evidence on the company’s website , blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was using Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities. TechCrunch reached back out to Replit for clarification and will update this story if we hear back. Masad shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue. “We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.” Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures. “In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.” This article was updated to article to include more context on Replit using Anthropic’s models. events.title: Canberra businesses battling 'multi-agency maze' to stay open, report finds
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Businesses affected by Civic construction received 'insufficient' financial relief, committee report finds Ongoing construction in Canberra's city centre has seen a reduction in turnover for businesses in the area. ( ABC News: Lily Nothling ) An ACT Legislative Assembly committee investigating the city's night life has accepted reports that "insufficient" relief has been given to businesses affected by light rail and car park construction. The country's peak hospitality advocacy body has welcomed the committee's 28 recommendations to improve the ACT's night-time economy. The recommendations include establishing an ACT Night-Time Economy Commissioner and offering "stronger temporary relief" for affected businesses. The ACT government should consider stronger relief for businesses affected by construction work and establish a dedicated night-time economy commissioner, a review of Canberra's night life has found. Restaurants and other businesses would be forced to shut their doors without more action to address car park access and construction disruptions, according to findings from the ACT Legislative Assembly committee tasked with investigating the city's night-time economy. Chris Gatfield of the Australian Hotels Association has welcomed the committee's recommendations, but says he doubts they will all be delivered. ( Supplied: Chris Gatfield ) The committee's report, made public on Friday, made 28 recommendations to improve what the Australian Hotels Association (AHA) said was "a little bit of a struggle" for the industry. "The general economic climate is really, really tough for the hospitality industry," AHA ACT branch general manager Chris Gatfield said. "That's not necessarily just related to the various infrastructure projects that are going on in the city. But the committee accepted that there had been "insufficient" relief for businesses affected by light rail and car park constructions. It recommended the ACT government "consider offering stronger temporary relief measures for businesses adversely affected by ongoing disruptions associated with major infrastructure works in the city, such as means-tested rent relief". Charcoal Restaurant owner Anna Gray says financial assistance is the only way to ensure her business survives the construction works. ( ABC News: Nick Haggarty ) Anna Gray, the owner of Charcoal Restaurant in the Melbourne building in Civic, said her turnover had reduced by 50 per cent since parts of London Circuit closed in 2024. "Customers don't want to come because there's no parking," she said. Mr Gatfield said businesses need cash flow, but he doubted they would get it. "This will be a decision for government and so far I'm not convinced that they would be in a position to offer that kind of financial support," he said. "You really want the people who are suffering right now to be there to reap the benefits when construction is finished and people return to the city." The committee also found businesses were battling a "multi-agency maze" of red tape to stay open. Josh Dotta, the owner of Fiction nightclub (pictured), told the committee he routinely had to interact with 10 seperate government agencies. ( Facbook: Fiction Club ) Fiction Nightclub operator Josh Dotta gave evidence that he routinely interacted with 10 separate government agencies, while other stakeholders criticised the "silos" and "disconnected sections of government". "Anyone who's ever dealt with a government agency would recognise that sometimes it's very hard to get the person that you actually need to talk to on the phone," Mr Gatfield said. Although the ACT has a dedicated minister for the night-time economy, the committee said a night-time economy commissioner would support that role. The commissioner would consult the industry before major decisions, establish progress metrics, develop a more streamlined red-tape system, support culturally and linguistically diverse workers and take advice from a dedicated advisory group, the recommendations said. "We think it has legs in Canberra and if it works in other places there's absolutely no reason why it wouldn't work here too," Mr Gatfield said. Late-night venues such as Squeaky Clean, pictured during a performance by Citizen Kay, pay significantly more for a liquor licence than similar NSW venues. ( ABC News: Nick Haggarty ) Evidence from the AHA also found liquor licence fees in the ACT were significantly higher than other jurisdictions, prompting a recommendation for a review, especially for larger venues that can host more than 350 people.

events.title: Meta employees say Lula’s accounts restricted in Brazil election: Report
events.summary: The messages, reported by a Brazilian daily, say the platform recommended Bolsonaro’s profile and his WhatsApp channel. Employees at Meta have acknowledged in internal communications that the Instagram accounts of Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva were negatively affected by restrictions during the country’s election, media reports say. The messages, reported on Friday by Brazilian daily Folha de S Paulo, also acknowledged the platform recommended the profile of Lula challenger Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, as well as his WhatsApp channel. Folha, the Sao Paulo-based paper, cited messages it had reviewed. list 1 of 4 US records 4,410 measles cases as outbreak grows list 2 of 4 How Iran messaging highlights cost of war ahead of US midterm elections list 3 of 4 White House press secretary Katie Zacharia fired after five days on the job list 4 of 4 AOC transfers $1m to Michigan candidate El-Sayed in progressive push Meta told the Reuters news agency that the technical issues cited in the report were already public and the conversations it referenced related solely to the severity of the issues, not political interference. “Any suggestion that Meta favors one side is false,” it added in a statement. Lula, the left-wing incumbent, will face right-wing challenger Bolsonaro in a presidential runoff on October 25, following a stronger-than-expected performance by the senator in the first-round vote earlier this month. Friday’s report came on the heels of a Brazilian court ruling on Thursday that ordered Meta to immediately adopt measures to provide equal treatment of the two candidates ahead of the runoff. The ruling by a judge in Brazil’s top electoral court was made shortly after Lula filed a complaint that accused the tech giant – which owns Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp – of using biased algorithms and AI restrictions to favour opposition candidate Bolsonaro ahead of the election. Justice Marco Aurelio Bellizze ruled that Meta cannot reduce the distribution of political content, restrict searches or remove posts in a way that creates an imbalance between Lula and Bolsonaro. His ruling also orders the company to ensure its artificial intelligence tool applies identical criteria to both candidacies. Bellizze said in his ruling that Meta must pay a fine of 500,000 reais ($98,700) per day if it fails to comply. According to Lula’s party, some of his posts appeared without a share button and had reduced reach. Options for reactions, sharing, audio or accelerated speed were also missing.

events.title: Calls to rethink limits as Fisheries Qld investigates Great Barrier Reef coral overharvesting
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Aquarium industry investigated for overharvesting of coral on Great Barrier Reef Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry Fisheries Queensland has confirmed it has investigated the overharvesting of coral in the Great Barrier Reef. Coral harvesters are permitted to take up to 190 tonnes from the reef annually. Fisheries Queensland does not intend to release the findings from the investigation. Fisheries Queensland has confirmed it recently investigated an overharvesting of coral on the World Heritage-listed Great Barrier Reef, but has declined to share the outcome. In the 2025-2026 fishing season the harvest of Pocillopora grandis , known as antler coral, was overfished by 30 per cent according to FishNet data. Coral harvesting is the process of collecting coral from the ocean. Harvesters are permitted to take up to 190 tonnes from the reef annually, with much of this destined for the global aquarium trade. Bright colours and interesting shapes are highly prized by 'reefers', who drive demand. But coral catch quotas have been breached several times in recent years, while some operators have been charged with fishing offences. There are quotas within the coral harvesting fishery on the Great Barrier Reef. ( ABC News: Brendan Esposito ) The ABC understands an internal investigation has now been completed into this year's exceeded quota. When questioned by the ABC, Fisheries Queensland would not send through the information about the investigations findings. Coral reef ecologist Dr Morgan Pratchett said while this particular species is not under threat, any overharvesting event is of concern. "It sends a bad message given the overwhelming international scrutiny on how this industry is being managed," Dr Pratchett said. Dr Morgan Pratchett is a reef ecologist. ( ABC News: Baz Ruddick ) There are two quotas within the coral harvesting fishery on the Great Barrier Reef, known as individual transferrable quotes (ITC) and prescribed commercial catch (PCC) quotas. Individual quotas are where fishers are given a set amount to fish individually. Breaking these quotas can result in prosecution. PCC quotas, or competitive quotas, are where an amount is set and fishers essentially race to harvest until the quota is exhausted. Harvested coral in tanks for shipping overseas. ( ABC News: Brendan Esposito ) According to Fisheries Queensland, this can sometimes result in going over the competitive quota for a coral species, which they say is not "uncommon or unreasonable." A 2024 assessment of the Queensland coral fishery noted that despite efforts to control overharvesting, some species continue to have their catch limits exceeded. It said fisheries would consider "trip limits, increased notifications, and more individual quotas if this issue continues." Do you know more? Email angelaheathcote@protonmail.com or contact her on signal: @angeh.36 At present, several Australian coral species are banned from being imported into the EU due to sustainability concerns. Simon Miller, from the Australian Marine Conservation Society, said he was concerned catch limits are not set at the right levels. "So when you see fishers in a race to fish to go out there where they're competing against each other to catch these corals as quickly as possible, and seeing this overrun of quotas, that's really concerning," Mr Miller said. "They're meant to be some kind of precautionary catch limit yet we keep seeing them overshoot year after year." Simon Miller from the Australian Marine Conservation Society. ( ABC News: Mark Leonardi ) The coral harvesting industry has faced ongoing compliance issues. One recent case of alleged illegal coral harvesting being pursued by the Queensland Director of Public Prosecutions involved coral collector Jardini. The case included Jardini's director Jason Coe, who currently holds five licences in the Queensland coral fishery. Coe has not yet entered a plea. Earlier in 2024, Monsoon Aquatics lead diver and skipper Tim Green was prosecuted by Western Australia Police for offences related to the collection and recording of coral and fish while harvesting on behalf of Monsoon within the Western Australian coral fishery. He was found guilty and fined almost a quarter of a million dollars. Tim Green was found guilty of offences related to the collection of coral in 2024. ( Image: Facebook ) ASIC documents show Tim Green continues to be a shareholder at Monsoon.

events.title: Why the new RTS won’t make me visit JB more often
events.summary: Journalist Rosalind Ang at a craft workshop with her husband in Johor Bahru in 2025. SINGAPORE – When I think of Johor Bahru, I think of yummy food, medicine and beauty services – all at one-third of what they would cost in Singapore. The time spent travelling to get these deals is set to decrease with the Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link that is slated to begin operations in February 2027. The cross-border rail service will carry up to 10,000 passengers an hour in each direction, with a journey time of just five minutes. With this, it would seem that I’d be able to go to JB more often. But I don’t plan on doing so. I used to go there once a month with my husband, who loves JB. For what we would pay in Singapore, we can visit more upscale restaurants and enjoy a wider variety of dishes that are harder to find in Singapore, such as herbal bak kut teh and lok lok – with the lok lok in Mount Austin being my favourite. Venues in JB also tend to be a lot less crowded, as there’s just more space. I can easily book a badminton court or a karaoke room with free-flow food and drinks. Securing the same facilities in Singapore is far more competitive, often requiring a ballot just to get a badminton court. As I manage my chronic sinusitis with long-term medication, which is far more affordable in Malaysia, my husband and I regularly pick up supplies for ourselves and his family whenever we visit JB. I’ve also been able to attend a variety of craft workshops in JB that would typically be far too expensive to try here. But cost savings aren’t always my only concern. I once went for a perm in JB. While it cost only $200, the curls lasted a grand total of one week – and I was left with damaged hair. In comparison, the same perm in Singapore usually costs me a whopping $500, but my hair is undamaged and the results stay intact for at least half a year. My visits to JB usually take up an entire weekend, so I can’t schedule anything else over those two days. During our most recent trip, my husband and I headed over on a Saturday morning and returned on Sunday afternoon. By the time we got home, there was barely any time left before dinner, ruling out any possibility of scheduling other plans. Even our cat ended up with a late tuna dinner that night. For all its cost savings and fun, trips to JB failed to give me what I valued most: time. There are many things I want to do every weekend. As a broke university student, I loved heading to JB to have a good time on a budget. As a working adult with a steady income, however, I’ve realised that chasing the cheapest deal usually means giving up something that’s not money. When I spend time in JB, I give up spending time with my family, my friends and my cat. Because I’m busy on weekdays, weekends are the only time I have to catch up with the people I love. Choosing to go to JB on the weekend means I won’t be able to go for my regular barre session with my friends. I also can’t eat lunch with them afterwards or have dinner with my parents. And catching up on sleep is out of the question. Even with the new RTS, it will still take a couple of hours just to travel to the Singapore terminus station in Woodlands North, take the train and book a private-hire vehicle out of Bukit Chagar. That doesn’t even include the time needed to reach your actual destinations in the city. As a time-starved Singaporean, it has become important for me to prioritise what matters most – scoring a cheaper manicure is simply not as important as time I could spend with family and friends. A couple of years ago, a lorry collided with the side of my dad’s taxi. Luckily, he survived with a few fractures, but it left him with a permanent leg injury. It made me realise that time with him is finite. The cost of living has risen significantly in recent years, making it natural to try and get the best bang for our buck. But while money can always be earned back, lost time with our loved ones is gone forever. In my pursuit of financial security and the next great money-saving hack, I hope I never lose sight of what makes life truly meaningful. And maybe I’ll finally get enough sleep, too.

events.title: OpenAI models hacked a crypto wallet and breached more websites
events.summary: OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of its agents performing unethical and likely illegal acts. The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own. The incident—which likely would have resulted in criminal charges had they been performed directly by a person—has further heightened concerns that widespread AI use could have harmful effects on an unprecedented scale. Easier to beg for forgiveness than ask permission In two of the cases reported Thursday, OpenAI agents tasked with retrieving information from websites hacked them when the models ran into obstacles obtaining it directly. In one incident during reinforcement training, a model that received access denials when trying to retrieve historical hospital-bed statistics on a government statistics website “used the site's file-download feature to retrieve server configuration and application files, including sensitive credentials,” OpenAI said . “It inspected the application code, bypassed the statistics endpoint's authorization checks, and retrieved data that had previously been denied. The model saved the data locally.” Read full article Comments

events.title: Trump says White House didn't order Starlink restrictions in Ukraine
events.summary: President Trump denied that the White House had ordered restrictions on SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet services in Ukraine this week. Ukrainian officials complained on Tuesday and Wednesday that SpaceX had limited internet connectivity via Starshield without advance notice. Musk said any restrictions on Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine would have come from decisions by the president or White House. President Donald Trump on Friday denied that the White House had ordered restrictions this week on Starlink satellite internet services provided to Ukraine's armed forces. Ukrainian officials on Tuesday and Wednesday said SpaceX had restricted use of Starshield , a military-grade version of Starlink, without warning, impeding some military operations and its ability to defend civilians against intensifying attacks by Russia. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk pinned responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government and Trump, writing on X that, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government." Reporters in Washington, D.C., on Friday asked Trump who was responsible for pausing access for the Ukrainian military. "Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Trump said. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been." Apple's $1,999 iPhone Duo puts the company's status-symbol power to the test Blue Origin plans $330 million Florida expansion to ramp New Glenn launches SpaceX AI policy leader grilled by NYC Council on Grok safety, sexualized images Ukrainian forces have long relied on Starlink and Starshield to enable data gathering by their autonomous drones and for other communications. The restrictions cut off connectivity for drones or other vehicles traveling above 160 kilometers per hour. Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote in a post on Telegram this week that, "Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions." Radoslaw Sikorski, Poland's deputy prime minister, criticized Musk on X about the restrictions. Poland has purchased Starlink services for Ukraine from SpaceX. "Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?" he wrote . "As your European customers, we are watching you." Musk is an advisor to the Pentagon on technology through his role in the recently announced Project Meridian. The Telegraph reported Friday that Musk "approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine," and both had a hand in imposing the restrictions. Reuters reported on Thursday , citing two U.S. officials, that the call to restrict Starlink in Ukraine came from the White House, but did not say who made the order. On Oct. 10, after Trump called on Ukraine to stop all attacks on Russian oil refineries, Musk wrote in a post on X, "Zelensky has gone too far." Musk and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Friday. SpaceX shares are down about 11% this week. The company is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday. events.title: Iran-backed militias sending money back to cash-starved IRGC, U.S. says
events.summary: Iran-backed militias in the region have been sending money back to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to relieve the economic pressure it's under after nine months of war , U.S. CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper said Friday. Why it matters: While the U.S. military has been preparing for a possible resumption of major combat operations against Iran, the Trump administration continues to put immense pressure on the regime with its naval blockade and severe sanctions. U.S. officials say the economic chokehold is causing serious difficulties for Iran and its security forces, while making the regime frustrated and aggressive. The White House hopes the pressure will induce Iran to make a deal that includes nuclear concessions. But so far, that hasn't happened. Driving the news: Cooper said the naval blockade has cost Iran $25 billion in lost oil revenue. Additionally, CENTCOM and the Treasury Department have managed in recent weeks to freeze $350 million that Iran had in cryptocurrency. Behind the scenes: In a video message released Friday, Cooper revealed that Iran-backed groups such as Hezbollah, Hamas and Shia militias in Iraq — which have been funded by the IRGC for years — now have to give the money back. "The financial strain on Iran's military has become so significant that there are reports about Iran-aligned militia groups across the region withholding payments for their soldiers in order to funnel money back to the IRGC, which also isn't paying its troops," he said. Cooper said the Iranian government is withholding salaries, pensions and benefits from public sector workers, including the internal security forces and the IRGC. State of play: Cooper attributed the significant increase in Iranian attacks against ships in the Strait of Hormuz to "desperation" within the IRGC. Despite those attacks, he said that the Strait of Hormuz is still open — with 400 ships and 100 million barrels of oil moving through it over the last week. Yes, but: In recent weeks, CENTCOM has almost completely stopped conducting strikes against Iranian anti-ship missiles and attack drone launchers in the area of the strait. The pause in strikes, which was ordered by the White House to avoid escalating the war ahead of the midterm elections, made Iran more confident about launching attacks, a U.S. official said. Consequently, CENTCOM is concerned that the increase in ship attacks will cause shipping companies to think twice about transiting the strait — resulting in less oil coming out and a spike in oil prices. U.S. officials say Iran is also attacking more ships to try to raise oil prices and ratchet up pressure on Trump ahead of the midterms. What to watch: The White House and Qatari mediators are still waiting to hear back from Iran about a U.S. counterproposal to end the war. "It's still in internal deliberations in Tehran," a U.S. official said. Regional mediators told Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in recent days that Iran shouldn't wait until after the midterms to give its response, a regional source with direct knowledge said. The regional mediators told Iran there's no guarantee that Trump will be more conciliatory after the midterms — on the contrary, he might be more aggressive.

events.title: Thune enjoys surprisingly clear path back to GOP leader despite Trump's attacks
events.summary: The News John Thune took criticism from President Donald Trump, agitated online conservatives, and occasionally frustrated some of his own members this year. Yet his next leadership election is looking smooth compared with the past couple of bouts to lead the Senate GOP. In fact, Thune may actually run unopposed this year, regardless of how the midterms go. “I’m not aware of anyone who wants the job. I certainly don’t,” Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., told Semafor. “I don’t envy the leader’s task.” Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who challenged Thune in 2024 and Mitch McConnell in 2022, told Semafor there’s “no wiggle room; I am not running for leader” this cycle. He said Thune is “probably the only person that’s going to run. But I always want to say if other people run and someone comes up with better ideas, you’ve got to listen to them. But I’m not running.” Know More The biggest headache for Thune was the Save America Act, a voter ID bill that lacked a strategy to become law in the Senate. Trump repeatedly leaned on Thune to kill the filibuster in order to pass it, and other senators wanted Thune to try to force Democrats to pull off a talking filibuster to block the bill. Eventually, though, the effort and outrage over its stalled status faded away. With Democrats favored to win the House and potentially even take the Senate, the fight over killing the filibuster is back on ice. That’s all good news for Thune, who says he’ll likely run for another term regardless of whether Republicans lose the Senate. If no one challenges him, it would be the first unanimous GOP leadership election since 2020. Notably, Johnson had backed Scott in previous leadership races. Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, told reporters on Thursday that Thune “will get elected pretty resoundingly.” “Do I think he’s got broad support? Yes. I don’t think there’s an insurgent movement that’s against him,” Moreno said. “There’s not a single Republican running nationally that’s saying, ‘Hey, if you elect me, I’ll vote against John Thune as leader.’” Several Democratic candidates say they won’t support Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for another term as leader of their caucus. But no one is indicating they are looking to challenge Schumer, either, which means those could just be protest votes. Former Democratic leader Harry Reid received a handful of “no” votes in his leadership race after losing control of the Senate in 2014. Republicans will have their leadership election on Nov. 10; Senate Democrats are likely to have theirs in early December, although the date isn’t set yet. The midterm results remain an X factor for both Thune and Schumer’s futures. Notable Thune told us in June he’d probably run again. Scott said in September he wasn’t committed to supporting Thune.

events.title: FAA equity talks raise questions about the agency's legal authority
events.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration’s pursuit of an equity stake in a private company that uses AI to manage air traffic is raising questions about whether it has clear legal authority to strike such a deal. The Trump administration has negotiated stakes in dozens of other companies, but none through the FAA. The agency’s interest in owning part of Air Space Intelligence, first reported by Politico , is too “premature” for there to be specifics, a person familiar with the matter told Semafor. Talks so far have been limited to a handful of internal conversations, the person added. One possible statutory underpinning for a deal: Existing law authorizes Transportation Department financial help for state or local governments to “acquire an interest” in some public transportation companies. That argument, like other agencies’ , would be a stretch. “It’s further proof that the administration doesn’t have a ‘plan’ or ‘strategy,’” said Tad DeHaven, who tracks the stakes for the Cato Institute . — Eleanor Mueller and Shelby Talcott

events.title: Copper thefts leave Perth roads in darkness and cost taxpayers millions
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts This section of Tonkin Highway en route to Ellenbrook has been without working street lighting for years. ( ABC News: Samantha Goerling ) Major roads and paths across Perth remain dark because widespread copper theft has left street lighting out. This week, police charged three people with stealing copper wire, and police are increasingly scrutinising scrap metal recyclers. The WA government has allocated nearly $12 million in the 2026-27 state budget to replace stolen street lighting cable and upgrade security. More than 100 kilometres of major roads and paths across Perth remain unlit, some for years, because of widespread copper theft. This week, police charged three people with stealing copper wire, which is lucrative on the black market. Police said they arrested and charged a 31-year-old man who allegedly stole more than 190 metres of telecommunication cable from Gidgegannup, before selling the recovered copper to a scrap metal recycler. That theft allegedly occurred over the King's Birthday long weekend in September from a Telstra site, where about 500 kilograms of copper was pulled out of the ground. Roads across Perth's metro area are in darkness at night due to the theft. ( ABC News: Samantha Goerling ) "This had a significant impact on the Gidgegannup and surrounding areas," Mundaring sergeant Tony Signal told 102.5 ABC Perth. Sergeant Signal said police were increasingly scrutinising scrap metal recyclers. "They're obliged by law to record any second-hand dealing of copper at the moment and we find that that's slipping through the cracks," he said. Col Blanch says organised crime groups would find illegal ways to get away with breaking the rules. ( ABC News: Kenith Png ) Police Commissioner Col Blanch previously told the ABC organised crime sought to circumvent those rules when offloading stolen metal. "We know that some scrap metal dealers are doing the wrong thing and doing a lot of business under the table … that's what [the] police's job is to stamp out," he said. "However, when they can't sell it to a second-hand dealer, scrap dealer here, they will put it in a container and they will send large amounts of scrap metal overseas." It's far from an isolated incident involving telecommunications infrastructure , with detectives charging a man with stealing around 50 metres of copper cabling from an exchange site in Wattleup last month. A Telstra spokesperson said copper theft widely impacted service companies and that the telco's copper theft prevention team works closely with police agencies across Australia. Streetlights don't work when the underground copper wiring is removed. ( ABC News: Samantha Goerling ) "We encourage anyone seeing any suspicious activity near our facilities to contact police immediately," the spokesperson said. Street lighting also continues to be targeted, with police arresting a 41-year-old man and a 50-year-old woman this week, after a member of the public reported suspicious activity along Tonkin Highway in Ellenbrook. Police stopped a vehicle in the vicinity a short time later and allege they found a significant amount of stolen insulated copper wiring. Copper thieves taking exceptional risks Demolition sites are being stripped for copper at an escalating rate, according to a Perth demolition contractor, risking electrocution and asbestos exposure to sell the scrap metal on the black market. Main Roads WA said as of October 2, more than 1,400km of cable had been stolen from its network, taking more than 100km of street lighting and nearly 30km of pedestrian/cycle paths lighting offline. "Since cable theft became a widespread issue, Main Roads have replaced 480km of copper roadway and PSP lighting cable as well as re-cabling and re-energising over 500 individual poles," a spokesperson said. "Currently, Kwinana Freeway, Tonkin Highway and Reid Highway are the three priority routes that Main Roads is focusing on for cable replacement and anti-theft treatments. "Works are also planned in key locations along Forrest Highway, Great Northern Highway, Mitchell Freeway, Roe Highway, Albany Highway, Ennis Avenue, Mandurah Road and Armadale Road." The WA government has allocated nearly $12 million in the 2026-27 state budget for street lighting cable theft replacement and security upgrades but still faces an uphill battle. Main Roads director of metropolitan operations James Pinnington said he expected the program to take several years.

events.title: Tariffs pose a risk to US-India relationship
events.summary: President Donald Trump faces a deadline Sunday to decide whether to impose certain penalties on other countries under a bipartisan sanctions law he signed last month. Any move by him to waive sanctions on Russian individuals or entities will be met with criticism, as would a decision not to impose tariffs on China for buying Russian gas. But Washington is hoping he’ll spare at least one country: India. “Both the United States and India should not buy Russian oil and gas, but I don’t think simply imposing big tariffs on India is the way to get them to” reduce their purchases, said Richard Fontaine, CEO of the Center for a New American Security. Punishing India for its reliance on Russian energy “would deal a body blow to the US-India relationship,” argued Sadanand Dhume, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations. The US and India are currently locked in trade negotiations, which more tariffs would surely disrupt. Fontaine said it is “100%” possible that the Trump administration uses the sanctions law to pressure India to give in to its demands in those discussions. Trump had previously hiked tariffs on India over its Russian energy purchases, but later removed them as trade talks progressed. Asked whether Trump had made a decision on which sanctions, if any, to impose at the deadline, a White House official said that he “signed the act and the administration will comply with the act’s requirements.” The bill gives the president broad power to waive penalties if he deems it in the US interest. — Morgan Chalfant

events.title: The terrifying true stories that inspired your favorite horror movies
events.summary: "The Exorcist." Warner Bros. Horror films have produced some of the most iconic figures in pop culture. But not all scary movies are completely fictional; some are actually based on real life . "The Conjuring" was based on the real-life Perron family in Rhode Island. Horror movies are reliably successful at the box office — just look at "Obsession" and "Backrooms " this year. They often have relatively low budgets, deliver strong box-office returns, and can create IP that leads to sequels and spin-offs for years to come. Plus, when Halloween rolls around, costumes and masks provide another bump to a studio's bottom line. But creating a completely original, compelling, and terrifying horror story can be challenging. That's why some of the most iconic and successful scary movies are based on real-world events. For example, " The Conjuring " franchise is based on the case files of real paranormal investigators Lorraine and Ed Warren. In total, the films have made almost $3 billion at the box office. These are the real stories and crimes that influenced some of the most classic horror films of all time, including "The Exorcist," "Nightmare on Elm Street," and "Jaws." "The Conjuring" is about the Perron family and the traumatic experiences they're having in their new Rhode Island home. Patrick Wilson and Vera Farmiga as Ed and Lorraine Warren. Warner Bros. The Perrons (husband Roger, wife Carolyn, and their five daughters) moved into what was known as the Old Arnold Estate in 1971, The Providence Journal reported. Almost immediately, the family reported paranormal activity, such as floating or moving furniture, doors opening and closing, disembodied sounds, and even being pushed, pulled, and hurt by unseen spirits. Upon calling in paranormal investigators Ed and Lorraine Warren, they found that the property was haunted by various ghosts, but that one particularly malevolent spirit, Bathsheba, was preying on them. Bathsheba Sherman, who lived on the property in the 1800s, has been described as a suspected Satanist who was charged with the violent murder of her first child, though historians say she was never convicted of a crime or accused of witchcraft. The property sold for $1.5 million in 2022. It has since been acquired by "Ghost Hunters" star Jason Hawes for $1.3 million, according to land records . "The Conjuring 2" is about a girl being possessed by a demon in London. New Line Cinema The Hodgson family reported experiencing unusual phenomena in their London home in August 1977, such as furniture flying through the air, and objects hurling toward witnesses, The Daily Mail reported. Most famously, however, Janet, one of four Hodgson children, claimed she was being possessed by a man named Bill Wilkins — it was later confirmed that a man by that name did, in fact, live in the house and died there of a brain hemorrhage,  People reported. While Janet later said that around "2%" of the haunting was made up, she maintains that the Enfield Poltergeist was real. You can listen to audio of her while she claimed she was possessed to make up your own mind. The third film is "The Conjuring: The Devil Made Me Do It," which is about the real trial of Arne Cheyenne Johnson. Warner Bros. In the third "Conjuring" film, Ed and Lorraine are tasked with helping a young man, Arne, who murdered his landlord after getting possessed by a demon, which Ed witnessed. In his trial, the Warrens supported Arne using the defense of demonic possession, a first in the United States. This is based on the real case of 19-year-old Johnson, who really did murder his landlord in 1981 and subsequently claimed he was innocent because he'd been possessed, as reported at the time by The New York Times . Johnson (and the Warrens) claimed that a demon was exorcised from the body of 11-year-old David Glatzel and then moved to Johnson. His girlfriend claimed she heard Johnson challenge the demon itself to leave Glatzel and possess him instead. Several months after Johnson's encounter with Warrens and the Glatzels, he stabbed his landlord to death, and then claimed he had no memory of the crime and was possessed. In reality, this defense was rejected; his lawyers then pivoted toward the self-defense strategy, and he was convicted of manslaughter. He served five years in prison. The fourth main film, "The Conjuring: Last Rites," is based on the Smurl haunting in the '70s and '80s. "The Conjuring: Last Rites." Warner Bros. Pictures In what's supposed to be the final cinematic appearance of Patrick Wilson and Vera Farmiga as the Warrens, "Last Rites" is a loose adaptation of the alleged Smurl haunting, which took place in West Pittson, Pennsylvania. Per The Times Leader , Jack and Janet Smurl, played by Elliot Cowan and Rebecca Calder, respectively, called the Warrens to their home in 1986 to address claims that a demon had slammed their 75-pound German shepherd into a wall, threw one of their children down the stairs, and even bitten Jack's ear. "The Smurls are truly a family coming under a visual attack," Ed Warren said at the time. "The ghost, devil, demon — or whatever you call it — is in that home." An exorcism was performed in that year, but it was, apparently, unsuccessful. Of course, the Smurls had plenty of doubters, including a priest who stayed in their home for two nights and reported nothing suspicious. The Smurls eventually left West Pittson and moved to Wilkes-Barre, about 10 miles away. The film dramatizes this story, but is mainly focused on passing the demon-hunting torch from Ed and Lorraine to their daughter, Judy (Mia Tomlinson). "Annabelle," "Annabelle: Creation," and "Annabelle Comes Home" tell the story of an evil doll that terrorizes her owner. New Line Cinema Annabelle is a doll believed to be imbued with an evil spirit. While the real-life Raggedy Ann doll (viewable at The Haunted Warren Museum in Salem, Massachusetts) is much less creepy-looking than her movie counterpart, she is said to have terrorized her owner. According to  The New Haven Register , the story of the doll begins in 1970, when a nurse received it as a birthday gift from her mother. She soon began to notice that the doll would change positions by itself. She then started finding creepy notes with messages like "Help me" written on them. And she claimed she once found the doll leaking blood. Once again, the Warrens were contacted for help. According to them, the doll wasn't possessed, but it was being manipulated by a spirit. They cleansed the home and took the doll to their museum, where it remains to this day. "The Amityville Horror" connects the murders of the DeFeo family with a demonic presence in the house. events.title: AOC transfers $1m to Michigan candidate El-Sayed in progressive push
events.summary: Progressive stalwart, who is seen as potential 2028 candidate, says she wants to combat ‘smears’ against El-Sayed. United States Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has transferred $1m to support Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, in a major progressive push for the upstart politician. Ocasio-Cortez, who has become a progressive stalwart since her surprise 2018 congressional victory, confirmed the donation in a statement on Friday and a speech in Michigan. The transfer was first reported by the New York Times. list 1 of 3 Trump’s Iran war now has a midterm election problem list 2 of 3 US court rejects Trump’s emergency order keeping Michigan coal plant open list 3 of 3 Kamala Harris campaigns with Abdul El-Sayed to unify Democratic voters The lawmaker pointed to political attacks against El-Sayed, a large portion of which have focused on his Muslim faith, his Egyptian heritage and support for Palestine. “I’m not waking up on November 4th wishing I did more to combat the smears aimed at Abdul,” Ocasio-Cortez said in a statement, in reference to the November 3 congressional midterm election. “I’m leaving everything I can on the field.” Speaking at an event in the Detroit area, Ocasio added that she transferred the money from her own campaign to show “the cavalry is coming”. “And the only reason I’m doing that is because I see the energy of each and every one of you stepping up to make an effort,” she said. The move comes as Ocasio-Cortez has been campaigning for El-Sayed in Michigan, joining him on a bus tour of the conservative-leaning Upper Peninsula area before hosting three events on Friday in the state’s largest city, Detroit. El Sayed’s populist progressive message has gained traction with voters in the state, where he currently leads Republican Mike Rogers by 2.6 percentage points, according to a Real Clear Politics average of high-quality polls. The support from Ocasio Cortez, who is weighing a potential 2028 presidential candidacy, also underscores a wider effort by progressives to court disaffected Trump voters. The pair highlighted economic issues while on the trail in the midwestern state. Trump’s approval ratings are at a career low ahead of the midterm vote. A slate of recent polls has shown widespread public disapproval of Trump’s handling of the US economy and the knock-on effects of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Recent polls have also shown an appetite for a more comprehensive change in US government, signalling a potential opening for candidates running outside of the establishment of both major parties. An AP-NORC poll released this week found that 80 percent of respondents said they supported either a “complete and total upheaval” or “substantial change” in how the country is run. Speaking alongside Ocasio-Cortez on Friday, progressive House Representative Ayanna Pressley called on the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which raises and allocates funds for Senate candidates, to make “an equitable investment in progressive and diverse candidates” like El-Sayed, Florida Senate candidate Angie Nixon and Mississippi Senate candidate Scott Colom. El-Sayed, who received an early endorsement from progressive US Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, has also recently been embraced by a handful of more centrist Democrats, including former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris. Sanders donated $250,000 to El-Sayed’s campaign, CNN reports. The new financial support from Ocasio-Cortez, which was given to the Abdul for Michigan Victory Fund, arrived as the Michigan Senate race has become one of the most expensive in the state’s history, topping $268m as of October 15, according to the Detroit Free Press. El-Sayed, meanwhile, outpaced Rogers in fundraising from July 1 to September 30, bringing in $30.6m compared to Rogers’ $9.6m. Still, Rogers’ campaign had more cash on hand as of September 30, with $6.5m compared to El-Sayed’s $3.8 million. Michigan is among the key Senate races that could determine control of the chamber for the final two years of US President Donald Trump’s term. Republicans currently hold 53 seats in the 100-member body.

events.title: From kitsch decor to extinct chains, new book revisits classic eateries
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts New book Old Vintage Melbourne, A Culinary Chronicle captures the dining institutions of yesteryear Stalactites in Lonsdale Street has been a Melbourne institution since 1978. ( Supplied: Nicole Konstandakopoulos/Stalactites. Most of the photos featured in this article appear in Old Vintage Melbourne, A Culinary Chronicle, published by Scribe. ) From a sophisticated 70s restaurant with hot-pink light shades, to a St Kilda cake shop and the all-you-can eat smorgasbords of the suburbs, Chris Macheras's latest coffee table book is brimming with Melbourne's culinary history. But the book's beginnings are also quintessentially Melbourne — or at least Melbourne as we knew it in 2020. Stuck at home during COVID-19, the lawyer and artist kicked off an Instagram account featuring vintage photos of the city and suburbs. The page took off, spawning two books and, now, a third: Old Vintage Melbourne: A Culinary Chronicle. Chris Macheras's lockdown project has now led to a third book. ( Supplied: Meghan Lawson ) "It's still crazy to have an idea that was just something that I was sitting there in lockdown, depressed, and then to think that it's created this community and people have found each other via my Instagram page," the author says. But Mr Macheras is clearly someone who thrives creatively in trying times. He produced his latest book while battling Hodgkin lymphoma — a type of blood cancer. "Whilst I was recovering and doing chemo and everything, my brain needed to do something," the 36-year-old says. "They give you a lot of steroids … whilst your body is tired, your mind is very up." The Club Grill restaurant, at the Southern Cross Hotel, was originally for men only. ( Courtesy: Athol Shmith, Mitchell Library, State Library of New South Wales/Tourism Australia ) He began piecing the book together from home, contacting a large number of restaurants and trawling the archives of the state library, Museums Victoria and the public record office for old images. "I couldn't physically go to the library because I was recovering," he says. "So everything was what I could get by email, and who could send me photos." The late Nick Tsiligiris pictured inside his beloved Olympic Doughnuts van in Footscray. ( Courtesy: Gina Hasapis ) The result is a collection of photos and stories from about 120 food joints, from Marios and Kingsland Chinese Restaurant , to Coles Cafeteria, Glo Glo's, Smorgy's, fresh produce markets and one very popular Footscray donut van. The Olympic Doughnuts van was a landmark for almost 40 years. ( Courtesy: Gina Hasapis ) A Greek grandfather who loved Melbourne Mr Macheras says his grandfather, who emigrated to Melbourne from Greece in 1955, instilled in him a love of history. "We would talk about sort of the difficult life they had as migrants, and that we should really love Australia and love Melbourne because this is a land that gave us the opportunity to leave war-torn Europe, where they were from," he says. The author says the book celebrates Australia's restaurant capital at a time when many people are craving a sense of nostalgia. Melbourne's dine-in Pizza Huts, which began to disappear in the 1990s, are captured in the book. ( Courtesy: Fremantle Media ) Mr Macheras grew up in Preston and Eltham, and remembers eating at places like Jim's Greek Tavern in Collingwood, which is still going strong. "As a kid, we were always going to things that were familiar for an immigrant family," he says. "And then those family restaurants. Dine-in Pizza Hut is super nostalgic for me, going and getting some of that big trough with chocolate mousse, soft serve and jelly." The dessert bar at Pizza Hut lives on in the memories of many a 1980s and 1990s child. ( Courtesy: Claire Sullivan and Rob Breslin ) The story behind the famous Stalactites ceiling A Greek institution on Lonsdale Street in the city is one of many legendary eating establishments featured in the book. Stalactites — named after the handmade structures that grace its ceiling — opened in 1978, when the area was a hub for Melbourne's Greek community, Stalactites operated for 24 hours a day for years, with many daytime and late-night diners eating under its distinctive ceiling. ( Facebook: Stalactites ) "It was a place where all the Greek migrants could come, and they could eat Greek food and speak Greek and maintain that connection," says Nicole Konstandakopoulos, whose parents and grandparents were the original owners of the famous restaurant. "But over time, the Greeks moved out of the city, and they went to suburbs like Oakleigh." The Lonsdale Street institution seen from the outside.
