events.title: Invasive fire ants return to organic farms not treated for 14 months
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Invasive fire ants are believed to have spread from organic farms left without treatment options for more than a year. ( Supplied: Scotty Yang ) Treatment on export-certified organic farms was paused in August 2025 after genetically modified ingredients were discovered in baits. The National Fire Ant Eradication Program (NFAEP) says there is evidence some areas have been reinfested from properties that did not have a treatment option for 14 months. A new treatment option has been found, but it requires direct nest injection, making it more labour-intensive than previous methods. Red imported fire ants have re-infested organic farms in Queensland, leaving them without options to control the pest for 14 months. Treatment was suspended in August last year on some export-certified properties in the south-east Queensland suppression zone after genetically modified ingredients were identified in baits used on nests. The National Fire Ant Eradication Program confirmed parts of a 1,110-hectare zone spanning the Lockyer Valley, Scenic Rim and Somerset agricultural hubs were re-infested, though the extent is yet to be determined. Fire ants can fly up to five kilometres, making their spread difficult to control. "We do have evidence of reinfestation of areas from properties that haven't been treated [since the suspension]," senior director of operations Robbie Wilson said. The genetically modified ingredients found in fire ant bait cannot be used on organic farms. ( Supplied: Johan Augustin ) He acknowledged organic farmers could not use ant-killing bait containing genetically modified (GM) corn and oil without risking their organic status. Fire ant treatment suspended on organic farms Fire ant treatments have been suspended on organic farms, and alternatives sought, after baits containing genetically modified soybean oil and corn grit were found to have been unwittingly distributed. "We've been working with (peak body) Australian Organic Limited … about how we support them in the eradication and limitations of infestation, which has been quite positive." Mr Wilson said the affected areas made up a small part of the 30,000 hectares identified as having gaps in treatment across the wider control area. "But that treatment may already be scheduled," he said. He said approving a treatment suitable for organic farmers was the "first phase" of bringing those properties back into the eradication program, which aims to eliminate fire ants by 2032. On Monday, the federal Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry announced it had granted a permit for a product using concentrated cinnamaldehyde, the organic compound that gives cinnamon its flavour and odour, for use in Queensland. "This treatment product has been assessed as compliant with the National Standard for Organic and Bio-Dynamic Produce," the department said. The tiny fire ants spread quickly and are easy to overlook. ( Supplied: National Fire Ant Eradication Program ) The permit requires application "by direct nest injection and/or as a nest drench" by people authorised by the NFAEP. Mr Wilson said the first shipment of the product from New Zealand was awaiting customs clearance at Brisbane port. "It is an organic product that can be used on certified organic properties," he said. Organic farmer Di Fyson welcomed the new treatment option. ( Supplied: Di Fyson ) But the labour-intensive method could not replace broadscale baiting, which Mr Wilson said authorities continued to work on for larger organic operations. Scenic Rim organic farmer Di Fyson welcomed the new treatment, but questioned why it took so long. Ms Fyson, who grows domestically certified organic leafy greens and pumpkins, received treatments during the suspension. But she said she would be willing to try the new product. "Definitely, particularly if that's going to be the only option," she said. Invasive fire ants detected in Sydney's inner west Specialist fire ant detection dog teams have been deployed to the site in Sydney's Enfield and a nearby area with no other nests having been discovered. Reece Pianta, advocacy director at the Invasive Species Council, which lobbies for better funding for eradication and prevention programs, said he was concerned that substitute treatments were taking too long to deploy "at mass scale." "I'm concerned about the lack of organic farm treatment alternatives creating gaps in fire ant eradication," he said. "We know from past experience when there have been gaps in fire ant treatments, that is when fire ants have spread." "The success of eradication is reliant on keeping those treatment gaps closed.

events.title: Brent oil touches $110 as Iran escalates Hormuz attacks, Ukraine vows to hit Russian refineries
events.summary: At least nine commercial ships have come under attack near Hormuz since Sunday as Iran tries to choke off crude oil exports through the strait. The "energy ceasefire" that President Donald Trump tried to broker between Ukraine and Russia has quickly unraveled. Iran allied Houthi militants in Yemen have repeatedly fired missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia this week. Crude oil prices rose sharply Friday as Iran escalated attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi militants fired missiles at Saudi Arabia and Ukraine vowed to keep striking Russian refineries. Brent futures hit a session high of $110 per barrel for the first time since May before easing slightly to close at $109.86, a gain of 3.7%. U.S. West Texas Intermediate rose 3.5% to settle at $101.41 per barrel. WTI added more than 10% this week while Brent advanced nearly 5%. Saudi Arabia intercepted several missiles fired over the Red Sea on Friday, including one that was heading toward the oil export terminal Yanbu, a military spokesman said. Three drones were also destroyed in the kingdom's Riyadh and southern regions, the military said. Iran-allied Houthi militants in Yemen have repeatedly fired at Saudi Arabia this week. Oil giant Aramco came under attack when one of its administrative buildings in Dhahran was hit Tuesday, the kingdom's energy ministry said . The Houthis attacked Riyadh's international airport on Oct. 10, killing 12 and injuring more than 300. In the Strait of Hormuz, at least nine tankers and cargo ships have come under attack since Sunday as Iran tries to choke off oil exports through the waterway. Iran sank the container ship GFS Pride on Wednesday, U.S. Central Command said. The crew of the Singapore-registered ship was safely evacuated, according to Singapore's maritime authority. The attacks have left three seafarers injured and two missing this week, according to the International Maritime Organization . Crude exports through Hormuz have pulled back after touching prewar levels in September. Shipments stood at 9.4 million barrels per day for the week ended Wednesday, about 70% of the average before the Iran war, according to data provided by the energy researcher Kpler. Meanwhile, the " energy ceasefire " that President Donald Trump tried to broker between Ukraine and Russia has quickly unraveled. The Kremlin continued attacking Ukrainian infrastructure despite the supposed truce. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv would resume strikes on Russian refineries in retaliation. Diesel prices have surged this year due to Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries and Iranian strikes on energy infrastructure in the Middle East. The fuel cost an average of $6.33 a gallon in the U.S. Friday, more than 70% above the same period last year, according to AAA data. U.S. crude oil prices were also driven higher by a big decline of more than 8 million barrels for the week ended Oct. 9 in commercial inventories due to production shut-ins on the Gulf Coast from Hurricane Isaias, according to the Energy Information Administration.

events.title: Debt is eating up a bigger chunk of your raise, research shows
events.summary: CNBC Global Financial Wellness Advisory Board Debt payments consume an estimated 52 cents of every dollar of inflation-adjusted take-home household income gained for a typical worker, new research finds. The share of families spending more than 40% of income on debt payments has reached its highest level since 2013, according to Federal Reserve data. Experts say understanding why you're borrowing, budgeting and comparing prices can help prevent debt from becoming a bigger burden. A version of this article first appeared in ″CNBC's Money 101 Newsletter with Sharon Epperson,″ an eight-week series with monthly updates to help improve your financial well-being. Subscribe now to receive the series in your inbox. It is also available in Spanish . Consumer spending has helped keep the U.S. economy resilient. Yet research shows debt payments are taking a growing bite out of Americans' income gains, leaving less money available to spend or save. A new analysis by the nonpartisan think tank The Century Foundation and the consumer advocacy group Protect Borrowers found that a typical U.S. household's estimated real take-home monthly pay rose $109 from late 2022 to early 2026. "Real" take-home pay is one's wage after accounting for inflation. Meanwhile, a worker's monthly debt payments rose $57. In other words, researchers estimate that for a one-earner household, 52 cents of every dollar of income gained in recent years goes to higher debt payments. For a two-earner household, they project that the entire real income gain, and then some, goes toward debt. The analysis also found inflation-adjusted debt payments rose nearly 15% over roughly three years — about eight times as fast as household income, which grew less than 2%. The Century Foundation and Protect Borrowers analyzed credit records for millions of working-age Americans ages 25 to 64, along with Census Bureau income data. The research includes payments on credit cards, auto loans and leases, student loans and home equity lines of credit. It excludes mortgages and some other borrowing, including many buy now, pay later loans and medical payment plans. Angela Hanks, chief of policy programs at The Century Foundation, said the findings may understate the financial pressure households face. "Even though it shows that workers' wages are getting eaten up by debt payments at a tremendous level," Hanks said, the findings represent "perhaps the rosiest analysis that we could have done using the data." She said adding mortgage payments as well as installment loans not included in a credit file — like buy now, pay later and payday loans — would have made household debt payments higher. Here's a look at more stories on how to manage, grow and protect your money for the years ahead. Living abroad doesn't end U.S. tax obligations. What young expats need to know Inheriting a home can leave siblings with financial headaches — how to avoid mistakes Is the K-shaped economy ending? Finance pros weigh in SEC proposes investor exam to expand private-market access — how it could work You can't 'borrow your way out of debt,' expert says, but more people are trying More consumers are relying on credit cards to cover basic expenses when their paychecks fall short, she said. Separate Federal Reserve data underscores the strain. The Fed's latest Survey of Consumer Finances found 8.6% of families spent more than 40% of their income on debt payments in 2025, up from 6.5% in 2022 — a level not seen since the 2013 survey. Mortgages and student loans are often considered "good debt" because they may help build wealth or earning power. But even potentially beneficial debt, or debt taken on for necessary expenses, can become a financial burden. "When that debt stretches out for six months or a year or longer, or if you're taking out a seven-year auto loan, or if you're taking out a longer mortgage than maybe you ideally would want to, or a bigger mortgage, that's when things get a little dicey," said Matt Schulz, chief consumer finance analyst at LendingTree and author of "Ask Questions, Save Money, Make More." To avoid taking on more debt than you can afford, he recommends three simple steps: Set a budget. Know how much you can realistically spend before you borrow or shop. Make a list. Shop with specific purchases in mind rather than giving in to impulse buys. Compare prices. Shopping around can reduce costs and how much you may need to borrow. Before taking on debt, consider the total borrowing cost, repayment terms and whether you have enough savings to handle unexpected expenses, Schulz said. — CNBC's Stephanie Dhue contributed reporting.

events.title: State Department warns travelers to China they risk “wrongful detention”
events.summary: The State Department is updating its travel advisory for mainland China to include an increased risk level for wrongful detention, according to a new plan seen by Semafor. The State Department’s move comes after two US citizens were labeled as wrongfully detained earlier this year, and at a complex moment in the relationships between the two most powerful countries in the world. Despite a personally warm relationship between the presidents, the countries’ deep differences from the Taiwan Strait to trade to artificial intelligence remain. A person familiar with the situation told Semafor the department’s change is connected to the continued detentions of the two Americans, Min Zin and Youlin Chen. Zin is a Myanmar scholar who was detained in June and accused of endangering China’s national security. Chen is a seismologist detained in 2024 and charged with espionage. Both are US citizens. The travel advisory as a whole remains at a Level 2, which urges Americans to “Exercise Increased Caution” when traveling to China, but the department is adding a “D” risk indicator for wrongful detention. Previously, the travel advisory for mainland China had an “O” risk indicator, which meant that there were “other potential risks not covered” by the department’s specific risk categories. “The U.S. Department of State has determined that Americans are at serious risk of wrongful detention in China,” a State Department spokesman said in a statement to Semafor. “The D risk indicator means the State Department has determined Americans are at risk of wrongful detention by the government of the country.” A group of bipartisan senators introduced a resolution last month pushing the department to add the wrongful detention indicator to its travel advisory, citing the two detained citizens. The spokesman added that wrongful detention is determined by a variety of factors, including having US citizenship or a connection to the US. This is the latest update to the State Department’s China travel advisory — in early September, the department added stronger warnings about wrongful detention, the “arbitrary enforcement of local laws,” and the usage of exit bans. Asked why the travel advisory remains at a Level 2 given the new wrongful detention label, the spokesman said it “identifies a specific risk of wrongful detention” and that “the overall Travel Advisory level reflects a broader assessment of safety and security conditions.”

events.title: Hill leaders brace for miserable 2027
events.summary: Have some sympathy for Capitol Hill's leaders next year, no matter who wins in November. 😩 Why it matters: The next Congress promises a thousand different ways to be miserable. And three of the big four leaders are expected to receive a two-year contract extension, with guaranteed long nights, bad days and short tempers. The fate of the fourth — Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) — rests on the outcome of the election. 🤕 The best (and worst) news for Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is that the job as party leader is likely his if he wants it, even if Republicans lose the majority. Like his first two years as leader, Thune's next two will be marked by constant second-guessing , or worse, from a president who commands his party, crushes his opponents and questions Thune's courage . Then there's the GOP base. MAGA influencers are seething over Thune's reluctance to try to nuke the filibuster and jam through a voter-ID bill . Between the lines: Four of Thune's confidants — DHS Secretary (and former senator) Markwayne Mullin and Sens. Steve Daines (R-Mont.), Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) and John Cornyn (R-Texas) — have left or are leaving the building. A fresh class of House conservatives will arrive in the Senate. They're likely to want to move fast and break things. The intrigue: Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) has not announced a third attempt to lead his party, but plenty of Republicans on the Hill suspect he will. Scott notably backtracked on his support for Thune in September. But Thune doesn't have to worry about his number two. Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) — who would be the top contender if Thune stepped down — has doubled down on his support. ⚠️ Thune's relationship with Speaker Johnson has been rocky throughout the year . If Republicans lose the House majority, Thune could find himself coordinating and strategizing with a new House leader. Most of Johnson's colleagues don't expect him to stay if the House flips. However, in the campaign's final weeks, Johnson has been playing Hamlet , publicly entertaining his next moves. With or without Johnson on stage, Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) are widely viewed as top contenders. 😎 Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) appears secure in his job as Democratic leader. His longevity in the role — or the Senate — is not. He's up for reelection in 2028 and could face a primary challenge from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.). Many Democrats expect him to retire. One possible result: YOLO Chuck , a 76-year-old majority leader with an angry base and ambitious colleagues, but nothing to lose. 🤬 One urgent task for Schumer is to get on the same page as House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), whose progressive members have some strong feelings about Schumer and the Senate. Jeffries and Schumer took dramatically different approaches to funding the government in March 2025. These differences would be harder to manage in the majority, especially if Jeffries struggles to maintain discipline within his ranks. However, Jeffries — like Schumer and Thune — doesn't appear to have any formidable challengers for party leader. Jeffries could face many of the same headaches Johnson did — a wing of his party that ran on anti-establishment principles and whose votes cannot be counted on . What we're watching: Trump and Schumer have a complicated relationship . But the president has indicated he sees Jeffries as someone he could work with.

events.title: Porsche’s electric Macan Turbo is an automotive existential crisis
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Maybe it was the grey color, the slightly bulbous roofline, or the vaguely SUV-like proportions of the electric Porsche Macan, but as I shuttled kids and groceries around city and suburban streets, I never once noticed a longing stare from other drivers. Unlike with other cars I’ve tested, no enthusiasts stopped to ask me questions. The 2026 Porsche Macan Turbo simply blended in, leaving in its wake a raft of existential questions. What is a sports car, anyway? Does it need to be overwhelmingly extroverted? Should it match the leaner, lighter look of its gas-powered sibling? Drive one and the questions cease. Maybe that’s because the acceleration makes it hard to breathe? Or maybe it’s because, by the numbers, the Macan is a sports car at heart despite its rather humdrum crossover body style. My passengers would agree. The kids I drove to soccer practice, both my own and others, gave the punchy acceleration high marks. The G-forces it reports on the head-up display ($2,660) can easily mimic the pull of gravity. Stab the accelerator at 70 mph and it lurches as though it were standing still. (Don’t worry, fellow parents. I did not try that with children on board.) On winding roads, the car comes alive, thanks in part to the four-wheel steering ($2,150). Drop it into Sport Plus mode, and the car literally drops on its air suspension. Are we sure this is another anonymous crossover? Maybe anonymity is a useful trait in a car this responsive and powerful. Unlike most two-row crossovers, you get the feeling of sitting in the Macan, not on it. The wheel extends far enough to make a sporty driving position possible, and the classic Porsche chronometer ($1,040) perched atop the dash ticks off the seconds it takes to get the kid to soccer practice. The 2026 Porsche Macan Turbo EV is a two-row crossover with 630 horsepower and a 100-kilowatt-hour battery. The EV, which the automaker provided to me for a week, starts at $112,700. However, the one I drove rang up at $149,610, including destination fees. Yes, the options alone could buy a nicely equipped Chevy Bolt . With Porsche and options, if you have to ask…well, it’s better not to. The Porsche Macan Turbo EV I drove came in Slate Grey Neo (a $2,620 upgrade), which was really well executed and among the best greys I’ve seen. If you crave luxurious anonymity, then this grey is your color. There were a slew of other options, and in my view, not all of them are worth it. I’d skip the passenger display ($1,710); my kids liked that it could play YouTube videos, but they can’t ride up front, and my wife was underwhelmed. “Our washing machine can play YouTube videos,” she said. I’d also forgo the illuminated Porsche wordmark on the front seatbacks ($690), puddle lamps that shine “PORSCHE” onto the pavement ($420), Porsche crests on the headrests ($640), and an illuminated Turbo badge on the door sills ($1,230). That Turbo badge became a point of contention for some of my friends, who were quick to point out that EVs technically can’t have turbos. That is true, though automotive names have long been divorced from reality. Almost every Porsche these days has a turbo, even those not labeled as such. It’s not just Porsche: BMW’s model numbers, for example, stopped reflecting engine displacement decades ago, and the Ford Galaxie never traveled between star systems using its hyperdrive. Sorry, friends, I’m not taking the bait. At least the Macan Turbo’s EV qualities don’t raise too many questions. It charges fast — exactly 20 minutes from 19% to 80% on a 350-kilowatt charger — and gets about 285 miles of highway range. Those big wheels ($4,110) and sticky tires ($660) sapped some range, but it was still more than enough to get from New York to Boston with charge to spare. The advanced driver assistance system ($1,140) works well enough, even if it hunts a bit in the lane. The AI-powered voice assistant did a solid job of interpreting my queries and commands. For a while, I thought it was the only way to turn on the heated steering wheel ($720), which was actually fine because it worked so well. (Surprise! There’s a small button hidden on the inner rim of the steering wheel between two spokes. IYKYK, I guess.) When it’s time to leave the Macan, you can just open the door and walk away. The Burmester sound system ($4,960) will keep bumpin’ until you lock the door, which is a helpful reminder. If you’re a Porsche traditionalist, you can also hit the vestigial power button to the left of the driver’s display. Good to have choices, I guess? At least Porsche doesn’t charge you for that. The navigation system, and specifically how it integrates with the EV, was underwhelming. When the car was at a 22% state of charge, I asked it to find the nearest fast charger. It directed me to two.

events.title: Here's who Netflix just brought in to run content — and what it means for the streamer
events.summary: Netflix has replaced its chief content officer, Bela Bajaria, with former Disney executive Peter Rice. Rice brings a wealth of experience in television and film, including scripted and unscripted shows, live sports telecasts, prestige television and theatrical distribution. Netflix's viewership has stagnated in recent quarters. It reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday. Netflix is shaking up its C-suite in an effort to fix its engagement woes. On Thursday, the streaming giant announced that former Disney executive Peter Rice will take over as the company's chief content officer, overseeing global content organization, including scripted and unscripted series, film and live events. Rice is replacing 10-year Netflix veteran Bela Bajaria , who most recently led the company's global content team with a focus on its live sports strategy . Bajaria was initially hired in 2016 to help the streamer launch an unscripted division as well as licensing and studio co-productions. She later transitioned to the top creative role, spearheading Netflix's $20 billion content budget. She oversaw popular TV series like "Stranger Things," "Wednesday," "Bridgerton," "Squid Game," "Adolescence" and "Beef," as well as Netflix films like "Frankenstein" and "KPop Demon Hunters." Bajaria also helped push Netflix into live sports and events, including deals with the WWE and the NFL as well as programs like "The Roast of Tom Brady." Prior to his stint at Disney, Rice was president of 21st Century Fox and CEO of Fox Networks Group as well as Fox's lead executive on the Hulu board. He was also the president of Fox Searchlight Pictures and helped release "Slumdog Millionaire," "Juno," "Little Miss Sunshine" and "Sideways." The executive change follows a tumultuous period for Netflix as it faces stagnating viewership and explores avenues for growth. It comes just days after the streaming giant laid off roughly 1,000 employees , or 6% of its workforce. The last time Netflix made cuts of this size was in 2022 when it reported its first quarterly subscriber loss in more than 10 years. "We believe this round of layoffs reflects more structural changes to the cost base than a reaction to near-term subscriber dynamics," wrote Brian Pitz, managing director and head of internet and interactive entertainment equity research at BMO Capital Markets, in a research note published Friday. In July, Netflix reported viewership increased just 2% in the first half of the year as the streamer suffers from a lack of shows with water-cooler-level hype. Co-CEO Ted Sarandos admitted last month during the Bloomberg Screentime conference that the company is "not growing as fast as I want us to." Those warnings, and now Bajaria's exit, have Wall Street bracing for more turbulence ahead. "The sudden departure of Bajaria likely signals to us that user engagement may have remained soft throughout [the third quarter]," Pitz wrote. Netflix is set to release fiscal third-quarter earnings on Tuesday. In July, Nielsen reported that Netflix had generated 7.8% of TV viewership, while YouTube accounted for nearly double that, at 14.2%. YouTube has been Netflix's biggest threat in the battle for viewers' time. In response, the streaming giant has sought to diversify its content in recent years, expanding into live sports, documentaries and video games in order to compete for share of consumer attention. "If the opportunity is to recast [Netflix] into a broader content hub, the risk is missing the watercooler originals," Steven Cahall, equity analyst at Wells Fargo, wrote in a research note last month. "We see breakout hits as a must for the stock to work again." Rice has a wealth of experience in television and film, most recently serving as the chairman of Walt Disney Television and chairman of general entertainment for the company. He managed a wide swath of channels across broadcast and streaming, including ABC, Disney Channel, Hulu and FX Networks. During his tenure, he oversaw the production of more than 300 shows, including "American Idol," "Modern Family," "Abbott Elementary," "The Bear," "Only Murders in the Building" and "Shogun." He also headed up major sporting events such as coverage of the Super Bowl, NBA Finals and FIFA World Cup. Under Rice's leadership, Disney earned roughly 300 Primetime Emmy nominations between 2021 and 2022. Of those nods, it won nearly 60 awards across its television networks and streaming platforms. Meanwhile, Netflix's Emmy wins have slowed. In 2021, it tied the record for most trophies won by an outlet in a single year with 44. This year, however, it only took home 16 prizes, its lowest Emmy haul in a decade. With Rice, Netflix is also getting an executive with theatrical experience. After he was ousted by then-Disney CEO Bob Chapek in mid-2022, he transitioned into an independent producer role. Since 2023 he has produced films like "Saturday Night" and "28 Years Later.

events.title: Questions about Katie Zacharia's credentials have recruiters talking about how they vet candidates
events.summary: Then-White House press secretary Katie Zacharia held her first press briefing Tuesday. Win McNamee/Getty Images Questions about now-former press secretary Katie Zacharia's legal credentials put résumé claims in the spotlight. Recruiters share how they've caught candidates inventing jobs, faking degrees, or exaggerating their past. Nearly 4 out of 10 Americans admit to putting inaccurate information on their résumés, a survey found. For corporate recruiters like Martha Heller, asking questions about a job candidate's credentials — like the kind that swirled around now-former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia this week — is par for the course. When a background check failed to verify an executive candidate's college degree a few years ago, Heller inquired about the discrepancy. The candidate, who was being considered for a job at a California insurance company, claimed a flood at his school had destroyed the records from the year he graduated. Skeptical, Heller called the college and learned that no such event had occurred. "It was like detective work," she said, adding that the problem wasn't whether the candidate had a college degree. It was that he misrepresented his education and then doubled down when questioned, she said. White House controversy Zacharia's self-described legal career has been the subject of intense scrutiny in recent days following her appointment as White House press secretary. When asked by a reporter what state she passed the bar exam in, she responded, "When I moved to China." Business Insider reviewed records for all 50 states and the District of Columbia and found no evidence that Zacharia had been admitted to any state bar in the US after she graduated with a law degree from Pepperdine University in 2011. Zacharia later defended calling herself a lawyer, saying that after failing the bar exam the first time, she did not take it a second time. On Friday, a White House official confirmed that she is "transitioning out" of the role. Vetting résumés One of a recruiter's jobs is to vet a candidate's background. Research suggests it's not uncommon for candidates to exaggerate their credentials. Some 37% of Americans said they've put inaccurate information on their résumés, according to a June report from Novorésumé, an online résumé-building service. Nearly 7% said they'd claimed a degree, certification, or other credential they didn't possess, while 6.1% said they'd listed a job that didn't exist or was substantially fabricated. The findings are based on a May survey of 2,000 US adults. Brian Fink, a managing partner at tech recruiting firm The ReWork Group, can relate. Last year, a candidate for a senior marketing job at a cybersecurity company was on the verge of being hired when a background check failed to confirm that he'd worked for a company listed as a past employer on his résumé and LinkedIn profile. Fink said he gave the candidate an opportunity to provide evidence supporting his claim, but the man refused. "I had no choice but to rescind the offer," said Fink. "If you're willing to lie about your education, what else are you willing to lie about?" Background checks Recruiters typically wait until a job candidate is a finalist to conduct a background check because the task is time-consuming and costly. They also tend to hold off contacting references early on to avoid tipping off the person's current employer that they're job hunting. Early in the process, though, some recruiters will look for potential red flags by probing inconsistencies or gaps in candidates' work histories. Doug Johnson, CEO of executive search firm Valor Partners, said he asks candidates at the end of an interview if there's anything embarrassing or potentially damaging in their past that might come up during a background or reference check. He tells them that disclosing it now gives them a chance to address the issue with a prospective employer, while discovering it later could cost them the job. Most candidates say there's nothing to be concerned about, said Johnson. But some subsequently fall off the radar, and others suddenly report receiving a raise or finding a better opportunity elsewhere. "It worries people who have a conscience," he said. Update: October 16, 2026 — This article has been updated to reflect Friday's news that Zacharia is out of the role. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Mine owner convinced tiny town's lead poisoning concerns are unfounded
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts IPC hearing on Bowdens Silver Mine concludes as lead concerns raised Protest signs outside the second day of hearings. ( ABC Central West: Hamish Cole ) The Independent Planning Commission (IPC) held a three-day hearing into a proposed silver and lead mine near Mudgee this week. A minerals expert told the IPC the nearby Lue Public School should be moved if the project was approved. The IPC is expected to hand down a determination by December 9. The NSW Independent Planning Commission (IPC) has been told a public school should be moved if a proposed silver and lead mine is approved, amid fears it could poison children. The IPC heard three days of evidence this week in Mudgee as it reassessed a proposal to extract 30 million tonnes of silver, lead and zinc over 23 years near Lue. The project has divided the community, with advocates touting the economic benefits and others raising concerns about potential environmental and health impacts. Proponent Silver Mines Limited's managing director Jo Battershill implored the panel to approve the development. "The project would provide investment and economic diversification for the mid-western region," he said. A tractor protest was held in Mudgee on Wednesday in opposition to the proposed silver mine. ( ABC Central West: Hamish Cole ) Almost 100 people spoke at the hearing, with the majority opposed to the mine. Only a few who spoke in support were not employees. On Wednesday, a group of farmers rode tractors and utes from Lue into Mudgee as part of their protest action. Along with dozens of local residents, experts from around Australia also addressed the hearing. Dozens of local residents spoke in opposition to the Bowdens Silver Mine at the IPC's reassessment. ( ABC Central West: Hamish Cole ) Among them was University of Queensland professor and principal research fellow at the Sustainable Minerals Institute Barry Noller. He told the hearing he believed the project's potential for lead exposure posed an unacceptable risk to children at Lue Public School, located two kilometres from the mine site. "I recommend that the Lue school, being at the boundary of dust deposition of [the] Bowdens mining project, be moved," Professor Noller said. "The management plan would be underestimating the true quantity of deposited lead that is relevant in terms of assessing the risk to adults and particularly children." Jo Battershill appeared before the IPC on Wednesday as part of its reassessment of the mine. ( ABC Central West: Hamish Cole ) Mr Battershill told the IPC that while the concern was understandable, the project had undergone extensive independent review. "Predicted health risks from the project, including from lead, are very low and are not expected to result in adverse human health impacts," he said. "It has been carefully assessed, and multiple layers of monitoring and management would apply throughout the life of the project." Mudgee-based general practitioner Peter Bryant told the panel dust from the project would threaten residents across the district. "There are no levels of lead exposure which are known to be without risk of harm," Dr Bryant said. "I don't want to find myself frequently requesting blood tests for children who live in this area to check their lead levels. "I really hope not to be talking with parents about the high levels of lead that have been found in their child's blood and discussing the long-term implications this could have on their blood development and ongoing health." GP Peter Bryant also spoke at the public hearing, citing his concerns. ( ABC Central West: Hamish Cole ) As part of the proposal, Silver Mines Limited would use approximately 2,000 megalitres of water a year for processing and dust suppression. Mr Battershill said assessments found average water supply reliability to be approximately 99.4 per cent. "The water balance monitoring found that except during extreme drought conditions, sufficient water would be available to meet operational demands," he said. Dozens of people drove tractors from Lue to Mudgee, where the IPC held its three-day hearing. ( ABC Central West: Hamish Cole ) Martin Krogh worked for the NSW government as a scientist for more than 30 years, including at the former Sydney Catchment Authority. "In my view, there are significant shortcomings in the Bowdens Environmental Impact Statement surface water assessment," he told the panel. "During drought conditions and very dry years, it appears highly unlikely there will be sufficient water falling in the catchment to support the environment, basic stock and domestic use, and downstream irrigation.

events.title: ICE shooting leads to rare Jeffries-Mamdani collaboration
events.summary: An October shooting by federal immigration officers in New York City has led to a head-turning show of unity from House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Why it matters: This unlikely collaboration between leaders of Democrats' competing establishment and progressive wings shows how opposing Trump-era immigration enforcement has become an area of party consensus. Democrats "are definitely unified across the spectrum re ICE," Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the chair of the Queens Democratic Party and a close ally of Jeffries, told Axios. He added that "the Mayor has also reached out ... to me in regards to local issues and I believe Leader Jeffries is also indicating he wants to work with the NY Congressional delegation." Driving the news: Mamdani led a letter dated Oct. 16 with over 100 other Democratic elected officials in New York City, including every Democratic member of the city's congressional delegation, to parking lot and garage owners. "In solidarity with immigrant New Yorkers and in our shared commitment to the City we love, we ask that you do not rent, lend, or otherwise make your property available to ICE as a staging area for its enforcement operations," the letter reads. The officials argued that the shooting of 28-year-old Oscar Belgal in New York's Marble Hill neighborhood in early October was "not an isolated case," pointing to past instances in Queens and Manhattan . "Owners who refuse to take part in these federal civil immigration enforcement operations advance public safety by protecting their own staff and customers, as well as fellow New Yorkers beyond their lots and garages." Between the lines: Jeffries and Mamdani have walked a careful line as two of the most prominent national figures within their respective Democratic Party factions. Jeffries rankled the left, including some members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, by waiting until 11 days before last year's election to endorse Mamdani for mayor. The two came into conflict this summer when Jeffries supported Democratic Reps. Dan Goldman and Adriano Espaillat while Mamdani campaigned hard for their primary challengers, though the Democratic leader notably downplayed the clash . Yes, but: The two have also had other notable moments of accord, such as when Mamdani opposed City Councilmember Chi Ossé 's ultimately aborted plan to try to primary Jeffries from the left. They also appeared together at a ribbon-cutting for a housing development in Brooklyn on Thursday. Zoom out: The letter's signers also include Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), who accused then-candidate Mamdani last year of making "references to global jihad," for which she later apologized . Goldman and Espaillat, who were ultimately unseated by their Mamdani-backed challengers, signed on as well. So did retiring Rep. Nydia Velázquez, who was burned by Mamdani endorsing Claire Valdez over her chosen successor, according to the New York Times . What we're hearing: "It's significant to see Mayor Mamdani lead a letter like this that includes both U.S. Senators and the full NYC Democratic House delegation (including the two he opposed in this spring's primaries)," a prominent Mamdani ally said in a text message to Axios. The person added: "It reflects both how universally hated ICE is by Democrats — and how much work the mayor has done to build bridges." The Mamdani ally spoke on the condition of anonymity to offer candid analysis of the delicate relationship between the mayor and the party establishment. The bottom line: Others argued that Democratic unity around opposing ICE was the overriding factor. One Democratic elected official from New York told Axios: "The fact that everyone signed on has more to do with the power of the issue than the power of the Mayor." A person in Jeffries' orbit similarly argued that immigration is simply "a unifying issue for Dems," but acknowledged that Mamdani "is consistently reaching out to the delegation to build ties and smooth things since the elections, which is smart."

events.title: SpaceX AI policy leader grilled by NYC Council on Grok safety, sexualized images
events.summary: SpaceX head of global government affairs for AI Gabriela Castillo Madrid faced questions about Grok's generation of sexualized images from the New York City Council on Friday. NYC Council Speaker Julie Menin asked why she was able to pull up sexualized images of herself when Castillo Madrid said Grok does not let users create such images of real people. Elon Musk's aerospace and AI company previously evaded a subpoena to testify as part of a legislative investigation and hearing held last week. SpaceX artificial intelligence policy leader Gabriela Castillo Madrid faced a tough line of questioning from NYC Council Speaker Julie Menin and other members on Friday as part of a council investigation into AI safety. When Castillo Madrid claimed that the company had appropriate "safeguards" in place around its AI products, Menin immediately confronted her. "I'm going to completely push back on that," Menin said. "I mean, just this morning — myself and my team — we put our own names, my own name, into Grok, and there's absolutely a sexualized image of myself. So then, how is it that within a second, I could find a sexualized image of myself using Grok?" Castillo Madrid responded that the company has "strict controls" and would have the safety team look into that specific instance. NYC Council Member Carmen De La Rosa, who leads the council's tech committee, told Castillo Madrid that "it is disgusting" that Grok enables users to easily "sexualize" images of real women without their consent. "I just don't understand how you can say that there are these safe models," Menin said. "It's just unacceptable." Castillo Madrid appeared in front of the council's tech committee by video. Elon Musk's aerospace, defense tech and AI company originally evaded requests and a subpoena from the city council to appear alongside leaders from OpenAI , Anthropic , Google and Meta on Oct. 5. SpaceX agreed to testify earlier this week after the council threatened to have its subpoena enforced by a judge. The council opened its probe following a month of intense debate surrounding the risks posed by advanced AI models, and is aiming to use testimony and information unearthed through the investigation to guide new regulations. Apple's $1,999 iPhone Duo puts the company's status-symbol power to the test Trump says White House didn't order Starlink restrictions in Ukraine Blue Origin plans $330 million Florida expansion to ramp New Glenn launches Before Castillo Madrid took a role in government affairs at SpaceX earlier this year, she worked at X, Musk's social media company that's now owned by SpaceX, according to her LinkedIn profile . Prior to that, she spent almost three years at the U.S. Department of Commerce. De La Rosa asked Castillo Madrid how many whistleblowers the company has fired, to which Castillo Madrid said she was "not aware" of any. "I just want to interject for a minute because Devin Kim, one of your former employees, was reportedly fired after he sounded the alarm about serious safety concerns," Menin said. "I'm not aware with that specific case," Castillo Madrid responded, adding that the company has a culture where "everybody has a an ability to say something when they see something." Kim is now President of the nonprofit Center for AI Safety, a think tank focused on AI risks and safety. Kim began his testimony before the council by outlining his experience as one of the first employees at xAI, saying that he "built the systems that researchers use to train and evaluate Grok." Kim said that he started raising concerns in January 2025 and those worries were shut down by his manager. "My supervisor responded that AI safety was useless, and that AI would kill us and all anyways," he said. Kim appeared by video, along with his attorney, following Castillo Madrid's questioning. Regarding Grok-generated images, Kim said under prior standards at the company, "tasteful nudity was acceptable and is the goal." "During my time there, there were only three employees working on AI safety, many of whom left after I resigned," Kim said. "And I think in large part due to the frustration with how safety was being handled." The council also pressed Castillo Madrid about other areas of misuse with Grok and the types of safeguards that were in place. Councilmember Mercedes Narcisse asked why the company promoted the idea of users uploading X-rays to Grok, asking if that was safe and if HIPPA protections applied. SpaceX's Castillo Madrid said Grok is "not meant to be a clinician, a doctor," adding, "in terms of privacy, users decide whether their Grok conversations are used to train our models or not." Narcisse said it was dangerous to tell people "openly on X, to put their MRI, X-rays," into Grok and expect "a definite answer" on health matters. The council member then upbraided the SpaceX representative for the vagueness of some of her replies. "You're supposed to give us answers. You're not," she said.

events.title: Private lenders scramble to recover funds after Bathla collapse
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Major Bathla lender La Trobe sells $31.2m loan as private credit firms seek to recover funds Topic: Construction and Real Estate Industry Private credit lenders of Bathla Group are striking deals to recover debts following the property giant's collapse. ( ABC News: Berge Breiland ) La Trobe Financial has sold its senior loan facility, tied to a Bathla Group development, to investors through a fund managed by 360 Capital. The $31.2 million purchase would give 360 Capital greater influence over the Marsden Park project. Morningstar expects private credit fund growth to slow substantially. The fallout from the collapse of property developer Bathla Group continues to reverberate through Australia's private credit market, with lenders taking matters into their own hands to recover money tied up in the failed construction giant. In one of the latest deals, property investment and funds management group 360 Capital has revealed it acquired a senior loan facility for about $31.2 million through its private credit fund, funded by private investors and entities within the 360 Capital group. A senior loan facility is the first mortgage debt in a commercial investment and ranks highest in repayment priority. The ABC understands the debt was acquired from major private lender La Trobe Financial, relating to a Bathla development at 137 South Street, Marsden Park, in Sydney's north-west. An artist's impression of 137 South St, Marsden Park apartments, as listed on the Bathla website. ( Supplied: Bathla ) The Marsden Park project comprises 72 apartments and is nearing completion, according to two sources close to the construction. Half of the apartments have already been pre-sold under contracts worth $25.8 million (excluding GST), 360 Capital said in a statement. In August, La Trobe disclosed it had $38.1 million in loans to Bathla, comprising four residential loans and one development loan. The ABC understands through this deal, La Trobe has sold its development loan, recovering all outstanding principal, interest and late-payment charges and significantly reducing its exposure to the collapsed developer. Deal gives 360 Capital greater control 360 Capital's ASX-listed mortgage investment trust, the 360 Capital Mortgage REIT, already held an $8.9 million loan secured against the development, which ranked behind La Trobe Financial for repayment. The trust has invested a further $5.2 million in the deal. Construction work has stopped at sites and the company is down to skeleton staff. "The step was not taken lightly, but is very important to protect the value of the trust's subordinated position," the company said. The deal means entities associated with 360 Capital now control both the first and second mortgages over the development, giving them greater influence over how the project is completed and the debts recovered. Morningstar equity analyst Winky Tan said lenders holding first mortgages were in a much stronger position to recover their money, while mezzanine lenders further down the repayment queue risked losing most, if not all, of their investment. "When you're able to finish the project, you can sell it as a finished product, which will have a much higher valuation than a half-finished project," she said. Ms Tan cautioned that the ultimate financial outcome for any lender would depend on whether the remaining apartments could be sold and at what price, particularly given the downturn in the property market. 'Perfect storm' unfolding in private credit sector Lenders including Centuria Bass and CVS Lane suspended withdrawals from some funds in August amid concerns about their exposure to Bathla. MA Financial, which says it has no exposure to Bathla, also introduced withdrawal limits on some of its funds amid concerns more investors could seek to pull out their money. Major private credit manager Metrics Credit Partners, which also says it has no exposure to Bathla, suspended withdrawals from some unlisted funds amid scrutiny of asset valuations.

events.title: Wall Street's fear gauge is ripping. Traders see it going even higher
events.summary: The sell-off in AI-related stocks pushed the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) above 22 for the first time in four months. A cluster of trades suggests it could go even higher. In a series of eyebrow raising trades, investors purchased a number of November VIX calls that payoff if the index stays elevated through November. Specifically, one trader bought 9200 of the November 18, 20-strike calls for $1.7 million and 12,500 of the November 18, 23-strike calls for $1.1 million, wagering that the VIX will close above 23 by the third week of November. "The speed at which VIX increased today, combined with elevated VIX options volume suggests traders are actively monetizing October VIX positions and rolling to hedge a larger market downturn. We note several +$1 million call VIX prints for November," said Brent Kochuba, founder of SpotGamma and a CNBC contributor. Cracks in the AI complex and fears around neo-cloud provider CoreWeave caused the Nasdaq to shed 2%, its worst day since June 5th. CoreWeave lost 13%. Of the top ten most popular VIX contracts to buy in Friday's session, nine were calls, and six were at strikes above where the VIX fell to after its initial spike. Nearly $27M in premium was traded across those nine contracts, or just about 36% of the total premium traded in VIX options on the day. The market faces a key test next week when Tesla, SpaceX and Meta report earnings.

events.title: The affordability crisis isn't hitting all voters equally. Here's why
events.summary: Affordability is a core issue in the upcoming midterm elections. Not all households are necessarily feeling the financial pressures of high inflation, according to economists and political experts. Seniors are more insulated from inflation because they are less exposed to certain categories such as home prices, mortgages and childcare than younger generations, economists said. Affordability is a major theme of the upcoming midterm elections — one that could have implications for how people vote in November. But not all households are feeling the financial strain equally, according to economists and political experts. Specifically, older Americans are more insulated from the affordability crunch than younger households such as millennials, the experts said. "Affordability is the central issue in the forthcoming midterm elections," said William Galston, a senior fellow and chair of governance studies at the Brookings Institution, a think tank. "Nothing else is close." "Who's feeling these pressures the least? Seniors," he said. Why seniors are 'doing pretty well' This isn't to say that older Americans — generally, those age 65 and older — aren't feeling any financial pressures . They're certainly paying more for food, gasoline, electricity and other items like everybody else amid stubbornly high inflation , economists said. It's also not to say that all young households find life to be more unaffordable. However, in aggregate, seniors disproportionately own their homes and are less likely to be first-time homebuyers — meaning they're less exposed to fast-rising mortgage rates and home prices, economists said. They generally drive fewer miles and keep their cars longer — making them less sensitive to high gasoline prices and rising bond yields, which have put upward pressure on auto loan rates, economists said. Most also don't need childcare, a category that has seen prices soar in recent years, economists said. And an important chunk of retirees' income — Social Security — is protected from inflation via cost-of-living adjustments, they said. The Social Security Administration on Wednesday announced a 3.6% boost to benefits for 2027, a larger-than-average COLA increase . "You put it all together, and I would say that — especially if you're 75 and above — you're doing pretty well compared to the rest of America," Galston said. "And the people who are feeling the most pressure are young families in the 30- to 45-year-old range." Young people are more 'disillusioned' Financial data supports this generational divide . Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's, conducted an analysis for CNBC that shows that baby boomers — which Moody's defines as those born between 1946 and 1964 — along with the Silent Generation and older — which it defines as those born in 1945 or earlier — experienced the lowest increase in consumer prices from January 2019 through August 2026. Zandi used Bureau of Labor Statistics data to generate a weighted consumer price index by generation. Those two oldest cohorts saw a roughly 31.5% cumulative percent change in consumer prices over that time period, Zandi found. Meanwhile, millennials — which Moody's defines as those born between 1981 and 1996 — saw the highest cumulative price growth relative to other groups — nearly 2 percentage points higher than that of the older cohorts, at 33.3%. Generation Z, the youngest adult group, born in 1997 or later, had the second-highest rate, at 32.7%. "Young people are definitely suffering higher rates of inflation than older Americans," Zandi said. "That comes through loud and clear in the data." "Younger Americans are arguably most disillusioned as they are facing the highest inflation, and thus may turn out to vote to a greater degree," a dynamic that should favor Democrats, he said. A Reuters/Ipsos poll published last week found 78% of Americans said the White House shares blame for higher costs. That includes 64% of Republicans, 76% of independents and 95% of Democrats, according to the poll , which surveyed 4,506 U.S. adults and had a margin of error of plus or minus 1.5 percentage points. "I think it's fair to say when people are feeling pinched, they look for somebody in leadership to come to them with a solution," said Michael Reid, head of U.S. economics at the Royal Bank of Canada. "I think you'll see some voters turn out and look for whoever is not currently in office as a solution." CNBC's No.

events.title: The AI behind Formula One race-day decisions
events.summary: Sunday, May 3, 2026, Miami International Autodrome, Miami Joseph “Joey” McMillan has been watching the numbers, and the skies above. With the start of the Miami Grand Prix just a few moments away, the Lead Race Strategist for the Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS F1 Team sits at his console, perched on the pit wall above the start line, listening to multiple different intercom channels at the same time, checking the weather reports and thinking about the race ahead. The team’s drivers have performed well over the race weekend, both in practice and in qualifying. British driver George Russell is starting fifth on the grid but, ahead of him, Kimi Antonelli is in pole position. The Italian teenager has been the breakout star of the season so far and is aiming to win his third Grand Prix in a row. At 19, Antonelli would be the youngest driver ever to achieve that feat. Antonelli and Russell are just two of Mercedes’ vast F1 team, around 1,300-strong, mainly engineers dedicated to making their cars go faster. But McMillan isn’t an engineer. His job is not about squeezing an extra ounce of speed from the engine, but saving time by executing a plan of action on the track, analyzing the variables his drivers can’t see and can’t control. “The strategist is sort of the black sheep in the sense that we are not really focused on making the car [go] faster,” explains McMillan. “Our job is to try and navigate those two cars through the race weekend. And to do that, we’re often looking at a lot more than just our car. We’re focused on every car on the grid, what every team is doing.” Like all sports, F1 is obsessed with marginal gains and McMillan’s mission is to find an edge on rival teams, making decisions based on multiple streams of data and running multiple simulations. In a sport where a thousandth of a second can be the difference between winning and losing, every factor needs to be considered. “By far the most important thing we do is decide what tire compounds to use in the race and what laps to make pit stops on,” he says. “That combination is known as the strategy.” There are five types of tires to choose from during a race, all color coded for different conditions: three types of slicks for dry conditions (soft, medium and hard), and two treaded tires (intermediates for light showers and wet tires for heavy rain). “If we knew the degradation rate of each of those compounds, essentially how much slower they get each lap in milliseconds, strategy would be so easy.” But things are rarely easy in F1. As well as monitoring the pace of rival cars and trying to judge how the tarmac will affect the tires, the strategy team’s simulations also need to know the answer to the question dominating McMillan’s thoughts as he sits at his trackside console. Is it going to rain? And in Miami, a storm is coming. The race is taking place at the start of May, six weeks before Florida’s Atlantic hurricane season usually begins, but the bad weather is ahead of schedule. The threat of lightning strikes is so severe that the organizers have brought the start of the race forward by three hours. Rain briefly fell in the morning, and McMillan is being fed local weather radar data that suggests rain might fall again during the race. Will it be a passing shower? Or a deluge? A decision has to be made about which tires to start on: the faster slicks, the intermediates or the wet tires. That choice could win or lose the race before it even starts. McMillan and the team make a play based on the data at hand and their instincts. The drivers will not start on wet tires, they will be on slicks and hope the weather holds. As the lights go out and the race begins, the drivers roar toward the first corner on a dry track under skies pregnant with rain. And then all hell breaks loose. “When we run our simulations, we run an entire race. We want to run thousands, if not millions of these races. Now, with Azure Batch, we can” McMillan has been a race strategist for a decade. The softly spoken Englishman was hired by the Mercedes F1 Team after finishing his mathematics PhD at Imperial College London. It was his first job after college and he’s been there ever since, moving up to Senior Race Strategist and, eventually, Lead Race Strategist. “We use about five or six strategists a weekend,” he says. “Out of those, maybe one or two of them will ever end up being the pit wall strategist who’s making the final decision, but you need a whole lot of people running models.” Mathematics is only part of the job. What separates a good strategist from a great one is the ability to function under pressure. “It’s not super difficult in the sense that I don’t need high-level mathematics, nothing like the mathematics I was doing for my PhD,” says McMillan. “What makes a good general strategist? Someone who is a logical thinker, really good at modeling and data analysis. But what really makes you good at the pit job is to be able to make the decision in the moment, to do it very, very quickly, with very good communication skills… when you’ve got drivers, team principals, race engineers, lots of excitement and intensity. Once you realize you can do that, I think it’s pretty clear you’re going to be good at this.” Machine learning, as McMillan calls it, has always been a huge part of his job – but in recent years, AI technology has greatly improved his ability to analyze more and more data at faster speeds. “My day-to-day, the actual Sunday doing the strategy, hasn’t changed a huge amount yet,” he says. So, what has changed? “I write quite a lot of code, but I’m really not a coder. I’m a mathematician, a statistician, a game theorist, but I’m not a coder. I understand what data we’ve got. I understand what I’d like to do with it. And [with] the advent of AI, like coding tools, I can do those things a huge amount quicker. I can now write models, write analysis, do things at a speed I could never dream of before.” At the start of 2026, Microsoft signed a deal with the Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS F1 Team, a partnership that put Microsoft technology at the heart of its operation. After dominating Formula One for much of the 2010s, winning seven consecutive drivers’ championships between 2014 and 2020 and eight consecutive constructors’ championships between 2014 and 2021, the team was looking to build on that legacy. With a radically reengineered car performing strongly in testing, there was growing belief that 2026 could see the Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS F1 Team challenge for championships once again. For the F1 strategy team, one of the biggest benefits of working with Microsoft is access to Azure’s vast cloud computing capacity. Using Azure Batch, they can run huge numbers of race simulations simultaneously, testing multiple scenarios before, and even during, a Grand Prix.

events.title: Celebrating the next generation of Latin American game creators
events.summary: Multiple Adventures Await as Stories: The Path of Destinies Arrives on Xbox One Free Play Days – NBA 2K27, Crusader Kings III, The Alters, Bus Simulator 21, Soccer Story and Ravenswatch Upcoming Changes to XBOX Cloud Gaming Coming to XBOX Game Pass: Battlefield 6, Valor Mortis, Forever Ago, and More Learn how XBOX is helping creators across Latin America bring new ideas to life through the ID@XBOX Developer Acceleration Program, the inaugural XBOX Game Camp Mexico City, and six upcoming titles from the region. Across Latin America, developers are creating some of gaming’s most distinctive new worlds by turning personal memories, local history, cultural traditions, and bold ideas into experiences that resonate far beyond the region. Games such as Despelote , Mexico, 1921: A Deep Slumber , and SOPA – Tale of the Stolen Potato show the remarkable breadth of this creative community, from intimate coming-of-age stories and interactive journeys through history to magical adventures filled with heart. For years, XBOX has worked alongside creators across Latin America, helping studios of all sizes bring their games to players around the world. Through the ID@XBOX Developer Acceleration Program (DAP), we’ve worked with more than 60 studios from Mexico, Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Peru, Honduras, Uruguay, and beyond, helping developers bring over 30 culturally distinctive games to XBOX since 2023, while strengthening the region’s growing game development ecosystem by providing access to technical resources, business support, and mentorship. XBOX Game Camp Heads to Mexico City As XBOX continues to support game creators across Latin America, XBOX Game Camp is expanding its reach with a Mexico City debut on October 17 alongside Xbox FanFest. Taking place during Xbox’s 25th anniversary year, the event will celebrate Mexico’s game development community and the extraordinary talent already shaping games across the region, while creating new opportunities for developers to learn, connect, and grow. XBOX Game Camp Mexico will bring together a select group of Mexican studios, including developers both within and beyond the existing XBOX ecosystem, for a day focused on industry knowledge, community, and connection. The program will feature advanced developer seminars, keynotes and fireside conversations with industry leaders, along with opportunities to connect directly with industry professionals and members of Team XBOX, including Jens Bergensten, Chief Creative Officer at Mojang Studios. His fireside conversation with Peter Zetterberg, Founder of XBOX Game Camp, will explore his career journey and lessons from Sweden’s game development ecosystem, with a focus on collaboration, supporting fellow creators, and the role community can play in building a stronger industry. With a passionate development community and a strong culture of collaboration, Mexico City provides an ideal setting for XBOX Game Camp to celebrate locally developed games, strengthen connections across the ecosystem, and create new pathways for Mexican creators to bring their ideas to audiences around the world. As we support the next generation of creators through initiatives like XBOX Game Camp, we’re also celebrating the developers shaping Latin America’s game development community today. Here’s a look at six upcoming games from Latin American creators to keep on your radar. Six Upcoming Games from Latin America to Watch Mariachi Legends — Halberd Studios, Mexico Studio Contact: Miguel Hasson, Creative Director Studio location: Guadalajara, Jalisco, Mexico Mariachi Legends is a brutal, combat-oriented Metroidvania wrapped in gorgeous pixel art and set in the heart of Mexico. Players step into the shoes of Pablo Cruz, a Mexican detective who strikes a deal with Death herself. Granted the ability to transform into the supernatural entity “La Sombra,” Pablo must battle an evil syndicate known as the Mariachi Legends. It’s a journey that blends intense hack-and-slash action with RPG mechanics, all unfolding around the Day of the Dead festivities. What truly separates Mariachi Legends is our deep, authentic integration of Mexican culture and folklore directly into the gameplay loop. Beyond standard combat and exploration we’ve also introduced a unique culinary mechanic: players explore the world to collect ingredients and cook traditional Mexican dishes to gain strength. Coupled with a Day/Night cycle driven by Sun and Moon gates, where different map sections are accessible depending on the time of day, the game offers a distinct flavor you won’t find in other Metroidvanias. How has DAP supported development of your title? ID@XBOX has been instrumental in helping us bring our vision to life without compromising on quality or cultural authenticity. The program provided us with the resources and technical support needed to ensure Mariachi Legends runs flawlessly on XBOX Series X|S, utilize features like XBOX Play Anywhere. The marketing amplification and the opportunity to bring the game to a massive audience via XBOX Game Pass has given our studio the runway to focus fully on creating a polished experience. What do you hope players take away from your game? We hope players walk away with a profound appreciation for the richness of Mexican traditions. We want them to experience the thrill of a tight, challenging Metroidvania, but more importantly, we want the world, the food, the music, and the folklore of Mexico to resonate with them long after they put the controller down. Studio Location: Villa Alemana, Valparaíso, Chile In Colorbound , color is more than just a hue. Join Anku on a heartwarming journey, using color to shape the world around you. In this puzzle-platforming adventure, you will solve challenging puzzles, uncover secrets, and help a family of musicians reunite, just like in the old days, for a farewell concert. Colorbound stands out primarily for its aesthetics and core mechanics. The ability to change the colors of the environment creates an experience that draws attention through its very concept. Furthermore, the narrative, music, and art reflect the Andean culture of Latin America, successfully connecting with the region and showcasing a culture unknown to many. Primarily by providing some of the funding for the project’s production and post-production, which allowed for a faster development process and more comprehensive publishing work. On one hand, I hope that during the process you are surprised by the different mechanics associated with the colors and enjoy solving the game’s challenging puzzles. But above all, I hope you take away a fond memory of a simple, touching experience about friendship and grief. events.title: Nvidia's communications team has undergone a shake-up as its public profile exploded
events.summary: Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia. Bloomberg/Getty Images Nvidia's communications operation has been reshaped as the company became the face of the AI boom. Roughly 15 staffers have left the lean team since 2025 as Nvidia reorganized its communications org. Former employees described growing workloads as responsibilities expanded. Nvidia's communications organization has been reshaped as the company became the face of the AI boom, with multiple teams brought under new leadership and a string of departures. Business Insider identified roughly 15 communications employees who have left Nvidia since 2025, based on LinkedIn profiles and interviews with former employees. The organization now numbers roughly 70 to 80 people globally, and has more than doubled in size since Mylene Mangalindan joined as vice president of corporate communications in 2023, according to a person close to the company. The departures have also included newer hires. Anna Soellner , who was recruited to lead corporate communications, left after roughly four months, Business Insider previously reported. Nvidia is known for high retention. It reported companywide turnover of 3.7% in fiscal 2026, up from 2.5% the prior year, and well below the tech industry average of 21.9% cited in its latest sustainability report . Mangalindan succeeded longtime communications chief Bob Sherbin, who retired in 2024. She previously worked at the advisory firm Brunswick Group. She was brought in to "bring fresh blood" and "upgrade the team" to meet Nvidia's growing profile, one former employee said. At the end of 2024, Nvidia restructured its communications organization. It brought enterprise public relations under Mangalindan's leadership alongside the corporate communications team she already led, according to two former employees. Corporate communications focuses on Nvidia's reputation and major media outlets, while enterprise handles product and industry messaging, including for its data center business . One former employee said the consolidation reflected the growing importance of Nvidia's data center business, which sells chips and systems that power AI and had become its biggest revenue driver. Analyst relations, social media, and influencer marketing also moved under Mangalindan's remit this year, another former employee said. Three former employees said Nvidia's communications team had long operated with relatively lean staffing, even as workloads grew alongside the company's public profile, leaving staff juggling multiple responsibilities. These employees said they experienced long hours, difficulty taking time off, and pressure to respond quickly to emails and Slack messages. A person close to Nvidia said the company's lean staffing allows employees to move quickly and also requires long hours. The person said Mangalindan encourages staff to take vacation, though the team's small size can make scheduling time off difficult, particularly in the summer. Nvidia is widely known for its demanding work environment. CEO Jensen Huang has emphasized operating at the "speed of light" and is known for fostering a culture of constant accountability. events.title: Kenya records third Ebola case, linked to first patient who died
events.summary: Nairobi says 65-year-old female patient in quarantine with Bundibugyo strain; no signs of community transmission. Kenya has recorded its third case of the Bundibugyo virus disease – a strain of Ebola that has killed thousands of people in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) – 10 days after reporting its first case and death in Nairobi. The latest confirmed case – a 65-year-old woman – was a “primary contact and a close relative of the first and second cases”, Kenya’s Health Ministry said in a statement on Friday, adding that the patient has been in quarantine since October 6. list 1 of 3 Why single Ebola death in Kenya has prompted fears of wider African spread list 2 of 3 Kenyan patient suspected of Ebola infection tests negative list 3 of 3 Ebola spreads in eastern DRC as Kenya confirms imported case After developing symptoms, she was isolated and then tested positive for the virus, it added in a statement. “Once she developed fever, sore throat and malaise, she was isolated and specimen collected for testing. She tested positive for Ebola,” the Health Ministry said. “She was diagnosed early and is currently receiving ⁠⁠supportive care improving her ⁠⁠chances of recovery.” Kenya’s cases are linked to the Ebola epidemic in the DRC, which is the second-largest on record globally ⁠ ⁠with more than 9,000 cases and over 4,300 deaths since it was officially detected in May. Kenya’s ⁠⁠first case emerged last ⁠⁠week after a Kenyan man, who had been ill in the DRC about a month before travelling by road ‌‌to Uganda, flew to Nairobi on October 3, where a relative drove him to ‌‌the ‌‌hospital. He died on October 5. In its statement on X, the Health Ministry moved to reassure the public that there was no community spread of the disease and that the risk to the Kenyan public remained low. Out of 130 contacts listed, 127 had been traced and were in quarantine, it said. Efforts to control the spread of the Ebola outbreak have been complicated because the Bundibugyo strain has no licensed vaccine. Research is under way to develop one or more vaccines that work against the strain and some of these vaccines are already in the early phases of testing in humans. Transparency demands over Ebola response funds The new case in Kenya was reported as Africa’s ‌‌top public health body and Congolese health authorities called ⁠⁠for greater transparency in how Ebola response funds are used. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) said financial information provided by aid organisations indicated that ⁠⁠more than $700m of donor money was unaccounted for. Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of ‌‌the Africa CDC, told the Reuters news agency that international donors disbursed about $962m to organisations ⁠⁠implementing Ebola response activities in DRC, rather ⁠⁠than to the government. Kaseya said those organisations reported receiving $228m, of which $127m had ⁠⁠been spent and roughly $100m remained available. But he said it was too early to speak of embezzlement. In a post on X, Congolese Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba warned aid groups were required to provide details on funding ‌‌sources to his ministry or risk being barred from working ‌‌in ‌‌DRC and blacklisted across Africa. Meanwhile, on the ground in the DRC, Ebola cases have been detected in a new province bordering the Central African Republic, two health officials told Reuters on Thursday. The two cases were confirmed in North Ubangi, the eighth Congolese province affected by the Bundibugyo outbreak, the officials said. Congolese authorities have not yet officially announced the outbreak has spread to North Ubangi.
