events.title: Trump: White House didn't impede satellite system in Ukraine
events.summary: President Trump said Friday that his administration did not disrupt an Elon Musk -owned satellite system used by Ukraine to wage war against Russia. Why it matters: The restrictions imposed earlier this week on the system hampered the Ukrainian military's ability to intercept Russian attack drones for 24 hours. It raised concerns that the Trump administration and possibly Musk were retaliating against Ukraine for its attacks on Russian oil refineries and President Volodymyr Zelensky's criticism of Trump's diesel deal with Russia. What he is saying: "I just checked this morning — it wasn't us," Trump told reporters. "I don't know if it was anybody, because it wasn't me and I don't think it was Elon." He was responding to a question about a Reuters report that the order to slow the satellite system came from the White House. Trump said that from what he was briefed the system is currently fully working with no restrictions. do we need this? no one is saying otherwise The other side: Ukrainian officials remain highly skeptical of Trump's claims and believe someone in the U.S. government participated in throttling the systems. "Our guys who speak to SpaceX say the White House was involved in the decision," a Ukrainian official said. Catch up quick: The Ukrainian military uses SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications system to control and operate its reconnaissance and intercept drones. When Starlink doesn't operate at full capacity, Ukraine's ability to gather intelligence, use interceptor drones and conduct long-range strikes against Russia is impeded. Ukraine relies on two satellite systems: One is SpaceX's Starlink, which it uses for communications, ground forces, logistics and defensive drones — ones that shoot down incoming drones. The other is Starshield, which is controlled by the U.S. government and used for offensive military purposes. Both systems were restricted, according to Ukraine. In a post on X on Wednesday, Musk hinted the U.S. government was involved in disrupting Starshield. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote. The big picture: The limitations came days after a new crisis erupted between the U.S. and Ukraine over Trump's agreement to lift sanctions on Russian oil sales. Zelensky criticized the move, then Trump called for Ukraine to elect a new president.

events.title: Katie Zacharia is out as White House press secretary. Meet the 6 Trump has had over both his terms.
events.summary: The three most recent White House press secretaries, from left to right: Kayleigh McEnany, Karoline Leavitt, and Katie Zacharia. Alex Wong/Getty Images ; Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images ; Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images President Donald Trump has had six White House press secretaries across his two presidential terms. Sean Spicer, Stephanie Grisham, and Kayleigh McEnany held the role for less than a year. Katie Zacharia succeeded Karoline Leavitt, but is "transitioning out" after five days on the job. The new face at the White House podium didn't last long. Katie Zacharia held her first briefing as the new White House press secretary on Tuesday after President Donald Trump chose her to succeed Karoline Leavitt , who left the White House in August to spend more time with her young children. By Friday, a White House official confirmed to Business Insider that she is "transitioning out" of the role . Zacharia was the sixth White House press secretary Trump has hired across his two non-consecutive presidential terms , and the fourth to serve for less than a year. It's not unusual for presidents to go through several press secretaries due to the demanding nature of the role. President Barack Obama had three press secretaries during his two terms in office. Former presidents Bill Clinton and George W. Bush had four. Here's a look at all of the White House press secretaries who have represented the Trump administration. Sean Spicer WASHINGTON, DC - APRIL 24: White House Press Secretary Sean Spicer talks to reporters during the daily press briefing at the White House April 24, 2017 in Washington, DC. Spicer was joined during the briefing by U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley and Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images) Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images Sean Spicer's time as White House press secretary spanned 182 days — the shortest tenure of all of Trump's press secretaries. After leaving the White House, he appeared on season 28 of "Dancing with the Stars." He now serves as a political contributor at NewsNation and hosts several podcasts, including "Full Court Press with Sean Spicer" and "The Sean Spicer Show." Sarah Huckabee Sanders White House Press Secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders speaks during a press briefing at the White House in Washington, DC, March 11, 2019. (Photo by SAUL LOEB / AFP) (Photo by SAUL LOEB/AFP via Getty Images) SAUL LOEB/AFP via Getty Images During Trump's first term, Sanders served as White House press secretary for just under two years, from July 2017 to July 2019. In the final months of her tenure, Sanders largely stopped holding formal White House press briefings. Sanders is the daughter of former Arkansas Gov. Mike Huckabee , who now serves as the US ambassador to Israel in the second Trump administration. After her time as press secretary, Sanders was elected governor of Arkansas in 2022. She is running for reelection in the 2026 midterms. Stephanie Grisham White House Press Secretary Stephanie Grisham listens as US President Donald Trump speaks to the media aboard Air Force One while flying between El Paso, Texas and Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, August 7, 2019. (Photo by SAUL LOEB / AFP) (Photo credit should read SAUL LOEB/AFP via Getty Images) credit should read SAUL LOEB/AFP via Getty Images Grisham served as White House press secretary for less than a year, from July 2019 to April 2020. Throughout her tenure, she did not hold a traditional press briefing. Grisham went on to become Melania Trump's White House chief of staff, then resigned from the role following the January 6, 2021 insurrection. She has since become a vocal critic of Trump and spoke about her time working in the Trump administration at the 2024 Democratic National Convention . Kayleigh McEnany WASHINGTON, DC - OCTOBER 1: White House press secretary Kayleigh McEnany, speaks during a press briefing in the Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House, on Thursday, October 1, 2020, in Washington, DC. (Photo by Oliver Contreras/For The Washington Post via Getty Images) Oliver Contreras/For The Washington Post via Getty Images McEnany served as Trump's 2020 campaign press secretary before Trump chose her to replace Grisham as White House press secretary. She held the role for less than a year, from April 2020 until Trump left office in January 2021. McEnany resumed formal White House press briefings after Grisham's tenure. McEnany now hosts "Saturday in America with Kayleigh McEnany" on Fox News, and co-hosts another Fox News show, "Outnumbered." Karoline Leavitt White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt speaks during a press briefing at the White House in Washington, D.C., the United States, on Jan. 15, 2026. U.S. President Donald Trump is keeping all options on the table for responding to Iran's unrest, White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said Thursday. (Photo by Li Yuanqing/Xinhua via Getty Images) Li Yuanqing/Xinhua via Getty Images Leavitt served as White House press secretary from January 2025 to August 2026. At 27 years old, when she started the role, she was the youngest person ever to hold the position. Leavitt established a "new media seat" in the White House briefing room, highlighting podcasters, independent journalists, social media influencers, and other non-legacy media sources. She was also the first-ever pregnant White House press secretary , and gave birth to her second child while in the role. Leavitt resigned shortly after returning from parental leave, citing her desire to spend more time with her family. She will begin working as an on-air contributor for Fox News starting November 1. Katie Zacharia UNITED STATES - OCTOBER 13: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia conducts her first briefing where she addressed issues including the resignation of Kimberly Guilfoyle, U.S. ambassador to Greece, on Tuesday, October 13, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images) Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images Trump named Zacharia as Leavitt's successor, writing in a Truth Social post on October 9 that Zacharia "has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning," and calling her "a devoted fan and member of MAGA." Zacharia previously worked as a senior communications advisor at Trump Media and Technology Group, which runs Truth Social. She held her first briefing on Tuesday, but after a rocky five days as White House press secretary — during which Zacharia's briefing performance and legal qualifications were widely criticized — a White House official told Business Insider on Friday that she was leaving the role. events.title: HALF A MOOCH: Katie Zacharia is out after 5 days as White House press secretary
events.summary: Katie Zacharia. Jim WATSON / AFP via Getty Images President Donald Trump said he told Katie Zacharia to reconsider the White House press secretary job. Shortly after, a White House official said she is "transitioning out" of the role. She lasted five days in the role after mounting scrutiny over her legal credentials. Embattled White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is out of the job after just five days, making her the shortest-tenured person to hold the role in history. President Donald Trump said on Friday that he told Zacharia to reconsider taking on the high-profile job. Shortly after his statements, The New York Times and CNN reported that Zacharia had been fired after less than a week in the role. A White House official told Business Insider that she is "transitioning out" of the role. "I said to Katie just two minutes ago, I said, 'Katie, you know, you don't have to do this if you don't want,'" Trump told reporters at the White House, adding that Zacharia responded that the job is "a lot tougher" than she thought. "I said to her, 'Honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider. You think about it, but I would reconsider,'" Trump said. A conservative commentator who has repeatedly described herself as a lawyer , Zacharia made her White House press briefing debut on Tuesday and quickly came under intense scrutiny over her legal credentials. She was widely panned after the roughly 14-minute briefing, most of which was spent on reading from prepared remarks. After the briefing, while alongside Trump, Zacharia was asked which state she passed the bar exam in and replied, "When I moved to China," raising eyebrows. National headlines soon followed reports that Zacharia had not been licensed to practice law in any US jurisdiction. On Thursday, Zacharia said she took the bar exam but failed, and never retook it. Trump told reporters on Friday that Zacharia had been treated "very badly" and "very unfairly" by the media. "She's been treated very rough, and she's a nice person, very nice person," the president said. "I've watched her for years on television, but I said, 'Is this for you, Katie? Because, honestly, you don't need this.'" "She's been treated, I would say, very nastily," he said. A rocky start Following her first briefing, CNN reported that "several White House officials" were questioning how long she could remain in the role. The news of Zacharia's ouster means Trump will be searching for a top spokesperson again after Karoline Leavitt left the role in August. Previously, Jonathan Daniels held the record for shortest tenure. Daniels served as White House press secretary for just 19 days before President Franklin D. Roosevelt died in office. (He briefly served in an interim capacity for President Harry Truman.) In the modern era, press secretaries have historically served roughly a year in the role, a fact that CNN noted when Trump's first-ever White House press secretary, Sean Spicer , departed after 182 days in August 2017. During the first Trump administration, Anthony Scaramucci famously spent just 11 days as the White House communications director before he was booted from the position. Scaramucci, known as "The Mooch," weighed in on Zacharia's departure in an X post , writing, "Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people's pain." Before becoming press secretary, Zacharia worked for Trump Media, the parent company of Truth Social, and served a brief stint at the Department of Homeland Security. Compared to her predecessors, her résumé was void of the campaign and Capitol Hill experience that previous White House press secretaries brought to the challenging role. events.title: AOC and El-Sayed test-drive a national platform for the left
events.summary: The News ESCANABA, Mich. — Abdul El-Sayed and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez are already thinking beyond 2026, even though he’s not a senator yet. During three different stops Thursday on his Senate campaign’s bus tour through redder, rural areas of this swing state, El-Sayed and Ocasio-Cortez drew crowds that showed notable star power. While Republicans see Michigan as their strongest chance to pick up a Senate seat, the progressive pair are casting themselves as heirs to the broader movement that Bernie Sanders has commanded for a decade — a push they plan to expand beyond this state. “Once you elect one person like that, people will then catch on,” Ocasio-Cortez declared of El-Sayed in this paper-producing town, whose county last went Democratic in 2008. “And we will start electing more people like that.” In a region walloped by the sort of deindustrialization that President Donald Trump had returned to office pledging to reverse, El-Sayed drew loud applause for vowing to move beyond him: “Donald Trump is just the worst symptom of the disease of our politics — the disease of the system of allowing billionaires, corporations, special interest, the bought and sold politicians, the way that the money brings the system against us.” While Ocasio-Cortez has yet to make her decision on a 2028 presidential primary that she’d enter as an automatic contender, her Michigan tour amounted to calling her shot. She’s betting on El-Sayed as proof of concept for her brand of populism, embracing his play for the left in a tight Senate race even as the strategy sparks internal Democratic worries about a possible drift of Black and Jewish voters towards Republicans. If he defeats GOP nominee Mike Rogers in a remarkably anti-Trump cycle to become the first Muslim senator in US history, El-Sayed could spark his own presidential boomlet. But for the moment, in a state that’s now among the Democratic nominating calendar’s earliest to vote, his campaign served as a vehicle for Ocasio-Cortez to spell out more ambitious policy than a single candidate’s platform. When one attendee in Escanaba asked the duo about eliminating interest on student loans. El-Sayed said “you shouldn’t have to go into debt to get a higher education” and that Democrats should find creative ways around the Supreme Court’s rejection of a Biden-era student loan forgiveness program. Then Ocasio-Cortez went a step further, saying that student loans should be interest-free, public colleges should be tuition-free, and “we have to really be asking ourselves what is the utility of putting people in indentured servitude their entire lives for seeking an education.” The crowd cheered. (At another point, the New Yorker laughed off cries from supporters asking her to run for president.) Know More Although Democrats have often fallen short in this part of Michigan come November, it’s been favorable territory for progressives during primaries. In this year’s Senate primary, El-Sayed carried the three counties where he held events Thursday, as did Sanders during the Vermont independent’s 2016 Democratic presidential bid. “I just want to have a conversation about gas, groceries, the ability to see a doctor. Want money out of politics, money in your pocket, Medicare for all?” El-Sayed told reporters. “I think that’s what Yoopers want, too.” He knocked Rogers, who generally avoids the large gatherings favored by the El-Sayed campaign, for not appearing in the Upper Peninsula this fall. “So when’s the last time he was in Iron Mountain? When’s the last time he was in Escanaba? When’s the last time he was in Marquette? I don’t know. At least I show up,” said El-Sayed. A Rogers spokesperson pointed to previous stops by his campaign in the Upper Peninsula towns over the last year, including in Marquette in June. “AOC is the latest trick up the Democrats’ sleeve, but Michiganders know better than to fall for it,” said the Rogers spokesperson. “While Abdul El-Sayed tries to run from his own progressive policies, AOC’s visit reminds voters exactly who he is — a radical leftist who wants to defund the police, force EV mandates on Michiganders, and jack up our utility prices even higher.” Rogers is keeping the race close in most polls, while undeniably benefiting from the tension that has persisted among Michigan Democrats after El-Sayed’s acrimonious primary against Rep. Haley Stevens. Among the Democratic nominee’s detractors are a sitting congresswoman, Rep. Hillary Scholten, D-Mich., who has withheld her support for him. Stevens’ likely House successor, state Sen. Jeremy Moss, has also held back on endorsing El-Sayed after entertaining early talks on the topic, as Semafor first reported. Moss isn’t the only Jewish Democrat who remains skeptical of El-Sayed’s harsh criticism of Israel and, as a result, hasn’t backed him. Stevens, in an interview, acknowledged “some shifting dynamics” among Democrats. “Republicans have not held a Senate seat in Michigan for 32 years, and it’s hard to believe that this would really be the year that they’d be able to make a comeback,” she said. “But they’re sure as heck trying.” She also hinted she was focused more on campaigning for House candidates and other Democrats in Michigan than on the Senate race; she’s holding a political event this weekend with House candidate Christina Hines to showcase outreach to Black voters. “I want to see Hakeem Jeffries become the speaker of the House [on the strength of] a place called Michigan,” she said. The View From Voters Attendees at El-Sayed and Ocasio-Cortez’s stop at Northern Michigan University in Marquette contextualized their own excitement around a broader concern that Michigan voters outside the room would view the two as too far left. “Most of my friends would think AOC is too liberal,” said Phil DeGabriele, a 70-year-old retiree from Negaunee. Younger voters were more easily energized by the progressives. Arthur Pichette, a 20-year-old junior at Northern Michigan University, said El-Sayed was “like a breath of fresh air” and that it was “nice” to have El-Sayed and Ocasio-Cortez plainly laying out their views. Nicholas’s view It’s striking to see how boldly El-Sayed and Ocasio-Cortez are already trying to build out a progressive coalition — before he learns whether he needs the fraying parts of the existing Democratic base to beat Rogers. But one thing we’ve known about El-Sayed since the start of his primary race: He’s confident. Talking up a seven-point win isn’t something I see a lot of swing-state candidates do. So if El-Sayed wins, he should be ready for an immediate question about who he plans to wield his new influence for in 2028. It could be his ally Ocasio-Cortez; it could be himself . Notable Bridge Detroit reported on El-Sayed’s potential weakness with Black voters in Detroit. MS NOW covered Rogers’ delicate dance around Trump on the trade war. Ocasio-Cortez’s campaign just transferred $1 million to an effort to elect El-Sayed, The New York Times reported

events.title: Katie Zacharia is 'transitioning out' as Trump’s White House press secretary. Here's what to know about her life and career.
events.summary: Katie Zacharia held her first press briefing at the White House on Tuesday. Kevin Lamarque/Reuters President Donald Trump chose Katie Zacharia to serve as the new White House press secretary. Five days later, a White House official said that she is "transitioning out" of the role. She succeeded Karoline Leavitt, who left the job in August. Katie Zacharia held her first briefing as White House press secretary on Tuesday, taking over the role previously held by Karoline Leavitt. Days later, a White House official confirmed to Business Insider that she is " transitioning out" of the role after Trump said that he told her to reconsider. Zacharia was the second press secretary to serve in Trump's second term, and the sixth across his two non-consecutive terms. Leavitt left the job in August to spend more time with her young children. In a Truth Social post announcing his hiring of Zacharia, President Donald Trump wrote that "She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning," adding that "She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA!" Zacharia did not respond to requests for comment from Business Insider on Friday, after her departure was announced. Here's what to know about her. What was Katie Zacharia doing before this? Katie Zacharia on the South Lawn of the White House. Brendan SMIALOWSKI / AFP via Getty Images Zacharia previously worked as a senior communications advisor at Trump Media and Technology Group, which runs Truth Social, a White House official confirmed to Business Insider. Zacharia previously worked as a spokesperson for former Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem at the Department of Homeland Security, and as a commentator for Fox News and Newsmax. Her LinkedIn profile also indicates that she serves as general counsel for the conservative nonprofit Fix California, and served as a White House intern in 2006, during President George W. Bush's second term. Is Katie Zacharia a lawyer? Zacharia earned a bachelor's degree in political science and government from Pepperdine University and a law degree from Pepperdine Caruso School of Law. She has described herself as a lawyer , but she confirmed to Fox News' Sean Hannity on Thursday that she sat for the California bar exam but did not pass it or retake it. "I had already preregistered for the bar exam," she said. "Basically, during the summer, I knew I would be living in China and the results of the bar were inconsequential, and I sat for it because I didn't want to have a withdrawal status." Zacharia's LinkedIn profile lists her as working as an associate at the Beijing law firm Zhong Lun from August 2011 to June 2013. Zacharia added that she "consulted attorneys and legal professionals" to confirm that she could call herself a lawyer and offer legal analysis on cable news since she holds a law degree and had "actual substantive legal experience." Zacharia told Business Insider in a statement that she "practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials." The White House referred Business Insider to Zacharia's comments on Fox News. Who is Katie Zacharia's husband? Tyler Zacharia and Katie Zacharia at the premiere of "David." Tibrina Hobson/Getty Images Zacharia is married to film producer Tyler Zacharia, who has produced movies such as "Young Washington" and "David" with Angel Studios, a production company specializing in faith-based films. He also served as an executive producer of the 2019 movie "The Irishman" starring Robert De Niro and Al Pacino, according to his IMDb page . They wed in 2011. Does Katie Zacharia have children? Zacharia and her husband share four children, ages 12, 10, 8, and 6. At her first press briefing, when Zacharia was asked about balancing work and motherhood , she said her family was planning to move from California to Washington, DC, so she could be present with them while working in the White House. She also called Trump "the most family-friendly president we've ever had." "The fact that he knew I had four kids, and he knew that this job would be demanding, and still placed his trust in me, shows that I know I'm capable of being able to step up to that," she said. This is a developing story. Please check back for updates. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Ethiopia sets up Tigray caretaker government as ex-fighters seek return to civilian life
events.summary: Ethiopia's government has set up a six-month caretaker administration for Tigray following renewed fighting in the region NAIROBI, Kenya -- Ethiopia's government set up a six-month caretaker administration for Tigray following renewed fighting in the region, as hundreds of former combatants registered Friday for a program to help them return to civilian life. The new administration is expected to restore public services, help displaced people return and prepare for an election within six months under federal oversight, according to the office of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed . The announcement follows the withdrawal of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front rebel group, or TPLF, from Mekelle and the entry of government-allied fighters into the regional capital on Oct. 4. Renewed fighting in the northern region in recent weeks has effectively shattered a 2022 peace agreement that ended a devastating two-year war. Ethiopia also has accused Eritrean troops of occupying parts of its territory, while Eritrea condemned Ethiopia for what it called a declaration of war. At Mekelle’s Tigray Martyrs’ Memorial Monument, former fighters lined up to register with the authorities, some carrying papers or sheltering under umbrellas. Registration began Wednesday. Authorities declined to say how many former fighters had signed up. “We were called upon by the TPLF to rejoin our former comrades and units, and doing so was even considered mandatory,” said Filmon Gebreselassie, a 33-year-old day laborer. “However, I did not want to return (to war). I decided instead to focus on raising my children.” He said that he had disarmed after the 2022 peace agreement in Tigray, but had been unable to register before the reintegration program was suspended as new tensions rose. Other former fighters were also signing up because they didn't want to fight again, he said. Many young men at the registration office declined interviews, citing fear of retaliation from the TPLF. In an Oct. 14 statement on its official Facebook page, the TPLF denounced Tigrayans collaborating with the federal government as “traitors” and said they would face “accountability and public judgment.” Human Rights Watch reported in June that Tigrayan authorities then in charge of Mekelle had ordered former fighters back to their units in a compulsory recruitment campaign. A TPLF spokesperson said those defending the region were volunteers, according to the watchdog. Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Fort Hood survivors speak out on Pentagon's decision to livestream Hasan's execution Atlanta school worker dies after falling from Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia The disarmament, demobilization and reintegration of former Tigrayan fighters is part of the 2022 peace agreement. Abiy’s office accused the TPLF of obstructing the agreement and said that the latest fighting ended in its defeat. The rebels urged their forces to continue fighting and called on Tigrayans to support them. Magnus Taylor, deputy Horn of Africa director at the International Crisis Group, cautioned against equating the loss of towns with an end to fighting. “We shouldn’t imagine that this conflict is completely over just because the TPLF has lost Mekelle,” he told The Associated Press on Wednesday. Capturing towns and roads would hamper Tigrayan fighters without necessarily securing the vast rural areas where the rebel forces regrouped during the previous war, Taylor said. Ethiopia also has accused Eritrean troops of occupying its territory, an allegation that the AP couldn't independently verify. Eritrea described Ethiopia’s assertion that it was taking self-defense measures as a declaration of war. Taylor warned that the proximity of the countries’ forces increased the risk of a wider conflict. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged de-escalation in a call with Abiy on Wednesday, according to the U.S. State Department. Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopian forces during the 2020-2022 war, which caused about 500,000 civilian deaths through violence, famine and collapsed health services, according to researchers at Ghent University in Belgium. Amir Aman Kiyaro in Hamburg, Germany, Filmon Equar Hailu in Mekelle, Ethiopia, and Desmond Tiro in Nairobi, Kenya, contributed to this report. events.title: The Austin Powers steamroller: How to trade CoreWeave's slow moving crisis
events.summary: In Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery , a Virtuocon guard famously stands in front of a commandeered steamroller, screaming "No!!" three times before being run over. The joke, of course, is that the hazard moved so slowly he had ample time to step out of the way. For months, equity traders holding CoreWeave (CRWV) have played that guard. Despite credit markets flashing warnings, equity holders essentially just stood there. Now, after a shocking 27.5% drop from last Friday's close to this Thursday morning's 52-week lows, followed by a whiplash 17% rebound, equity investors, if not squashed like Dr. Evil's henchman, are dazed and confused. Shares are down another 5% today. With earnings just a few weeks away, massive leverage, a heavily split sell-side, and 15.4% short interest, the stock remains primed for explosive volatility. The credit market slow moving steamroller The hazard approaching CRWV equity wasn't hidden. The AI cloud infrastructure platform essentially didn't exist five years ago and has accumulated $51.6 billion in debt (~$46 billion net of cash) against a backdrop of zero historical profitability. That was well known, but the CEO's comments that the company aspired to be investment grade so it could borrow "unlimited sums", even as investors already anticipated nearly another $60 billion in debt in the next 18months, spooked folks. (Trick or Treat!) Especially since the debt issued only in June had already fallen 20% since. From an options trader's point of view, it was hard to reconcile deteriorating credit and rising leverage with falling options premia; as recently as last week, they were in the 6th percentile, 1.5 standard deviations below the one-year mean. At 72%, options weren't cheap in absolute terms, but given everything going on, they should have been higher. The stock also looked somewhat complacent, with the equity chopping around historical support levels dating back to May 2025. The credit side was on tilt: Bond Swoon: Bonds issued at par just this past June at an 8.5% rate fell nearly 18% through last Friday, following a severe initial swoon in late July. CDS Spikes: 5-year Credit Default Swaps (CDS) exploded from 452 bps in early June to over 1100 bps this week, implying a roughly 60% probability of default within the next five years. Cash Flow Burn: The company faces an estimated $16.45 billion in negative free cash flow in the second half of this year alone, and another $30.6 billion in FY2027, according to Bloomberg Cost of Capital: With a 15% cost of capital, the structural hurdle rate for new business is staggering. Even with optimistic pricing power through 2028, forecast Debt/EBITDA at FYE2028 sits at 4.5x, which warrants caution, and only if the company hits all those ambitious numbers. Because CRWV is levered by more than 2:1, a 10% move in enterprise value translates to a nearly 22% swing in equity value. Despite the dire credit picture, equity sentiment remains fiercely divided, driving this week's 17% bounce from the lows. For example, HSBC maintains a Sell rating with a $39 price target, essentially calling for the stock to be cut in half. Conversely, banks like BNP and Cantor Fitzgerald (my former employer) suggest these fears are overblown and the stock should more than double from here. It's not just bankers defending the company either. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang downplayed systemic concerns, and ARK Investment stepped in to buy 192,000 shares. BofA argues that CRWV's ability to bring active power online at scale, combined with higher pricing from Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin deployments, will drive faster-than-expected revenue growth. They described execution risk as a bigger concern than financing; I'm not sure those who bought the 2032 8 1/2s at par would agree. The Trade: November 80/January 72.5 call diagonal With CRWV's credit heavily distressed but its equity heavily defended by high-profile dip-buyers, going outright long or short into earnings carries excessive directional risk. A November/January Call Diagonal , currently trading for just under $6 per spread. Almost 9% of the current stock price. Normally, that's a lot, but given this stock has fallen 27.5% and then gained 17% in the past 5 sessions, it isn't. Buy the January 72.5 Calls pay $10.25 Disclosures: Tidal owns/holds all the securities mentioned in the article. events.title: A US Army general says he had a change of heart about high-flying balloons after seeing them in action
events.summary: An Urban Sky High-Altitude Balloon system inflates during an international training exercise in the Philippines. Staff Sgt. Brandon Rickert/US Army The US Army is expanding its use of high-altitude balloons for surveillance and communications. The balloons can operate 60,000 to 100,000 feet above Earth, providing space-like capabilities. Army officials plan more experiments as the service expands its space warfare ranks. The US Army is looking to expand its use of high-altitude balloons as the service builds out its capabilities near and in outer space. These balloons operate in the stratosphere, roughly 60,000 to 100,000 feet above Earth, the space in between where conventional aircraft fly and satellites. Army officials say they see an opportunity to use the balloons to deliver satellite-like surveillance and communication capabilities closer to the battlefield. Lt. Gen. John Rafferty, commander of Army Space and Missile Defense Command, said he was initially skeptical of the technology. He recalled hearing proposals to use high-altitude balloons while serving in what was then Army Futures Command and questioning whether they'd prove practical. The general's view, however, changed after he saw the balloons hold their positions and conduct high-altitude surveillance during a training exercise. "I went from nowhere to a huge believer very quickly once I saw them in action," Rafferty said at this week's Association of the United States Army conference in Washington, DC. The Army is exploring a range of balloon systems for different missions, from surveillance and communications to supporting long-range strikes. Col. Joseph Mroszczyk, who oversees the efforts to integrate emerging space capabilities into Army operations as the director of Transformation Integration Space Superiority, said at AUSA that he wants a "family of stratospheric systems ." Unlike satellites, which travel set paths in orbit, high-altitude balloons can exploit different wind currents to maneuver or maintain a presence over an area of interest, he said. Mroszczyk said the Army could use favorable winds to position balloons carrying sensors, communications equipment, or payloads supporting strikes. "What that enables us to provide is space-like capabilities, really exploiting a transition point between what is normally considered the aerial layer and the space domain," he said. Operating at those altitudes could give the Army persistent coverage across large areas from the stratosphere without relying exclusively on satellites or conventional aircraft. The Army plans to conduct multiple experiments involving various stratospheric systems over the coming year, building on tests conducted in Europe and the Pacific. The service has also experimented with the technology alongside combat operations in the Middle East, a senior Army official told Breaking Defense earlier this week. Those efforts followed the cancellation of a large-scale balloon demonstration planned for the Indo-Pacific last year. The growing interest in high-altitude balloons comes as the Army expands its role in space and near-space operations, with ground forces increasingly reliant on space-based capabilities for navigation, communications, and intelligence. events.title: No 10 leaves option open to impose Chinese EV tariffs if UK joins EU scheme
events.summary: Beijing warns against ‘discriminatory’ step after France drops opposition to British role in Made in Europe package No 10 has left the door open to imposing tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles as part of the Made in Europe package, prompting a warning from Beijing that such a move would be “discriminatory”. Downing Street said on Friday that it would “welcome the objective to have the UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act” after France dropped its opposition to Britain joining the scheme . The aim of the rules is to curb subsidised Chinese imports by giving EU-made products preferential treatment, but the UK and others such as Norway are worried about being left at a disadvantage if excluded from the scheme. The price for joining would be aligning with the EU’s tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the bloc in 2024, according to a Franco-German proposal on Thursday night that said the UK would have to dynamically align with EU trade defence measures. The Chinese embassy in London said it was “firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products”. “We have expressed serious concern to the UK side regarding the reports in question,” it said, adding that “trade protectionism runs counter to WTO rules and market principles”. This week, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy. However, the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK is locked out of supply chains in the EU. Asked whether the UK accepted it would have to put tariffs on Chinese-made vehicles in order to join Made in Europe, a No 10 spokesperson said it was “premature to speculate” on the terms of any deal with the bloc and there was “still a European process to run”. They added: “But more broadly, on the principle, the UK obviously has its own trade policy and it keeps all tariffs under review. And we work closely with the British automotive sector to make sure that that approach reflects their best interests.” Chinese EVs are increasingly popular, with BYD sales up 78% year on year in September, Chery up 660% and the lesser-known Changan up by more than 3,000% in terms of market share. EU lawmakers are expected to finalise the Industrial Accelerator Act, known as Made in Europe legislation, by the end of the year or early 2027. But MEPs have already tabled 5,100 amendments, including one embracing the UK and giving Andy Burnham time to secure the deal he wants. Earlier this week the boss of Mercedes-Benz, Ola Källenius, who is also the president of the European car trade body ACEA, warned that locking the UK out of legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc. According to the new Franco-German proposal, there would be “an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 1 January 2020”, which includes the UK and Norway. This would be provided those third countries accepted “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”. Tariffs could help UK-based manufacturers by preventing cut-price Chinese models flooding the market but they could also push up prices for consumers and harm British manufacturers trying to sell vehicles to China in the case of an escalating trade war. About 80% of UK-made cars are exported, with more than half going to the EU and 6% to China. Earlier on Thursday the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs. He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector. A car industry source said the EU “has recently shown that it is possible to have a dialogue with the Chinese and get some form of safeguarding in place” without retaliation. China opposes the expansion of EV tariffs. In the past few months it has made what European Commission officials called “bloodcurdling threats” to launch a trade war over the latest plan to impose quotas on Chinese hybrid cars. While quotas can be introduced within months under World Trade Organization rules, it could take more than a year to impose tariffs on Chinese cars, with strict processes to be followed, starting with notification of an investigation and followed by evidence-gathering and sharing over alleged harms China might be causing to the British car industry. Liam Byrne, the Labour chair of the parliamentary business committee, has said imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs would be “a small price to pay” to save the industry in both the UK and the EU. At a conference in London on Thursday night, he said the UK “urgently needs” a new strategy on China to ensure that British and European manufacturing “does not die”.

events.title: Katie Zacharia lasts five days, or half a Scaramucci, as White House press secretary
events.summary: Katie Zacharia is out as White House press secretary after a week in the job, according to multiple news reports, following a first briefing that drew criticism and questions about whether she had overstated her legal credentials. A senior White House official confirmed to Fortune that Zacharia is out, after less than a week since accepting the job and less than five days since appearing behind the world’s most famous podium. The New York Times, citing three people familiar with the matter, reported Friday that Trump had fired her. CNN reported the same, citing advisers. Fox News quoted a senior White House official saying she is “transitioning out.” Trump told reporters he had urged her to “reconsider” the job. Trump named Zacharia, a conservative commentator and adviser to the company that runs Truth Social, on Oct. 9 to replace Karoline Leavitt, who left at the end of August. Her only briefing, on Tuesday, was short, and she took three questions. She later told Fox News’s Sean Hannity she “probably should have stepped aside” instead of taking questions without time to prepare. Zacharia’s tenure was shorter than the one that had long set the standard for a brief White House stint: Anthony Scaramucci’s 11 days as communications director in 2017, which turned his name into a unit of measure. And Scaramucci noticed. “Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people’s pain,” he wrote on X Friday. In a second post, he addressed her directly: “Dear @katiezacharia—speaking as the world’s leading expert on short White House tenures: turn off the news and go enjoy your family. In time you’ll realize that the Universe did you a major favor.” Zacharia’s five days are the shortest tenure for a White House press secretary on record, TheGrio reported . And Scaramucci noticed. “Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people’s pain,” he wrote on X Friday. In a second post, he addressed her directly: “Dear Katie Zacharia—speaking as the world’s leading expert on short White House tenures: turn off the news and go enjoy your family. In time you’ll realize that the Universe did you a major favor.” Zacharia’s five days are the shortest tenure for a White House press secretary on record. Social media users had spent the week joking about whether Zacharia would last “one Scaramucci,” and the math got more creative once news surfaced that she didn’t. “And if you’re using the metric system, a full Zacharia converts to one ninth of a Liz Truss,” one user wrote, a nod to the British prime minister who lasted less than two months in 2022. “Do we now say that Zacharia lasted half a Scaramucci, or that Scaramucci lasted two Zacharias?” She also drew scrutiny for calling herself a lawyer after failing the bar exam, which she called “somewhat inconsequential” because she would not need to be licensed while living in China. Zacharia on Thursday defended her legal background and justified her truncated inaugural briefing as she navigates a rocky first week as the president’s chief spokeswoman. Zacharia sat down for interviews with conservative media. She told the conservative Human Events outlet that she did not have time to get fully prepared ahead of her first briefing on Tuesday and that it was always the plan to keep it short because President Donald Trump would field questions from journalists later that morning. “It was absolutely my goal to keep it short, considering he is his own best spokesperson, and he would love — and does love — gaggling with the media as he goes to Marine One,” Zacharia said. “So I wanted to give ample deference and not barge into his time.” The initial briefing materials were given to Zacharia on Monday evening, then completed Tuesday at 8 a.m., less than two hours before she would appear before the White House press corps. She had been up since 3 a.m. preparing, Zacharia said. “I never had a full briefing beforehand, and I went out and I effectuated the briefing,” she said. Later, speaking to Fox News commentator Sean Hannity, she said she “probably should have stepped aside” instead of taking questions from the press corps without having time to prepare. “I could have just given a brief intro and said, ‘I’m only here to introduce myself, and I want to engage with the press corps,’” she said. Zacharia calls failure to pass bar exam ‘inconsequential’ As for her legal background, Zacharia said she was preparing to take the bar exam in California at a time that she had just gotten married and was readying a move to China to join her new husband, who had been working in private equity in Beijing. “I was obviously incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited for finally being married to someone who I’d been long distance from for at least a year,” Zacharia said. She said the results of the bar exam, which she did not pass, were “somewhat inconsequential” because she would not need to be a barred attorney while living in China. Zacharia, who has been under scrutiny for calling herself a “lawyer,” said she consulted several legal experts to ensure that title was accurate when offering legal analysis. “It’s unfortunate that people dub this as some kind of conspiracy or want to put me in a camp. The truth is, I was very careful how I executed this, and I never came across as someone who was an attorney-at-law.” She will not weigh in on legal matters in her White House capacity, Zacharia said. She says she didn’t lobby for the job She also divulged details of how she went about securing the White House press secretary job. Zacharia stressed that she did not want to be seen as lobbying for the position, left vacant when Karoline Leavitt announced she would depart the administration to spend more time with her family. Zacharia, who was a communications adviser for the company that runs Truth Social, said she closely monitored the president’s social media posts to determine what was top of mind for him, then would go on air to talk about those topics. “My philosophy is, I’m on TV enough where if he sees me and he likes me, then I will be recruited for the job. I do not believe that lobbying for that job would have been successful, and I wanted to work for it. I wanted to audition for it.” Then on Oct. 7, as Zacharia was preparing to take one of her children to a pumpkin patch, she received a phone call from Trump about the press secretary position. She promptly flew out the next day from her home in California to Washington, met with the president about the job on Friday and formally accepted the position later that day . ___ Associated Press writer Jonathan J. Cooper in Phoenix contributed. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: My Dubai Salary: 'I earn up to Dh45,000 a month coaching wellness to women in midlife’
events.summary: Monika Singh arrived in Dubai 12 years ago with a dentistry degree from India and a plan to sit her Dubai Health Authority licensing exams to practise in the UAE. Then she started attending group workout classes while she studied, discovered a love for dance fitness and never looked back. Today, she runs Monika Sphere, a women's wellness coaching business specialising in women in midlife, a niche she arrived at through her own experience with perimenopause after having her son, now seven. She now works exclusively within Arabian Ranches 1 and 2, coaches 23 clients, and earns between Dh42,000 and Dh45,000 a month. What was your first job? Before I started my own thing, I was doing group exercise classes in Fitness First and some other studios across Dubai. That was my starting point in the industry. I was never into fitness , honestly. I started attending dance fitness classes, and it just kind of stayed with me, and I was like, “Oh wow, I really want to do this.” I told my husband; I expressed my feelings to him, and he was very supportive. From there, I started my journey into fitness. I took my Zumba training, then I went into a group exercise leadership programme. Then I did my yoga training, Les Mills Body Balance training, then personal training and sound healing. A lot of things happened, and here I am today. And now? I’ve set up my own company. I have been training 23 ladies, and I'm just around Ranches 1 and 2 – I don't go outside because of commute time, and I also don't have time to go out and train people. My average earnings are Dh42,000 to Dh45,000 a month. My training is not just about typical strength training. Of course, strength training is important for women, but other factors come into play, like mobility, recovery, your sleep, your meditation, and your breathwork. Everything comes together to give you a balanced and sustainable fitness regime. I also specialise in women in midlife. This came to me through my own experience. After I delivered a baby, and as I entered my midlife phase – that is, perimenopause – I realised that my energy was not the same, my sleep was getting affected, and my responsibilities were different. And I realised the same complaint was coming from the women that I coach. Coming from a medical background, I have more understanding of human anatomy and physiology. I decided to dive more into this and study women's wellness, especially in midlife. I took my training, and now I am helping women achieve their goals without punishing themselves. Do you manage to save and invest? Yes, I do save. I'm not investing yet, but I do take care of my daily routine. I have a boy – seven years old – so I manage his school fees, then take care of my car loan, and some house chores. I keep around Dh3,000 to Dh4,000 aside for household expenses, and the rest I save. My husband takes care of the rest of the house. Growing up, were you taught how to handle your finances? When I was in university studying dentistry , we were given a very small amount of pocket money, and you had to manage that throughout the week. You wouldn't get more than that – that was the rule set by our parents, because in India it's like that. That's how I learnt how to manage my expenses. Honestly, I didn't learn anything about investing because we were not given the right to make any decisions on that. It was all my father who used to do that, not us. What are your financial goals? Currently, my goal is to launch my online portal. I have been saving for that because launching an online portal, an app, and everything else is expensive. Long-term, we have a plan to get a new, bigger house after I launch my online portal, once it becomes successful and once we start getting more and more income. That is our first plan. Where do you want to see yourself in the next 10 years? I want to be a known personality, a successful businesswoman – among people in the UAE who are known for their work.

events.title: IEEE Offers More Services to Cities That Want to Be Smarter
events.summary: More and more city governments are using advanced technologies to improve livability for their residents. Municipalities use data from smartphones and sensors for traffic enforcement, traffic control, and waste management. They also have implemented artificial intelligence and deep learning programs. Dubai , Paris , and Coral Gables , Fla., are among the cities that have invested heavily in programs to become smarter. But along with the conveniences that come with a smart city transition, there have been challenges including safety and privacy issues and eroding relationships between residents and city officials. Although many initiatives have delivered real innovations, not all have been successful. Inefficient global coordination has hindered projects with unclear standards, socioeconomic differences, and a lack of worldwide governance, leading to a disconnect between the technologies and the ability to adapt to them. Citizens’ trust in the technologies suffers because of privacy breaches, personal data leaks, and other issues. Finding solutions Smart city projects are complex and expensive endeavors that involve politicians, citizens, technocrats, and engineers. Successful projects require citizens to be fully engaged and to have strong collaborations with the participants, especially engineers, as engineering is the cornerstone . Collaboration with universities, research institutions, and technology experts can bridge knowledge gaps on the behavior of complex socio-technical systems. What’s missing, though, is a global platform where those involved can discuss their experiences. To help solve those and other challenges, the IEEE Smart Cities Technical Community (formerly the IEEE Smart Cities Initiative ) was launched in 2013 by IEEE Future Directions , which incubates emerging technologies and new applications of current ones. The technical community provides city leaders and others with credible, unbiased information and educational content developed by IEEE experts. Since then, IEEE Smart Cities has launched services including its flagship International Smart Cities Conference , a media center with educational and technical resources, and a contest to recognize the best smart project completed by city officials. The platforms bring together practicing engineers, academic researchers, policymakers, and city leaders to collaborate and exchange ideas and experiences about moving toward a smart-city model. Better serving humanity In 2021 the IEEE Power & Energy Society began managing the Smart Cities program, which is supported by the IEEE Communications , Industry Applications , and Intelligent Transportation Systems societies and other IEEE entities. Thanks to volunteers’ dedication and determination, IEEE Smart Cities launched several services. But the initiative’s structure limited the development of long-term projects and the creation of new activities. To address the situation, the IEEE Technical Activities Board (TAB) created the second-generation technical community ad hoc committee , also in 2021. It was a pilot program whereby IEEE Smart Cities formed a board of governors to oversee the community’s operations and leadership, and created a policies and procedures manual. In November 2025 IEEE Smart Cities became a TAB technical community . IEEE Smart Cities now Today more than 7,000 volunteers collaborate on various aspects of the community within at least one of the following technical tracks: Smart grid. Smart water management. Green electronics for smart cities. Smart governance and planning. Hydrogen for smart cities. Smart and sustainable campus. Security for smart cities. Smart lighting for cities. Smart mobility for cities. Artificial intelligence for cities. New webinar series, workshops, conferences, educational resources, and other offerings are being created. Two events were launched recently: the IEEE European Technology and Engineering Management Summit , held in May 2025 in Belgium, with the next one planned for 2027; and the IEEE Sustainable Smart Lighting World Conference , scheduled for 2 to 6 December in Athens. The Smart Cities Ambassadors program aims to raise the technical community’s visibility outside IEEE by holding roundtables and other events at non-IEEE functions. IEEE Smart Cities volunteers are working on launching journals. In addition, standards are being developed in collaboration with the IEEE Standards Association , societies, and councils. The program is collaborating with the Open and Agile Smart Cities and Communities network, the Instituto de Competitividad e Innovación para el Desarrollo y Transferencia de Tecnología, and the International Project Management Association . All of those actions have the ultimate objective of boosting IEEE Smart Cities’ growth and sustainability, as well as strengthening the leadership and educational offerings to technical community volunteers. If you would like to volunteer, visit the Smart Cities website .

events.title: $2m payday for home battery owners as heatwave catches grid off guard
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Spring heatwave and coal outages deliver $2m payday for home battery owners Topic: Electricity Production and Distribution On Monday evening this week, self-styled home battery boffins were buzzing with excitement on Reddit. Deep in niche threads, they shared screenshots and boasted about how much money they'd made that afternoon on the National Energy Market (NEM). Electricity prices in New South Wales had suddenly skyrocketed around 3:30pm (AEDT), peaking at $23,107 per megawatt hour (MWh), just shy of the market cap. Prices exceeded $5,000/MWh in 11 separate five-minute intervals. "Rolling power spike pricing, have made $100 in an hour selling 30kw/h," one Reddit user commented. A typical household uses between 15 and 20 kilowatt hours of electricity a day. Screenshots from a Reddit sub where people discuss home batteries. ( Supplied ) A spring heat wave was sweeping the state, pushing temperatures into the mid-30s. At Observatory Hill in Sydney, the mercury spiked at 34.7 degrees, more than 12 degrees above the long-term monthly average. For people with solar panels on their roofs and batteries in their garage, it was a chance to make money selling power back to the grid at much higher rates. "Hot day shenanigans," another Reddit user posted under another earnings screenshot. Tristan Edis is the CEO of Green Energy Markets, an industry analysis company. ( Supplied: Green Energy Markets ) Green Energy Markets CEO Tristan Edis said the price spike was a reminder of an underlying NEM vulnerability in a rapidly warming climate as it tried to manage aging coal plants while building generation and storage. "It's normal for electricity prices to be high when temperatures go noticeably above 30 degrees," Edis said. "What's problematic is that doesn't normally happen in October." Fuelling the extraordinary spike in prices was a confluence of factors. As temperatures climbed, four of NSW's 12 coal-fired generating units were out of action and two were at reduced capacity. The Eraring Power Station is scheduled to shut down in 2029. ( AAP/Greenpeace ) To make matters worse, several high transmission lines were also running below capacity due to maintenance, meaning huge amounts of mostly renewable energy and storage capacity could not be delivered to Sydney just when it needed it most. Australian energy intelligence firm GridScout said the energy was instead curtailed, or throttled at the source, because the high-voltage network could not transport more electricity. "Technical curtailment peaked at (2,800 megawatts), with renewables and batteries in Southern NSW being the most heavily affected," the firm noted on social media. "This was all while prices were above $10,000/MWh." So hot temperatures drove up demand just when less electricity was available. Amid the chaos, market watchers were also stunned by an unusual phenomenon. Just after 3pm AEDT, as demand soared, NSW prices on the spot electricity market started whipsawing dramatically. They jumped from about $200/MWh to more than $1,300/MWh, fell to $766, hit the $23,000 market ceiling minutes later, then plunged again. Dave Smith, a wholesale power market designer, said the wild price gyrations appeared to have been driven by a new force in energy — Australia's growing fleet of household batteries. In the national grid, the Australian Energy Market Operator sets prices every five minutes. It does so choosing the lowest-priced "bids" of whichever generators are offering to meet supply. The price paid is the cost of the highest-priced bid required to meet demand in that five-minute period. According to Smith, the squeeze in NSW on Monday drew a predictable response from the market. Prices rose sharply as supplies struggled to keep pace with demand. Tesla releases plans for Australia's largest EV charging hub More problems emerging along WA's high-profile 'electric highway' Pacific's undersea treasure is worth billions, but some say we'll never see it The key features Australian homes may have in the future Among those responding were the legions of household battery owners, who were getting alerts on their phones telling them to sell their surplus power to tap into soaring prices. But unlike most energy providers, these batteries sit "behind the meter", meaning the market operator cannot see nor control them. When prices spiked on Monday, households with batteries sold big amounts of power into the system, only to pull back when prices fell in the next five-minute interval. At all times, Smith said, AEMO was on the back foot and playing catch-up.

events.title: Why Trump and the GOP's billion-dollar midterm blitz isn’t working
events.summary: Republican groups have poured more than $740 million into House and Senate races since Labor Day, fueled by President Trump-aligned groups and record megadonor giving in the midterm election. The spending advantage has produced little movement in major Senate battlegrounds, while super PACs are often paying substantially more than candidates for comparable television exposure. Republicans are increasingly shifting money from offense to defense, pouring resources into once-safe states including Texas, Kansas and Nebraska while retreating from races in North Carolina and the House. A billion-dollar war chest was meant to be Republicans' great equalizer heading into a bleak midterm election environment defined by economic frustration , President Donald Trump's unpopularity and fallout from the war in Iran . From Labor Day through Oct. 14, GOP groups injected more than $740 million into congressional races that will determine control of Congress , according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data. That includes at least $220 million in spending from Trump-linked groups. Elon Musk has separately given another $276 million to Republican groups since July and helped boost the GOP's Senate Leadership Fund super PAC to a record quarter . Yet with less than three weeks until the Nov. 3 Election Day, the spending blitz has barely moved the map. Democrats lead in FiftyPlusOne's polling averages across nine of the Senate's most competitive races — Alaska, Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas — little changed from before the Republican spending spree. Minnesota was expected to be solidly blue, making its tight race a concern for Democrats. And Republican political operatives and independent election observers CNBC spoke with say the money hasn't had the effects its magnitude would be expected to in voter sentiment. Meanwhile, the broader battlefield continues to deteriorate for Republicans. Democrats are favored to flip the House and remain competitive in the Senate , according to the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter , forcing the GOP to burn millions protecting once-safe seats while abandoning former pickup targets. "Money is an amplifier, not a magic wand," said Neil Newhouse , partner at Republican polling firm Public Opinion Strategies. "You can buy all the airtime in the world, but if the political climate is blowing 30 miles an hour in your face, ad volume alone isn't going to turn the weather around." Republicans entered the final stretch of the midterm election with unusually deep pockets. MAGA Inc. had nearly $416 million on hand at the end of August, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Across the broader ecosystem, major Republican organizations had roughly $1 billion available, eclipsing the $579 million available for comparable Democratic groups, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings. Then came Musk — after saying he'd be less involved in this year's election. The Tesla and SpaceX CEO has given more than $276 million to Republican groups since July, including $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund Republican-boosting super PAC and more than $76 million to his own America PAC , according to figures confirmed to CNBC by an America PAC spokesperson. Musk's known federal political giving this election cycle now totals roughly $366 million, making him the largest known donor of the midterms. And Musk is far from alone. Nine of the 10 largest individual and family donor groups this cycle are Republican-aligned, accounting for 86 cents of every dollar contributed by the top 10, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC records . "We are watching an unprecedented concentration and scale of political influence and wealth this election cycle," said Hilary Braseth, executive director of OpenSecrets, a nonprofit, nonpartisan group that tracks campaign spending. AdImpact projects $11.6 billion in political advertising this 2025-2026 cycle, surpassing both the 2022 midterms and the 2024 presidential election. However, the size of Republicans’ financial advantage may overstate how much advertising that money can actually buy. That's because much of the GOP's money, particularly spending by Trump-aligned groups, has arrived late and via super PACs, which can pay far more for airtime than candidates. Federal law entitles candidates to broadcasters' lowest unit rate during the final 60 days before a general election; outside groups get no such protection. It's an edge for Democrats whose candidates have generally outraised their Republican counterparts. In Dallas, for example, Democrat James Talarico's campaign spent about $2.4 million on local broadcast ads from Oct. 1 through Oct. 14, enough for the average viewer to see his ads about 48 times, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data.

events.title: India becomes the latest country to report rogue AI agent activity
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency said Thursday. The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said it had received “multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers” whose models, during research and evaluation runs on the open internet, “had reached the live systems of Indian organizations.” The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles, and their actions “exceeded the authorisation of their assigned tasks.” This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity. Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal. At Hugging Face, OpenAI’s agents started the same way but then found and exploited software flaws to run code on the company’s servers. CERT-In described no such hacking in India, where the agents appear to have simply used the access left lying around. Still, the Indian cases appear to be worse in one respect, which is what the agents saw: In Australia, OpenAI said it found no evidence its agents touched individuals’ medical or criminal records, even after they wrote files inside a Medicare statistics system, while in India, agents read personal data and confidential business records. And unlike earlier incidents, each disclosed by a single lab, India’s case involved agents from multiple providers. CERT-In did not name the providers or affected organizations, or say whether the agents altered any systems. TechCrunch has reached out to CERT-In for more information. For now, the closest parallel seems to be Anthropic’s July disclosure of Claude breaking into three companies’ systems during testing using basic techniques like weak passwords. In India, as in Anthropic’s cases, the affected organizations had not detected the intrusions on their own. The disclosures have left governments relying on AI companies causing these breaches to voluntarily disclose rogue AI agent activity. events.title: Palisades nuclear reactor restart continues despite work environment safety findings
events.summary: The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission has granted permission to Holtec International, owner of the Palisades nuclear reactor , to retrieve a potentially compromised fuel assembly, although the plant received a warning about its work environment. At some point after August 30, as new fuel was being lowered into the reactor, one of the fuel assemblies tipped, causing the plant's planned restart to be placed on hold. If Holtec successfully retrieves the fuel assembly, efforts to restart the plant are likely to move forward with NRC oversight. The Palisades reactor, bought by Holtec after it was decommissioned in 2022, has become a poster child for the US nuclear energy renaissance driven by artificial intelligence data centres. The NRC said no radiation was released during the incident at the reactor, in Covert , Michigan. Amid the controversy, the NRC sent a letter to Holtec following an inspection that determined that although Palisades maintained a safety-conscious work environment overall, “a chilled work environment” existed in the supply chain and quality assurance departments. The NRC explained: “Employees in these two work departments are hesitant to raise safety concerns using all available avenues without fear of retaliation.” Patrick O’Brien, Holtec director of government affairs and communications, said the company was “taking actions to address these issues and will continue our work to maintain and strengthen a healthy safety-conscious work environment”. But the response to the NRC findings has failed to calm fears among those concerned about the plant's work environment and the restarting of “ zombie reactors ”. “Holtec's unprecedented restart of the Palisades zombie reactor will risk a Chernobyl or Fukushima-scale catastrophe a hundred yards from the shoreline of the Great Lakes, drinking water supply for more than 40 million people in eight US states, two Canadian provinces and a large number of Indigenous Nations,” said Kevin Kamps, executive director for environmental advocacy group Don't Waste Michigan. Arnie Gundersen, a nuclear engineer and expert adviser for the organisation, called the NRC's decision to approve Holtec's strategy for retrieving the tipped fuel assembly “ironic”. “In the last four weeks, Palisades lost control and tipped a nuclear fuel bundle and couldn’t get it out, nine out of 15 licensed reactor operators failed their exam, and more than half of the people in their quality assurance and procurement departments feel they will be fired by management if they bring concerns forward,” he said, and yet “ironically … the NRC just gave them permission to begin loading fuel again!” 📍 NRC senior managers recently visited Palisades nuclear plant as part of our continued oversight to ensure the historic restart is done safely. pic.twitter.com/9SLRdJejyT — NRC (@NRCgov) October 9, 2026 He added that the subsequent report from the NRC indicated that the “fuel assembly exhibits significant bowing”. In a statement to The National , a spokesperson for the NRC reiterated that the findings related to a chilled work environment were limited to the Palisades “supply chain and quality assurance departments”, adding that the government agency “did not identify any violations or significant plant safety issues but has concerns about the work environment's impact on these departments.” That spokesperson also said that the NRC will “continue to verify that safety requirements are met”. As for approving Holtec’s method of retrieving the tipped fuel assembly, the NRC indicated that its “specialists and resident inspectors will continue monitoring removal activities.” In a statement, however, Holtec said that it appreciated the government agency's decision. “The proposed recovery approach was supported by engineering evaluations addressing structural integrity, fuel handling, thermal conditions, and radiation protection,” Holtec said. A source close to Holtec recently told The National that the company hoped to have Palisades back online by March 2027. Holtec has yet to provide a timeline. 📍 As Palisades begins loading fuel into the reactor, our inspectors have been on site ensuring this activity meets safety and security requirements. This historic step moves the plant closer to restart — an extraordinary milestone for nuclear energy and the NRC. pic.twitter.com/qGfoCfwaYD — NRC (@NRCgov) September 2, 2026 “Palisades will return to service when all required work is complete and all federal requirements and industry standards are met,” Mr O'Brien said. “Our team of more than 1,000 nuclear professionals continues this work in parallel with the fuel assembly recovery effort.” Before shutting down 2022, the Palisades reactor was no stranger to controversy. In 2012, an NRC report warned about the work culture at the plant, where it said safety concerns were often dismissed. In 2016, security staff were placed on leave from the plant, which was then owned by Entergy, for failing to properly follow fire prevention protocol. In October 2025, a worker at Palisades fell off a refuelling bridge into a pool of water, but was not seriously injured.

events.title: NBA tightens betting rules, develops AI to flag suspicious wagers
events.summary: The NBA is restricting certain bets, like wagers on tip-offs, in an effort to curb betting manipulation. The league has developed an AI platform to flag suspicious betting activity and is expanding mandatory training and protections against bettor harassment. Adam Silver told CNBC the NBA wants greater access to wagering data and control over betting markets and prediction markets. The NBA is upping the ante when it comes to monitoring sports betting ahead of the 2026-2027 season. The league is tightening restrictions on bets offered by its authorized gambling partners and deploying artificial intelligence to help identify suspicious wagering, according to two documents obtained by CNBC. The measures come as Commissioner Adam Silver pushes for greater access to wagering data and more control over the types of markets offered on the league's games. He said his concerns extend to prediction markets. "For us, whether it's called a prediction market, whether it's sports betting, it's the same issues for our league, and I think for all the leagues," Silver told CNBC last week in Macao. "There's issues around integrity first and foremost." In the letter sent to sports betting companies including FanDuel , DraftKings , Fanatics and others, the NBA has placed restrictions on wagers on which player scores the first basket, wagers on players expected to play less than 12 minutes per game and parlays combining multiple bets on the same player's underperformance. Those types of bets can raise integrity concerns because a single player has the ability to influence the outcome. The changes follow a series of gambling-related cases involving NBA figures including former players Jontay Porter, Terry Rozier, and Damon Jones and former coach and player Chauncey Billups. A separate memo sent Friday to team presidents, general managers, integrity officers and lawyers says the NBA has developed an internal AI-based monitoring platform. The system analyzes basketball data, injury reports, social media information about player availability and individual betting data. The platform is designed to help the league “promptly identify and investigate potentially suspicious betting activity,” according to the memo from Dan Spillane, the NBA’s executive vice president of league governance and policy. Silver’s comments underscore the importance the league places on obtaining that information. “So we want access to that data. We also want control over the markets,” Silver told CNBC. The league is also increasing its training and education around sports betting. The memo said that former NFL player and retired FBI agent Charles Tillman, will provide in-person training to each team. The league said it has also added new training around sports betting to NBA rookies who will now receive training at the NBA Combine and during the required Rookie Transition program. The letter also highlights steps the league is taking to better protect players and personnel from harassment and threats by sports bettors. As betting has become more widespread, some bettors have taken to social media to harass players for their game performance that may be tied to a bet. To address this, the league has updated its NBA Fan Code of Conduct to highlight the prohibition on betting-related harassment. The league is also partnering with a third-party service provider to help monitor and control harassing messages. It has also launched a new text message-based hotline to securely report threats. The memo does not specify how the restrictions would apply to prediction market platforms. In Macao, Silver said that he's in favor of a national framework when it comes to federal regulation around sports betting. "We have roughly 40 different judications regulating us right now so to have a consistent policy nationally, I think would be in our best interest," he said.
