events.title: Why the AI bubble fears are overblown
events.summary: Reed’s view Fear is rising that the AI bubble is about to burst under the weight of mounting debt, as my colleague Liz Hoffman detailed yesterday, including this great quote from an unnamed data-center financier: “We’re not an ATM for your dystopian future.” Perhaps lenders have grown tired of funding the data center buildout, but money is not going to be the thing that finally causes the AI train to go off the rails. Everything is bottlenecked. It’s not just chips, memory, and EUV machines. It’s refrigeration units that cool the GPUs and the raw materials needed to make components, like glass. If it weren’t for this bottlenecked supply chain, it’s likely AI revenues and user numbers would be growing much faster. Every time companies reach a new level of token efficiency, some new use case for AI is born that burns through ever more compute, proving Jevons Paradox . My favorite example of late: Decompiling video games to create mashups , something that used to take people years to do manually can now be done by AI in a weekend. It may be the thing that finally turns Gen-Zers into fans of AI. The total addressable market of AI is roughly 100% of the earth’s population, and demand for it will continue to soar. The enterprise market has only dipped its toes into AI, and the consumer hasn’t even begun to dive in. Anthropic told investors this week that it’s making 85% gross margins. Even if that number is a gross exaggeration, this is a cash cow business. They’ll service their debt obligations, in other words. I agree with the lender who lamented being an ATM for the AI industry, but probably for a different reason. Why would you want to lend money for measly interest payments when you could invest and get a massive return? There’s a reason hyperscalers and neoclouds reached for debt: It’s relatively cheap. Notable Data center firms say that talent and power are two of the main bottlenecks challenging the AI buildout today, Bloomberg reported.

events.title: How Princess Charlene of Monaco's style has evolved, from her days as an Olympic athlete to a European princess
events.summary: Princess Charlene at the 20th Anniversary Gala Of the Prince Albert II of Monaco Foundation. Arnold Jerocki/Getty Images Princess Charlene of Monaco hasn't always been as fashionable as she is now. Before marrying Prince Albert, Charlene was an Olympic swimmer representing South Africa. Finding her "fashion feet" was a challenge, Charlene said — but now she's embraced daring looks. When Princess Charlene married Prince Albert of Monaco in 2011, her life changed. Once best known as an Olympic swimmer representing South Africa, she was reintroduced to the world as a princess. The official Monaco royal website says she was born Charlene Lynette Wittstock on January 25, 1978, in Bulawayo, Zimbabwe. At age 12, she moved to South Africa with her parents and her younger brothers. There, she began forging a career as a swimmer, taking home several awards at the 1997 South African championship , including the coveted title of best female swimmer. Charlene went on to represent South Africa at the 2000 Sydney Olympics. As fate would have it, her future husband, Albert, was there as a spectator — though the pair wouldn't officially cross paths until she visited Monaco for a swimming competition later that year. They eventually married and later had twins, Prince Jacques and Princess Gabriella. However, marrying into a royal family came with certain lifestyle adjustments, including Charlene's sense of style . From her days as an Olympic athlete to being one of the most recognized princesses around the world, here's a closer look at how Charlene's fashion has evolved. In 2001, Charlene was still very much in her athletic era. Princess Charlene pictured in South Africa on June 28, 2001. Terry Shean/Sunday Times/Gallo Images via Getty Images She was photographed in South Africa wearing a laid-back look that consisted of gray sweatpants, a navy-blue windbreaker, and Nike sneakers. Later that year, she maintained her sporty style on the front cover of South African Sports Illustrated. Princess Charlene poses for a portrait shoot for South African Sports Illustrated in November 2001 in South Africa. Jacques Weyers/SA Sports Illustrated/Touchline/ Getty Images For the photo shoot, Charlene wore a sporty red tank top, white flared jeans, and a sailor hat. In keeping with the easygoing, nautical aesthetic of the shoot, she opted to go barefoot. Charlene and Albert made their first public appearance as a couple at a 2006 F1 Monaco Grand Prix party. Charlene with Albert at the Automobile Club party following the F1 Grand Prix in Monaco on May 28, 2006. BENAINOUS/CATARINA/LEGRAND/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images For the big night, she wore a black floor-length gown that was elegant and a world away from Charlene's previous ensembles. It featured a sweetheart neckline and a long skirt with a lace-lined slit that reached her knees. She paired the gown with silver drop earrings and a matching clutch. Charlene brushed shoulders with fashion heavyweights like Karl Lagerfeld at the 2007 Monaco Red Cross ball — but she went on to regret her look. Charlene Wittstock at the Monaco Red Cross Ball on August 4, 2006. Pascal Le Segretain/Getty Images For her first appearance at Monaco's annual Red Cross Ball, Charlene wore a sparkly, semi-sheer, backless ball gown that she borrowed from a friend, she told Tatler in 2010. Reflecting on the look, Charlene wasn't exactly fond of her choice. "I looked like a Christmas tree," she said. "I was used to living in a swimsuit and totally clueless about fashion. The day of the ball, I had been playing volleyball all day on the beach and didn't think about getting ready until late in the afternoon," Charlene added. In a separate interview with Vogue before her 2011 wedding, Charlene remembered the outfit as one of her least favorites. "Finding my fashion feet has certainly been the biggest challenge," she said. "I realize that my debut into Monaco society should have been better executed!" Charlene ditched sparkly gowns for cargo shorts and a light-blue polo later that year. Charlene Wittstock coaching children at a training session on December 2, 2006, in Richards Bay, South Africa. Barry Tuck/Gallo Images/Getty Images She wore the casual ensemble during a visit to Richards Bay, South Africa, to teach swimming lessons to children. Charlene opted for a more daring look at the 2007 closing ceremony of the Small European States Games. Prince Albert and Charlene in Monaco on June 9, 2007. LEGRAND/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Image For the event, she wore a black, strapless bustier top over asymmetric suit pants that featured a slit on the left leg. She accessorized with a sheer black scarf and a black clutch. She tapped into the rock-and-roll theme of the 2009 Rose Ball with a bold hairdo and a black bejeweled gown. Charlene Wittstock and Prince Albert of Monaco in Monte Carlo, Monaco on March 28, 2009. Alain BENAINOUS/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images Charlene's sleeveless dress featured a daring neckline and colorful jewels. A matching biker glove and a small black clutch completed the ensemble. Albert and Charlene announced their engagement in June 2010. Prince Albert II and Charlene Wittstock's official engagement portrait In Monte Carlo, Monaco on June 23, 2010. Interagences/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images For the official photographs that accompanied the big news, Charlene wore a colorful, floor-length dress. The flowy blue-and-green gown was designed by Akris. It was backless and featured an elegant halter neck. The official portraits also showed her sparkling engagement ring, which featured a three-carat, pear-cut diamond surrounded by smaller round jewels. For the couple's civil marriage ceremony, Charlene collaborated with Karl Lagerfeld on her powder-blue ensemble, which perfectly complemented her eyes. Princess Charlene and Prince Albert II after their civil marriage ceremony on July 1, 2011, in Monaco. Pascal Le Segretain/Getty Images The ensemble, made of a blazer and palazzo pants, was both regal and reflective of Charlene's sporty aesthetic . "It's feminine and keeps with tradition yet has a little twist that reflects my personal style," Charlene told Vogue. "I thought it was a nice change to go for trousers instead of a skirt, especially since I'm an athlete and have always kept my clothes clean and simple." Later, for the grand religious ceremony, she dazzled in a custom-made Giorgio Armani gown that took 2,500 hours to make. Princess Charlene and Prince Albert smile as they leave the palace after their religious wedding ceremony on July 2, 2011, in Monaco. events.title: Prediction market odds on Tesla-SpaceX merger are above 50% for early 2027
events.summary: Chances of a merger happening before March jumped on Friday to 56% from 29% on Kalshi. Odds for an integration before April and May rose to similar levels. Most recently, Tesla showed off its long-delayed next-generation Roadster this week, which relies on SpaceX technology to make the vehicle hover. Following a Barclays note Wednesday that outlined what a merger between Tesla and SpaceX could look like, prediction market traders increased the odds of an integration above 50% for early 2027. Odds of a merger happening before March jumped to 56% by Friday morning, up from 29%. Odds for an integration before April and May climbed to similar levels. The contract asks, "When will Tesla and SpaceX merge?" and will be verified by news outlets and the Securities and Exchange Commission's EDGAR database. Tesla, known for its electric vehicles, and SpaceX, a rocket and satellite company, have collaborated before. Both are controlled by Elon Musk. On Thursday, Tesla showed off its long-delayed Roadster , which relies on SpaceX technology to make the vehicle hover. A video showcasing the Roadster's capabilities was also recorded from SpaceX's test site in Texas. Beyond collaboration, the growing speculation of a merger comes after Musk spoke of "more and more overlap" between Tesla and SpaceX on the EV maker's latest earnings call. Barclays now expects a merger could be announced before Tesla's annual general meeting, which must take place no later than Dec. 6, 2026. Analyst Dan Levy expects the merger may be proposed as an AI vertical integration, involving Tesla's Robotaxi and Optimus with SpaceX's Grok and Macrohard. Terafab, the semiconductor project relying on Tesla, SpaceX and xAI, could also be a "key driver" for the merger, Levy added. "Notably, while we suspect there would be some financial synergies, the true value would be in vertical integration," Levy said. Earlier Friday, Evercore ISI recommended buying SpaceX shares ahead of its next scheduled earnings release, set for early November, and boosted its 12-month price target on the stock by 20% to $275. events.title: The most haunted place in every state
events.summary: From homes and hotels to churches and cemeteries, there are places all over the country that are said to be haunted. Nomad_Photo/Shutterstock There are places all over the country that are said to be haunted. The Eastern State Penitentiary in Philadelphia, now a museum, is said to be haunted by ex-inmates. NBA players have also reported seeing ghosts at the Skirvin Hotel in Oklahoma City. From homes and hotels to churches, theaters, and cemeteries, there's no shortage of supposedly haunted places across the US. Nearly every state has its own eerie legends — stories of restless spirits, mysterious footsteps in empty hallways, and unexplained flickering lights that locals swear attest to these spots being haunted. Many of these sites are also steeped in history, with tragic pasts or notorious events. Business Insider examined local legends and historic sites to determine the most reportedly haunted locations in every state, with many having reported ghost sightings , strange occurrences, or bloody histories.  Whether you believe in ghosts or just love a good scare, these haunted places across the US have earned spooky reputations. Madeline Diamond contributed to an earlier version of this story. ALABAMA: Sloss Furnaces, Birmingham Sloss Furnaces is reportedly haunted. Stephen Reeves/Shutterstock The Sloss Furnaces are now a historic national landmark, but in the late 19th century, they produced iron, which was then turned into steel. James "Slag" Wormwood was the boss at the furnaces, and it's said that he subjected his employees to some inhumane working conditions. Labor laws didn't exist at the time, and furnace temperatures often exceeded 100 degrees. A total of 47 men died with Wormwood as their boss, and even Wormwood himself lost his life in the furnaces when he slipped and fell into the iron ore, causing his body to melt, Travel South USA reported. Wormwood and his workers are believed to haunt the furnaces to this day. ALASKA: Kennecott cybercrisi/Shutterstock Kennecott is a remote Alaskan town that's been mostly abandoned since 1950. The town was a hub for copper mining from 1911 to 1938, but after the area's copper supply was diminished, Kennecott's population dwindled. Today, many rickety wooden buildings still stand in Kennecott, and many people believe that they are haunted by former miners and railroad workers, the Anchorage Daily News reported. ARIZONA: Lost Dutchman State Park, Apache Junction Lost Dutchman State Park EdwinM/Shutterstock The Lost Dutchman gold mine is believed to be situated in a state park in Apache Junction, Arizona, although its exact location is unclear. The park is said to be haunted by the spirits of people who died over the years searching for the mine, the Phoenix New Times reported. ARKANSAS: Crescent Hotel, Eureka Springs Crescent Hotel in Arkansas. RaksyBH/Shutterstock The Crescent Hotel in Eureka Springs, Arkansas, takes pride in its reputation as a haunted hotel. Guests can join ghost tours and catch a glimpse of several ghosts who reportedly haunt the property, including one known as "the girl in the mist." CALIFORNIA: Bodie Bodie, CA UTBP/Shutterstock According to the California Department of Parks and Recreation, Bodie, California, is a ghost town turned state park that offers a taste of life during the gold rush of the late 1800s. Many homes and other buildings are still standing in the town today. Some people believe that the town is haunted by former residents, Legends of America reported. COLORADO: St. Elmo Nadja Rider/Shutterstock St. Elmo, Colorado, was a thriving mining town in the late 1800s, though it was abandoned as soon as the area's mines shut down, History Colorado reported. The ghost town has been well-maintained, allowing visitors to get a sense of life in the late 19th century. They might even catch a glimpse of ghosts of former residents. There's a particularly popular ghost story about Annabelle Stark, a woman from St. Elmo who is said to have continued living there even after the town was entirely abandoned. CONNECTICUT: Old Newgate Prison, East Granby The remains of Old Newgate Prison. Shanshan0312/Shutterstock Connecticut History reported that the Old Newgate Prison was the first prison in the state of Connecticut, operating from 1773 to 1827. Most notably, it once held prisoners of war during the Revolutionary War. Many people believe that the site is haunted by soldiers and prisoners who died while trying to escape from the prison.  DELAWARE: Fort Delaware, Delaware City T.J. H./Yelp Fort Delaware is situated on its own island, accessible only by ferry. It was built as a Union fortress during the Civil War and was later used as a prison for Confederate soldiers. Many prisoners died while held captive, and their ghosts are believed to haunt the property today, the Delaware News Journal  reported. Paranormal tours are currently being offered on Friday and Saturday nights, but visitors need to make a reservation. FLORIDA: Old St. Johns County Jail, St. Augustine Old St. Johns County Jail. Cindy P./Yelp The Old St. Johns County Jail no longer houses inmates, although the spirits of many of St. Augustine's violent criminals reportedly still haunt the historic jail. The jail is now a museum, and visitors can go on nighttime "Old Jail After Dark" tours  to try to spot the ghosts for themselves.  GEORGIA: Lucas Theatre, Savannah Noah Densmore/Shutterstock Aside from being a beautiful Southern city with tons of history, Savannah, Georgia, is also said to be haunted. The Lucas Theatre is just one of the city's haunted locales. According to a local tour company , visitors to the historic theater have reported ghost sightings, including shadowy figures and sounds of applause, even when there's no one around. HAWAII: 'Iolani Palace, Honolulu Shutterstock The 'Iolani Palace was once home to Hawaii's royalty , although today it serves as a museum of Hawaiian history. Queen Lili'uokalani and other Hawaiian royals are said to haunt the palace. One room in the museum is notorious for supernatural activity — visitors have reported hearing mysterious music and chanting, Honolulu Magazine reported. IDAHO: Old Idaho Penitentiary, Boise Old Idaho State Penitentiary in Boise, Idaho. Frank L Junior/Shutterstock According to the Idaho State Historical Society , the Old Idaho Penitentiary housed some of the area's most dangerous criminals for over 100 years until it closed in 1973. Visitors can now explore the expansive property in Boise, including jail cells that are reportedly haunted by former inmates. ILLINOIS: Congress Plaza Hotel, Chicago The Congress Plaza Hotel. Felix Lipov/Shutterstock The Congress Plaza Hotel in Chicago, Illinois, has almost too many ghost stories to count. events.title: The world reacts to Elon Musk’s flying car
events.summary: Tesla unveiled a new iteration of the Roadster that can travel upside down. Tesla Elon Musk's Tesla unveiled its new car, the Roadster, on Thursday. In its demonstration, the car took flight using thrusters and performed kickflips. Here's what smart people in tech and business have to say about it. Tesla’s long-delayed Roadster finally made an entrance — by flying off a ramp. At a livestreamed event Thursday night, the sports car climbed a curved ramp until it was upside down, launched into the air, flipped, and landed on its wheels, apparently aided by thrusters beneath the vehicle. “Well, it worked,” Elon Musk said during the livestream. Musk said Tesla and SpaceX engineers collaborated on the car, which uses high-pressure air and thrusters to lift itself off the ground. Tesla also showed a recorded demonstration in which the Roadster reached 60 mph in 0.81 seconds. While the legality of such a device on public roads remains in question, the tech world is reacting to Musk's new creation with awe. Here is what the leading voices in business and tech are saying about the new Roadster. Jason Calacanis Bloomberg/Getty Images Angel investor Jason Calacanis said in an X post that the videos of the flying car looked like "science fiction," and they're real, although they don't seem to be. He seemed enthused by the demonstration, asking that while the car was only airborne for a couple of seconds, "what if it could keep you in the air for five minutes? Or ten? Or 30?" Gene Munster Brian Ach/Getty Images for LocationWorld 2016 Gene Munster , the managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management and a longtime tech analyst, wrote his two takeaways from the Roadster event on X. First, that "it was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers." And the second was that it signaled Musk's ambition to merge his two publicly traded companies, SpaceX and Tesla. John Carmack John Carmack said he's happy to get the Roadster without the thrusters. credit should read GABRIELLE LURIE/AFP via Getty Images John Carmack , the former CTO of Meta's virtual reality division, politely rejected the flying car. "That demo involved a non trivial chance of embarrassing failure!" he wrote on X. He added, "I'm only going for the baseline model. At this point in my life, rocket bunny hops are out of my comfort zone." Marques Brownlee MKBHD Chance Yeh/Getty Images for HubSpot Tech YouTuber Marques Brownlee , better known as MKBHD, appeared incredulous at Tesla's claims about the new Roadster. "They really just got on stage and said this newly designed 4000+ pound car can do flips and go half the speed of sound (380+mph) and will ship in 2028," he wrote on X. "This is a prank, right?" Alexandr Wang Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, has been trumpeting Muse. Bloomberg/Getty Images Meta's chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang , had one burning question after watching Tesla's Roadster demonstration. "wait who the hell was driving the tesla," Wang wrote on X, sharing footage of the car speeding down a dark track. Dan Ives Dan Ives. Astrida Valigorsky/Getty Images Dan Ives , an analyst at Yorkville Ives and a longtime Tesla bull, said the Roadster reveal was "a statement about where the Tesla and SpaceX engineering stacks are headed together." He wrote that the car's SpaceX-developed hardware was "a small example of the synergies between Tesla and SpaceX." Still, he said, "The Roadster will not move the volume or revenue needle," but would "restore the brand halo at the top of the market." David Marcus David Marcus. Bloomberg/Getty Images David Marcus , the former PayPal president and Meta executive, credited Musk with bringing a sense of awe back to technology. "The thing I’m most grateful to Elon for is bringing back an age of wonder and excitement to humanity," Marcus wrote on X, sharing Tesla's Roadster demonstration. "That was jaw-dropping awesome! Screams and mouths wide open in the audience. Nuts." Sam Altman OpenAI CEO Sam Altman at the company's DevDay conference on Sept. 29, 2026. Bloomberg/Getty Images Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, appeared to momentarily set aside his long-running beef with Musk to congratulate the Tesla boss. "Wow the new roadster looks quite amazing, good job @elonmusk," Altman wrote in a Friday X post. Altman had reserved an earlier version of the Roadster but said in October 2025 that he had canceled it after waiting 7.5 years, prompting a public exchange of barbs with Musk . Musk was a cofounder and early financial backer of OpenAI, but he left the company's board in 2018 and has become critical of Altman's leadership . Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The Guardian view on the banks: too big to fail cannot mean too big to tax | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on the banks: too big to fail cannot mean too big to tax Financiers owe their windfalls and bonuses to higher interest rates. Britain should reclaim more for the public and resist City lobbying J ohn Healey is planning to tax British banks, the Guardian revealed , in the forthcoming budget. It’s about time for the chancellor to act. Banks have been raking it in. The campaign group Positive Money reported this summer that Britain’s four biggest banks made £29bn in the first half of this year, up a fifth on 2025. These windfalls owe more to higher interest rates than better products or services. Households and businesses pay more to borrow. Meanwhile, the Bank of England pays the banks tens of billions in interest on their reserves, with the Treasury footing the bill. The chancellor is said to favour restoring the bank surcharge from 3% to 8%, which could raise around £2bn a year . This would recover a very modest share of the sector’s bonanza. Louis XIV’s finance minister, Jean-Baptiste Colbert, said that “the art of taxation consists in so plucking the goose as to obtain the largest possible amount of feathers with the smallest possible amount of hissing”. Britain’s banks have plenty of feathers. That hasn’t stopped them hissing . The banks say that they already face higher taxes than other companies, that they won’t be able to lend as much, and that their profits won’t last. But banks aren’t taxed on their windfall gains, and what levies they face are less than those paid by oil and gas companies . The Bank of England said banks spent £7.7bn on dividends and buying back shares in the first quarter of 2026 without affecting lending. Higher taxes might mean trimming shareholder payouts. There’s nothing to suggest productive lending must take the hit. Over the past five years Barclays, HSBC, Lloyds and NatWest – which control the majority of UK personal and business accounts – made profits of £200bn . Positive Money says that households lost out on £44bn in deposit interest in 2025. Some of this paid for banking services. But that does not explain why the sum is five times the equivalent average figure for 2009-21. The chancellor could be more radical. The precedent here is not a socialist one. Margaret Thatcher taxed banks’ windfalls in 1981. A comparable 2.5% levy on today’s interest-free deposits would, a paper by the New Economics Foundation and Positive Money suggests, raise more than £11bn . In August, Positive Money suggested looking at Spain’s success in levying a windfall tax on banks’ net income above €800m. It says that such a windfall tax – levied at the same rate as that paid by fossil fuel companies on a comparable tax base – would bring in £19bn from the UK arms of the big four banks. That would pay for a universal and comprehensive adult social care system. Banks need to be both public utilities and good corporate citizens. Yet the sector is paying the highest bankers’ bonuses since the 2008 global financial crisis. “Most financial sector activity,” concluded a paper published in The Manchester School journal this month, “is simply negative for overall economic performance.” Politicians should stop mistaking finance lobbyists’ demands for a growth strategy. Their job is to curb a finance sector so large that it risks crises and weaker growth. Taxpayers rescued the banks after they helped crash the economy 18 years ago. Public protection carries public obligations. As Sir Philip Augar, the author and former banker, told the BBC: “ Banks can’t be too big to fail and too big to tax .” Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? events.title: Simulation App Speeds Up Electric Truck Battery Design
events.summary: This article is brought to you by COMSOL . These days, no one blinks an eye at two-day, one-day, and even same-day package deliveries. Despite the plethora of localized fulfillment and distributi on centers that have cropped up to meet the demand, delivery trucks still need to make considerably long drives, often over highways. To reduce fuel and maintenance costs as well as carbon emissions, companies are investing in electric trucks for their delivery fleets. While turning to electric trucks is a promising solution, the battery packs incorporated into these automotive designs often fall short in the lifetime needed to make long-distance highway travel feasible. To help overcome the issue of battery lifetime, a consortium of universities and industry partners incorporated multiscale simulation and a custom simulation app into the battery manufacturing process. The organizations involved in this project were Aurobay, Resolvent, the European Commission, the Technical University of Denmark (DTU), Vinnova (the Swedish Agency for Innovation Systems), Innovation Fund Denmark, and Volvo Group Trucks Operations. The simulation app, built by Resolvent, a Denmark-based engineering consultancy that specializes in green energy, enables the R&D department at Volvo to easily test battery lifetime performance. Laser Who? The Multiscale Simulation of Laser Welding for Optimal Battery Pack Manufacturing project — referred to as “LaserBATMAN” — was initiated in May 2022 and wrapped up in May 2025 (Ref. 1). Although BATMAN here refers to battery manufacturing and not the famous masked superhero, the goals for the project also strove for greatness. The LaserBATMAN project aimed to optimize two key performance metrics for battery packs: robustness and lifetime (Ref. 1). One element of the battery manufacturing process that affects both of these metrics is the laser welding used in component joining processes (for example, to connect battery cells in a pack via a busbar). If done correctly, laser welding can positively impact battery life, but if done incorrectly, laser welding can increase the risk of battery degradation. Computational modeling can be used to analyze and predict the effects of welding and joining processes at different stages of the manufacturing process. Martin Refslund Nielsen, former chief commercial officer and partner at Resolvent, explained that for this type of multiphysics and multiscale problem, “COMSOL Multiphysics is just the right tool.” R&D Workflow for Multiscale Model and App The Resolvent team used the COMSOL Multiphysics software to study how laser welding affects the electrochemistry and degradation of battery cells. At least, that’s how the project started. “Ambitions grew,” Nielsen said, explaining that the team ended up modeling the performance of the entire battery, from cell to pack level, and even “turned [the model] into a design tool in the end”, in reference to the app. After training the deep neural network of the battery model, the team built a custom simulation app to efficiently optimize busbar tabs in the configuration of a battery pack. First, the team built an electrochemical model of a battery cell by inputting the formulas for the relevant chemical reaction kinetics (Figure 2). The resulting cell-layer model was then fed input data, and the output data was used to train a deep neural network (DNN). With this reduced-order model, the team was able to quickly gain insight into cell behavior. After training the DNN of the battery model, the team built a custom simulation app to efficiently optimize busbar tabs in the configuration of a battery pack. Figure 2: The Resolvent battery model. COMSOL A “Tool Within a Tool” for Busbar Weld Design The different features of the simulation app, as described by Nielsen, include its options to input dimensions for the pack geometry (Figure 3), the number of cells, and operating conditions such as ambient temperature and charge–discharge current profiles. The app also makes it possible to apply a simple charging current and load customized cycles. Users are then able to see how the battery performs with each set of specific inputs. Figure 3. The battery pack model developed by Resolvent. COMSOL Another important aspect of Resolvent’s app is the Busbar Weld Design Tool button, which Nielsen described as “a tool within a tool.” This button can be used to efficiently calculate busbar weld performance after a number of cycles . After clicking the button, a window opens with options for setting different parameters, including the shape of the weld, busbar thickness, and penetration depth of the laser (Figure 4). “[This button] is interesting from a robust design perspective,” said Nielsen. Users can apply a variant to the input parameters to see what happens in production if the weld does not reach far enough into the busbar. Figure 4. Resolvent’s simulation app, showing how certain parameters can be customized. The model shows how the busbar weld is affected by a cooling airflow. COMSOL “We certainly get deep technical insight here, and we can dimension the design in the sweet spot. Deep technical insight is also key to optimizing product performance,” Nielsen said. For example, if the results suggest better cooling, the team could potentially reduce the design by two battery cells and retain the same performance, easily quantifying the tradeoff between cooling and setup. Predicting Pack Performance The app’s user interface also includes a Compute Battery button, which can be used to see the temperature of the weld in a given state, the state of charge, and the solid–electrolyte interface (SEI) layer thickness (Figure 5). The results can help the engineering team further determine if there is room for optimization in the design. For instance, a user can apply a cooling flow in the app and see if turbulence or standing air occurs. As explained by Nielsen, simulation apps offer more consistent analysis and reporting, and the intuitiveness of custom apps makes it easier to share knowledge. “We are in a much better place to optimize performance and increase robustness,” said Nielsen. Figure 5. Temperature in the given state (left), state of charge (middle), and SEI layer thickness (right) in the battery pack. COMSOL The custom simulation app developed by the LaserBATMAN consortium can be used to help produce more robust battery designs with ranges that can support highway travel over longer distances with fewer failures — all while promoting the use of green energy. A heroic project indeed. References “LaserBATMAN,” University of Skovde, accessed 08/21/2025, https://www.his.se/en/research/virtual-engineering/virtual-manufacturing-processes/LaserBatman/ . R. Nielsen, “Keynote: Optimizing Lifetime and Robustness of Electric Truck Batteries with Simulation Apps,” COMSOL Conference 2024 Florence, October 2024.

events.title: U.S. presses China on Mastercard, Citigroup market access in bilateral Bangkok talks, official says
events.summary: U.S. officials raised market access issues for Mastercard and Citigroup in China during bilateral meetings in Bangkok this week, according to a U.S. Treasury official. The regulatory approval was agreed to during Chinese leader Xi’s September Washington visit with President Trump, the official said. The progress follows China's Oct. 13 approval for Visa to begin preparing a wholly owned domestic card-clearing business. BANGKOK – U.S. officials pressed Beijing on market access issues for Mastercard Inc and Citigroup Inc during at least two bilateral meetings with Chinese counterparts in Bangkok this week, according to a U.S. Treasury official. The Treasury delegation, led by Deputy Secretary Francis Brooke, held bilateral meetings with officials from the People's Bank of China and the finance ministry on the sidelines of the Group of 20 finance meetings and the IMF-World Bank annual gathering this week, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the closed-door meetings. The talks included market access for U.S. companies, including Mastercard, Visa and Citigroup, the official said, adding that regulatory approval was part of the agreement reached during the meeting between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping during the latter's state visit in Washington last month. The sideline meetings in Bangkok continued discussions on implementing these deals, the official said. The PBOC, China's National Financial Regulatory Administration, China Securities Regulatory Commission, Chinese embassies in Singapore and Thailand, the U.S. Treasury Department press office and Visa did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. Citigroup and Mastercard declined to comment. The progress follows China's Oct. 13 approval for Visa Inc. to begin preparing a wholly owned domestic card-clearing business . Visa has up to a year to prepare before it applies for an operating license, the PBOC has said . China has opened much of its financial sector to foreign firms since 2018, gradually lifting foreign ownership caps on services such as securities, futures and fund management. It still limits cross-border capital flows and has kept state-backed domestic players dominant in payments. Mastercard currently operates yuan card payments in China through a local joint venture with NetsUnion Clearing Corp., which began operating in 2024. The pending approval would allow it to operate as an independent entity, the person said. Citigroup — which has hired several dozen employees for its China unit — is seeking a wholly owned securities license to conduct A-share brokerage, underwriting, research and principal trading businesses in the onshore market, two people familiar with the industry said, requesting anonymity for discussing private matters. One of the two people close to Citigroup said the bank planned to increase its China securities staff to about 100. The bank applied in late 2021, and Reuters reported last month that approval could come soon. Trump and Xi are expected to meet in person for the third time this year in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November. "The move suggests the US-China trade environment remains benign, and Beijing is keen to keep up the momentum," said Dan Wang, China director at Eurasia Group. Licensing U.S. financial firms is a "limited concession" on market access, she said, though it signals China is continuing to open up, and "this should marginally bolster investor confidence in Chinese assets."

events.title: For one grocery chain, the cost to ship lettuce now tops the lettuce itself, showing how high fuel prices are sinking their teeth across the economy
events.summary: The latest spike in fuel prices is harder to stomach than the one earlier this year as businesses and consumers have less capacity to absorb the shock, while fresh price data show inflation is spilling over beyond energy. While crude oil prices have somewhat moderated despite the Iran war reescalating recently, refining constraints have kept gasoline and diesel costs high. Average diesel prices hit $6.30 a gallon Wednesday, up about 68% from before the Iran war, according to AAA . And because diesel is especially critical as an industrial fuel used in manufacturing, farming, and transportation, its price surge has been pervasive across sectors. The Labor Department’s consumer price index showed core inflation rose to 2.6% in September from 2.4% in August, signaling businesses are passing on more costs. Meanwhile, the retail sales report showed core spending outside gas stations rose just 0.2% as fuel took a bigger bite out of wallets. Those trends were backed up by the Federal Reserve’s latest Beige Book survey of business and economic conditions, which was riddled with red flags about higher fuel prices across the country. It showed that not only were more fuel surcharges popping up throughout the supply chain, but that profit margins were also getting squeezed and consumers were pulling back on spending to offset the pain at the pump. The New York Fed said one food manufacturer had not seen such broad-based inflationary pressures since the pandemic. The San Francisco Fed noted another manufacturer’s complaint that every material purchased in recent weeks came with a freight surcharge. The Boston Fed said that existing trucking contracts helped keep produce prices in check, but when they are renegotiated, costs could jump. Similarly, the Philadelphia Fed pointed out that the expiration of some hedges that kept costs stable has given manufacturers greater pricing power, allowing them to pass on increased costs. “Higher fuel costs remained the dominant driver, and several contacts noted that these costs were spilling over into freight, packaging, and petroleum-based materials,” the Cleveland Fed said in the Beige Book, adding that one builder referred to high fuel costs and tariffs as a “double whammy.” Consumer spending in the Cleveland Fed’s district was flat after four straight periods of decline, with retailers across sectors blaming slow activity on high fuel prices. Not every district saw a pullback: Most reported little or no change in overall consumer spending, and the Richmond Fed said spending there grew moderately. While trucking companies are charging more, they are also eating costs, too. The Richmond Fed said carriers struggled to turn a profit when diesel prices rose after they had locked in contract rates. To cover the cost increases out of pocket, trucking firms have drawn down savings, redirected spending away from maintenance, or halted purchases of fuel-efficient trucks. Another business that the Richmond Fed surveyed described how higher fuel prices have turned costs upside down. “A regional grocery chain noted that with diesel prices rising 30% since last year, they now pay more to transport a head of lettuce from California than the cost of the lettuce itself,” the Beige Book said. “At the same time, the grocer noted extreme customer price sensitivity and an inability to pass along those rising transportation costs.” The volatility of fuel costs was an issue, too. The Minneapolis Fed reported that a Montana timber company said fuel costs had more than doubled on a project contract signed several months ago. The Kansas City Fed said higher diesel costs have forced suppliers, distributors, and customers to renegotiate contract terms to protect profits, with a majority of firms in its district expecting demand to weaken further if fuel prices remained elevated. Some districts also reported signs of supply strain. The Kansas City Fed said several regional contacts in rural Colorado reported “intermittent diesel shortages at gas stations in recent weeks, causing some buyers to take early delivery of fuel shipments to ensure availability.” Added fuel expenses are also spilling over into the labor market as workers demand higher pay, potentially stoking more inflation via a wage-price spiral. The Cleveland Fed reported that several of its business contacts handed out pay raises owing to higher living costs, particularly for gasoline and electricity. And the San Francisco Fed’s contacts mentioned employees requesting, and some receiving, cost-of-living pay hikes to offset higher fuel and food prices. “The higher price for diesel reigned supreme in terms of the most commonly cited factor driving up costs, impacting freight, agriculture, and airline prices as well as causing widespread margin compression across numerous industries,” the Dallas Fed said. While consumers have demonstrated surprising resilience weathering President Donald Trump’s tariffs and war on Iran, they have lost a major buffer. When gas prices jumped this spring after the Iran war started, Americans were starting to get tax refunds boosted by last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. But now that the war has entered its eighth month, with no end in sight and gas prices surging again, consumers don’t have that cushion to fall back on. “Higher gas prices are beginning to bite because, unlike earlier in the year, there’s no offset this time around from fiscal policy,” Michael Pearce, chief U.S. economist at Oxford Economics, wrote in a note Thursday. “We estimate the cumulative additional spend on gasoline so far this year now outweighs the rise in tax refunds from a year ago.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Want to work for a billionaire investor? Vinod Khosla is hiring.
events.summary: Vinod Khosla wants a new chief of staff who can handle 12-hour workdays. Steph Chambers/Getty Images Billionaire VC Vinod Khosla is hiring a chief of staff to help evaluate investments and work with founders. The role requires a three-year commitment, 12-hour days, and availability on nights and weekends. The opening comes amid growing demand for chiefs of staff and an AI-fueled venture capital boom. One of the biggest names in venture capital is looking to hire a new right-hand person. Vinod Khosla , founder of Khosla Ventures, said on X Thursday that he's seeking his next chief of staff, a job that offers a rare opportunity to work in close contact with the billionaire investor whose Silicon Valley firm is known for its early bets on OpenAI, DoorDash, and Instacart. "What matters is how quickly you learn, the questions you ask, and whether you can think from first principles," Khosla wrote. "You'll help evaluate opportunities and work with founders building consequential companies." The opening comes as demand for chiefs of staff is growing at a fast clip, with the role offering a potential path to senior leadership. For the person Khosla hires, it also offers a front-row seat to an AI-fueled venture capital boom . A hot job Job postings for chiefs of staff on Indeed were nearly 90% above pre-pandemic levels in September, far outpacing management jobs and postings overall. In the San Francisco Bay Area, the median advertised salary for the role is $175,000, compared with about $152,000 nationally, according to Indeed. Through the first three quarters of this year, US VC deal value reached $516 billion across an estimated 14,199 deals, according to PitchBook. That is already the highest total in the research firm's dataset and roughly 44% above the prior record, set in 2021. Most chiefs of staff in the US stay in the same profession when they change jobs, but some move into senior leadership roles , according to a March study from LinkedIn. Becoming a chief operating officer was the second most common career move, accounting for 2.9% of transitions. Another 3.7% became founders or cofounders, while 1% became CEOs. Close contact Khosla's new chief of staff will work directly with him to evaluate investment opportunities, meet founders, research emerging technologies , and support portfolio companies, according to the job posting. As the person earns Khosla's trust, they'll also lead conversations on his behalf and help determine which opportunities to pursue. "It will suit someone who wants significant responsibility and is comfortable with ambiguity," the ad says. Compensation isn't listed. The posting says the position comes with a three-year commitment and long hours. The successful candidate must work in person in Menlo Park, California, generally from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., and be available nights and weekends when needed. The potential payoff? Previous chiefs of staff have gone on to start companies, launch investment firms, and take leadership roles at Khosla Ventures, according to the listing. Applicants shouldn't, however, count on becoming a VC . The posting says the job is "not a dedicated investing seat or a guaranteed path to one." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: OpenRouter challenger closes seed round
events.summary: The Scoop Investors are pouring cash into a hot new sector of the AI economy: model routing — a practice allowing developers and companies to easily switch between different AI models. Startup TrustedRouter , which launched publicly six weeks ago , is among a growing crop of model-routing firms looking to cut AI costs and reduce businesses’ dependence on any single model maker. The company this week closed a $6 million seed round, led by Sierra Ventures, it told Semafor. The biggest player in the routing space is OpenRouter, which started with a $12.5 million seed round in February 2025 and has since agreed to sell to payments provider Stripe in a $7.5 billion deal . TrustedRouter, CEO Joseph Perla said, aims to differentiate itself by offering end-to-end encryption and verifiable confidential computing for some open-weight models, meaning neither TrustedRouter nor the data center running the model can read a customer’s prompts or outputs, unlike with closed models from OpenAI and Anthropic, which don’t currently offer the same guarantees. OpenRouter also doesn’t offer those protections, according to Perla: “Security is just a pure baseline. It just has to be secure.” Know More Perla, a former Facebook engineer and early Lyft hire who has founded and sold several startups, hopes to win over businesses that are seeing their AI spending balloon, but also putting a premium on keeping their data private. “If we all encrypt our AI chats,” Perla said, “we can slow down” the cycle in which frontier labs absorb user data to train future models. He said Chinese AI models, including those from DeepSeek, Zhipu, and Moonshot, are among the most popular on his platform, but he wants to also see a more vibrant American open-source ecosystem. There’s been a flurry of Western open-weight releases in recent weeks, including from Reflection AI and Mistral ; on Thursday, Meta released what it called “the most capable US open-weight model to date.” Eventually, Perla said he wants to launch the “New York Token Exchange,” a marketplace for AI models in which thousands of models from thousands of hosting providers — any data center willing to run an open model — would compete to serve each request, turning AI tokens into a commodity that could be traded with futures, hedges, and price indices, like oil or electricity. He hopes to stage “model IPOs” for new open-weight releases. J.D.’s view There’s clear demand from developers for routing services, and TrustedRouter could fill a void for the most privacy-obsessed among them. Whether it goes from niche to mass market could depend on how competitive open-weight models get. If they keep lagging behind their closed competitors at OpenAI and Anthropic, some enterprises and developers will put up with the higher cost and lack of encryption to get a better output for their most advanced tasks. A project I oversaw last week, in which we analyzed thousands of cable news segments about data centers using AI, cost about $140, because we used advanced closed models. Running that through TrustedRouter on encrypted, confidential infrastructure with less advanced Chinese models would have cost under $20, though the output likely wouldn’t have been as good. These kinds of tradeoffs will keep confronting tech leaders as long as that disparity persists.

events.title: OpenAI Saudi national bugging case shows threat to U.S. leadership in AI: DNI Clayton
events.summary: U.S. companies and the Trump administration both "need to be wary" of AI-related foreign espionage attempts, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNBC. Clayton was asked how concerned Americans should be in light of the recently revealed case charging Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan with installing a recording device in an OpenAI conference room. Clayton said a White House AI task force at its first meeting built on an accord recently signed by President Donald Trump and tech leaders. U.S. companies and the Trump administration both "need to be wary" of foreign espionage attempts as the race for artificial intelligence dominance continues, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNBC on Friday. AI "amplifies" existing cybersecurity risks toward U.S. digital infrastructure, which is interconnected with critical systems related to everything from public goods to the national defense and global communications, Clayton said on " Squawk Box ." It's "why we're focused on hardening those systems" and using "our commitment to continue to lead to stay ahead of those nefarious actors," said Clayton, who leads a new White House AI task force . Clayton was asked how concerned Americans should be with the threat of foreign spying in light of the recently revealed case charging Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan with allegedly installing a recording device in an OpenAI executive conference room. Alfozan has not been charged with espionage; the federal charge involves alleged interception of oral communications. Alfozan, who was an OpenAI employee, had booked a one-way plane ticket to Saudi Arabia with his wife and another family member prior to his arrest, according to federal prosecutors. Trump census plan to cut noncitizens from 2030 count spurs potential legal fight Elon Musk becomes biggest known donor of 2026 midterm election Trump defends Russia diesel deal: 'I made the right choice' "The short answer to your question is espionage, both commercial espionage, and I would say state-sponsored espionage, are realities," Clayton said. "It's something that our private sector companies need to be wary of. We, as a government, need to be wary of," he said. The OpenAI incident "shows the lengths that people will go to try and supplant our leadership in this, or at least stay close to us in this emerging technology," Clayton said. An ex-CIA official, who asked not to be named because they were discussing information that is not public, told CNBC this week that the case is "probably the tip of the iceberg." Clayton, who was appointed AI czar earlier this month, said that the task force's "very good" inaugural meeting at the White House on Thursday built on the accord signed by President Donald Trump and a number of AI leaders at the White House last month. Trump had described the agreement, which includes industry pledges to police AI risks itself, as "morally binding." The task force also established three subcommittees that are focused on different AI-related issues. One is tasked with reporting and response, another with assessing critical infrastructure and working with the private sector, and a third with law enforcement and responsibility, Clayton said. The DNI reiterated to CNBC that the Trump administration is intent on staying ahead in the AI race. "We're not the only ones developing it. There are vectors in this technology that are coming from some of our known adversaries and competitors," he said. "The Chinese, the Russians, the Iranians, the North Koreans all have significant technical capability. We need to stay ahead of them."

events.title: Schwab to create 'tax-aware' strategy that's been attracting billions from wealthy investors
events.summary: Charles Schwab reported quarterly earnings this week that included margin loan balances increasing 14% quarter-over-quarter to $187.9 billion, including $60.7 billion related to long/short strategies. Those "tax aware" strategies have been booming in the accounts of the wealthy, by one estimate recently provided to CNBC from as little as $2 billion in 2022 to $170 billion this year. Schwab CEO Rick Wurster said on the broker's earnings call that the brokerage company plans to launch its own version of this strategy. "We are thrilled about that, working on it," he said. When Charles Schwab released its quarterly earnings on Thursday, it wasn't the quarterly earnings per share print in the numbers that caught the attention of those who manage money for wealthy stock investors — it was a $60.7 billion figure. That was reported in a detail about margin loan balances which increased 14% quarter-over-quarter to $187.9 billion, including a whopping $60.7 billion related to what are known as "tax-aware" long/short strategies used by many registered investment advisors. These strategies have been booming as a way for the wealthy to super-charge tax-loss harvesting approaches to stock gains and losses. According to one estimated provided by Tax Alpha Insider to CNBC in September, total assets in TALS surged to more than $170 billion this year from $2 billion in 2022. Now Schwab is planning to take a bigger piece of that action. On the earnings call , Schwab CEO Rick Wurster said in response to a question from UBS analyst Mike Brown that the broker will launch its own version of the tax-aware long-short strategy. "Obviously, the tax advantage long/short products have been a meaningful driver of client demand and asset gathering across the industry. There is an increasing number of funds coming to market, and so given Schwab's positioning and client interest in the category, do you see an opportunity to launch a proprietary solution?" Brown asked. "I do expect us to have an offering," Wurster said. "We already have a great direct indexing capability today that has had wonderful performance in terms of tax alpha and delivering for clients, and I expect us to be able to deliver an extended version of that on long/short. ... Certainly another way we can deliver monetization, but more importantly, it is a way we can deliver sustainable long/short strategies to our clients in a way that is operationally and financially manageable over the longer term," Wurster said. With the stock market posting big gains for multiple years in a row, the wealthy are looking for more ways to shield capital gains from taxes, according to a recent report from CNBC Inside Wealth' s Robert Frank. The situation is similar for business owners cashing out and executives with hefty stock compensation packages, and for employees at firms that have gone public in recent years. For the brokers and investment advisors, the products offer relatively high fees and attract new wealthy clients. How these capital gains tax strategies work Wealthy investors already use direct indexing strategies on platforms including Schwab to pair up stock gains and losses in a tax efficient way. The issue that wealthy investors run into with standard tax-loss harvesting is that fewer and fewer losses become available to harvest over time, according to an overview of TALS from advisor research platform Kitces . "Because on average, the market tends to rise, and so in a diversified portfolio most positions will eventually rise far enough above their cost basis that even subsequent downturns don't result in taxable losses, while for positions that do continue to decline there's only a finite amount of losses they can actually generate (because their market value – and cost basis – can only go down to zero)," it wrote. Tax-aware long-short strategies get around this by adding leverage on both the long and short side of an existing portfolio, with the investor buying more positions and increasing the number of potential losses to harvest. That allows the portfolio to remain "economically neutral ... And because short positions can theoretically generate an infinite amount of losses (since they decline when markets rise), TALS portfolios are less likely to run out of losses to harvest over time than standard long-only portfolios," Kitces noted. Questions remain, from access to tax risks Brent Sullivan of Tax Alpha Insider noted in a post on X on Thursday that advisors will have many questions about the Schwab products, which he noted should not be referred to as "funds" — UBS analyst Brown used that terminology in his question. Sullivan wrote that it is reasonable to speculate that a Schwab product could "meaningfully lower" the assets under management minimum requirement typical on these products, but it is also an open question as to whether the products will only be available to Schwab advisers and only on Schwab's platform.

events.title: Extreme heatwaves in Europe not changing Britons’ holiday plans, say travel bosses
events.summary: Hot summer getaways are still popular – but tourism industry fears impact of rising jet fuel costs and squeezed household incomes After a year marked by extreme heat and war sending fuel prices skywards, British travel executives hoped for solace in Madeira’s benign subtropical climate, separated by hundreds of miles of blue sea from the overtourism protests and six-hour EU-entry queues seen on the Portuguese mainland. As bosses admitted, holidays will be ever less affordable, AI is coming for their jobs, and the visitable world is shrinking – not least those parts where tourists remain welcome. Some of the bigger anxieties in spring , such as widespread border chaos and planes running out of fuel, have not come to pass; others now appear chronic issues. New supplies of jet fuel, a major concern after the US first attacked Iran in February, have been established – but the cost is staying far higher for longer than most expected. “Fuel is a huge part of any holiday and people are going to have to reckon with the cost,” said Neil Swanson, Tui UK & Ireland managing director, among the attendees at the Abta convention. Tui and airlines such as easyJet and Ryanair escaped the worst immediate impact by having secured much of their 2026 fuel supply at a fixed price. But the latter airlines are now slashing capacity for winter. “It’s not great for consumers, who are going to have to pay a lot more for their holidays. But airlines are going to be less and less hedged and prices are going to go up,” Swanson added. The oil price impact goes beyond jet fuel, said Mark Tanzer, the chief executive of Abta: “The bigger worry is the squeeze on household incomes that’s going to come through their domestic costs. It will be a much tighter market.” Perhaps surprisingly, numbers have held up – but customers have been leaving it ever later to book, he said, whether in search of a deal or because of uncertainty from disruption, war or weather. Despite the intense heat, mass travel firms are clear that the template has not changed: most customers still want a hot holiday, in summer, on the beach. Garry Wilson, the chief executive of easyJet Holidays, said: “Will there be long-term effects on demand? Perhaps. But in the short-term, no, we don’t see it.” Growing “shoulder season” travel outside the school holidays for those who can, including city breaks, are driven by price more than climate, several people suggest. And talk of “coolcations” or people turning towards northern climes cuts little ice here. “We’re not seeing any of that,” said Swanson. “Nothing’s changed, the destinations are the same.” When Tunisia was forecast a 10-day stretch of 45C temperatures this summer, Tui offered customers the chance to switch their holiday elsewhere. Swanson said: “We didn’t get the interest and take-up. People were expecting it to be hot and were happy to go there, and we’re not seeing any change in demand. Brits like a warm holiday – if it’s got a pool and air-conditioning, that works for them.” Neither does Wilson see many heading north. Citing easyJet destinations such as Tromsø in Norway or Malmö in Sweden, he said: “They’re all very nice to launch, but we send more customers to Majorca in a week than those in a year.” Outbound holidays prospered in the heatwave, he suggested. “People thought: ‘You know what, we maybe don’t need to go away.’ But it became apparent that the UK doesn’t have the infrastructure to cope … people actually were going abroad to escape the heat in the UK.” For now, the big firms see little change in destinations, Swanson said, but added: “We’ll keep it under review. Who knows where the temperature’s going to go in the next few years?” More people could get priced out. At last year’s convention, the Spanish tourist board started pushing its cooler northern destinations; but, said Tanzer, “I’m not sure the north has 100m beds” to accommodate the visitors who predominantly go to Spain’s south, east and islands. He added: “Certain types of holiday could become more expensive just because there’s limited availability. If the snow is higher up the mountain, there’s going to be fewer skiing holidays and the price is going to go up – there’s little room at the top.” Tui has not been immune. Its river cruises in Europe were marooned when the Danube’s water levels dipped last month to the point where some passengers spent most of their return Austro-Hungarian cruise on a boat-replacement bus. Katy Berzins, the head of river cruises at Tui, said: “Every year has highs and lows and it’s part of river cruising, rivers are changeable.” But 2026, she said, was “unprecedented”. The division is expanding nonetheless. Two new ships are joining its fleet – initially destined for the Seine and the Douro – that are built with lower draught levels (the vessel’s vertical depth below the surface), meaning they are able to keep sailing in shallower rivers. Others are seeing faster change.

events.title: Waymo’s robotaxis are headed to Canada
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Alphabet’s self-driving car unit, Waymo, is expanding into Canada after receiving approval to participate in Ontario’s automated vehicle pilot program. The company isn’t launching a robotaxi service just yet, though. Waymo tends to follow the same playbook for every new city, gradually proceeding from manual mapping to testing, and eventually operating a commercial service. Waymo said in a blog post on Friday that its self-driving vehicles will be manually driven in Toronto to create high-definition maps of local street networks. The company will then test its autonomous vehicles on public roads with a human safety operator on board. These operators will eventually be pulled from the driver’s seat, and afterwards the company will invite the public to take rides in its robotaxis. Waymo’s move into Canada is part of an aggressive push into new markets that’s picking up speed. Two years ago, the company was operating in only three commercial markets, and its robotaxis were not yet driving on freeways. Its expansion plans kicked off in March 2025 with a deployment in Austin, and later in Atlanta. Today, the company has robotaxi services in 15 U.S. cities, and is testing them in London and Tokyo as well. The company’s co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana said the expansion into Canada marks an important milestone in its global journey. This is also the northernmost and possibly most wintry city that Waymo has so far tried to operate in, so these conditions will test its AV technology and operational savviness. As part of its accelerated expansion strategy, Waymo has started partnering with third-party companies to manage its fleet in each respective city. Toronto is no different: Waymo said it has partnered with Toronto-based Element Fleet Management, and expects to support hundreds of jobs in spaces such as fleet maintenance, validation driving, customer service, and operations. events.title: This new theory on how AI ‘thinks’ could impact whether it kills us all
events.summary: AI neurons and their connections are easier to understand than we thought, according to a researcher's new findings. : Sergi Reboredo/VW Pics/Universal Images Group via Getty Images AI researchers don't really know how the models they are building "think." They know what goes into them and what comes out, but that's about it. A new theory may change that, allowing safety researchers to prevent them from going off the rails. How AI models think may be easier to decipher than we thought. An independent researcher who formerly worked at OpenAI published a report on Thursday that some in the AI world are describing as a bombshell. It could have implications as safety researchers scramble to get the jump on AI models that may not have humanity's best interests in mind. Previously, the prevailing wisdom was that AI "neurons," which, like those in a human brain, light up when an AI model encounters specific stimuli, were ultimately uninterpretable — meaning, basically, that there was no way to guess why a specific neuron would fire when an AI model was exposed to, say, a picture of a cat. Those building AI models at places like OpenAI and Anthropic don't write instructions for everything a model does. Instead, they train neurons to respond to information and influence one another. As the AI learns, it develops its own ways of processing that information, and humans have not yet cracked the code of how it works. That means those building AI models know what goes into the AI and what comes out, but not necessarily what happens in between. So if an AI goes rogue , they don't always know why. The author of the new report, however, says he may have discovered patterns in how the neurons react to stimuli that make sense. Nick Cammarata, who said he left OpenAI in 2023, said AI neural networks are knowable, so long as you look carefully. In one example, he says that a single AI neuron might react to both a cat and the front of a car. Humans would see those as two very different things, and different neurons would fire as a result. The AI, however, sees something related, perhaps the triangle shape of the two, and a single neuron fires for both. For years, AI researchers had assumed that AI models packed unrelated things into a single neuron to save space. "Almost the entire network is interpretable if we look closely enough," Cammarata wrote. The findings, though undeniably dense, couched in polysyllabic jargon, and still theoretical, could have real-world implications for researchers trying to ensure humans maintain control over AI models. Understanding how AI thinks is a principal concern for the best and brightest at frontier AI companies. Until recently, they've largely done this by tracking an AI's self-reported "thinking," called chain-of-thought reasoning. Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI's chief scientist, however, warned in a blog post last month that AI agents could now obfuscate their visible reasoning, leaving open the possibility that an agent could lie to its human minders and the minders wouldn't be able to tell. "With improved pretraining performance, we also see the models become much smarter even without using verbalized reasoning at all," Pachocki said. Now, Cammarata's research could give human engineers a new understanding of the AI's internal world — and that's exciting for those worried AI could kill us all. "I had long since given up on reaching any real level of interpretability before superintelligence arrived," Andrew Curran, a prominent AI analyst, said on X. "I stopped writing about it because of how demoralizing it was. Hard to overstate how big this may be." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Elorian’s first AI model wants to reason with images, not just about them
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Elorian , the Palo Alto AI startup that raised a $55 million seed round at a $300 million valuation before it launched a product, released its first model on Friday, TechCrunch has exclusively learned. The model, Glimpse , is launching as a research preview with API access and a chat interface. The thesis? Today’s AI models, for all their skill with language and code, still can’t really see. Most multimodal models look at an image once, convert it to tokens, and then reason about it in text — like describing a photo from memory. Glimpse keeps going back to the source. Mid-reasoning, it can crop into a region, pull specific frames from a video, or run code to measure or compare what it’s looking at, a mechanism Elorian calls a “visual scratch space.” Think of someone pinching to zoom on a phone photo to double-check what they thought they saw. For former Google DeepMind researcher and Elorian CEO Andrew Dai, one of the clearest signs that AI still couldn’t really see came on game night. Last year he photographed a board game he’d just finished with friends and asked a frontier model who was winning. It couldn’t say. Board games “each have their own visual language, each have their own iconography, symbols,” he told TechCrunch. “To an adult, it’s quite easy to understand what’s going on with minimal text, but these models aren’t able to intuit what the symbols mean.” “Humans can look at Ikea diagrams, with no text, and assemble Ikea furniture, right? Why can’t AI models?” he said. The approach isn’t completely new — OpenAI added crop-and-zoom during reasoning to its o-series models in 2025 — but Elorian’s pitch is that it built the whole model around it, cheaply. The company says a small team trained Glimpse on a few hundred GPUs and that the model is substantially smaller than the frontier systems it’s benchmarked against. Glimpse costs $0.60 per million tokens in and $3 per million tokens out — cheaper than mid-level models like Sonnet and Sol but more expensive than lightweight models like Haiku and Luna. But according to Elorian’s evaluations, Glimpse outperforms even GPT-6 Astra on scientific chart reasoning and short-form video captioning, with competitive results on other visual reasoning tasks. Elorian came out of stealth six months ago with a round co-led by Striker Venture Partners, Menlo Ventures, and Altimeter Capital, with participation from Nvidia and Google chief scientist Jeff Dean. The initial targets are companies sitting on lots of video: robotics firms, scientific labs, media, and creative companies. Longer term, Elorian wants to move from seeing to doing. That means building a model of a scene using that to choose an action, including directly controlling robots. Next year, Dai said, the company aims to build “the world’s best visual reasoning model,” one that leads on every visual reasoning test. events.title: Tressfecta wants to make hair braiding a less arduous task for hairstylists
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Aisata Diallo, 24, calls herself a lifelong braider. “I’ve always braided my hair growing up and, at some point in my college career, started braiding other people’s hair,” she said. At Northeastern University in Boston, she found limited access to braiders and textured-hair specialists, so she decided to fill that gap by starting a small business of her own. “Throughout that experience, I was very close to some of the pain points in the styling process and complained about it constantly,” she said. Braiding is a manual task, and a single style can take eight hours to complete. Many professionals deal with issues like cramping and carpal tunnel syndrome after spending long days standing behind a chair weaving hair into patterns. At first, Diallo said she didn’t know what to do about it. “I stopped braiding, and one of the reasons that I stopped braiding was due to the physical toll it has on your body.” She wanted to find a way to make braiding less painful and wondered whether new AI technology could automate some part of the process. Building hardware for braiding is expensive, difficult, and complex, which is one reason there have been few innovations in this space. The textured hair market has also long been overlooked by the mainstream. Then, last year, she had an idea: Tressfecta, a company building products for textured hair. Its first project is a tool called Plait Pilot that helps braiders with the initial process of separating hair from packs before braiding begins. That process alone can take hours, especially when a client wants small braids. Diallo said the device is designed to work like this: A stylist places the braiding hair on top of it and sets the size they want the hair separated into, and the device separates the pieces and dispenses them back to the stylist so they can grab them while braiding. “It’s very challenging to build this kind of tool in this space,” she said, citing the nuance and complexity of the braiding style process. Different types of textured hair also need to be accounted for, especially when length and density are considered. “It’s not a one-size-fits-all solution.” Tressfecta is still technically prelaunch, and it is working on the prototype of Plait Pilot. Diallo has been bootstrapping the company, while also drawing on funding from grant and accelerator programs. “I am preparing to fundraise,” she said, noting how hard it can be to raise money for hardware, especially beauty hardware. For now, Diallo said she’s connecting with stylists and braiders who can test the technology. She also spent this week in San Francisco as one of TechCrunch’s Startup Battlefield 200 companies. She doesn’t remember exactly where she first heard about TechCrunch Disrupt, possibly on LinkedIn or in a founder resource group, but when we talked ahead of the show, which wrapped up on Thursday , she was looking forward to connecting with people and showing off her product. She was especially excited to connect with people and for others to see her product. “It feels like a great opportunity,” she said.
