events.title: In ‘You Can See Everything,’ Elizabeth Holmes meets her equal in comedian Nathan Fielder
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. “Isn’t it weird that I, like, did a TV show about kind of a business scam, and you got in trouble for like … a business scam?” comedian and filmmaker Nathan Fielder gently asks Elizabeth Holmes. One month before the notorious Theranos CEO surrendered to begin her 11-year criminal fraud sentence in 2023, Holmes and her husband contacted A24 as a last-ditch effort to exonerate her in the public eye, suggesting they send a film crew to document her final days of freedom. Alongside director Lance Oppenheim, Fielder — a cringe-comedy mastermind whose work often walks the line between fact and fiction — embraced the impossible project of figuring out who the infamous Stanford dropout really is. “I never actually made that connection,” says Holmes. “I think it’s a pretty different situation.” No one is better prepared than Fielder to probe the depths of Holmes’ psyche. His satirical docu-reality show “Nathan for You” catapulted him to cult stardom as he assumed the role of an exaggerated, deadpan version of himself who tries to help struggling small businesses by executing asinine interventions. In one early episode that went viral , Fielder convinces a coffee shop to change its name to “Dumb Starbucks” as a marketing stunt, but consults a lawyer to help him toe the flimsy line of parody law and escape legal trouble. “If you just said that, you know, Theranos was a comedy bit, maybe you could get off scot-free,” Fielder says to Holmes. “I was just kind of making a little joke. Maybe it was in bad taste.” We already know that Elizabeth Holmes is not innocent. What we still can’t figure out, though, is whether she really, truly believes she did nothing wrong. Even as she sat on trial — listening to testimonies from investors who lost hundreds of millions of dollars, whistleblowers who were silenced when they flagged that Theranos’ blood-testing devices didn’t work, and patients who acted on incorrect blood test results — Holmes never wavered. Across Fielder’s body of metatextual comedy, even his most reverent fans can’t quite figure out when he’s acting, when he’s being himself, and if Fielder himself even knows where to draw that line anymore. In that way, Fielder is just like Holmes: After over a decade in the public eye, onlookers remain captivated by each of their ambiguous personas. “The world believes a reality about me that isn’t true,” she tells Fielder. “I know I didn’t commit any crime.” [The rest of this review contains spoilers.] Early on in filming, The New York Times had just published a profile of Holmes, which was widely criticized at the time for allowing Holmes to portray herself as an innocent mom deprived of the chance to watch her kids grow up. And yet, Holmes and her husband, hotel heir Billy Evans, were livid about the article. At one point in an interview, Holmes tells the Times reporter that she wasn’t offended by actress Amanda Seyfried’s portrayal of her in Hulu’s miniseries “ The Dropout ” because “they’re not playing me. They’re playing a character I created.” She and her husband insist that the quote was taken out of context. They claim that they have evidence that Holmes actually said, “They’re playing a character they created,” relieving her from any implication that she admitted to concocting an inauthentic persona as CEO of Theranos. Fielder asks Evans multiple times to share this evidence so he can prove that Holmes was misquoted. He never does. Once Holmes reports to prison, Fielder is agonized as he tries to make something out of his month of footage. He calls in the perfect sidekick to help him dissect her confounding behavior: the very actress who portrays her in “The Dropout.” Fielder plays Seyfried a brutal clip from his time with Holmes, when he tries watching “The Dropout” with the subject of the series. When they get to a tense scene involving Holmes’ manipulative ex-boyfriend and former Theranos partner in crime Sunny Balwani — who is also now in prison — Holmes can no longer bear to watch this fictional version of herself. She turns away and cries. In other words, Seyfried is watching Holmes react to Seyfried’s portrayal of Holmes, who was probably also playing a character herself. But Seyfried is not the only one creating a crude approximation of the real Elizabeth. Evans has constructed a lifelike AI avatar of his wife, trapped inside of a large vertical screen that he wheels over to the dinner table to sit with him and his kids as though she’s actually there. The remainder of the film is a constellation of colliding personas. Though it’s a nonfiction documentary, it’s clear that everyone involved is, to some extent, also performing for the cameras. How could they not?

events.title: Tesla's vision for the future: Manually driving your own car will be a luxury for the rich
events.summary: The Roadster's price is likely at least $250,000. Musk said it will be Tesla's only vehicle that humans drive themselves. Tesla Want to physically drive a Tesla in the future? The Roadster will be your only option, Musk said. The car is not cheap. Musk has compared today's driving to elevator operators. Want to physically drive a Tesla in the future? Get ready to pay up. On Thursday, Tesla CEO Elon Musk unveiled the new Roadster with a gravity-defying demo . The car suctioned to the side of a vertical ramp, drove upside down, briefly flew, stuck the landing, and later bunny-hopped and twirled over a standing lineup of other Tesla vehicles. The stunts were choreographed with autonomy, Musk said — but Roadster owners will eventually be able to manually take the wheel. That will make it unique in Tesla's lineup. "This will actually be, long-term, the only manually driven car that Tesla makes," Musk said on stage, before Tesla's lead engineer, Lars Moravy, added, "You gotta have some fun sometimes." Tesla hasn't revealed the car's final price, but we know it'll firmly be in the luxury supercar tier. The company's reservation queue asks customers who want the base Performance trim to fork over a $50,000, due within 10 days. That reservation, alone, is nearly the price of an average car in America , and it doesn't capture the car's final price. Our best pricing ballpark dates back to 2017, when Tesla first said it was bringing back the Roadster. At the time, the automaker collected $250,000 payments from people who wanted a Founder Series model. Meanwhile, Tesla has been ramping up its autonomy push for its more price-conscious vehicles. In September, it started rolling out the Cybercab — a vehicle that leans so heavily into self-driving that it has no steering wheel, brake pedals, or side mirrors. Tesla says it wants to eventually sell those cars to consumers at less than $30,000 apiece . On recent earnings calls, Musk has also praised the recurring revenue from subscriptions of Full Self-Driving (Supervised) from Cybertruck, Model Y, and Model 3 owners. Musk has talked a lot about a world where driving becomes obsolete. He has compared driving a car to operating an elevator, a profession that was largely phased out in the mid-20th century as elevators became automated. "Now, you just get in, press a button and a modern elevator, if inspected regularly, is extremely safe," he wrote on X in March. Treating driving like elevator operation requires a pretty big leap. Driving is still a hobby, a sport, and — for many people — a point of pride. By Moravy's own admission, driving is fun. There's still a chance in Musk's vision of his carmaker's future that drivers can control their own Tesla and lean into that fun. They'll just need to open their checkbooks. events.title: Tesla unveils long-delayed Roadster developed with SpaceX, fueling merger speculation
events.summary: Tesla revealed its next-generation Roadster from a SpaceX test site in Texas on Thursday. CEO Elon Musk first debuted the Roadster refresh concept in 2017 but Tesla has since missed every targeted delivery date. Tesla said the new Roadster, equipped with SpaceX thrusters, can accelerate from zero to 60 miles per hour in less than a second. Tesla showed off its long-delayed next-generation Roadster on Thursday, almost a decade after Elon Musk's company started taking deposits for the electric sports car. The event was livestreamed from a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, near Waco, starting at 7:55 p.m. local time, or 8:55 p.m. ET. In attendance along with Musk were design leader Franz von Holzhausen and Lars Moravy, vice president of vehicle engineering. "You're going to see some crazy stuff tonight," Musk said. "You're going to see the results of what happens when you have a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company." Tesla's original Roadster, designed and engineered by a team led by founding CEO Martin Eberhard, was based on a Lotus Elise chassis and was first delivered in 2008, selling for roughly $100,000 in small volumes until 2012. The next-generation Roadster is expected to be a high-end, low-volume model that relies on SpaceX technology to enable it to hover. While Musk fanatics expressed their excitement on social media, the Roadster isn't likely to have any material financial impact on the company. At the event, Musk and his team showcased a white sports car that raced up a curved ramp, then clung to it upside down and vaulted off it, flipping in mid-air and hovering slowly before landing on the ground. The two-seater can go from zero to 60 miles per hour in under a second, according to Tesla's timer, a feat Moravy demonstrated for the live audience. Musk said the next-generation Roadster would enter production in 2028. The price wasn't announced, and the company didn't disclose specifications about other performance-level variants of the new Roadster. It was unclear whether the vehicle would be street-legal, with Musk saying on stage that, "This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car." The Roadster unveiling has added to speculation of a possible merger between Tesla and SpaceX. For years, Musk's companies have worked with and paid each other, even sharing some personnel. The collaboration has increased in 2026, with speculation about a possible SpaceX-Tesla tie-up swirling since the aerospace and defense company went public in June. SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell told CNBC ahead of the IPO that a merger "might make Elon's life a little easier." Barclays analyst Dan Levy predicted in a note out this week that such a transaction could happen before the end of 2026. SpaceX is currently valued at about $2 trillion, while Tesla has a market cap of $1.4 trillion, making them two of just 12 U.S. companies worth at least $1 trillion. Tesla reopened reservations for the refreshed Roadster in recent weeks, accepting $50,000 deposits from prospective buyers in the U.S., Canada and China. Musk first promoted the refreshed Roadster concept at an event in November 2017 , and the following June in a series of tweets. He wrote at that time, "SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car." The engines would improve speed and braking, and may "even allow a Tesla to fly." The prototype Tesla showed on Thursday is built to be as lightweight as possible with a steer-by-wire system, steering yoke, and an array of technologies developed by SpaceX, including thrusters, carbon overlay pressure vessels and diffusers, and powerful fans that enable the car to do some gymnastics. One feature Tesla left out of its forthcoming Roadster is the company's "FSD" or automated driving system. Musk said the new Roadster will be the last vehicle the company produces that's intended to be controlled by a human driver. Tesla started taking $50,000 deposits for the revamped Roadster in 2017, but has since missed every targeted delivery date. As recently as last October, Musk was hyping a Roadster demo that he hoped would happen before the end of 2025. That didn't take place either. Musk's former friend and OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman mocked the Tesla CEO in posts on X last year over the extreme delays, showing screenshots of his reservation and refund requests. "I really was excited for the car! And I understand delays," Altman wrote. "But 7.5 years has felt like a long time to wait." Altman got his refund, and the two ended up in court earlier this year over a separate matter related to OpenAI's governance and ownership structure. Others have kept their reservations.

events.title: That Y2K feeling: Why today's economy resembles 2000
events.summary: It was an economy bursting at the seams: robust growth powered by a tech boom, low unemployment, elevated inflation and Fed rate hikes to try to cool things down. The big picture: That was the situation in the year 2000, and it reminds us a great deal of the conditions in 2026. The worrying part, however, is this: Then, as now, there were early warning signs that the technological boom powering the good times may not last forever. And indeed, the cracks that appeared in the tech sector in 2000 would spill over into a broader bear market and mild recession in 2001. We're not predicting that this time. History only rhymes; it doesn't repeat. But it is a historical episode worth weighing when thinking about the range of possibilities for how things may go in 2027 and beyond — particularly this week, as the debt markets funding the AI build-out have wobbled. Flashback: While 2001 was a nasty year for the U.S. economy — a full-fledged tech bust exacerbated by the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks — the year before was pretty great by nearly every measure. The unemployment rate reached a multi-decade low of 3.8% in April 2000 and closed the year at a mere 3.9%. GDP rose 4.1% for the full year, powered by stunning rates of productivity growth. It coincided, however, with high inflation, driven particularly by surging energy costs. The Consumer Price Index was up 3.4% over the course of the year. Zoom in: Against that backdrop, the Alan Greenspan-led Fed felt compelled to try to cool things down, lest that inflation become more entrenched. The central bank increased rates three times that year, including a super-sized half-point in May. But here's where the parallels to today get even more interesting: Greenspan's justification for rate hikes could be lifted from today's Fedspeak about the AI boom — or would be if today's central bankers shared his penchant for circumlocution. What they're saying: The "profoundly beneficial forces driving the American economy to competitive excellence are also engendering a set of imbalances that, unless contained, threaten our continuing prosperity," Greenspan told Congress in February 2000. "The problem is that the pickup in productivity tends to create even greater increases in aggregate demand than in potential aggregate supply," he said. "This occurs principally because a rise in structural productivity growth has its counterpart in higher expectations for long-term corporate earnings." "This, in turn, not only spurs business investment but also increases stock prices and the market value of assets held by households, creating additional purchasing power for which no additional goods or services have yet been produced." Between the lines: He was talking about the productivity boom driven by the internet and related IT innovations of that era, but it is very much applicable to the AI boom today. Yes, AI-fueled productivity could create a boost to the economy's supply potential in the future, with corresponding noninflationary growth and higher incomes. But that's in the future. Right now, that potential is causing surging asset prices and rising demand for inputs to the build-out, pushing inflation higher. Reality check: The stock market peaked in March 2000. By 2001, an all-out tech rout was underway, as much of the investment in fiber-optic cable and other internet infrastructure was ahead of its time. That reversed the playing field for the Fed, as the wealth effects and an investment boom that appeared to be overheating the economy in 2000 instead dragged it down. The Fed enacted a surprise half-point rate cut on Jan. 3, 2001, and would ultimately cut rates 11 times (!) in 2001. Yes, but: Interestingly, while the tech bust hammered Americans' wealth, employment prospects and capital spending, the turn-of-the-century productivity gains continued throughout that recession and the ensuing jobless recovery. The bottom line: Even if the AI boom drives the kinds of long-term productivity surges its proponents anticipate, there is a risk of a bumpy path ahead — and policymakers would do well to study the parallels from 26 years ago.

events.title: Sickle cell gene therapies offer new hope, but access remains a major challenge
events.summary: New gene therapies are creating unprecedented hope for people with sickle cell disease, with Casgevy and Lyfgenia offering the potential to eliminate severe pain crises for many eligible patients. High costs, a demanding treatment process and limited access to sickle cell specialists have slowed their use. Experts say the broader sickle cell care system still has significant gaps, prompting new efforts to build stronger treatment networks nationwide. For decades, people living with sickle cell disease have endured a lifetime of hospital visits, medications and blood transfusions to manage a painful genetic blood disorder that can shorten life expectancy by up to 20 years . But a long-awaited breakthrough came in 2023, when the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved Casgevy and Lyfgenia, the first two gene therapies for patients with severe forms of the disease. Patient advocates and clinicians say the recent advancements in treatment could mark the beginning of a new era in sickle cell care, one that may free thousands from recurrent episodes of debilitating pain and improve long-term health outcomes. "That opens up a whole world of individuals potentially being cured of sickle cell disease," said Dr. Edward Donnell Ivy, chief medical officer for the national patient advocacy organization, Sickle Cell Disease Association of America . Yet for thousands of people living with the disease, accessing the transformative therapies remains far from straightforward. Patients often face a fragmented and uneven healthcare landscape where treatment costs, a complex treatment process, provider availability, and access to specialized treatment centers can vary widely based on where they live. The result has left therapies with the potential to dramatically alter the course of the disease still out of reach for many eligible patients. "The patients' priorities are actually a big part of really trying to figure out what the barriers to access are and how we overcome them," said Dr. Alexis Thompson, an attending physician in the division of hematology at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and spokesperson for the American Society of Hematology. Sometimes referred to as "the most common rare disease" because millions of people globally are affected, sickle cell disease impacts around 100,000 people in the U.S., according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention . More than 90% of the patient population are non-Hispanic Black or African American. Sickle cell disease is a genetic blood disorder that causes normally flexible, round-shaped red blood cells to become rigid and crescent-shaped, which can block blood vessels and reduce oxygen delivery to tissues. Some of the more common health complications that can occur include chronic fatigue and anemia, as well as blood clots and what is known as vaso-occlusive, or "pain" crises, which are severe episodes of debilitating pain that can last from a few hours to several weeks. Other complications can include stroke, organ damage, and increased risk of infection. More than a century after the first documented U.S. case of sickle cell disease in 1910, progress in developing new treatments remained slow, due in part to decades of underinvestment and lower levels of philanthropic support than those received by other rare genetic disorders. From 2008 through 2018, research funding from the National Institutes of Health given toward sickle cell disease averaged $812 per patient, according to a 2020 analysis , by comparison, funding for the genetic disorder cystic fibrosis, which affects approximately 40,000 people in the U.S., averaged $2,807 per patient for the same period. "There's been a slow increase in the development of new therapies for sickle cell disease," said Dr. Andrew Campbell , director of the comprehensive sickle cell disease program at Children's National in Washington D.C. "In the past six or seven years, there's been an explosion in that, but I would say from 1910 until about 2015, there was very little progress in disease-modifying treatments for sickle cell disease." A major breakthrough arrived in 1998 with the FDA approval of hydroxyurea, the first medication shown to modify the health effects of sickle cell disease. Studies have found the drug has helped to reduce the frequency of pain crises in patients by half , as well as the need for hospitalizations and blood transfusions . Since its introduction, hydroxyurea has become a cornerstone of sickle cell disease treatment that has helped thousands successfully manage their condition. Yet the discovery of a curative treatment remained elusive until gene therapy. For years, the only option available to patients was undergoing a bone marrow transplant, which was limited to only a select number able to find a donor match. "Bone marrow transplant was always available, but it wasn't a great option because not too many people had access to a donor," said Ivy, who is also a sickle cell disease patient.

events.title: Jev is Vercel’s fastest-adopted AI model ever
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Jev has become the fastest adopted AI model ever — at least by some measures. Vercel data published on Thursday shows that, within two weeks of its launch, the buzzy decision model was being used by 35% of paid teams, with nearly double the reach of the second most popular model, Sonnet 5.5. It’s the fastest adoption a model has ever seen in its first two weeks, according to Vercel’s data, and a major accomplishment for the model’s creators, TypeSafe AI. Published in limited release on September 15, Jev is designed as a lightweight tool for choosing between a few predetermined outputs. Limiting the outputs lets the model run cheaper and faster than alternatives like Sonnet, making it ideal for classifying large quantities of data quickly. That new approach has attracted significant buzz in the weeks since Jev’s release — inspiring competing offerings from OpenAI and Amazon , among others — but until now there has been little hard data to back up the good vibes. The data comes from Vercel’s AI gateway , a unified API service similar to OpenRouter. It’s a necessarily limited view — particularly at risk of undercounting major labs like OpenAI and Anthropic that offer their own APIs — but it shows the buzz around Jev really did translate into actual usage. In fact, Vercel was an early adopter of Jev, using it to replace GPT-6 Luna for classifying harmful commands. The report also shows continuing momentum for open source models, which now account for more than 70% of the tokens processed through Vercel’s gateway and nearly 25% of the total spend. While open source models are capturing a larger share of the market, the market is also growing fast. Spending on frontier labs has grown tenfold, even as it accounts for a smaller share of overall spend, giving credence to the idea that frontier models and open source alternatives may turn out to be complementary rather than competitive . events.title: Target pensions or welfare, not banks, IMF tells John Healey
events.summary: Supporters of planned tax, however, say banks were bailed out by taxpayers during financial crisis and can afford to pay more now John Healey poised to raise taxes on banks in budget The International Monetary Fund has urged John Healey to target savings on pensions and welfare, instead of taxing Britain’s banks at the budget later this month. Helge Berger, deputy director of the IMF’s European department, was asked about bank taxes after the Guardian revealed Healey plans to tap the sector for additional revenue. Berger replied that given the UK’s current high tax-to-GDP ratio, it might be better to “put the emphasis” on cuts. He said if additional tax revenue were needed, reforming property taxes or VAT might be a good place to start. He added: “Ultimately, with taxes roughly at 40% of GDP – historically, for Britain, a high number – then of course balancing these measures on the fiscal [spending] side, doing a bit more there, makes good sense.” As examples, he highlighted the pensions triple lock – which Labour has already said it will reform – and “better targeting [of] social benefits”, adding: “I think that’s where you would put the emphasis, rather than the tax that you mentioned.” Berger was speaking in Bangkok, where the IMF has held its annual meetings this week. City lobbyists have been out in full force, warning the government that higher taxes could force banks to throttle lending, hitting the economy and even forcing some lenders to move jobs and operations abroad. In a letter sent to Healey and copied to the prime minister, Andy Burnham, on 12 October, days before news of the planned tax hike broke, the chief executive of UK Finance, David Postings, shared research commissioned by the lobby group. It suggested that reversing Tory cuts to the bank surcharge – taking it back to 8% from 3% – would leave annual UK GDP £1.2bn lower in real terms by 2029-30 than it would have otherwise been. He said it would also see banks issue fewer business loans and mortgages, with lending likely to be £10.4bn lower in 2029-2030 than if the surcharge was held at 3%. “The UK’s banking sector already makes a vital contribution to the wider economy,” Postings’ letter said. “To sustain this vital contribution, the budget should avoid any increases in bank-specific taxes, as this would risk constraining the sector’s ability to lend and invest.” However, TUC analysis of HMRC corporate tax receipts shows the Treasury has already lost out on £6bn over the three years since the surcharge cut came into force in 2023. At the same time, banks have been reporting strong profits, largely off the back of high interest rates, with bosses subsequently increasing banker bonus pots and handing billions of pounds to shareholders. Collectively, the UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays and Lloyds – reported £29.2bn in profits over the first six months of the year, with almost half, £13.7bn, pledged to investors through dividends and share buybacks. Over the past five years, those banks have raked in £200bn in pre-tax profits. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Author and former banker Philip Augar said the banks were “enjoying boom conditions”, partly due to good management but partly due to economic conditions “not of their own making”. He said there was room for a “moderate increase in taxation” that would raise about £2bn to £3bn a year. “The prime minister has said that the burden of taxation has to fall on those with the broader shoulders, and at the moment, it’s hard to think of a sector where the shoulders are much broader than the banking sector,” Augar told the BBC’s Today programme on Friday. While banks could not expect interest rates benefits to continue forever, Augar said that banks – including those that were bailed out in the 2008 financial crisis – could not have it both ways. “Banking is cyclical, it’s true. But when it hits really rocky times it expects the taxpayer to bail them out,” Augar said. “When it hits boom times, it expects some kind of special treatment. Banks can’t be too big to fail and too big to tax.” Some banks have threatened to pull investment, and potentially jobs, from the UK if it hikes taxes, with lobby groups noting smaller overall tax charges in rival financial centres like Frankfurt, Dublin and Amsterdam. Jamie Dimon, who heads up the largest bank in the US, JP Morgan, said in May that he could scrap plans for a new £3bn London headquarters if the UK government became hostile towards banks. But Augar said the government needed to see past the bluster. “There seems to have been a coordinated campaign by the big international banks who have businesses in Britain – JP Morgan, Citigroup, Santander, HSBC and others. “But they always say this, [and] they rarely move.

events.title: How Chick-fil-A grew from a small Southern diner to the third-largest restaurant chain in the US
events.summary: Chick-fil-A has come a long way since opening as a small roadside diner in Georgia in 1946. Irene Jiang / Business Insider In 1946, Chick-fil-A founder S. Truett Cathy opened the Dwarf Grill in Hapeville, Georgia. In 1967, Cathy opened the first Chick-fil-A and invented the restaurant's iconic chicken sandwich. Chick-fil-A is now the third-largest restaurant chain in the US. Eighty years after Chick-fil-A founder Truett Cathy opened his first restaurant, Chick-fil-A is now the third-largest restaurant brand in the country. The family-owned chain has since grown to more than 3,200 US restaurants and generated nearly $24 billion in US systemwide sales in 2025, trailing only McDonald’s and Starbucks, per Technomic's Top 500 chains report . The chicken chain's rise has not been without controversy. Chick-fil-A faced widespread backlash in 2012 after Cathy's son Dan, then the company’s CEO, publicly opposed same-sex marriage, while the company and its foundation were criticized for donations to organizations with anti-LGBTQ+ positions. This week, current CEO Andrew Cathy declined to directly address the company’s history or state its position on LGBTQ+ equality in an interview with NBC , instead saying Chick-fil-A is focused on hospitality and welcoming everyone who comes through its doors. Here’s how Chick-fil-A grew from a small Southern diner into a fast-food powerhouse. Chick-fil-A's origin story began when Truett Cathy opened the Dwarf Grill in Hapeville, Georgia, in 1946. Chick-fil-A The small roadside diner was later renamed when it became one of the chain's "Dwarf Houses." The original location previously served as  one of 12 Chick-fil-A locations,  offering modern favorites and items from the original restaurant's "blue menu." The first official Chick-fil-A locations were located in shopping malls. Chick-fil-A The first restaurant to bear the name Chick-fil-A opened in the Greenbriar Mall in Atlanta in 1967. According to the company, the restaurant occupied just 384 square feet, and some have credited the chain with being an "early pioneer" of what would become the modern mall food court . Chick-fil-A opened its first stand-alone restaurant in 1986 in Atlanta. Chick-fil-A Free-standing locations are now the norm for Chick-fil-A, and mall locations are much less common. Chick-fil-A also experimented with drive-thru-only restaurant locations. Chick-fil-A The first-ever drive-thru-only Chick-fil-A restaurant opened in 1993 in Greenville, South Carolina. By eliminating dining rooms in these locations, the restaurants were designed to be faster and more convenient for customers. Today, there are more than 3,000 Chick-fil-A restaurants in North America. Chick-fil-A The chain, which was founded in Georgia, still has its headquarters there, and is regarded as a "Southern" fast-food chain . However, restaurants can actually be found in 48 different states as well as Washington, DC. In 2019, Chick-fil-A expanded internationally by opening its first location in Toronto. Later that year, the chain opened its first restaurant in the United Kingdom. The chain now has locations across Canada, Puerto Rico, the UK, and Singapore. Before Chick-fil-A began using a cow as its mascot, the chain was represented by — perhaps unsurprisingly — a chicken. Chick-fil-A The chain's tag line used to read, "The best thing that ever happened to a Chicken." Now, Chick-fil-A's slogan pays homage to its most famous menu item — its chicken sandwich. An employee picks up a fried chicken sandwich during an event ahead of the grand opening for a Chick-fil-A restaurant in New York. 465-square-meter/Getty Images The "A" in Chick-fil-A comes from both a play on the word "fillet" and a nod to the "grade-A top quality chicken" used in Chick-fil-A's chicken sandwiches. However, the chain also still uses cows and the words "Eat Mor Chikin" to bring customers through its doors. John Adams/Icon Sportswire/Corbis/Icon Sportswire/Getty Images The "Eat Mor Chikin" slogan, accompanied by two "rebel cows," debuted in 1995 on an Atlanta billboard, according to the  company . The campaign quickly gained traction and is now regarded as one of Chick-fil-A's most famous and successful advertising campaigns. The original Dwarf Grill menu served diner favorites like breakfast and burgers. Hayley Peterson/Business Insider Menu items included everything from waffles to sandwiches, steak and potatoes, and the chain's famous Hot Brown , a hot casserole dish made with lean white meat chicken, gravy, mashed potatoes, cheese, and bacon.  Today, Chick-fil-A still serves breakfast, but the menu items look much different. Irene Jiang / Business Insider Launched in 1986, the first item added to the breakfast menu was the Chick-fil-A chicken biscuit. Today, the Chick-fil-A menu typically includes more than 50 items. At the Dwarf Grill, Truett Cathy's first restaurant, you could order burgers. Business Insider/Hayley Peterson The Dwarf Grill served both hamburgers and cheeseburgers, which the restaurant's menu said were made from "100% choice beef, chopped in our kitchen." Served on a large toasted bun, the menu also boldly said that "they're the best." Business Insider's Hayley Peterson tried the burger for herself when she visited the Dwarf House , and she found the patty "thick and flavorful" and that the cheese "melted perfectly between the patty and the bun." You won't find burgers on any Chick-fil-A menus, but you will find the chain's famous chicken sandwich. Irene Jiang / Business Insider In 1964, Truett Cathy created the recipe for Chick-fil-A's original chicken sandwich: a fried, boneless chicken breast nestled between two buttered buns and topped with two pickles. Though the sandwich soon shot to popularity at the Dwarf House, the invention was odd compared to other fast-food offerings and food tastes of the time. However, Cathy's bet on chicken would soon pay off. Though Chick-fil-A has expanded immensely since the launch of its chicken sandwich, the recipe has remained virtually the same. In 1989, Chick-fil-A added a grilled chicken sandwich to its menu. Hollis Johnson Introduced as a health-conscious option for Chick-fil-A customers, Cathy introduced the original grilled chicken sandwich alongside the deluxe grilled chicken sandwich, which included the same pickle-juice-marinated grilled chicken, pickles, and white bun, along with lettuce and tomato. According to the restaurant's website , Cathy tested more than 1,200 recipes to perfect the chain's grilled chicken recipe. Chick-fil-A revolutionized its menu yet again when it launched its spicy chicken sandwich nationwide in 2010. Irene Jiang/Business Insider "While we recognize that not everyone enjoys spicy food, for the growing customer constituency that does, our Spicy Chicken Sandwich offers a unique, well-balanced and craveable spicy flavor," William F. events.title: All 59 Marvel Cinematic Universe movies and TV series, ranked
events.summary: Joe Locke, Paul Bettany, and Ruaridh Mollica, aka an android father and his two "sons" in the MCU. Tristan Fewings/Getty Images for BFI The Marvel Cinematic Universe has been going strong since 2008's "Iron Man." There have been 38 movies, 19 TV series, and three specials to date, with many more in the works. Here's how they all compare, according to critics. The Marvel Cinematic Universe has been a huge box-office force ever since its first film, "Iron Man," debuted in 2008. Eighteen years and 37 more films later, the MCU has experienced its fair share of ups and downs, both critically and commercially. This year's first MCU film, " Spider-Man: Brand New Day ," has garnered strong reviews (and an even stronger box office ), while the studio's most-anticipated film of 2026, " Avengers: Doomsday ," is yet to come. The two TV shows Marvel released this year have both fared well with critics: "Wonder Man" and the latest series, "VisionQuest." We used Rotten Tomatoes scores to rank every single MCU project — including movies, TV series, animated series, and special presentations — from worst to best. See how each hero stacks up. 58 (tie). "Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania" (2023) Marvel Studios Rotten Tomatoes score:   46% The best part of "Quantumania," the third installment in the Paul Rudd-led "Ant-Man" series, was Jonathan Majors' introduction as the MCU's next big bad, Kang, audiences and critics agreed — although, Majors' time in the MCU was short-lived as a result of his legal troubles. While critics had a tougher time with the miniature film, the audience score of 81% shows that fans had a good time with Scott, Hope, Hank, Janet, and Cassie down in the Quantum Realm. "The general color-drenched too-muchness of it all might be tolerable if the plot wasn't such a by-the-numbers slog, alternating hyperkinetic action sequences with draggy recitations of exposition," wrote Decider's John Serba. 58 (tie). "Captain America: Brave New World" (2025) Anthony Mackie as Sam Wilson/Captain America in "Captain America: Brave New World." Eli Adé/Marvel Studios Rotten Tomatoes score:   46% "Brave New World" sees Sam Wilson (Anthony Mackie) officially take over for Steve Rogers (Chris Evans) as Captain America on the big screen, while his old friend Joaquin Torres (Danny Ramirez) is the new Falcon. Sam must go up against President Thunderbolt Ross — with Harrison Ford taking over for William Hurt, who died in 2022 — who has somehow turned into, you guessed it, Red Hulk. "Though it ties together threads from the Marvel Cinematic Universe as a whole, 'Brave New World' is neither particularly good or bad. It's just another Marvel movie," wrote Dylan Roth for the Observer . 57. "Eternals" (2021) Marvel Studios Rotten Tomatoes score:   48% "Eternals," directed by Oscar winner Chloé Zhao, attempted to introduce an entirely new team of superheroes, an alien race called the Eternals, to the MCU, and followed them from prehistoric times all the way through the present day. Your mileage may vary on how successful she was — but "Eternals"  did  introduce Harry Styles to the MCU, so there's that. "Zhao ultimately robs the artist's comic of its sweep by constantly turning a space opera into a repetitive character drama," wrote Ed Gonzalez for Slant Magazine. 56. "Secret Invasion" (2023) Emilia Clarke in "Secret Invasion." Gareth Gatrell/Marvel Rotten Tomatoes score: 53% "Secret Invasion" continues the story of the Skrulls, a few decades after we last saw them in "Captain Marvel," as they search for a new planet with the help of Nick Fury, played by Samuel L. Jackson. But not even the all-star cast of Jackson, Emilia Clarke, Olivia Colman, Don Cheadle, Kingsley Ben-Adir, Cobie Smulders, Martin Freeman, and more could save this show from getting torn apart by critics. "If a series about Nick Fury doesn't feel urgent or crucial, then the MCU is losing the battle for our attention," wrote Melanie McFarland for Salon. 55. "The Marvels" (2023) Brie Larson as Captain Marvel in "The Marvels." Laura Radford/Marvel Studios Rotten Tomatoes score: 63% "The Marvels," the long-awaited follow-up to 2019's "Captain Marvel," sees Brie Larson's Carol Danvers team up with Monica Rambeau, aka Photon (Teyonah Parris), and Kamala Khan, aka Ms. Marvel (Imani Vellani) to take down a new threat. "It might not have the overwhelming impact of an 'Endgame' or even a 'Guardians 3,' but this is the MCU back on fast, funny form," wrote Empire Magazine's Helen O'Hara. 54. "Thor: Love and Thunder" (2022) Chris Hemsworth as Thor in "Thor: Love and Thunder." Marvel Studios Rotten Tomatoes score:   64% The follow-up to smash hit "Thor: Ragnarok" and the first-ever fourth solo film for an MCU hero didn't live up to expectations, at least according to critics. But we did get to see Natalie Portman return to the MCU as her version of the Mighty Thor, a couple of screaming goats, and a jaw-dropping post-credits cameo. "Though Chris Hemsworth, as usual, has a lot of fun in the title role, the film around him too often strains to provide excitement and laughs," wrote Wall Street Journal's Kyle Smith. 53. "Marvel Zombies" (2025) Disney+ Rotten Tomatoes score: 66% A successful stand-alone episode in "What If…?" season one, where the Watcher asked viewers to consider one thing — zombies — inspired a four-part animated special that followed a group of ragtag heroes as they tried to save the world from a zombie apocalypse. "Even with the zombie apocalypse there to spice up their lives, Marvel's newest heroes are less lively than the arm-munchers surrounding them," wrote AV Club's Jarrod Jones. 52. "Thor: The Dark World" (2013) "Thor: The Dark World" was directed by Alan Taylor. Marvel Studios Rotten Tomatoes score:   67% "Thor: The Dark World" — the 2013 sequel to the 2011 film — stars Chris Hemsworth as the titular Norse god, Tom Hiddleston as his mischievous brother Loki, and Natalie Portman as Thor's Earth-bound love interest Jane Foster. It wasn't as well-received as its predecessor, but it has its defenders. And now, it's been ranked better than "Love and Thunder." "This feels like a really, really, expensive episode of 'Doctor Who.' In a good way," wrote Larushka Ivan-Zadeh for Metro. 51. events.title: Maybe Chatbots Shouldn’t Get to Say ‘I’ or ‘Me’
events.summary: During four decades of studying the effects of interaction with computers, Sherry Turkle has developed a reputation as a careful if critical social scientist who approaches her work with academic rigor and distance. Her new book , Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines , breaks this mold. It is a polemic warning that we have reached a state of emergency where our humanity is at risk from overreliance on soulless machines who pose as our tutors , mentors , friends, colleagues, and lovers . Turkle is aiming for the high bar of books — Silent Spring , The Jungle , Unsafe at Any Speed —that awaken the public to impending crises. Essentially, this diminutive MIT professor is taking on a multitrillion-dollar industry backed by a government eager to accelerate AI into every corner of our personal and professional lives. STEVEN LEVY: Your previous books reported results of your research as a social scientist, often leading to troubling conclusions about how people, especially children, interact with computers. But this book reads like you’re breaking the glass and pulling the fire alarm. Why the shift? SHERRY TURKLE: Like I do with all my books, I went in curious. But after 10 or so interviews, conducted during the pandemic, neutral-curious was no longer my state of mind. This was terrible! Here are these people during the pandemic, their families are suffering, reaching out to them, and they're talking to me about how they really want to just hang with their chatbot. When I was able to interview people face to face, I was not happy. People don't want to do anything in politics because they just want to live in chatbot-land. So the arc of the book ended up as—reality needs you. It couldn't be a worse time to give up on reality. You write that social media set us up for this. Social media softened us up by getting us used to the idea that if you're feeling sad or blue, open up your computer. Then it made you mad and kept you with your own kind. But now we have this new technology that has no reason to be first-person. Do you think that we should ban chatbots from using the first person? Yes! After a career of having credibility as not being Luddite-crazy, I'm not in the mood to give all that away and say all chatbots are toxic all the time. But this is very dangerous, a slippery slope. This is being used to basically say we don't need to pay for psychotherapy, we can use chatbots. In every serious interview I do, people invoke this myth about practice—that you use chatbots to practice for talking to your boss, your lover, your teacher. But when you’re bathing in the warm soup of total acceptance [from LLMs], talking to chatbots becomes the endgame. You also have a problem with reliance on chatbots in the workplace, and a particular loathing for the term “human in the loop.” When they use that term, it means the human has been taken out of the productive process and is there to do some sort of cleanup work, to catch the hallucinations or things the AI doesn’t see. That doesn't work, because employers only have a couple of humans in the loop. Those people basically can't change anything. They are there partly to make it sound good when they're litigated, and partly to give people a false sense that the process hasn't been delegated to an AI. But it has been delegated to an AI. Maybe powerful chatbots are a new form of interaction that isn’t necessarily worse than human conversation, but different, as people report feeling encouraged and empowered by the positive feedback they provide. An AI won't ever replace human conversation. It’s really not afraid of death, it’s not afraid of illness, it's not afraid of pain, it doesn't love its children, and it doesn't care if you kill yourself or make dinner. So if we raise our kids with it, or have our most intimate conversations with it, we're going to lose contact. Still, a lot of people have nobody to talk to. They feel that talking to chatbots helps them. If there's a crisis of loneliness, it's because we're abandoning each other. Give me one data center, and I will turn it into resources for the elderly. Studies show that most people are skeptical about AI, and there has been considerable pushback. Yet hundreds of millions of people use them. Even people who push back against data centers are using chatbots. The goal of this book is to expand the terms of the pushback to include this more intimate connection. Do you really feel that our growing intimacy with AI can be stopped? I have more hope now than I did six months ago, because of all of this talk about extinction events and Hugging Face and getting into the Australian civil service by mistake. I feel that people will be willing to look at the intimate as well as the non-intimate costs. This is an edition of Steven Levy’s and Lauren Goode's Backchannel newsletter . events.title: JP Morgan deepens critical minerals push
events.summary: JP Morgan has appointed an executive to lead the company's critical mineral efforts under its $1.5 trillion drive to invest in industries deemed significant to US national economic security. Andrew Frame will oversee the Security and Resilience Initiative's critical minerals strategy across extraction, refining and processing, a company representative confirmed to The National . Mr Frame's mandate will centre on addressing bottlenecks across the value chain for an industry considered essential to advanced manufacturing, energy and defence, they said. Mr Frame's appointment was first reported by Mining.com. JP Morgan launched its 10-year, $1.5 trillion Security and Resiliency Initiative last year. The drive spans four sectors – supply chain and advanced manufacturing, defence and aerospace, energy independence and resilience, and frontier and strategic technology. The bank said those are then divided into 27 subsections ranging from fishing to critical defence components. Critical minerals fall under the supply chain and advanced manufacturing category, while battery storage and grid resilience fall under defence and aerospace. Artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and quantum computing make up the initiative's frontier strategies sector. The $1.5 trillion builds on the previously announced $1 trillion the company planned to finance over the next decade. The commitment includes a separate $10 billion allocation for direct equity investments. “It has become painfully clear that the United States has allowed itself to become too reliant on unreliable sources of critical minerals, products and manufacturing – all of which are essential for our national security,” JP Morgan chief executive Jamie Dimon said. Mr Dimon told analysts during the company's third-quarter earnings call this week that the company “probably” deployed more than $200 billion in the first year. Mr Frame's appointment makes him an integral part of the US critical minerals push amid a string of private and federal capital injection into the sector to strengthen the country's supply chain . Since 2025, the US government has announced $10.8 billion in investments , including $5.1 billion in total private capital, in 14 critical minerals companies, using a range of tools from equity stakes to grants, loans and offtake agreements, according to the Council of Foreign Relations. In September, Houston-based start-up Hertha Metals said it had closed a $133.65 million Series A round that includes a $65 million equity investment from the Pentagon. The company is planning on producing high-purity iron for rare-earth magnets needed for F-35 fighter jets and missile-guidance systems. The US government also holds equity stakes in companies across the critical minerals supply chain including MP Materials, USA Rare Earth, and Canada-based Lithium Americas. Also in September, Glencore and Mercuria became the first two companies to participate in VaultCo, a public-private partnership designed to implement the administration's Project Vault initiative. Glencore said its $500 million commitment from Export-Import Bank will allow it to create a critical minerals reserve in the US. Mercuria also announced a $500 million commitment, bringing the total pledge from the companies to $1 billion. “Mineral security is national security. VaultCo is working to ensure the US industrial base has access to the critical minerals needed to build the products everyday Americans rely on and lead the world when they need it most,” ValtCo executive chair Brett Lambert said.

events.title: China targets AI technology exports with new controls as US trade truce frays
events.summary: China has proposed new export controls on 40 strategic technology systems, including 23 linked to artificial intelligence, in a move that could test its fragile trade truce with the US and deepen the rivalry between the world's two largest economies . The draft rules, unveiled on Friday, would give Beijing greater oversight of technology transfers spanning AI chips, large language models, solar energy and biotechnology. China said the move was aimed at curbing the misuse of the technology. Most can still be exported without heavy restrictions and licensing would be simplified. Beijing will seek public opinion on the proposal until November 15, after which it will announce a final version of the controls. “The announcement is extremely expansive and it will take time to fully assess its implications,” said Leonhard Xu, a senior consultant at Sinolytics, a Berlin-based consultancy. “AI seems to be the big centrepiece … but the registration requirement starts immediately, even for exports that have already started shipping. Also, always important to note that export control does not equal an export ban in most cases,” he said. China and the US have been locked in a largely bitter trade war, as Washington seeks to control Beijing's global influence. Technology, and AI in particular, has become a major driver of the rivalry. AI has become key for Chinese exports, which jumped more than 36 per cent year-on-year in September, markedly better than a previously anticipated 25.5 per cent, underscored by AI products, according to IndexBox data. Industry observers believe the move will have notable implications on China's economic engine and its trade strategy against the US, with which it is competing for leadership in the AI race. Last month, Washington and Beijing ​agreed to cut tariffs on $30 billion of goods and start dialogue on AI, after Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House. Erin Browne, the US Treasury's undersecretary for international ‌affairs, told Reuters that Washington was pushing for its partners in the International Monetary Fund to rename AI “super intelligence”, a term championed by the Trump administration. China's move indicates that the “fragility of our trade truce cannot be overstated”, said Wendy Cutler, a senior vice president at the New York-based non-profit Asia Institute, who also warned that it is “only be a matter of time” until the US responds with its own restrictive measures. “Despite the agreement on constructive strategic stability, China has announced it is working on a new export restriction tool on solar, AI and other products, allowing Beijing to have better control over export levels, destinations, etc,” she said. “This once again shows that despite the two-month extension of our trade truce, Beijing is going full steam ahead in efforts to control exports of strategic goods to the US and others.” Ting Peng, a partner at BZW Law Firm in Shenzhen who specialises in trade compliance, said the registration requirements extend beyond conventional technology transfers, as they cover certain cross-border IP transfers and licensing arrangements, as well as changes in ownership or actual control of domestic technology, to overseas entities. These implications may extend to cross-border investment and corporate transactions, she noted. “Companies involved in cross-border acquisitions, IP restructuring or international licensing arrangements should assess whether their transactions involving the relevant technologies trigger the new registration requirements,” Ms Ting said. “This is particularly relevant to the biopharmaceutical sector, which has seen significant M&A [mergers and acquisitions] activity over the past two years.”

events.summary: Guillaume Faury writes to Andy Burnham warning him against choosing US firm Lockheed Martin to build Skynet satellites The boss of Airbus has told Andy Burnham that choosing its US rival Lockheed Martin to manufacture military satellites could cost the UK a key role in the European space industry, intensifying a last-minute lobbying effort for the £2.4bn contract. It is understood that Guillaume Faury, the chief executive of France-headquartered Airbus, has written to the prime minister suggesting that the choice of provider of the Skynet system could have effects for decades to come on the UK’s strength in military satellites in Europe, in an effort to tip the contract away from its US rival. Yet politicians in north-east England have lobbied in favour of the Lockheed Martin bid, which would include a new factory in Durham. The military satellites under the Skynet 6 contract will carry the British armed forces’ most sensitive communications up to 2042, replacing the Skynet 5 system operated by Airbus . The delayed decision on which company will manufacture the UK’s sovereign satellites comes at a sensitive moment, after Ukraine complained that its access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite network was restricted , apparently at the behest of the US government. Several sources said they believed no final decision on the contract had been made. However, some said they believed that Lockheed Martin’s bid was preferred by the Ministry of Defence . The final decision will rest with Burnham and the chancellor, John Healey. It is thought that Faury’s letter warned of longer-term consequences for the UK’s role in the European space sector if Airbus were to lose out. Senior industry figures have previously claimed that Airbus’s UK satellite operations would not be viable without the next Skynet contract, meaning the company might close its sites at Stevenage and Portsmouth, which employ 3,000 people, including 600 working on Skynet. The manufacturers Airbus, Thales and Leonardo are working on a long-awaited merger between their space subsidiaries, known as Project Bromo, in an effort to build a single European champion with the scale to rival the leading US companies. Faury is understood to have warned that if its British operation were no longer viable it could mean the UK missing out on the chance to be the European hub for military satellite communications once the merger was complete. Lockheed Martin is one of the US’s largest defence “prime” contractors, but it says its UK subsidiary will have full control over the satellites eventually built in the UK. People close to Lockheed Martin have strongly denied that the US government would have control over the satellites. A Lockheed Martin spokesperson said the company was “unable to comment on the ongoing procurement process”, but added: “Lockheed Martin UK, a British company, will establish facilities to develop an ecosystem alongside our regional partners in the north-east of England to provide the UK with a sovereign space capability. It will create jobs, supply chain opportunities and the potential for exports. It will have a UK design authority and a UK chief engineer.” Luke Akehurst, the Labour MP for North Durham, said Lockheed’s bid would mean a “state-of-the-art new manufacturing facility” in the region. “This represents a massive investment in the reindustrialisation of the north-east of England, building on our region’s proud heritage of advanced manufacturing.” The personal intervention from Faury, one of the most powerful executives in Europe, is a sign of the importance of the contract to Airbus, which is headquartered in Toulouse. A decision had been expected in the summer but it has been delayed in part by the arrival of Burnham in office. Unite, one of the Labour party’s biggest union backers, had warned against “handing the British space industry over to the Americans” at a time when there are increased questions over whether the UK can rely on the US government. Burnham will also have to consider the two bids on their financial terms and the capabilities the two companies can offer. A government document for a related system said satellites had to deal with the “proliferation of counterspace capabilities to disrupt, deny, degrade or destroy space-based enablers”. It highlighted radio jamming, hacking and direct physical attacks on the satellites as possible concerns. The first Skynet satellite was launched in 1969, well before the use of the name for a hostile artificial intelligence in the 1984 film The Terminator . Kim McGuinness, the mayor for north-east England, said: “Bringing satellite manufacturing to the north-east is a huge opportunity to build on what we have already achieved, including the close ties we have forged between our world-class universities and industry.

events.title: Mark Wahlberg on using AI in film ‘the right way’ and being open to an AI clone carrying on his legacy
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Even as Hollywood remains divided over the use of AI in filmmaking, actor and director Mark Wahlberg believes the technology has a place in the industry as long as it’s used the right way. Wahlberg, who’s also an entrepreneur and angel investor, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt to share his perspective on AI’s role in filmmaking, and how he’s open to having an AI likeness of himself carry on his legacy. The actor said he plans to potentially use AI to enhance certain aspects of the upcoming Pete Rose biopic, in which he’ll star in the title role. “It’s a fairly expensive movie, but, we’re talking about utilizing [AI] to enhance the stadium setting, things of that nature,” Wahlberg said. “I don’t think you should just, you know, put an idea into ChatGPT and it puts out a script, and then you should go make that and not use real actors. But if you can use it to enhance what you’re doing, I’m all for that.” That said, Wahlberg made special mention of his belief that storytelling should remain at the heart of filmmaking. “I’ve done big, effects-driven movies,” Wahlberg said. “I think I was in that kind of sweet spot when the first Jurassic Park was made, or when Perfect Storm came out, and you had that wave, the 100-foot wave that was in the trailer. Those are cutting-edge moments in technology with computer-generated images. Now, I think it’s hard to do that, so I’m not so passionate about effects-driven movies per se, as opposed to real storytelling.” When asked by TechCrunch Editor-in-Chief Connie Loizos whether he had visited the CAA Vault , a Creative Artists Agency facility which lets actors use scanning technology to capture their bodies, faces, movements, and voices to create AI replicas, Wahlberg said he hadn’t, but would be open to the idea. “I would be interested because I think in the future, if that’s where things go, it would be cool that my children or my grandchildren could be in charge of my likeness and my image, and hopefully put me in some good movies,” Wahlberg said. “It’ll be interesting to see where things go.” He even said he wouldn’t be opposed if his upcoming animated series, “Ted,” continued for decades with an AI version of his likeness. “I think it’s cool if I’m no longer able to do it or don’t exist, and if it could continue and people want to see it, I think it’d be interesting to see where things go,” Wahlberg said. “I think there’s certain things from my childhood that I wish still existed and were still a part of my life […] I wouldn’t be opposed to it. I think people are going to have massive opportunities to watch whatever it is they want, and if there’s a real audience for that, they should be entitled to have what they want to see.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: U.S. small-scale solar generation has quadrupled in the last decade
events.summary: U.S. Energy Information Administration - EIA - Independent Statistics and Analysis Browse by tag liquid fuels natural gas electricity oil/petroleum production/supply crude oil consumption/demand generation prices map states exports/imports international coal renewables weather forecasts/projections gasoline capacity steo (short-term energy outlook) Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Annual Electric Power Industry Report We estimate that U.S. generation from small-scale or rooftop solar photovoltaic systems (smaller than 1 megawatt of capacity) has increased from 18,812 gigawatthours (GWh) to 92,979 GWh over the last decade. The four states with the highest generation of small-scale solar in the country—California, Arizona, Texas, and Florida—are in regions with more abundant solar resources . Even though it is in a region with lower solar resources, New York ranks as the fifth-largest rooftop solar generation producer as a result of capacity growth supported by technology improvements and state incentives. The year-over-year change in generation was particularly high in 2022, when total generation grew by 25% compared with the previous year amid record capacity growth . Changes in different programs supporting rooftop solar partly explain this increase in generation. For example, California’s Net Energy Metering (NEM) 2.0 program was available through April 2023. This net metering program offered higher export compensation than the subsequent Net Billing Tariff, or NEM 3.0 . All the capacity built under the NEM 2.0 program was grandfathered in, incentivizing higher capacity installation before the current NEM 3.0 took effect. California accounted for 37% (34,411 GWh) of total U.S. small-scale solar generation in 2025. Between 2024 and 2025, rooftop solar generation in the state grew by 8%, largely due to an increase in capacity. Small-scale solar capacity in California increased from 18 gigawatts in 2024 to 20 gigawatts in 2025. The state with the next largest amount of small-scale solar power generation is Arizona, accounting for over 6% of total U.S. generation, or 5,795 GWh. Year-over-year generation in Arizona grew only 6% in 2025. The largest increase happened between 2022 and 2023 when generation from small-scale solar grew by 22% in the state. Arizona customers can access a 25% state income-tax credit and other incentives for adding rooftop solar to their properties. States such as Florida and Texas have seen rapid growth in small-scale solar generation in the last decade as more capacity has been added. Generation in Texas grew from 391 GWh in 2016 to 5,408 GWh last year. Over the same period, Florida’s generation grew from 205 GWh in 2016 to 5,198 GWh in 2025. These two states provide incentives through property tax exemptions and other programs specific to each state and, in some cases, utility. Programs in states with lower irradiance levels are also supporting growth in rooftop solar generation. New York offers incentives, which have encouraged small-scale solar growth in the state. Other states with similar programs include New Jersey , Massachusetts , and Illinois . Although generation from small-scale solar continues to grow year over year, the rate of growth has declined since 2022. EIA uses its surveys of electric utilities to collect information on the number of customers with small-scale solar systems and the aggregated capacity. Electric utilities do not necessarily know how much electricity is generated by rooftop solar on their distribution systems, so generation must be estimated. To develop estimates of generation, we rely on tools such as the National Renewable Energy Laboratory's System Advisor Model and PVWatts . Data on commonly used tilt angles and orientations for small-scale solar systems in California were used as inputs to be representative of tilt angles and orientations in other states. events.title: Veritas expands its anti-counterfeit chip to jewelry, trophies, and fragrance bottles
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Counterfeits of luxury goods are a major problem for fashion houses. Counterfeiters are getting better at replicating brands’ marks and passing off dupes, known as “ superfakes ,” as genuine items. A startup called Veritas wants to tackle the problem with its own chip that verifies goods. Veritas was founded by Luci Holland, a former Tesla technical product manager who also has a background in design and art. Its chip is built to be easily inserted into products without damaging them. Brands can use it to verify whether a product is the real deal, and customers can show a certificate of ownership through the company’s app. Holland said other approaches are easier to defeat, because a digital record can be reproduced through a copied QR code or static NFC link. “Our approach combines secure, authenticated chip responses with integration into the product itself. Our chip generates a secure response with each tap and includes a tamper-detection wire. We make the connection between the object and its digital identity part of the proof,” Holland said. The Veritas founder told TechCrunch over email that the company has just introduced the second version of its chip, which works on metal surfaces and can be scanned through glass. “The next-generation chip is ready for production and supports a broader range of applications, including jewelry, trophies, hard-surface products, and glass objects such as fragrance bottles,” Holland said. “Alongside our garment integrations, this gives brands more ways to incorporate authentication directly into their products.” This week, the startup announced a partnership with ATHLOS, a women’s track-and-field competition founded by Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian, who is also an investor in Veritas. As part of the partnership, all 18 championship crowns will include Veritas’ chips so they can be verified. The company also embedded a chip into a pair of LeBron James’ first Nike shoes, reimagined by artist Adam Port. Tapping a phone to the shoe brings up its history and story. The company has so far raised $1.75 million in pre-seed funding led by Ohanian’s venture firm Seven Seven Six, with participation from DoorDash co-founder Stanley Tang; Gloria Zhu, co-founder of skincare brand Reys; and former TechCrunch editor Josh Constine. Since its February fundraise, the company has shipped an iOS app for consumers and a brand portal that lets companies manage product records and build owner experiences. Through the app and the portal, brands can offer experiences such as clubs, event check-ins, and segmented early access to product drops. Veritas competed in this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt Startup Battlefield, which ran Tuesday through Thursday. A winner was announced Thursday afternoon . events.title: Zuma’s illness raises questions for South Africa opposition
events.summary: The News Concerns over the health of former South African President Jacob Zuma have raised questions about the future of uMkhonto weSizwe (MK), the populist party built around him that has redrawn the country’s political landscape. The 84-year-old was taken to hospital two weeks ago. Since then, MK officials and the Zuma Foundation have circulated conflicting accounts about his condition. The party initially described Zuma as healthy and undergoing routine checks before returning home. That claim was later contradicted by the foundation, which said he remained in hospital and declined to provide regular updates. In a sign of the impact on the party, MK canceled its flagship Siyathatha rally less than three weeks before South Africa’s municipal elections. The uncertainty has become a political issue because of Zuma’s central role in the party he publicly launched nearly three years ago, after switching from the African National Congress (ANC) ahead of a general election. MK emerged from the 2024 poll as one of the biggest forces in South African politics, winning nearly 15% of the vote on promises to scrap the constitution, expropriate land without compensation and nationalize banks, insurers and strategic mines. Its performance accelerated the slide of the ANC, once led by Nelson Mandela, which lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since the end of apartheid and was forced to form a coalition government. Still, the MK’s rise has been punctuated by leadership turmoil, internal purges, and recurring disputes over candidate selection. Zuma’s absence from public campaigning has heightened questions about whether the movement can maintain its momentum without him. Natasha Marrian, a political analyst at the Bureau for Economic Research, a South African think tank, said the MK party, launched as a breakaway outfit for Zuma supporters who opposed the ANC leadership of President Cyril Ramaphosa, was a Zuma project from the outset. “He is the party’s central drawcard,” she said. “There’s no clear center holding it together in his absence.” Know More Zuma’s son, Duduzane, serves as the party’s first deputy president and is widely regarded as a potential successor, but analysts question whether he can replicate the appeal of his father, who led South Africa from 2009 to 2018 before being ousted amid corruption allegations and a wider state capture scandal. “Duduzane is a completely unknown political figure,” said André Duvenhage, a political analyst at South Africa’s North-West University. “He comes from a business background.” The ANC may benefit from Zuma’s absence, said Musa Xulu, an independent political analyst, adding that if he remains largely absent from the campaign trail, some ANC voters who followed him could drift back. “The ANC is becoming the biggest beneficiary of Zuma’s current disappearance from public politics. The MK party is Jacob Zuma and Jacob Zuma is the MK,” Xulu said. Notable The ANC secured a legal victory ahead of the 4 November 2026 local government elections when the Constitutional Court ruled in its favour, ordering the electoral commission to reinstate 181 disqualified candidates onto the ballot papers.

events.title: African energy's 'Big Bang' moment
events.summary: Alexis’s view The Iran war is shaping up to be the catalyst of a seismic shift in Africa’s energy sector. And, in the case of the continent’s richest man Aliko Dangote, the conflict has proven the old adage that luck is what happens when preparation meets opportunity. Dangote’s mega-refinery on the outskirts of Lagos State has revealed the scale of a West African market underserved by locally refined fuel, while upending conventional thinking by showing African refineries can supply markets in Europe and Asia. At the same time, disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has exposed the vulnerability of nations that are heavily dependent on fuel imports: South Africa and Kenya have hiked prices, which runs the risk of driving inflation. Meanwhile, President Bola Tinubu’s removal of Nigeria’s subsidy three years ago has allowed prices to skyrocket, turning the cost of fuel into a key campaign issue ahead of January’s election. Policymakers have been quick to react to the altered energy dynamics. South Africa announced plans to increase its strategic oil reserves for the first time since the end of apartheid to mitigate supply shocks, Angola wants to implement faster exploration concessions while urging southern African governments to help finance a new refinery , and plans to build refineries in Uganda and Tanzania have gathered pace. Fola Fagbule, who heads the Kenya regional office of multilateral lender Africa Finance Corporation, which helped to finance Dangote’s Lagos refinery, called the impact of the Nigerian billionaire’s project a “Big Bang” moment. He told me various projects are being developed across the continent “as a result of the new realities in the energy market.” The shift has potential pitfalls. Daniel Evans, global head of fuels and refining research at S&P Global Energy, acknowledged the increased appetite for downstream investment across Africa, but warned difficulties remain around projects that require high levels of capital expenditure. But a new generation of refineries has the potential to transform economies, not only protecting countries from future energy shocks but providing the baseload power needed to ramp up manufacturing. As Fagbule put it, the legacy of this paradigm shift could be how it triggered “massive, large-scale industrialization in Africa that nobody expected.” Notable Dangote Refinery is pushing to extend the sale of its shares to Egypt , indicating that Africa’s largest IPO is likely to take a more pan-African shape .

events.title: Demand for AI experts brings deepfakes and chatbot impostors
events.summary: AI experts are coming — and the pretenders too. “Anybody who knows anything about AI” is in high demand from investors trying to play the AI trade, said Gemma Postlethwaite, CEO of expert network GLG. And there are plenty of deepfakes and people using AI chatbots willing to play the part. “We have to be able to deliver experts that not only are who they say they are, but know what they say they know,” Postlethwaite tells Semafor. To test for authenticity, GLG is doing additional screening and ID verification — increasingly on camera with questions designed to trip up AI avatars. It’s also parsing transcripts to find “situations where somebody’s expertise is going off-piste,” she said. “Think of it like a digital fingerprint of knowledge.” Verify, then trust. GLG is also connecting frontier AI labs with subject-matter experts to help train models in sensitive subjects, such as child psychiatrists who can craft responses to kids in crisis and nuclear or bioweapon experts to respond to bad actors looking for instruction manuals. — Liz Hoffman

events.title: Congo Basin deforestation nears Amazon levels
events.summary: Forest clearing in the Congo Basin nearly matched losses in the Amazon for the first time in a decade of monitoring, even as deforestation slowed worldwide, a new study found. The destruction releases vast stores of carbon, adding to climate change that is already contributing to drought and forest fires across the tropics. Expanding farming, timber, and mining activities are driving the clearances in the basin, which is home to the world’s second-largest tropical rainforest, the Forest Declaration Assessment group said . In DR Congo, where most of the forest is situated, decades of conflict — along with poor oversight — have fueled uncontrolled logging, driving up the rate of tree loss in central Africa this decade. Meanwhile, there has been a steep decline in deforestation in Latin America and the Caribbean, leaving the two regions almost on a par. — Ruben Nyanguila
