events.title: Singapore-listed firm faces Indonesian probe over suspected land clearing by burning amid haze
events.summary: Several Singapore-listed plantation and agribusiness companies have faced scrutiny over fires in Indonesia. Indonesia has opened a preliminary probe into suspected land clearing by burning in a Kencana Agri subsidiary’s North Kalimantan concession, after fires and haze spread across the region. Kencana Agri, Wilmar, GAR, Bumitama Agri and First Resources said fires affected some concession areas, but many started outside their land or in community areas before spreading. Singapore’s National Environment Agency will issue preventive notices to seven Indonesian firms, mostly in timber and pulpwood, as authorities step up action over the haze risk. SINGAPORE – The Indonesian authorities have started a preliminary inquiry into suspected land-clearing fires in a concession area operated by a subsidiary of Singapore-listed palm oil producer Kencana Agri. The company disclosed on Oct 16 that investigators had inspected the affected area in North Kalimantan in September, and that the inquiry was ongoing. Kencana acknowledged that fires had affected approximately 62ha within concession areas operated by its subsidiaries in North and East Kalimantan, although it maintained that the fires had spread from adjacent land rather than originating from its operations. The disclosures came in response to queries from Singapore Exchange Regulation (SGX RegCo) over recent forest and peatland fires in Indonesia and the resulting transboundary haze affecting Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia. Kencana is among several Singapore-listed plantation and agribusiness companies that have faced scrutiny over fires in Indonesia in recent days, with some acknowledging fires within their concessions but disputing that they had started them. The company, which has plantations and mills in Sumatra, Kalimantan and Sulawesi, said the affected area was small compared with its total planted area of around 67,862ha. It said its firefighting teams had worked with local authorities and communities to contain the fire, using drones and fire observation towers to identify active fire fronts and to direct ground crews. “The incidents are under control, with ongoing monitoring and precautionary response measures being maintained.” Agribusiness giant Wilmar International also acknowledged on Oct 16 that fires had been detected in small areas of some of its Indonesian concessions, but said they had originated outside its concession boundaries or on land farmed by local communities within them. The group said its field verification indicated that the fires had subsequently spread into areas under its management. Wilmar said its firefighting teams, working with local authorities and communities, had extinguished all such fires quickly. It also said it had not undertaken any new oil palm planting at its company-owned plantations in Indonesia since 2013. Its field activities since then have been limited to replanting existing cultivated areas, which it said was carried out mechanically without the use of fire. Wilmar added that it had maintained a strict no-burning policy since 2006, covering its subsidiaries and third-party suppliers. Suppliers that breached the policy could have their commercial relationships terminated. Meanwhile, Golden Agri-Resources (GAR) said on Oct 16 that the recent forest and land fires had not materially affected its operations. GAR, which operates oil palm plantations across Sumatra, Kalimantan and Papua, said it had received inquiries from various stakeholders about the fires and whether its concessions or activities were connected to the incidents. However, it said that, to the best of its knowledge, there had been no allegations, claims or findings that its operations had contributed to the recent fires and haze. The company also said neither it nor its subsidiaries had received any formal notice of investigation, enforcement action or allegation from regulatory or government authorities in connection with the fires. Its Indonesian-listed subsidiary, Sinar Mas Agro Resources and Technology (SMART), had separately responded to queries from the Indonesia Stock Exchange on Oct 15. SMART said the fires had not materially affected its operations, 2026 production targets, revenue, profit or asset values. Indofood Agri Resources also disclosed on Oct 16 that its Indonesian-listed subsidiary, Salim Ivomas Pratama (SIMP), had responded to queries from the Indonesia Stock Exchange over forest and land fires. SIMP, which operates plantations across Java, Sumatra, Kalimantan and Sulawesi, said it is monitoring hot spots using satellite data, and any detected hot spots would be addressed promptly to prevent fires. It did not specify whether any hot spots had been detected within its plantation areas. Bumitama Agri, which requested a trading halt on Oct 16, said fires had damaged some areas within or adjoining its Indonesian concessions, particularly community-managed and unplanted land.

With the highest adult obesity rate in Africa , at 30%, the drugs are in high demand in South Africa, but the cost of the trademarked version puts them out of reach for most people. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

events.title: South Africa’s Black firms face $45B funding gap
events.summary: South African Black-owned businesses face a funding shortfall of $45 billion, a new report shows, citing “explicit investor bias” alongside barriers such as limited collateral and governance concerns. The findings come three decades after the democratic government introduced a raft of measures — known as Black Economic Empowerment (BEE) — aimed at reversing the dispossession suffered by Black people under apartheid and colonialism. Despite the efforts to redress the problem, South Africa remains one of the world’s most unequal societies. The study, published by British International Investment and Sweden’s Swedfund, both state-owned development finance entities, lands as Washington steps up pressure on Pretoria to dismantle BEE. US Ambassador Leo Brent Bozell III has put scrapping the policy on a list of demands tied to improving the investment climate. Pretoria has refused, despite disagreements within the coalition government. Instead the policy conversation has moved to creating a $60 billion fund to help scale up small Black-owned businesses. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

events.title: Wee Hur enters Singapore student housing market with 1,398-bed NTU project
events.summary: A hall of residence at Nanyang Technological University. The new development will mainly house postgraduate students. Wee Hur Holdings is entering Singapore’s purpose-built student accommodation market with a 1,398-bed Y-Suites project at NTU. NTU issued a Letter of Award after a competitive process. The award covers design, construction, financing, operation and maintenance. The project may become Singapore’s largest privately developed and operated student housing on an autonomous university campus. Construction is due in Q3 2027, with operations by the start of the 2029-30 academic year. Wee Hur says the project will grow its pipeline and regional Y Suites platform. SINGAPORE – Wee Hur Holdings is entering Singapore’s purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA) market with a 1,398-bed Y-Suites development at Nanyang Technological University (NTU). The Singapore-listed property and construction group said on Oct 16 that NTU had issued it a Letter of Award for the project, following a competitive expression-of-interest and request-for-proposal process. The award covers the design, construction, financing, operation and maintenance of the accommodation facility. The parties are working towards finalising an agreement, with the award subject to its terms and conditions. Upon completion, the project is expected to be Singapore’s largest privately developed and operated student accommodation facility within an autonomous university campus, Wee Hur said. The development will mainly house postgraduate students, with a limited number of beds allocated to undergraduates. It will also be Wee Hur’s first Y Suites-branded asset in Singapore. Construction is targeted to begin in the third quarter of 2027, with operations scheduled to start by the beginning of the 2029- 2030 academic year, subject to approvals from NTU and the regulatory authorities. The project will be undertaken through a special-purpose vehicle, with Wee Hur responsible for the development from design and construction through to operations and maintenance. The roughly 6,000 sq m greenfield site is located next to 30 Nanyang Link within NTU’s main campus. The project vehicle will be granted an initial 20-year land lease, with options for two five-year extensions, subject to the definitive agreement. Wee Hur Property chief executive Goh Chengyu said the award will add to the group’s development pipeline and provide greater visibility for its construction activities. He added: “By developing the PBSA from the ground up and operating it over the long term, we can apply our experience across the full real estate life cycle – from design and construction through to operations.” The project also expands Wee Hur’s student accommodation business into a third market, after Australia and Hong Kong, as the group builds out its Y Suites platform across the Asia-Pacific. Goh Wee Ping, Wee Hur Holdings’ chief investment officer and chief executive of Wee Hur Capital, said bringing Y Suites to Singapore was “an important step” in the group’s ambition to build a regional PBSA platform. “Working with NTU allows us to bring our experience to our home market while further scaling a platform that we believe can create long-term value for the group,” he said. events.title: Neet rates higher in England’s smaller cities and towns than in biggest cities
events.summary: Initiatives to address youth employment crisis and offer training are being launched in towns such as Telford Smaller cities and towns across England have higher rates of young people not in employment, education or training than the nine largest cities, analysis shows. The Centre for Cities, an independent thinktank dedicated to improving the economies of the UK, used 2021 census data to work out the rates across 41 cities and towns in England. Of those places, 10 of the smallest cities and towns had higher rates of 16- to 24-year-olds out of employment and education – an average of 15.7% of their youth population, compared with an average of 13.9% across the nine largest cities . It comes amid a national debate over chronic youth unemployment in the UK, with the latest ONS data showing just under 1 million young people are not in employment, training or education (Neet). An interim report published by the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn in May found that the UK was “at risk of a lost generation”, with young adults facing a “perfect storm” of challenges. His final report is expected soon after the budget on 28 October. The Centre for Cities analysis shows London (117,095) and Birmingham (44,995) have the highest number of Neets in absolute terms, representing rates of 13.1% and 15.9% respectively. The average Neet rate across England is 12.6%. In Blackpool , 2,660 of young people are not in education, employment or training, a rate of 21.2%. In Slough, 2,170 young people are Neet (14.1%). The Shropshire town of Telford has 2,780 Neets (15.1%). Rob Johnson, a senior analyst at the Centre for Cities, said the higher rates of Neets in smaller towns and cities were often a reflection of their general economic performance. In particular, he said such areas could be affected by their proximity to larger cities, but the figures could also be a reflection of the weakness of bigger city economies in the north and Midlands. “A big root cause of higher rates of Neets in these places is because we know these are cities that have weaker economies,” he said. “The big headline [is] of 1 million Neets across the country but it’s actually more important to understand where those people are. The scale is important, but you just need to know the extent of the variation across the country.” Johnson said the picture was mixed across smaller cities and towns. “Somewhere like Slough, which is actually quite a productive economy, does have a relatively high rate of Neets. There’s an issue there about connecting those people to the local economy.” For some in Telford , 30 miles north of Birmingham, the answer to the UK’s chronic crisis of youth unemployment may lie in its local shopping centre. The Skills Shop, a new youth employment hub opened by Telford College in partnership with the Department for Work and Pensions, aims to connect young people with education, local employers and mentors to tackle the high Neet rates in the region. Sarah Davies, the executive director of employer engagement and partnerships at Telford College, said there were multiple drivers for the Neets crisis, including the Covid-19 pandemic, mental health disorders and changes in the job market, and there was no “one size fits all” solution. “It’s a national concern because young people are our future. If you’re out of work, you’re more likely to stay out of work,” she said. “If you ask any young person, they’d rather be working than sat at home. Nobody wants to sit at home on TikTok all day.” Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning One of those benefiting from courses at the college is George Bate, 21, who is learning to become a HGV driver after graduating from university with a degree in games design. He said he had been unable to pursue a career in gaming due to a lack of opportunities and so embarked on the HGV course after he was signposted by the jobcentre. “I’d applied to most of the stuff around the area and just didn’t get a response, so that was the disheartening part. I couldn’t find anywhere that was willing to take me,” he said. “A lot of the time, it’s not even a person who reviews any of your [applications].” When asked about narratives surrounding young people being “lazy”, Bate said there was a lack of employment opportunities as well as an absence of career progression. “It makes it so much more stressful to find a career when you know that some of them don’t have the correct amount of upward mobility,” he said. Charlie Pryce, 19, is also taking the HGV course and said he had applied for other jobs but faced several barriers to further training and employment. “People our age, we’ve got a long life ahead of us and we actually want to do work. We might not start off the best but I think we can grow into the role,” he said. “It’s not nice sitting around not doing anything. It’s nice to get out there and do stuff and feel like you’re actually providing something and just working hard.

events.title: The ultra-rich are spending one million dollars a day fighting California’s proposed billionaire tax
events.summary: Tech billionaires have raised more than $340m to defeat Prop 40, a one-time 5% wealth tax that will fund healthcare and education Tech billionaires have been dumping hundreds of millions of dollars into the fight against a wealth tax in California . They’ve raised more than $340m, and the campaign they’re funding is spending more than $1m a day to defeat the measure, according to state financial disclosures. With the election less than a month away, those funds are being spent at a stepped-up pace. During the first 19 days of September, according to the most recent campaign filings, the opposition campaign plowed through at least $21.2m to fight the billionaire tax – surpassing $1m per day. Voters are being inundated with robotexts, mailers and advertisements that warn a tax on billionaires would “expose all Californians to higher taxes”, as one ad reads. Californians will vote on the ballot measure, Proposition 40, in early November. If passed, it would require a one-time 5% tax on the state’s billionaires, with the proceeds mostly funding healthcare programs, along with some education and food assistance. The measure has divided Democrats in the state, with some giving enthusiastic support and others rejecting the proposal because it’s just a one-time levy and the bulk of it would only fund certain healthcare programs. The state’s major unions and progressive politicians like the Vermont senator Bernie Sanders and California congressman Ro Khanna back Prop 40. But both the Democratic and Republican candidates for governor, as well as organizations like Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, a lobbying branch of the healthcare group, oppose it. Among its fiercest critics, however, are the tech billionaires it would most directly apply to. The donors to the no campaign are a who’s who of Silicon Valley , including the Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison, crypto magnate Chris Larsen and several prominent venture capitalists. The biggest donor, by far, is the Google co-founder Sergey Brin , who has contributed at least $102m to fight the tax, according to campaign finance filings. The runner-up is Schmidt, who has donated more than $42m. For comparison, the yes on 40 campaign has raised a total that’s just shy of $33m, mostly from the healthcare union sponsoring the measure. Proponents and opponents alike are casting the billionaire tax as a potential first step toward wealth taxes in more states. While those against the measure see it as populist contagion , those in favor connect it to the top issue of the midterms – affordability. And with California having more billionaires than any other state, Prop 40 is seen as setting the stage for more referendums on wealth inequality throughout the country. “There’s a lot of volatility among the electorate surrounding a pushback against Marie Antoinette and her tech friends,” said David McCuan, a political science professor at Sonoma State University who studies ballot measures. “And that’s what the ‘yes’ forces are relying on.” Recent polling on Prop 40 shows that it’s favored to pass, but its lead has shrunk over the last few weeks as the opposition campaign has increased spending. A late-September poll by the University of California shows 45% of voters likely to vote yes on the tax with 42% voting no. Just a month earlier, the proposal enjoyed a 7% lead . Complicating matters are two separate countermeasures that Prop 40’s opponents successfully placed on the November ballot, Proposition 41 and 42. Prop 41 directly targets the billionaire tax, while Prop 42 is more of a general proposal to protect individuals from certain new taxes. If either of these measures receives more yes votes than Prop 40, they will stop the billionaire tax from taking effect – even if it passes. “Props 41 and 42 have poison pills in them to destroy 40,” McCuan said. “And when voters are confused, when they are uncertain … it’s much easier to get a no vote.” Earlier this month, the campaign fighting the billionaire tax placed an ad on television, digital and streaming platforms across the state. It starts with quiet, foreboding music and the president of the California Medical Association, René Bravo, dressed in a white lab coat, saying: “The people pushing Prop 40 say it’s supposed to improve healthcare. That’s not true.” The campaign has debuted similar ads saying teachers, carpenters and firefighters also oppose the wealth tax, saying it’s “a dangerous experiment”. The messaging around the campaign centers on how the tax would hurt “doctors, teachers, small businesses, working families and public safety”, without mention of the state’s billionaires. The no on Prop 40 campaign calls it “an everyone tax”. Likewise, the campaigns for the two measures that would pre-empt the billionaire tax argue these proposals promote transparency and have the backing of small businesses and taxpayers.

events.title: For restaurants Covid-19 was a crisis – pandemic loans are proving a disaster
events.summary: Low-interest loans kept many eateries afloat. But the industry never recovered enough for them to repay the debt F or almost 20 years, Jai Mazumdar has served vegetarian curries, samosas, gulab jamun and other Indian delicacies at Spice N Curry, a cafe and grocery nestled inside a modest strip mall near Florida International University (FIU) in Miami. When the Covid-19 pandemic devastated his business, as it did with so many restaurants, Mazumdar took out a $370,000 economic injury disaster loan (EIDL) from the federal government in early 2021. At the time, it provided a desperately needed lifeline. He was confident that once business returned to normal he could begin repaying the 30-year loan, which came with a low 3.75% interest rate and a 30-month deferment period. But when his business didn’t recover, the disaster loan turned out to be a disaster of its own. The Spice N Curry cafe relied heavily on traffic from FIU. Since many students and faculty were studying and working remotely both during and after the pandemic, Mazumdar’s lunch business took a major hit. As the losses mounted, he applied for additional EIDL funds and was extended another $87,000 loan the following year. Borrowers with EIDLs totaling more than $200,000 were required to personally guarantee the loan, which meant that if they default, the government would be able to seize their personal assets. Five years later, Mazumdar is struggling to make his monthly payments, and he’s losing faith that he’ll ever be able to fully repay the loans. Since Congress passed the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (Cares) Act in March 2020, the federal government has issued 3.9m Covid-related EIDLs totaling $378.4bn to businesses that faced hardship as a result of the pandemic. The Small Business Administration (SBA) was tasked with administering the loans – up to $2m per individual applicant. Despite the attractive rates and flexible terms, according to a congressional report released earlier this year, EIDL defaults have steadily risen to over 30%, resulting in $75.2bn in charged-off loans as of last June. “Covid was an extinction event for tens of thousands of restaurants,” said Erika Polmar, executive director of the Independent Restaurant Coalition, a non-profit advocacy group for independent bars and restaurants in the US. “The ones that survived, if they didn’t receive [restaurant revitalization fund] grants, had to pay off all that debt from small businesses loans or EIDLs. Local initiatives that promised rent relief or eviction moratoriums often fell through. So they moved through 2022 and beyond trying to pay off their debt and weren’t able to reinvest in their businesses.” Mazumdar says his business is worse off today than it was during Covid – a sentiment echoed by other operators whose businesses have been negatively affected by rising food, labor and energy costs. “There is a tsunami going on right now,” he said. “Rents are very high. The average population doesn’t have spending power. There is a lack of qualified labor. Tourism has also declined here. Everyone is just nervous about when the next leg of the stool is going to collapse.” Five years after he took the loans, Mazumdar says the EIDL money is gone. Initially, he used the funds to refurbish the space and upgrade equipment, installing new refrigeration and freezer units to increase his retail inventory. He used the rest to cover operating expenses. After finally reopening the cafe in 2022, sales declined so badly that he decided to close the dining room permanently after just a year and a half. “My monthly EIDL payment is $1,900, and my home mortgage is $1,600,” he said. “I had to rent out a room in my own home so I could have extra income to cover part of the payment.” His business has lost money every year since Covid, yet he’s managed to stay current with his loan payments. “I’ve been working seven days a week, 12 hours a day for the last three years. It’s become a completely hand-to-mouth existence.” When borrowers exceed 120 days past due on their EIDL payments, the loans are transferred to the US treasury department for collection. That results in additional fees and penalties that typically amount to about 30% of the principal. When the loans are personally guaranteed, the IRS can garnish the delinquent borrower’s wages, tax refunds or a percentage of their social security benefits. Randy Barnette, founder of the Virginia-based Ornery Beer Company, is almost two years past due on a $500,000 EIDL he took out in February 2021. Before Covid hit, he was actively searching for a space to open a second location of the Ornery Beer Company Public House, his restaurant and bar that features Ornery brand beers.

events.title: Replit’s CEO says the future of work is the ‘self-driving company’
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Replit CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad has seen how AI is impacting the workplace firsthand, with businesses adopting his company’s AI coding tools to develop and launch their own software. At TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco on Thursday, Masad shared what Replit has learned about what that means for the future of work in the AI age, including how humans will still play key roles as AI agents come to work alongside them. He described his vision of a “self-driving company,” referring not to robotaxi makers, but how agents will come to do much of the grunt work at companies while people become more valued for their judgment and taste. “The reality is, all of our jobs — perhaps everyone in this audience, especially — changed over the past year,” he said, addressing the audience at Disrupt. “But a big part of America and the world, they still don’t know that that change is coming, and it’s going to be surprising to a lot of people,” Masad said. He said Replit’s team had been reflecting on how AI technology impacted their own workplace over the past year, particularly after AI agents became more reliable sometime earlier this year. “Our company entirely changed how we operate, and I would say the closest analogy is a ‘self-driving company’,” Masad said. “The company is sort of self-improving, so a lot of the work that’s going on is driven by agents.” Illustrating the shift, Masad said that when support tickets come in at Replit, they’re first examined by an agent, which performs the initial triaging by looking at GitHub issues, the codebase, and Linear tickets. By the time the support request reaches a person, they have all the additional information that helps them decide how best to proceed. And when that support person decides to submit a patch to apply a fix, it’s just a click to deploy another agent. “You have an entire loop where agents did most of the work, but crucially, there’s human judgment in the middle, and we don’t think that’s going away anytime soon. You need human judgment; you need taste,” Masad explained. The end result is that instead of taking jobs from people, agents are changing what people work on. “We’re spending a lot more time figuring out what to work on,” Masad continued. “I go around the company, I see a lot more discussions, a lot more whiteboarding. We spend a lot more time on architecture, how to build things. And so I think the future of work — the self-driving company idea — is really trying to discover what AI transformation means.” He also noted that when Replit talks with other businesses, the conversations are more about how AI can help people become more productive and happier at work. (The latter because the AI agents make work less boring and more creative, he said.) “There’s a positive vision of the world that Silicon Valley is not really putting out, and we’re hoping to do that,” Masad added. events.title: Houthi strikes expose Saudi Arabia's vulnerabilities
events.summary: The deadliest week for civilians in the Gulf marks a turning point in the US-Iran war that has engulfed the Middle East from Beirut to Aden, and from Irbil to Salalah . Saudi Arabia stepped up strikes on Yemen’s Houthis after the group hit Riyadh’s airport 20 times this month, killing 17 people and injuring 333 . Despite Riyadh’s considerable air defenses and vast military spending, the militants have been able to outsmart the systems using relatively cheap drones and missiles. Iranian attacks on the Gulf have brought the region closer together, and the latest strikes by Tehran’s allies in Yemen have galvanized support for Saudi Arabia. Authorities in the region are reinforcing this message of unity: In today’s Friday prayer sermons in Kuwait, imams were instructed to praise the kingdom’s support during Iraq’s 1990 invasion and condemn the Houthis . Similar expressions of support were also voiced in Bahrain, Qatar, and the UAE. While security is by far the most pressing priority, new projections from the IMF have revealed the war’s deepening economic toll. Jihad Azour, the fund’s regional director, told Asharq Bloomberg that the Gulf’s financial reserves, diversified export routes, and government interventions have cushioned the shock . But the IMF now predicts a deeper contraction than previously expected, with GDP trailing pre-war forecasts even after energy production and trade recover. — Mohammed Sergie

events.title: British food and drink exports to EU collapse by more than a third since Brexit
events.summary: NFU analysis of official data shows falls in exports to UK’s largest trading partner since 2019 include 70% for sugar and 74% for egg products Exports of British food and drink to the EU have collapsed by more than a third since Brexit with eggs, chicken and potato producers badly hit, new figures show. Analysis by the National Farmers’ Union (NFU) of HMRC data shows a sharp fall in exports in the year to July compared with the same period in 2019, with sugar dropping the most, down 70%. Data for the first seven months also shows poultry exports fell 53%, with eggs and egg products sold for confectionary and baking industries down 65% for the same period. Full-year data from 2019 to 2025 showed an even deeper impact since Brexit with exports of eggs and egg products down 74%. The NFU president, Tom Bradshaw, said: “The EU is our largest trading partner for agri-food products, accounting for 68% of agri-food exports last year, but trade volumes have fallen over a third since 2019.” Boris Johnson’s government signed a deal on the UK’s future trading and security relationship with the EU in late 2020, after the UK’s formal exit earlier that year. Andy Burnham is reconsidering Labour’s red lines on EU membership under pressure to repair the economic damage of Brexit. Economists estimate the cost to the UK economy has been up to £240bn so far. Food exporters have long complained over the added paperwork that Britain’s exit has brought. Since Brexit all food exports are required to have customs paperwork with different codes for every single product. This includes, for example, every variation of an egg product, whether it is fresh, dried, steamed, shelled, or contains added water or sugar. The paper pulp used in egg cartons as well as the eggs also need health certification to show they are free of disease. Also hit hard by Brexit is the horticultural sector with seed potatoes from Britain, mainly Scotland, banned from the EU after trade negotiators failed to agree on equivalent standards in the Brexit trade and cooperation agreement in 2020. Horticultural exports fell more than 50%. Pre-Brexit, Scotland exported around 20,000 tonnes of seed potatoes, worth almost £11m, to Europe each year. Speaking in parliament earlier this week Andy Burnham said that Brexit trade barriers meant “entire truckloads of plants or fresh product can be destroyed because of a single missing stamp or minor paperwork delay”. He hoped to “land a positive outcome” in the upcoming UK-EU reset talks with a new agreement removing many of the sanitary and phytosanitary checks on fresh farm produce exports that came in after Brexit. Burnham told MPs: “Our largest food export, Scottish salmon, faces a 100% rate of document checks at the border, costing us around £100m in lost exports. “British burgers and other fresh meat products cannot be sold in the EU. Seed potatoes from Scotland and shellfish from Wales are banned. This is having a real impact on businesses and the agreement on the table could reverse some of that damage.” A deal to ease sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) checks was largely agreed in May giving food producers time to prepare for changes expected to come in next summer, but key details remain to be finalised. The NFU is calling for “transition arrangements” for some UK crops that have been grown with fungicides or breeding techniques not yet approved in the EU. This is to allow those harvesting this autumn and winter to make use of the new export freedoms when they come in next year. Bradshaw said: “British farmers and growers must retain access to precision breeding technologies that will help to strengthen food resilience to extreme weather and to science-based plant protection products that help protect food being grown for 29m households from pests and diseases. “Any changes must also provide an appropriate transition period to minimise disruption for farm businesses and we will continue to make this case to government while we await the final agreement.”

events.title: Remote work made these colleagues more open with each other, not less
events.summary: Many employees see having the freedom to work from home as a benefit. DigitalVision/Getty Images If you need to participate in video meetings for work, you’ve probably experienced more than one disruption, whether it’s kids darting around or home renovation noise. Meetings that use Zoom and similar software are a fixture of remote work, which surged during the COVID-19 pandemic and remains prevalent. As of August 2026, 36% of American workers in management, professional and related occupations did at least some of their work from home, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. I’m a management scholar who studies how, when and where people work . Before the pandemic began, I was studying a professional services company. That made it possible for me to follow how its staff transitioned from primarily working in person to mostly remote through 2024, which gave me more insight into how remote work has changed people’s lives. The study included 275 interviews and about 330 hours of observation. Most people in the groups I followed ended up working from home four or five days a week, joining meetings by video. What I found was the opposite of what I expected. Learning more about colleagues Rather than pulling colleagues apart, remote work brought them closer and made them more willing to be open with one another. The findings were peer-reviewed and will be published in an upcoming issue of the management journal Organization Science. Before the shift to remote work, I assumed – consistent with the predictions made by many prominent researchers of workplace relationships – that moving people out of the office would break down social connections. But I was wrong. In the office, before the shift to remote work, I found that people primarily viewed one another as work colleagues rather than whole people. Reflecting this relationship, workers sometimes said they felt uncomfortable sharing with one another aspects of their lives that might limit their ability to do work. For example, one worker I interviewed, Patrick, was afraid to tell his colleagues he could not work late one night because he was helping his mom. All the names I’m mentioning are pseudonyms to protect the privacy of the people involved and their employer. “Even though you didn’t sleep last night, you’re expected to show up and smile and be fine,” said Tamara, an exhausted parent with two young children, when she was still commuting regularly to the office. Surprisingly, people told me that they learned a lot more about one another once they began to work remotely instead of being together in an office. During my research, I heard about children yelling in the background and pets wandering in front of cameras. A spouse arriving home from work stopped to say hello on screen. In team chat channels, people posted photos of their children, their animals and the meals they had cooked. “Everyone has noises in the background, or they have something going on or whatever, and so we get to know each other quicker and on a deeper level than we would otherwise,” Tamara told me. In some cases, this increased sense of closeness happened to people who had known each other for years prior to switching to remote work. When you’re a remote employee, you may get more quality time with your pets. Moment/Getty Images Growing psychological safety Psychological safety is the sense that you can take an interpersonal risk at work, such as admitting a mistake, asking for help or raising a problem, without being judged negatively. Decades of management research tie psychological safety to important outcomes for both workers and organizations, including learning, creativity and speaking up . Over time, working remotely seemed to improve psychological safety for many of these co-workers. People became “less afraid to talk about the interface of their personal and professional lives,” Leah said. Before, she added, no one would have volunteered that a breakup was affecting them and that they needed a day off to decompress. After the company went remote, people told me they felt more comfortable sharing their own challenges as they tried to juggle their work and the challenges they faced in their personal lives. Supporting work and nonwork activities And as people started sharing these problems with their co-workers, they also told me they felt as if they could then better support one another. When one worker’s father fell ill, his colleague, Brooke, took over the tasks the two had planned to do together. “I’m just going to take this over for you right now,” Brooke told him. “And then, whenever you can, come back and swoop in.” The colleague was able to dedicate time to caring for his father. And importantly, because help circulated this way, Brooke said, a task no longer “stopped dead in the water” when one person could not get to it. This deeper collaboration did not seem to come at the expense of getting tasks completed. As an employee I’m calling Charles explained, having co-workers sharing details about their personal lives has “helped us to work more effectively in a lot of ways.” Crucially, these improvements were experienced by people with many different living arrangements – young and old, those with and without kids or partners, men and women. And these benefits were positively reinforcing. For instance, sharing more meant learning more about others, which further reinforced psychological safety. My findings suggest that remote work can be a benefit that employers and employees may overlook. Rather than treating time out of the office as a cost to social connection among employees, they might treat it as a way to grow personally and get to know co-workers better. Vanessa M. events.title: The Download: failed social media bans, and extending pets’ lives
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Kids are outsmarting social media bans. That’s not a problem we need to solve. —Michal Luria, Aliya Bhatia, and Danah Boyd Social media bans are stacking up. In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds.  The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15. But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented.  Here’s what we ought to do instead to keep kids safe . Can’t bear to say goodbye to your pet? Biotech’s got you covered. —Jessica Hamzelou I don’t remember much about Peppy, my first and only pet cat. What I do vividly remember, though, is the day she went missing. I was 10 years old, and I searched everywhere for her, scouting nearby fields and woods until sunset. I made posters. We never found her. I was devastated. Almost 30 years later, pet owners have an expanding set of options to potentially prolong their years with their furry companions. The possibilities include drugs, cloning, and even cryonics. But is that a good thing? Read the full story on the promises and pitfalls of pet life extension . This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday. 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Form Energy and its iron batteries Form Energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s  10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026 , available  exclusively to subscribers . As wind and solar power grow, utilities need cheaper ways to store electricity for longer periods. Form Energy aims to meet that need with batteries that can store energy for 100 hours. The company has developed a new type of battery using iron, a far more abundant and cheaper metal than those used in many existing batteries. It uses a process that Form calls “reversible rusting,” in which iron turns to rust as the battery discharges and back to iron when it charges. See how Form Energy hopes to make renewable power more reliable . —Jonathan W. Rosen Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch , spanning everything from electric buses to portable rubber dams . The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 Insurance is the next big obstacle for AI  AI companies are racking up billions of dollars of legal liabilities from the damage their products cause. ( WSJ  $) +  The FTC has sent subpoenas to OpenAI and Anthropic over consumer harms.  ( Axios ) + AI hacks leave a mess, and AI companies still aren’t cleaning them up.  ( Wired  $) +  Who’s liable when AI agents go rogue?  ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 A Russian drone entered NATO waters for the first time Attacks like those near Bulgaria and Romania are spurring requests for better defenses. ( TechCrunch ) +  Criminals stole $90 million from crypto wallets last week in a highly sophisticated hack.  ( FT  $) 5 Big Tech gave Trump $92 million for his ballroom  Meanwhile the president himself won’t be spending a dime. Residents responded by building wildlife tunnels beneath the road to help them reach their breeding ponds safely. The crossings became popular. But a few years later, researchers found the local toad population had crashed from more than 10,000 to fewer than 1,000. events.title: How to dress a tech oligarch: The Social Reckoning’s costume designer on Zuckerberg’s style evolution
events.summary: Susan Lyall worked with actor Jeremy Strong to research the Meta CEO’s favorite Nikes and luxury sweaters The first Aaron Sorkin Facebook movie, 2010’s The Social Network, helped cement the early aughts image of Mark Zuckerberg rebelling against corporate norms in rumpled hoodies and T-shirts. The follow-up, The Social Reckoning, is carbon-dated from 2019 to 2021. This is “post-hoodie”, as the movie’s costume designer, Susan Lyall, describes it, “post-thumbing his nose” to formality. It is also peak robot. Zuckerberg’s reserved wardrobe of suits or interchangeable long-sleeved shirts echo his chilling composure throughout, even as fury simmers under the surface. The costume was based on deep research by Lyall and also by actor Jeremy Strong who, she says, is “very into costume”. Having worked together before, on the Sorkin movies Molly’s Game and The Trial of the Chicago 7, they would text a lot during the preparation process. “He reaches out before I even get to reach out to him. It’s my third movie with him, so I’m pretty used to it. He’s very proactive. He’s one of my favourite actors because of that. He would know exactly where [Zuckerberg] wore what. He wanted the exact Nike shoe – the footwear was very important to him – and the exact Brunello Cucinelli T-shirt and sweater, and so on,” she says. Strong has become notorious for method acting, and method dressing, too, seems to be part of his process. “It’s sort of the first step in the performance. That and the haircut,” says Lyall. The conversations went deep. “It’s actually kind of nerdy, you know, to sit there and talk about the color of the shoelaces. There aren’t that many people who want to talk about that. I always joke with him, if the acting thing doesn’t work out, you can have a position in my department!” she says. Lyall found those Nikes – to be specific, the 2018 Nike Flyknit trainer in black anthracite – on Grailed. For the sweaters, it was Strong, she says, who worked out how to reach the eye-wateringly expensive Italian luxury brand Brunello Cucinelli, in order to buy specific pieces, “because we don’t want the latest. We want stuff from five or six years ago, and they were very helpful at procuring it. And that was because of him. He was really proactive.” Lyall has spent a lot of hours thinking about how tech oligarchs dress. Not only Zuckerberg but Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos and others too, who were partial inspiration for another of her recent credits, the 2025 Jesse Armstrong movie Mountainhead about four devilish plutocrats. They, too, wore a lot of Brunello Cucinelli. That brand sells cashmere cardigans for $16,500 and ribbed sweaters for $4,600. Amusingly, it currently has the Immanuel Kant quote “beauty is the symbol of the morally good” in prime place on its website homepage. In Lyall’s view, Brunello Cucinelli is a “safety net for people like Mark Zuckerberg. If they’re not sure about what they’re wearing, if they pay a lot for it, they feel a little better about it. You know, if this little sweater is $2,000, it must be good. It’s kind of a security blanket, or just an affirmation of your own success. You’re going to be OK if you’re wearing this tasteful thing.” The Zuckerberg of The Social Reckoning had moved on from the earlier antifashion stance that prompted him to declare, in 2014, that he was “not a cool person”, and only wore grey T-shirts because he wanted to make “as few decisions as possible … I feel like I’m not doing my job if I spend any of my energy on things that are silly or frivolous.” By the period captured in the movie, says Lyall, “I believe Zuckerberg was trying to be relatable, but also starting to understand Silicon Valley’s obsession with taste and the cost of things.” He was also more buff than he had been. In her interpretation, he seemed to be thinking: “My fit physique looks very nice in this clingy but expensive sweater. And ‘if you know, you know’ – I think there’s a bit of that. But I also think, he’s nouveau riche without being gaudy. It’s not without taste.” Since then, Zuckerberg’s outward presentation has graduated to outright peacocking. For the tech billionaires, in general, says Lyall: “I think something happened. I think they have discovered a new way to flex. And it’s not quiet luxury. It’s loud.” For Zuckerberg specifically – whose makeover came suddenly with ostentatious gold chains, Loewe shorts and Alexander McQueen suits embellished with dragonflies in around 2024 – it could not feel much more strategic. Dabbling with fashion allows Zuckerberg to look like a different guy from the one we have seen so many times sweating in a suit in front of Congress. It also provides a distraction from the reality of his products and work, giving him something soft and harmless to talk about. Zuckerberg has even used the classic fiction writer’s trick of embedding backstory within his jewellery.

events.title: NVIDIA RTX Spark PCs Available Today — A New Beginning for Windows PCs
events.summary: News Summary: NVIDIA RTX Spark laptops are available today from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI — with additional systems to follow — bringing RTX acceleration and NVIDIA’s full-stack AI platform to slim, premium Windows PCs for creation, gaming and local AI. RTX Spark delivers up to 1 petaflop of AI compute and up to 128GB of unified memory — enabling AI developers, creators and gamers to run frontier AI models locally, render 90GB+ 3D scenes and play AAA games at 1440p at over 100 frames per second, all on a slim, portable device. Day-one support across local AI agents, creative apps and major games helps users put RTX Spark to work immediately — from editing with Adobe Photoshop and Premiere to running Hermes and OpenClaw agents and playing titles including Gears of War: E-Day and NBA 2K27 with NVIDIA DLSS 5. NVIDIA today announced the availability of  NVIDIA RTX Spark ™ laptops, bringing together RTX graphics and NVIDIA’s full-stack AI platform in slim, premium Windows PCs for accelerated creation, immersive gaming and powerful local AI — rolling out from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI. Combining decades of NVIDIA innovation into a single superchip, RTX Spark delivers up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of FP4 AI performance to run large language models and AI agents locally. On a single device, creators, developers and gamers can move seamlessly between their everyday workflows and emerging AI agents on the familiar Windows platform. “RTX Spark brings the power of NVIDIA AI, RTX graphics and CUDA together with Microsoft Windows in one PC for creating, gaming and running personal AI agents,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “Together with Microsoft and our PC industry partners, we’re bringing creators, developers and gamers a new generation of Windows PC, built for the work they do today and the personal AI agents they’ll work with next.” “We’re building Windows to be the platform for hybrid intelligence, where AI can run locally when it makes sense and reach the cloud when needed,” said Yusuf Mehdi, executive vice president at Microsoft. “Windows PCs powered by RTX Spark unlock powerful new local compute for creators and developers, expanding what they can create, build and run on Windows.” A New Beginning for Windows PCs RTX Spark brings NVIDIA’s accelerated computing platform to a new generation of portable Windows PCs. At its foundation is a single superchip combining an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU and an NVIDIA Grace CPU with up to 128GB of unified memory and up to 1 petaflop of FP4 AI performance. That shared memory allows demanding creative projects and local AI models to run simultaneously and efficiently. MediaTek collaborated with NVIDIA on the custom CPU design, contributing to its best-in-class power efficiency, performance and connectivity. All of NVIDIA’s platform innovation comes together in RTX Spark — NVIDIA CUDA ® , DLSS, OptiX™, Reflex, G-SYNC ® , TensorRT™ and hardware-accelerated video — in a device that fits in a messenger bag. Slim, efficient designs and all-day battery life bring these capabilities wherever users create, develop and play. From Tool to Teammate RTX Spark gives users the capabilities to deploy local AI agents that turn the PC from a tool into an everyday teammate that can complete tasks, generate assets and write code. Users can put agents to work immediately. Guided setup and easy installers help users get started with agents, including GitHub Copilot, Hermes, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi and WorkBuddy, without requiring a command line. “Personal AI becomes more useful when it can work with your tools and help get things done,” said Dillon Rolnick, CEO at Nous Research, creators of Hermes Agent. “We brought Hermes to RTX Spark so people can put open AI models and agents to work locally on a Windows laptop, with greater control over their data and the freedom to shape AI around their own workflows.” NVIDIA’s models and tools build on that ecosystem. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, a 74-billion-parameter model optimized for tool calling and multistep tasks, brings more capable local AI to supported RTX Spark configurations. The NVIDIA OpenShell ™ secure runtime and Microsoft Execution Containers help users control agent permissions, while NVIDIA agent skills let compatible agents work with tools including NVIDIA Broadcast , RTX Remix and Omniverse ™ libraries. For example, compatible agents can adjust Broadcast effects during a stream or batch-process recorded clips, all on a local PC. That experience extends across devices with NVIDIA PAIR , letting RTX Spark serve AI inference to compatible Windows, Linux and macOS computers on a home network while keeping other PCs free for creating and gaming. Create, Innovate, Play RTX Spark helps creators move from an idea to finished content wherever they work, with the ability to edit 8K 4:2:2 video and render large 3D scenes up to 90GB, even when unplugged. With the arrival of RTX Spark, Adobe is enhancing its industry-leading creative applications, including Photoshop, Premiere and Substance 3D, with NVIDIA TensorRT acceleration in AI-editing features. In Premiere, creators can work faster across some of the most intensive parts of post-production, from playback and rendering to effects, color grading and more. Photoshop and Premiere offer native RTX Spark support through beta releases available at launch, with Substance coming soon. “Creatives are pushing the boundaries of what’s possible across image, video, audio and 3D, and they need tools that can keep up with their ambitions,” said Deepa Subramaniam, vice president of product marketing for creative professionals at Adobe. “By combining NVIDIA’s advanced computing technology with Adobe’s industry-leading creative applications, we’re delivering enhanced experiences that empower creatives to bring their ideas to life with greater power and speed.” For enhancing recorded content, NVIDIA Broadcast 2.3 lets creators remove background noise from existing recordings and shape their voice with Studio Voice Mic Profiles. Beta RTX Video features enable up to 4K super resolution and 4x frame generation. In ComfyUI, new RTX Video nodes can turn 15 frames-per-second (fps) AI-generated video into smoother 60 fps footage and convert it to high dynamic range without requiring per-use cloud inference charges. Code, Test and Deploy With One Machine As AI shifts software development from writing code to directing agents, work often spans a laptop, a cloud AI model and a cloud virtual machine for testing. events.title: Lowball retention bonuses doomed Perella-Piper Sandler merger
events.summary: The Scoop A merger between two Wall Street boutique firm collapsed after senior bankers balked at their retention bonuses. The deal between advisory firm Perella Weinberg Partners and investment bank Piper Sandler envisioned paying Perella’s highest producers $2.5 million in shares of the combined company to stay on for as long as three years, according to people familiar with the matter. The rest of its partners were split into tiers and offered bonuses of between $500,000 and $1.5 million. Perella CEO Andrew Bednar called some partners individually to describe their retention packages and gauge their reaction, the people said. They were almost uniformly negative, with the offers deemed “offensively low,” in the words of one banker, compared to the millions that top dealmakers at the firm make per year. That opposition led to the talks ultimately falling apart, some of the people said. The Financial Times earlier reported that the deal had collapsed . A spokesperson for Perella did not respond to requests for comment. Perella Weinberg went public in 2020 and had seen its shares lose half their value since early last year. Bednar had sought a deal with at least one other bank earlier this year, although talks only progressed with Piper, some of the people said. Rohan’s view Expect to see a wave of departures from Perella in the coming weeks and months. Recruiters at rival banks are already fielding calls and making their own, I’m told. Bankers don’t want to work at troubled businesses, and seeking a deal signaled just that. Perella, the junior partner in these talks, had been seeking some kind of deal for months before alighting on Piper. Bankers, especially rainmakers, have healthy egos. It’s difficult enough to lock them up, but it’s a critical step in talent-driven mergers like this. Failing to do so highlights exactly the risk that companies take when they try to strike deals.

events.title: Elon Musk reveals ‘world’s first flying car’ at Tesla event
events.summary: The Tesla Roadster 2 drove up a curved ramp before using SpaceX rocket thrusters to fly, flip and land Elon Musk has revealed Tesla’s latest model, which he claims will be the world’s first flying car, using technology from his aerospace company SpaceX to “basically fly like a rocket”. The billionaire, who hosted a demonstration of the Tesla Roadster 2 at the SpaceX rocket development and testing facility in Texas, said the sports car could go from 0 to 60mph in a record time of less than a second and had thrusters. A video of the event shows the Roadster, which he said was controlled remotely “to make sure we don’t kill anyone”, driving up a curved ramp using suction to grip upside down, before using thrusters to flip, fly and land . Later in the demonstration the Roadster is seen using the jets to leap over a line of Tesla’s existing models and then accelerate to 60mph in record time. “Turns out the future does have flying cars,” Musk said in a post on his social media site, X, accompanying a video from the event. Speaking at the event on Thursday, Musk said: “Flying cars are real. It’s got altitude controls, thrusters and main thrusters in the rear. So it can basically fly like a rocket, it can do rolls, crazy gymnastics.” “I’m not sure it’s necessarily legal in all jurisdictions,” Musk said, adding that the prototype was “not necessarily a safety optimised car but it takes the fun meter to 11”. In 2014 Musk expressed his scepticism about a future with flying vehicles . However, three years later he announced the development of the Roadster 2, which will go into production in 2028 and is priced in excess of $200,000, (£150,000), to create an electric sports car “to give a hardcore smackdown to gasoline cars”. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning After the event, a Tesla reservation website for expressing interest in the two-seater Roadster 2 showed that a “performance” version of the vehicle would require a £50,000 deposit. A “thrust” version would require a $250,000 deposit. Meanwhile, a one-seater “rocket” variant with “full flight system” was labelled as being available only by invitation. The car company added that flying it was not permitted on public roads.

events.title: China plans AI export curbs to exert control over key tech
events.summary: Restricted technologies would include model weights and source code for products exceeding certain performance thresholds. China proposed adding advanced artificial intelligence technologies to its export-control list, potentially restricting overseas transfers of AI models and chip designs in an effort to tighten control over homegrown advancements in a strategically important sector. The draft proposal covers 23 AI technologies, including large language models, agents, chip designs and computing clusters. Restricted technologies would include model weights and source code for products exceeding certain performance thresholds. Chinese AI startups have in summer 2026 made significant progress in closing the gap on US industry leaders. Models like Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and DeepSeek’s latest editions offer better pricing and Chinese companies also favour the approach of sharing the weights – used to steer an AI system toward finding an answer – of their models to encourage developers to build on top of them. They are also increasingly looking for markets beyond China, with the likes of Z.AI making their wares available on US cloud service providers like Amazon Web Services. The proposal forms part of a broader effort to control 40 technologies across industries where Chinese companies have become increasingly competitive. It would also cover five biomedical technologies and 12 solar technologies, including proprietary cell and gene-therapy platforms and production technology for certain advanced solar modules. “This is more than routine maintenance,” said Ryan Etzcorn, a senior director at Ankura China Advisors. “By targeting AI, solar and biotech – industries where China holds a growing edge – Beijing is signalling that steadier relations with the West do not mean it will stand still.” China regularly updates its catalogue of technologies that are prohibited or restricted from export. In 2020, Beijing added algorithms to the list, after the first Trump administration threatened to ban TikTok unless the app sold its US assets to an American company. The proposed AI export curbs are aimed at ensuring “the safety and controllability” of the technology, a spokesperson for the Commerce Ministry said, citing the risk of misuse for attacking critical infrastructure, defense industries and core government systems by non-state actors or malicious entities. “The Chinese government’s necessary management of these technologies aims to solidify the security baseline, prevent misuse and abuse, ensure that AI remains under human control, and promote international governance of AI,” the spokesperson said in a statement. The proposal would restrict exports of core technology for models trained on “important data” and containing at least 2 trillion parameters – like Kimi K3 or Alibaba Group Holding’s Qwen3.8-Max – or ranking among the world’s top 10 on measures including performance, usage and safety. China’s cyberspace regulator broadly defines such data as information that, if leaked, may endanger national security, economic operation, social stability or public safety. The new Chinese guidelines are likely to stoke uncertainty in an AI industry already grappling with strict content controls, a licencing regime and potential US sanctions. The proposed restrictions against shipping mega-parameter models abroad are likely to hamper development given AI labs are training ever larger platforms: in September , Alibaba declared plans to develop models with between 5 and 10 trillion parameters, far larger than what’s common today, for longer and more complex tasks. Open-source technology and research already in the public domain would not be covered, and the government will provide streamlined procedures, such as automatic licensing, to exports involving open-source AI technologies. Deploying a covered model overseas would constitute a technology export, according to a statement. Deployments on overseas infrastructure owned by the Chinese provider could qualify for automatic licencing. Companies that allow overseas customers to use restricted AI models through apps, websites or online services would not be subject to the proposed controls, the Commerce Ministry said. Beijing said the measures were not aimed at any particular country, region or entity. The ministry also proposed to restrict the export of design technologies for AI chips built using 14-nanometer or more advanced techniques or employing 2.5D or 3D advanced packaging. The proposed restrictions also cover design technologies for certain advanced memory chips. China simultaneously imposed a temporary registration requirement for exports of the technologies covered by the proposal. The measure took effect on Oct 16 and applies to transactions already underway but not completed, including intellectual-property transfers, overseas licencing and changes that place Chinese technology owners under foreign control. events.title: Apple and Meta to collaborate on new AI model

events.title: ‘We should all be worried’: calls grow to limit London rollout of robotaxis
events.summary: Protest planned at Wayve HQ as Uber drivers fear for their future and city’s politicians demand TfL should have power over licences For passengers in Britain who want to try the latest ride, robotaxis are eagerly awaited: more than 100,000 are on Uber’s waitlist in London after the first UK services started in September. Others view them with trepidation. “I think we should all be worried,” said Florentina Ghiuzan, an Uber driver from Essex. “I was shocked TfL approved it so soon . I knew change would come. But I thought it would come with a solution for us.” London’s rollout is facing mounting opposition, from drivers fearing for their future and the capital’s politicians, with a critical report demanding Transport for London (TfL) is given full powers to permit or suspend operations. Drivers will this weekend protest outside the headquarters and depot of Wayve, which has partnered with Uber to supply London’s first autonomous cabs for hire . The direct action marks the latest salvo between unions and the global tech companies, whose driverless cars trials expanded this week to Manchester, with fears that hundreds of thousands of driver jobs could be lost. Although only a handful of driverless cars now ply the streets, Uber has announced plans to deploy 100,000 Nvidia robotaxis worldwide starting next year, and its senior executives have talked about all new cars being autonomous by 2040. In San Francisco, Waymo’s fully autonomous cars already operate more than a quarter of all rides. The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, and bosses at TfL have expressed unease, and the London assembly’s transport committee has called for the government to devolve authority over autonomous taxi services. In a report published this week, the committee said there was “considerable uncertainty around many of the claimed benefits of autonomous passenger vehicles”, and fears over the impact on public transport and congestion, as well as safeguarding and accessibility for disabled passengers. The chair, Caroline Russell, said they were not convinced that London should welcome robotaxis. “Rather than just accepting the autonomous passenger service model proposed by operators, London should be looking at the transport problems it is trying to solve and then considering what solutions this technology could provide,” she said. TfL is understood to see little benefit in the addition of robotaxi services to its crowded city streets , even if the numbers turn out to be relatively few in comparison to the wider traffic. For the robotaxi companies, London is a tempting challenge to crack. Commercially, it is one of the biggest private hire markets in the world and a foothold in Europe; logistically, it is a tricky test bed to prove their vehicles are viable anywhere. Compared with the grid system of US cities in particular, it presents narrower, twisting and unruly streets, without the kind of rules on jaywalking that give cars priority on the road. Under current rules, TfL licenses passenger services, but the government decides whether autonomous vehicles can operate. TfL has approved the start of Uber and Wayve’s limited robotaxi services, which retain a human safety driver in the front seat. As it stands, when it comes to fully autonomous passenger services, the Department for Transport would issue permits for robotaxis with TfL only able to grant or refuse consent, rather than regulate their usage on London’s streets. That has alarmed TfL, which sees parallels with when Uber first started business in London, creating problems few had considered, and was twice rebuffed in licence renewals as not a “fit and proper” operator. Quite how driverless cars will affect the capital’s transport ecosystem is unknown – and TfL wants to retain the power to intervene. City hall is also concerned about the social implications of more than 100,000 licensed drivers losing income or a living. Those at the frontline in the App Drivers and Couriers Union (ADCU) are planning protests outside Wayve’s London base from this Saturday. Their members include Ghiuzan, 42, who started working as a driver four years ago after going back to college. She said: “Our earnings are the same or even lower since I started – and with the robotaxis on the market it could get even worse.” Ghiuzan said she was notified of the start of autonomous services as an Uber customer – but received no notification as a driver. She thinks people will switch to robotaxis: “Young people like them, it’s new, and you don’t have to pay the driver … I might have other skills, but for lots of drivers who are older and have done it their whole life, it’s going to be quite a challenge.” Faisal Osman, 51, from east London, has been an Uber driver for 12 years, after switching from a long commute to an IT engineering job to allow him to work nights when he had children. He knows four other engineers who joined Uber: “We all used to talk about AI taking our jobs in IT.

Time: 3pm – 4pm | Location: Bank of England, Threadneedle Street, London, EC2R 8AH and MS teams The Chair opened the meeting by welcoming Members and outlined the purpose of the meeting. Namely, to consider the results of the 2026 banknote imagery consultation in light of the Bank’s objectives to support counterfeit resilience, and to consider which four animals to recommend to the Governor to feature as the central imagery on the next series of banknotes. The Chair reminded Members of the Bank’s obligations under the Public Sector Equality Duty throughout the imagery selection process. Decision: Members agreed to sign off the updated Terms of Reference adding the Banknote Innovation Programme Director as a new Core Member. Members were reminded of the key milestones in the imagery selection process, including the recent consultation asking for the UK public’s views on a shortlist of animals which could feature as the central imagery on the next series of banknotes. Respondents were able to choose up to two animals from each of three different categories: Mammals; Birds; and Amphibians, Insects and Fish. Members discussed the response to the public consultation, which received nearly 500,000 responses via an online survey, post, emails and phone calls. Members were pleased with the level of public engagement and suggested it showed that the theme resonated with the public. Item 4 – Choosing which animals should feature on Series H banknotes Members were asked to consider the Bank’s objectives that the chosen imagery supports counterfeit resilience, reflects public preference and celebrates the breadth of UK nature. Members were encouraged to consider the four proposed animals as a set to ensure they are sufficiently varied in their forms, movements and habitats to maximise differentiation between each denomination, thereby aiding counterfeit resilience. Members considered the results of the June 2026 public consultation and agreed on the importance of reflecting the public’s views on banknote design alongside the Bank’s wider objectives to ensure secure and resilient banknote design. Members discussed the proposal to feature the Atlantic puffin, barn owl, buff-tailed bumblebee, and European hedgehog as the central imagery on the next series of banknotes. The Atlantic puffin would bring a marine environment that would not be possible with the fox or kingfisher, which had received more selections in their respective categories. This set would include the most popular animal from each of the three categories as well as the most popular marine animal in the shortlist. Members considered how each of the proposed animals’ forms and habitats could be differentiated to help the public easily identify each denomination, as well as how the proposed animals’ movements could be incorporated into security features to support authentication. It may also be possible to include some of the other animals from the shortlist as secondary imagery in the final designs. This would be subject to further engagement with the members of the Banknote Imagery Expert Panel about the animals’ habitats and note design decisions later in the process. Members concluded that the proposed set of animals met the Bank’s objectives for counterfeit resilience and took into account the outcome of the public consultation.

events.title: ‘Clean air is not a favour’: Indonesia’s neighbours fed up with acrid haze as Singapore threatens to prosecute
events.summary: Millions affected by smoke from wildfires as schools close, respiratory illnesses soar and diplomatic tensions rise S ingapore is threatening to prosecute companies responsible for some of the worst fires in years in neighbouring Indonesia, as the region grows increasingly frustrated with a persistent, acrid haze that could result in diplomatic relations fraying. Lawrence Wong, the Singaporean prime minister, said his government was distributing masks to vulnerable citizens and working with countries in the region to deal with the smoke. “At the same time, we are looking into which companies may be responsible for the fires,” he said in a Facebook post on Thursday, adding that he was exploring the idea of “joint action with other countries”. Singapore has no plantations or forests of its own, but several companies with concessions in Indonesia are reportedly based in the city-state. Haze is a persistent problem in Indonesia, but drier-than-usual conditions mean the thick smoke has been drifting into nearby Singapore, Malaysia , Brunei and Timor-Leste, and as far afield as the Philippines and Vietnam. Millions are affected, with school closures, respiratory illness spiking and air pollution indexes reaching unhealthy levels. Malaysians and Singaporeans have been sharing images online of their cities, with skyscrapers disappearing into the smog, and frustration with the region’s most populous country is boiling over. “Year after year, the haze comes back. It affects our health, closes schools, hurts businesses, and costs us billions,” a veteran Malaysian social activist and former politician wrote in a public letter this week. Lee Lam Thye said that real enforcement and “not just polite words” were needed. “Those responsible must be named, investigated, and punished. Clean air is not a favour. It is a basic right.” While Indonesia regularly battles wildfires in the dry season, these blazes are the most intense in more than a decade and exacerbated by slash-and-burn practices to clear land for agriculture, including palm oil, of which Indonesia is the world’s largest producer. Regional diplomats have offered to help Indonesia, but their offers have not always been immediately accepted. On Monday, an Indonesian official said the country was “still capable of handling it”. By the end of the week, Jakarta said it would accept assistance . Such delicate diplomacy is routine among the region’s Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), which is built on ​quiet engagement and non-interference. A meeting of regional foreign ministers in the Philippines is due next month, but that might be too late. Nerves are fraying. In remarks that went viral on social media, Syahganda Nainggolan, the head of Indonesia’s government communication agency, hit back at the criticism on Saturday. “We don’t only send haze,” he said, “the oxygen in Singapore and Malaysia comes from our forests.” Rare strong words came earlier this month from Anwar Ibrahim, the Malaysian prime minister. He said he had been in contact with Indonesia’s president, Prabowo Subianto , “who agreed to take the necessary steps, and this commitment must be followed by immediate and effective action from the Indonesian side to tackle the root causes of the haze”. At the same time, pressure is growing on Jakarta to declare a national disaster, first from civil society groups but now also from Indonesian politicians and neighbours. According to the Jakarta Post, Indonesian students have been holding protests across Kalimantan and Sumatra, demanding accountability and government action. In one video posted online , a child in a mask stands outside under a dark orange sky and calls on the local and national government to help. He holds a sign that says: “Save our little lungs”. The country has dispatched firefighters and announced a crackdown on arsonists, but declaring a disaster would unlock funds and help thousands with medical expenses. On Friday, the Indonesian forestry ministry said four firefighters were killed in a national park in Java. Longtime onlookers say the issue is not just firefighting, but targeting the companies involved. In recent years, several attempts to take legal action against the companies exacerbating “transboundary haze” have failed, both locally and internationally, and posed a diplomatic minefield. Haze is complex for Singapore and Malaysia, as they host companies working in Indonesia. A Greenpeace report published this month identified businesses based in Singapore and Malaysia that it claimed were linked to burning land in Indonesia. Ultimately, Indonesians bear the brunt of the blazes. The health ministry has reported nearly 280,000 people in the country with respiratory infections linked to the fires, with children under five accounting for more than 60,000.

PHOTOS: SINGAPORE NATIONAL EMPLOYERS FEDERATION SNEF has named Poon Hong Yuen as its next chief executive. He starts as chief executive-designate on Nov 1 and takes over on Dec 1. Poon is now deputy secretary at the Ministry of Digital Development and Information. He also held senior roles at MOM and Spring Singapore, giving him strong policy and digital economy experience.
