SINGAPORE - The Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF) has named Poon Hong Yuen as its next chief executive, replacing Hao Shuo after a two-year tenure. Poon will join as chief executive-designate on Nov 1 and take over formally on Dec 1, SNEF said on Oct 16. He is currently deputy secretary at the Ministry of Digital Development and Information. He previously served as deputy secretary (workforce) at the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) and chief executive of the former Spring Singapore. SNEF president Kuah Boon Wee said Poon’s experience would position him well to lead the federation through technological and economic change. “His leadership experience and contributions to workforce policy, enterprise development and the digital economy will be invaluable as SNEF champions employers’ interests, strengthens tripartism and helps businesses harness emerging technologies for workforce transformation and sustainable growth,” he said. Hao, who joined SNEF as chief executive in December 2024, will leave to take up a new appointment in the public service. SNEF did not disclose his next role. Before joining SNEF, he was divisional director for manpower planning and policy at MOM, where he oversaw workforce planning, labour market policies, foreign workforce policies and HR sector development. Under him, SNEF strengthened its policy, research and communications capabilities, while membership grew to more than 4,000 corporate members employing about 900,000 workers. More than 700 employers have taken part in workplace and workforce transformation programmes administered by SNEF in the last two years, benefiting over 3,200 employees. Kuah said Hao also worked with MOM and the National Trades Union Congress on policy reviews, including the Employment Act review and tripartite work on senior employment. events.title: Coffee’s coming glut may not be enough to calm volatile prices
events.summary: The 2026-27 season is widely expected to produce the biggest surplus in years, helped by a potential record crop in the world’s top grower. Coffee supplies are rising after years of shortages, but exchange-certified stocks are still at their lowest since 1999, keeping arabica prices near US$3.50 a pound. A 2026-27 surplus, led by Brazil, could boost private inventories, but traders doubt enough beans will reach exchange warehouses to stabilise futures. Low exchange stocks may keep prices volatile and risk a short squeeze, which could raise costs for roasters and consumers, including latte prices. After years of shortages, the world is finally getting more coffee. The question is how much of it will reach the exchange warehouses that underpin prices across the industry. The market for arabica coffee has been unusually volatile in 2026, due in large part to a deeply depleted repository of beans available to settle expiring futures. Exchange-certified stockpiles have fallen to their lowest point since 1999, helping push prices close to their highest levels this year, near US$3.50 (S$4.50) a pound (454g). Those stockpiles need to rebuild for prices to become more stable. Otherwise, coffee roasters – and ultimately consumers – could remain exposed to sharp price swings even as global supplies improve. There should be plenty of beans to go around: The 2026-27 season is widely expected to produce the biggest surplus in years, helped by a potential record crop in top grower Brazil. But traders and analysts are unsure whether current futures prices offer enough incentive to send those beans into exchange-managed warehouses rather than private stocks. Exchange deliveries were a “slam dunk” when the premium for delivering coffee sooner rather than later was higher, said Judy Ganes, president of J. Ganes Consulting and a veteran commodity analyst. “The math changed, and all of a sudden it didn’t make sense to deliver as much of that.” That distinction matters because exchange warehouses act as a backstop for the coffee industry. They absorb beans when other buyers show little interest and provide a readily available reservoir when supplies become scarce. Roasters have drawn heavily on that reservoir and are now actively buying beans in the physical market at higher prices, intercepting supplies that might otherwise reach the exchange. Growing private inventories would still be good news for roasters and consumers after years of shortages and record prices. But without a significant recovery in exchange stocks, futures could remain volatile. Prices may have to rise to encourage more deliveries, potentially forcing traders with short positions to buy back futures and amplifying the rally. “There’s the possibility that someone gets squeezed,” Ganes said. That can ultimately feed through to the price of a latte. Futures serve as a basis for the prices that many roasters pay for beans, with their final cost typically based on the futures price plus a premium or discount for quality. Consumers are still feeling the pinch of a historic run-up in coffee costs two years ago, and Folgers maker JM Smucker has cited elevated futures as a reason for delaying plans to cut prices. Oliver Broster, senior manager of coffee analysis at Expana, said the looming surplus creates the risk of a steep decline in prices, meaning the exchange should already be an attractive destination for some beans. Some beans are starting to arrive. More coffee from Brazil entered certified stocks in September than in each of the prior 18 months. But the sudden influx of tens of thousands of bags sent futures plunging, and arrivals have since slowed. The fact that around 72% of Brazilian coffee bag arrivals passed an exchange quality test that month – an unexpectedly high rate in line with past years – also pressured prices, since heavy rains had raised fears about potentially widespread damage to the crop. “It’s a huge crop. So in comparison with last year, there’s still a large quantity of excellent-quality Brazil,” Broster said. Still, Brazilian growers have little reason to rush. Flush with cash from record coffee prices in previous harvests, producers have been able to hold beans for longer than usual while waiting for higher offers. Brazilian coffee likely to meet the Intercontinental Exchange’s quality standards is also good enough to be “really getting a premium in some markets” beyond what the exchange can pay, said Marcelo Moreira, a Brazil-based analyst with Archer Consulting. A surge in Brazil’s currency in October on election results may further discourage farmers from selling unless the dollars they receive for exports also rise. Beans from sought-after origins like Colombia are likewise commanding higher premiums, making near-term deliveries to the exchange a less profitable option, according to StoneX senior trader Tomas Araujo.

events.title: The UAE’s ‘Zero Hormuz’ strategy runs through Fujairah
events.summary: The Scene From the deck of one of the large tugboats used to guide giant crude tankers into Fujairah’s port, the UAE’s race toward its “Zero Hormuz” strategy is visible in every direction. A carrier capable of moving two million barrels of oil was loading at the port’s lone jetty able to handle such vessels. Smaller ships occupied other berths, and one tanker was loading at an offshore mooring, with a UAE naval corvette standing guard nearby. On the horizon, in the haze, several more tankers lay anchored, engaged in ship-to-ship transfers, taking on oil shuttled through the Strait of Hormuz under US protection for delivery to customers around the world. Fujairah — one of the UAE’s poorer emirates better known for its low-cost resorts and mountain escapes — is at the center of a regional push to reduce Iran’s leverage over Gulf trade through the Strait of Hormuz. Geography has become its biggest asset, and it’s not alone. Saudi Arabia is expanding its pipeline network, and Kuwait is in talks with Riyadh and the UAE to move crude through their respective links. Oman is also a likely beneficiary of the Hormuz disruption, with separate pipeline plans for its ports to safely ferry fossil fuels trapped in the Gulf. For Fujairah, this race to bypass the strait could lead to a new liquefied natural gas plant, a refinery, and “a much bigger port,” Fereidun Fesharaki, chairman emeritus of energy consultancy FGE NexantEC, told Semafor. “This wretched war has created for Fujairah a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.” Kevin Zweerink/Semafor Know More Fujairah had been preparing for this opportunity long before the US-Iran war erupted on Feb. 28. Abu Dhabi opened a pipeline to the port in 2012 with a daily capacity of 1.8 million barrels of crude, giving itself an outlet beyond Hormuz, just in case. Photos of the port and coastline in the late 1990s show minimal oil storage and loading infrastructure. Today, tank farms line both sides of the coastal highway near the port, and a network of pipes moves products among terminals and to ships. A rail link from Abu Dhabi moves goods and recently began carrying passengers. Glancing at a map of the UAE makes shifting assets east to the Gulf of Oman seem a relatively simple feat for a wealthy country dependent on exporting its resources. But the topography is a challenge: Craggy mountains press against the coastline, making land reclamation the only way to expand. And while the opportunity is clear and few doubt the UAE government’s ability to execute, the territory is still subject to the same risks affecting the region. Being outside Hormuz provides some protection for ships, but the vessels, tank farms, and port infrastructure remain vulnerable. Iran has attacked them all. War insurance has always been an issue for operators in Fujairah, and insurers have indicated they would need to see six months of stable peace before lowering premiums, according to two people familiar with the matter who have negotiated with insurance companies. Thus far, Fujairah’s port has focused on the most valuable trade, leaving the import and re-export of building materials, consumer goods, and machinery to the much larger facilities in Dubai and Abu Dhabi. That is changing. Cargo trucks now line the highway for some 10 miles, waiting for a chance to enter the ports. Ship-to-ship transfers are rising rapidly, from just a handful before the war to 80 in August and 120 in September, according to a person familiar with port operations. They mostly involve crude, but also aluminum, bauxite, and steel. At a dinner during the Energy Markets Forum, organized by Dubai-based consultancy Gulf Intelligence, the word “resilience” was overused, but in this setting, it was appropriate: These are the people who have helped move oil consistently from one of the world’s most volatile regions for almost a century. The business’s boom-bust cycle also came up. Fujairah’s historic advantage was as a link for ships coming through the Strait of Hormuz, but there are other ports to call at in Oman, which has friendlier relations with Iran than anyone else in the Gulf, and the question no one could answer was whether the boom during a crisis would carry on once shipping companies could return to their old routes. For the people of Fujairah, though, the vacant plots of reclaimed land near the port that may soon accommodate an LNG plant and other productive assets may be enough to help them catch up to their wealthier compatriots in Abu Dhabi and Dubai. Mohammed’s view Iran has been threatening to close Hormuz for decades, and while Gulf states didn’t necessarily ignore the threat, they largely operated as if freedom of navigation through the waterway would remain the norm. Saudi Arabia’s and the UAE’s investments in pipelines were prescient. But like their neighbors without outlets beyond Hormuz, they concentrated most of their investment in cities and industrial zones inside the Gulf, within reach of Iranian missiles, opting to prioritize domestic economic development. Today, the direction of travel in the region is redundancy and resilience. Gulf states don’t have much of a choice other than to invest in different routes and use whichever works best. If there’s peace, some pipelines and ports could lie dormant at times. That’s the price of keeping energy and goods flowing when enemies strike at the lifeblood of their economies. All these contradictions are evident in Fujairah’s boom, where its geographic blessing offers no immunity from conflict. Iranian attacks there and on other pipelines in the region signal a future where Gulf states may also need alternatives to their alternatives. Room for Disagreement Fujairah and Oman are beneficiaries of efforts to keep oil and other exports flowing. But making the Strait of Hormuz, in US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s words, a “worthless piece of water,” has always been hyperbole. It’s true that crude flows have largely recovered thanks to pipelines and US military escorts of tankers. But liquefied natural gas, fertilizer, metals, helium, and other exports, as well as all the imports that more than 60 million people rely on, can’t all move efficiently through alternative routes. Qatar’s energy minister, meanwhile, has been emphatic in rejecting gas pipelines and relocating processing facilities to other countries, committing instead to LNG expansion in Ras Laffan. For other exporters, the trucking math doesn’t work: The CEO of Fertiglobe, one of the world’s largest exporters of urea and ammonia fertilizers, told me a typical ship carries 50,000 tons of fertilizer. Replacing it would take some 2,000 truckloads . Notable Fujairah’s wartime role reflects years of investment in pipelines, ports, and trading capabilities , energy expert Robin Mills writes in The National. events.title: Warsh signals steady Fed outlook despite inflation jump
events.summary: Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh said Friday that the economy has largely performed as expected since September's rate hike, hinting that little has changed in the central bank's outlook. Why it matters: The Fed is weighing another interest rate increase later this month as inflation heats up and the economy remains strong. What they're saying: "Over the month or so that's transpired since then, the world has broadly conformed to our expectations," Warsh said at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, referring to the Fed's September meeting. Warsh, interviewed by IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva, offered no explicit signal about October: "I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year." His remarks come just before the Fed's standard pre-meeting blackout period ahead of the Oct. 27-28 policy meeting. "It's hard to be in a discussion with central bankers and not compare notes and hear the same thing about the surge in prices," he said, alluding to conversations with international counterparts in Bangkok. State of play: The Fed raised rates last month for the first time since 2023 to contain inflation fueled by the Iran war. Minutes showed most officials expected another hike this year, though the timing remained unclear. Vice chair Philip Jefferson, New York Fed president John Williams and governor Christopher Waller have signaled that the Fed could hold off in October, with Waller noting that rate hikes need not come at consecutive meetings. Friction point: Fresh data this week showed inflation accelerated in September, with signs of price pressures extending beyond energy into services. Odds of an October hike jumped to 50% from 22% after Wednesday's hotter-than-expected inflation report, before retreating to 28% Thursday afternoon, per CME FedWatch. Between the lines: Warsh acknowledged that AI is boosting spending before its longer-term productivity benefits materialize, while investment beyond AI is also strengthening the economy. Warsh said AI was contributing to a "massive investment surge" in the U.S., calling the investment boom "probably the most important thing that's happening in the global economy on the upside." Warsh said AI could ultimately make economies more productive and generate greater wealth. But he said the AI transition was "likely to be a very bumpy one." What to watch: Warsh announced that the Fed will hold the first field hearing of its productivity and jobs task force on Nov. 16 in the Bay Area, bringing together outside experts to examine how AI and other technologies are reshaping the economy. The task force is one of five Warsh launched shortly after becoming Fed chairman to rethink how the central bank approaches monetary policy.

events.title: Banks expect to be hit with higher taxes in Budget
events.summary: Chancellor John Healey is planning to increase taxes on the bank sector, senior banking executives have told the BBC. Healey has described banks as part of "the crown jewels" of the UK economy, but leaders in the sector have said it will be "on the menu" at the Budget in two weeks' time. The biggest four banks collectively made about £15bn profit in the first six months of this year, and trade unions have called for them to face additional taxes. The trade body for the banking sector, UK Finance, warned "further increases in bank taxes would weaken competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government's ambition to deliver growth in every postcode". Barclays fell only slightly and HSBC actually rose as both have large international businesses and would be less affected by a hike in UK taxes. What is the Budget and what could be in it? There are a number of ways the chancellor could extract more money from the sector. One option is for Healey is to reverse a reduction in the surcharge that banks pay on corporation tax, from 8% to 3%, introduced in 2023, by Conservative chancellor Jeremy Hunt. Critics argue this would be unfair noting the cut coincided with a rise in corporation tax from 19% to 25%. Healey could also raise the bank levy - a small percentage charged on loans. The BBC understands that the Treasury is leaning towards changing the surcharge if they were to go ahead as it is easier to change an existing tax rather than impose a new windfall tax. Reversing the 2023 surcharge rate would raise around £2bn. However, the last government was persuaded that adding 8% on top of corporation tax of 25% would leave UK banks struggling to compete with European and US rivals - so it may be that it is raised, but not all the way back to the 8% level. Speaking to the press in Bangkok, Healey praised the role banks play in the British economy. Adding that he has "decisions to take in the Budget", he said: "My observation on the banks is that people too often see ​them as big, distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future ⁠prospects." In the past banks have successfully argued that higher taxes would risk making the UK uncompetitive with other jurisdictions and would reduce their ability to lend, and therefore be anti-growth. Sir Philip Augar, an author and former banker in the City of London, told the BBC's Today programme there was "room for a moderate increase" in taxes on the sector that could raise up to £3bn a year. He said lenders were enjoying "booming conditions", benefiting from higher interest rates which boost their profits. Rising interest rates have expanded the margin between the rate at which banks lend to customers and the rate they pay savers. Sir Philip added that when the banking sector "hits really rocky times it expects the taxpayer to bail them out - when it hits boom times, it expects some kind of special treatment". He said banks cannot simultaneously be "too big to fail and too big to tax". Paul Nowak, general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, which represents trade unions, said Britain's four biggest banks are making a billion pounds a week, with bonuses at post-financial crash records. "These are bumper profits - driven by high interest rates and households' mortgage misery," he said. "Now it's time to make sure banks pay their fair share," he added. "But if the chancellor does ask the Banks to pay a fairer share of tax in the Budget, that's 100% the right call," he added. Burnham announces scheme to help first-time buyers onto housing ladder Published 27 September Healey says surprise UK growth is 'sign of resilience' ahead of Budget Published 1 day ago Faisal Islam: What surprise praise for UK economy tells us about the Budget Published 2 days ago Banks were pleased to have avoided being targeted at the last Budget, given the large profits they have made in recent years. There is another option that has been discussed with Treasury officials. Currently banks can use losses from the past to offset against profits - thereby reducing their tax bill in any given year. Lloyds in particular has been a beneficiary of this policy, as large losses from the financial crisis have been used to lower tax bills ever since. Some analysts and bank executives have pushed the idea of a moratorium on this practice for a few years, which would yield an estimated extra £1bn per year for the Treasury. That would provide a windfall while being "a lot more bearable", in the words of one bank executive. It would also spare foreign banks from an additional hit, including JP Morgan, whose chief executive Jamie Dimon has warned that the UK already has one of the highest tax burdens on banks in the world. He warned that adding further sector-specific taxes could discourage investment and damage competitiveness.

events.title: Oil prices head for weekly gain on continued uncertainty over Middle East supplies
events.summary: Brent crude touched $110 for the first time since May on Friday, as oil prices headed for another weekly gain amid mounting Middle East supply concerns. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, gained 3.7 per cent to close at 109.86 a barrel. West Texas Intermediate, which tracks US crude, rose 3.55 per cent to $101.41. For the week, Brent gained nearly 5 per cent, while WTI is on track to jump by more than 10 per cent. Global energy prices remain volatile and elevated as the war in Iran, now in its eighth month, continues to choke energy supplies. That has prompted moves to ensure ample supplies globally. The International Energy Agency on Thursday said it had agreed to release more than 20 million barrels to the market amid a surge in diesel prices. The IEA said wholesale diesel surpassed $200 in Singapore and hit roughly $220 in Europe and the US. The average US diesel price at the pump was $6.32 a gallon on Friday, compared to last week's average of $6.27 a gallon. The Paris-based agency also pointed out that exports out of the Middle East have recovered to pre-crisis levels and that oil storage globally is not tight. Gulf oil producers, meanwhile, have pushed tanker transfers as far as India’s coast and slashed prices to keep crude flowing to Asia, as the makeshift export network around the Strait of Hormuz buckles under congestion and persistent attacks . There were 82 ship-to-ship transfers in India's Gulf of Kutch last month, equivalent to about 680,000 barrels per day, shipping analytics company Vortexa said. Refined products accounted for about 65 per cent of the volume, with crude making up the remainder. Current oil market levels “still seem to be somewhat lofty compared to market realities … [but] we are not running out of oil, as flows out of the Middle East have largely recovered,” said Norbert Rucker, head of economics and next-generation research at Swiss lender Julius Baer. “Instead of tilting the oil market into a deficit, the Iran war has mainly erased the surplus that had been built in 2025.” G7 leaders pledged this month to accelerate the IEA's co-ordinated emergency stock release by releasing 100 million barrels of diesel and other reserves to help stabilise markets. And in a surprise move last week, US President Donald Trump's administration lifted sanctions to enable Russia to supply millions of barrels of diesel to global markets. Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries continued on Thursday after Moscow was accused of violating President Trump's ceasefire on targeting energy sites last week. Russia's Ryazan oil refinery suspended operations at one of its crude distillation units following a drone attack, Reuters reported. The IEA on Wednesday warned that the global diesel shortage triggered by the Iran war was set to persist well into next year, with depleted inventories not expected to recover until the second half of 2027.

events.title: Geothermal finds rare political sweet spot amid AI boom
events.summary: Geothermal — power drawn from the Earth's natural heat — is pulling off something remarkable in today's hyperpolarized America: Winning fans across the political spectrum. Why it matters: The bipartisan appeal, combined with surging electricity demand from AI , is helping fuel investment in a niche energy source yet to prove it can compete at scale. Driving the news: Geothermal received unusually extensive attention in a bipartisan Senate bill introduced late last month to expedite infrastructure permitting . The House this summer passed a package containing several of the same geothermal provisions, including measures sponsored by lawmakers as ideologically distant as Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Mike Kennedy (R-Utah) . The rising cachet of geothermal is the product of three trends converging: Technologies adapted from the oil and gas industry, including fracking, are making it possible to tap heat in more places than just far-flung hot springs and volcanoes. Tech companies, on the hunt for reliable electricity, are willing to pay a premium for next-generation geothermal to power data centers. Investment is surging as companies race to scale a renewable energy source that can generate power around the clock. Catch up quick: The geothermal-specific provisions in the Senate bill go further than the broader permitting reforms offered to other renewable energy sources, including wind and solar. The bill would make it easier for geothermal developers to explore and lease federal land, speed up drilling permits and exempt certain activities from environmental reviews. Geothermal retained federal clean-energy tax credits in Republicans' sweeping tax law last year, even as wind and solar faced an accelerated phaseout. State of play: Fervo Energy, an advanced geothermal company that went public earlier this year, is at the leading edge of this convergence. It was founded nearly a decade ago by Tim Latimer, a former drilling engineer in the oil and gas industry. "I don't think any of us saw in 2017 that a few years later we would be in the biggest demand power boom for electricity that we had ever experienced," said Latimer during a recent on-stage interview with Axios in an event aptly titled "The energy source nobody argues about." The AI boom has "accelerated our business tremendously." Chart: Amy Harder/Axios; Note: Other includes project finance and debt. Fervo's IPO proceeds reflect capital raised at the time of its listing, not its current market value; Data: Currence The intrigue: Geothermal's appeal crosses traditional political divisions precisely because it doesn't fit neatly into Washington's usual energy-policy boxes. Its renewable characteristics appeal to Democrats. Its reliance on drilling expertise and overlap with the oil and gas industry appeals to Republicans. Its ability to provide stable, carbon-free electricity makes it attractive to utilities and tech companies. By the numbers: The average winning bid for federal geothermal leases has surged, reflecting growing commercial interest. The average winning bid in 2023 was $10 an acre, and so far this year, the average is $182, according to Guy Cohen, a geothermal analyst at the market intelligence firm Currence. A record $1,207-an-acre bid was placed for a single parcel in Utah this summer . Reality check: Geothermal's political popularity and investment boom are running ahead of its commercial reality. The technology remains expensive, and questions persist about whether it can reliably generate electricity over decades. Geothermal currently generates less than 1% of U.S. electricity, and those eye-popping leases are for the right to explore for geothermal, not for active geothermal wells. Fervo's stock has fallen nearly 70% from its first-day closing price following its IPO earlier this year, amid what Axios Pro calls a broader slowdown among energy startups. Tom Erb, Fervo's government affairs and policy manager, says the construction costs at its flagship project in Utah are about half those of new nuclear plants. He acknowledged that underground heat can diminish over time, requiring additional drilling, but said those costs are factored into company projections. What they're saying: Jigar Shah, a former Energy Department official under President Biden, says geothermal's current momentum still depends on state policies encouraging clean electricity and tech companies willing to pay a premium. "I don't think this moment would work without above-market mandates from states or the data centers," Shah said. Friction point: Geothermal has also encountered local opposition, particularly over water. Traditional geothermal projects can disrupt hot springs and wetlands critical to wildlife, said Patrick Donnelly of the Center for Biological Diversity. Newer technologies like Fervo's avoid some of those risks, he said, but questions remain about their water consumption. What we're watching: Geothermal has found something rare in Washington: Political consensus. The test now is whether that consensus survives the industry's growth.

events.title: EU promotes sovereign, trusted AI as it struggles to catch US and China
events.summary: EU pushes homegrown AI agenda as US, China retain lead At an international AI summit in Dublin, EU leaders promoted trusted and independent artificial intelligence. Critics question whether the bloc can close the gap with the US and China while maintaining strict regulation. If supremacy in artificial intelligence was an Olympic discipline, there would only be two serious contenders for gold on current trajectories: the US and China . The European Union, as has been the case in many areas of cutting-edge technology in recent times, is barely in the AI conversation. Former European Central Bank President Mario Draghi, whose 2024 report highlighted the EU's desperate need to be more innovative to become more competitive, said recently that AI is "perhaps the most promising" route the EU has to raise growth today. However, he decried the fact that the European Union controls little of the value chain. "Being cut off from AI, once the economy runs on it, would be more like being cut off from the US financial system," he wrote in an opinion piece for the Financial Times. "The effects would be catastrophic." Draghi's spirit was on full display in Dublin on Wednesday at an international AI summit the Irish government convened as part of its six-month stint hosting the rotating EU presidency. The summit's motto, "Harnessing AI to Revolutionize Europe's Competitiveness," might as well have been dreamed up by the Italian former prime minister. AI safety concerns shadow growth agenda Harnessing AI has become a lot more complicated. A slew of controversies around AI agents going rogue, from the Hugging Face attack in June when 1,200 agents hacked an online platform, to an Anthropic-designed agent sending a fake tip to US police over an unsolved murder, have caused alarm. Many from within the tech industry, including Microsoft founder Bill Gates and the leading AI frontier labs themselves, have called for a development pause in order for safety measures to catch up. Trump announces creation of new 'AI Force' Yet positivity was largely the name of the game at the summit, with tech and AI industry leaders joining Irish and EU politicians to declare AI's transformative economic and societal potential — while also emphasizing the need for strong regulation and safety standards. Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin made it clear that Ireland was all in on AI. He echoed European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen 's recent assertion that the technology represented a "tipping point." He also repeatedly highlighted what he sees as the bloc's commitment to safety. "We are determined to capture the dividend by mitigating the risks," Martin told the event. "In Europe, we have charted our path ... balancing innovation and opportunity with a trustworthy, human-centered approach to AI." AI critics say key concerns overlooked Meanwhile, Henna Virkkunen, the European Commission executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, security and democracy, revealed at the event that the EU had begun its first enforcement actions under its new AI Act , requesting information around security and safety from advanced AI model providers. However, other topics that concern AI's many critics, from those fearing the massive environmental impact of data centers to others warning about possible AI-related job losses, were largely absent from the discussions. Outside the venue, a group of protesters led by People Before Profit, a left-wing Irish political party, criticized the summit for not focusing on these issues. "There is a deliberate blurring of the line here with the type of AI that is being promoted," Alexandra Day, one of the protest organizers, told DW. "It is really being pushed on workers with very little consent. There's no right for workers to opt out of using AI now that it's coming into the workplace." A sense of urgency was palpable from the speakers inside the summit. Executives from some of the world's biggest AI and tech firms talked up Europe's potential. Yet the EU evidently has plenty of ground to catch up on in terms of AI development. Despite ramping up its data center capacity, it still lags far behind the US and China. It hosts 5% of the world's AI computing capacity compared to around 75% for the US. Trump proclaims US 'golden age' of science The EU is conspicuously absent from lists of the leading AI frontier labs, with only French company Mistral coming close to rivaling the top labs. Its production of leading-edge chips is also nowhere near that of the top US or Taiwanese producers. As part of its plan to make ground on the US and China, the Irish government, in its role as EU presidency host, presented a policy document at the event. The so-called "Dublin Declaration" outlines political commitments to strengthen Europe's AI capabilities, including infrastructure investment and financial backing for European AI companies.

events.title: Banks are pulling back as AI's massive debt pile disconnects from economic reality
events.summary: Wall Street appears to be hitting its limit on AI, and financiers are starting to say the quiet part out loud: All of this AI spending doesn't look like it can pay off, at least not for everyone. Why it matters: The gap between what it costs to build AI infrastructure and what companies are actually paying to use it is widening. Wall Street's anxiety is surging as the debt piling up to fund data centers and chips looks increasingly disconnected from economic reality. Driving the news: A massive gap is opening up between AI infrastructure spending and expected returns. While AI providers are projected to spend $7 trillion on infrastructure through 2030, research from Gartner forecasts they will generate no more than $3.6 trillion in related revenue over that same period. More than $4 trillion in AI infrastructure spending could be at risk of write-downs by the end of 2032 if companies maintain their current investment pace. Gartner also predicts that more than 80% of specialized AI cloud providers, known as neoclouds, will cease operating independently by 2030. Case in point: CoreWeave, one of the largest neoclouds with among the closest ties to Nvidia — the AI boom's financial and spiritual foundation — has faced a multi-day selloff of its stock and debt. Yields pushed above 15% and its stock tumbled 15.5% before rebounding after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang spoke up on the company's behalf. Follow the money: Sources on Wall Street used to tell Axios that as long as the AI buildout was paid for in cash, there was nothing to worry about. But today, a third of the capex being spent on AI is coming from debt, and capital markets are showing signs of severe fatigue. It's getting harder to secure financing. Global AI-related debt issuance plunged to $23 billion in September 2026, down sharply from $113 billion in June, per the Financial Times . Banks are actively pulling back to avoid concentration risk, with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon confirming his bank is tightening up on credit. Infrastructure projects and providers are struggling: approximately $18 billion in bank loans for an Oracle data center campus recently slid into stressed territory, while Nvidia-backed AI cloud provider Firmus shelved an IPO that sought a valuation north of $30 billion. Zoom in: The constant spending relies on the belief that compute demand will never falter — a belief that has structural cracks. Reflection AI co-founder Ioannis Antonoglou told Semafor that businesses may need "a decade or two decades" to fundamentally redesign their operations around AI. That's 10 to 20 years of companies slowly adopting the technology that's being built (expensively) today. Between the lines: This creates a mismatch: Data centers and chips require enormous investment today, but the returns that could justify that spend will take years to materialize. Put bluntly, there is a massive gap between AI spending and AI revenue, one that won't close for many, many years. At the same time, companies that are adopting AI quickly are getting smarter about using tools more efficiently, turning to open-weight models that are less compute-intensive to cut costs. Reality check: Look at Anthropic's latest financials for a counterpoint to the bears. The company is raking in cash, turning free cash flow positive in the third quarter and growing revenue nearly 50% compared to the April-to-June period. But even Anthropic's staggering growth has slowed, albeit expectedly because trees can't grow to the sky. The bottom line: The debt-fueled AI buildout is not an isolated problem for tech investors alone to worry about. The stock market and economy have become increasingly tied up with the AI boom. If the AI bet doesn't work, markets and the economy could falter as well.

events.title: Trump's MAGA allies openly discuss martial law
events.summary: MAGA activists are pushing for President Trump to resort to extraordinary measures — including martial law — if they believe the midterm elections are "rigged." Why it matters: Some of the proposals go far beyond Trump's legal authority — and there's no evidence that the elections will be rigged. But people in this orbit have close access to the president. Prominent MAGA election activist Tina Peters met with Trump this month. Convicted in 2024 of crimes tied to a breach of election equipment, Peters was released this year after Colorado Gov. Jared Polis (D) commuted her sentence. Peters and her attorney, Peter Ticktin, also visited Trump at the White House in late June . Peters did not respond to attempts to contact her for comment. Zoom in: On a September 30 video call for MAGA election activists streamed on Rumble, speakers warned of widespread election security breaches they believe will occur in November — and urgently pushed for remedies. Ticktin, Trump's childhood friend, said on the call "there would have to be martial law in the event... [of] another rigged election." "They'll probably need to be commandeering of ballots and election equipment to make sure that we can get to the bottom of it before anything further occurs," he later told Axios. Gregory Stenstrom, who testified about alleged voting irregularities in Pennsylvania in 2020, said he most wanted the election paused over security concerns. Alternatively, he proposed Trump invoke the National Emergencies Act to force states to change how they run elections. Stenstrom could not be reached for comment. Peters was also on the call. She's been promoting her own plan online since August, which calls for switching to hand-marked paper ballots and a manual recount of all votes where feasible. "Her plan is secure the paper ballots and recount by hand," Ticktin said. In an interview with Colorado Public Radio, he further explained this "would eliminate whatever effect the machines have." State of play: The streamed call is a regular feature in this activist community, drawing voices from across the country. Steve Stern, the host, directs his viewers to sign up through the Republican Party to become poll workers and observers for November. Stern declined an interview request. Reality check: "Emergency powers are not just a blank check for the president to go do whatever they want. The president still has to act within the Constitution and within statutes set by Congress," said Derek Tisler, counsel for the Brennan Center's elections and government program. He said those legal limits include : Election timing: Congress sets the date of federal elections. Trump cannot unilaterally delay the midterms. Counting and voting systems: States choose their voting systems and determine how votes are counted, subject to federal law. Trump cannot mandate a nationwide hand recount or order machines replaced. Emergency and martial law authority: Emergency powers do not allow Trump to override state election laws or constitutional restrictions. Martial law would not give Trump authority to seize control of election materials or override federal and state election laws. The big picture: Skepticism about the 2020 election extends into Trump's administration, including officials now involved in election integrity. Heather Honey, most known for denying the results of the 2020 election in Pennsylvania and Arizona, is now the Homeland Security Department's deputy assistant secretary for election integrity and senior advisor to the ICE Director. White House adviser Peter Navarro continues to promote his own report of mass election fraud and irregularities around the 2020 election. Between the lines: "This election did not sneak up on the administration. They've been in office for 21 months. We're 20 days away from this election, and they haven't done any of this stuff," said David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation & Research. White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told Axios in a statement: "Americans deserves elections that are safe, secure, and transparent to ensure full confidence in the results. President Trump believes every legal vote must count, every election must be protected, and Americans must have complete confidence in the integrity of our elections."

events.title: This implant can restore sight for patients with macular degeneration
events.summary: More than 5 million people around the world with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) experience atrophy in their retinas. And until now, no treatment could restore their vision. The PRIMA system, which was approved in Europe in July and is awaiting FDA clearance in the US, changes that. It combines a retinal implant with camera-­equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision due to advanced AMD. After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients were able to read, do crosswords, and use their phones. The retina processes light in three layers of cells: Photoreceptors convert light into electricity, bipolar cells process that signal, and ganglion cells transmit the signal to the optic nerve and the brain. PRIMA replaces the photoreceptors. BROWN BIRD DESIGN Developed by the California-based Science Corporation, the system takes advantage of the fact that AMD doesn’t damage all retinal circuitry; only photoreceptors—the cells that convert light into an electrical signal—die off. PRIMA’s implant mimics those cells and transmits visual information directly to healthy eye circuitry and on to the brain. “We’re leveraging all of the body’s own natural functions to process and transmit the information,” says Frank Brodie, an ophthalmologist at the University of California, San Francisco, and Science Corp.’s chief medical officer for ophthalmology.  BROWN BIRD DESIGN CAPTURE Glasses outfitted with a miniature front-facing camera capture what someone is seeing in real time. The video feed is roughly five megapixels running at 30 frames per second, which is similar to TV. The raw video is transmitted to a connected processor via a fiber-optic cable . CONVERT A small, handheld processor, which can be set on a table or tucked in a pocket, converts the video feed into infrared light signals that route back to the glasses. The device also includes physical buttons that let the wearer adjust contrast, brightness, and zoom. BROWN BIRD DESIGN DISPLAY A laser projector on the glasses faces the wearer and shines pulses of near-infrared light directly at the eye at 880 nanometers—an invisible wavelength. This signal passes through the pupil and on to the retinal implant in the back of the eye. SEE The implant is made up of 378 pixels, each with an electrode and two photovoltaic cells , which do double duty. They convert the light into a current that healthy bipolar and ganglion cells pass on to the brain. They also act as solar cells to power the chip, eliminating the need for a battery. Update : This story has been updated to clarify the specific cases of AMD the PRIMA system treats. Linda Marsa is a former Los Angeles Times reporter and an author who covers medicine, health, science, and the environment.

events.title: Love is infrastructure
events.summary: I. Meet cute Barnabas and Mainspring grew up near at hand, about an hour apart with good traffic, but for a long time they weren’t close. They traded glimpses and occasional hellos and then went about their business. Both of them carried on livelier conversations with farther-flung neighbors, who were richer and had more to offer. When Mainspring did interact with Barnabas, it was cringe. Mainspring liked to puff themself up, to strut around like a big deal—an innovator, a titan of industry—but they would turn shy at the worst moments, especially in any intimate conversation. Barnabas, meanwhile, had a dancer’s flair, an artsy, enigmatic glamour, except that when they tried to talk about real life, they’d blurt out hundreds of rapid-fire words—overtalking, overthinking, and generally overwhelming whomever they were trying to impress. So when Barnabas and Mainspring were young, they minded their own business. Until they’d both come into their own, and they saw each other properly. A group of geographers got together every year in a different place to talk about everything they had learned, and they were considering coming to visit either Mainspring or Barnabas. Both of them put on their best faces and tried to coax the geographers into choosing them as host. “Uh, hi-hello,” Mainspring said haltingly to Barnabas, whose full official name was St. Barnabas. “I really think it would be better if those geographers came to my place. I have more space, you see, and … and I am a titan of industry. I can show them practical applications of their research. It just makes more sense.” “Oh, really?” Barnabas laughed, making Mainspring more antsy. “Well, I can give them an elevated, artisanal experience. I have fresh croissants that were just written up in the Times . And I have plenty of space! I have so many friends who are great thinkers and architects. It’ll be lovely.” Barnabas carried on, basically calling Mainspring uncultured. Mainspring had a prickly feeling, like the worst heat dome of midsummer. For their part, Barnabas couldn’t bear the meanness they were inculcating inside themself. This feeling that they were small-time, no-account, a dilettante. They couldn’t stop aiming a flood of nervous words at Mainspring. At last, Mainspring had had enough—with the help of their city council and mayor, they offered the geographers a much-too-lavish deal that Barnabas could never hope to match. Totally worth it to hear Barnabas’s stream of self-aggrandizing nonsense peter out as they realized they’d been defeated. “There,” Mainspring said. “I’m going to show these geographers a time they’ll never forget. Now if you’ll excuse me, I’ve wasted enough energy—I have some sewer maintenance and a lovely parade to deal with. Goodbye.” Mainspring was skilled enough at multitasking that they could have fixed the sewer, ensured the smooth running of the parade, dealt with the geographers, and done a thousand other things all at the same time. But they were making a point. “St. Barnabas is such a fool,” Mainspring complained to their friend Turnbull. “They are totally unserious but determined to be taken seriously. It drives me to gridlock.” “I know what you mean,” lamented Turnbull. “We live in a world of posers.” Turnbull lived an hour and 15 minutes from Mainspring but at least two hours’ travel from Barnabas. Turnbull was even richer than Mainspring and had a certain surety of purpose that made Mainspring feel even more like a stammering numpty. “Whatever,” said Mainspring. “It’s over, and now I’ll never worry about St. Barnabas again. I have better things to fuss about. Like ensuring that every last detail of this geographer meeting goes perfectly.” II. How they came alive Everybody voted all the time. Well, some people voted more than others, but the median resident of the cities of Mainspring and St. Barnabas voted a dozen times a day—though of course some outliers might vote occasionally, or constantly. A lot of the votes were more like complaints, or bug tickets. Like: “The storm drain on my street corner clogs and becomes a lagoon every time it rains.” Or: “The cars go too fast on my block.” Or: “I can’t get to work because the bus is too slow.” But there were also votes along the lines of: “There should be a park here.” And: “This neighborhood is a food desert—we need a grocery store.” And: “The crossing guard by the elementary school is a hero who deserves some recognition and maybe a raise.” Nobody expected that by voting, they were prodding their cities to grow minds of their own; they just had stuff to get off their metaphorical chests. But it transpired that every vote was a building block of thought. Much later, some fancy expert summed up: “Turns out the smallest unit of consciousness is a vote.” Take Sandi, the librarian at the Nine Corners branch in Mainspring. She noticed things all day, like the people using the book drop box as a trash can, or the folks who came in off the street who could use easier access to social services. There were books she knew her patrons wanted, books that undoubtedly sat unwanted on people’s shelves all over the city. But also, Sandi shared things that came to mind—like, hey, what if the library book sale were a block party? What if the shopping district on the West Side were easier to get to from the Longneck neighborhood, where all the warehouses had been converted to housing and hipster coworking spaces, during peak after-work hours? Sandi had opinions about everything from street cleaning to the power grid, because she listened to people all day. Then there was Raeford, a bartender at the Wild Goose Chase in the middle of Gallery Row in St. Barnabas. He also listened to people’s problems from evening until the wee hours, and solutions came to him like clockwork when he woke at noon the next day. He saw St. Barnabas at night, so he knew the unsafe blocks that could use brighter streetlights, the places where hydroelectric jitneys drove too fast at 3 a.m., and the teens who needed an all-ages hangout. He also knew about the fish fry at the Black church in the Uptilt District that kept being disrupted by noxious smoke from the incinerator two blocks away. And the yarn store on the edge of Gallery Row that needed a disabled parking spot for its many customers with mobility issues. People voted with their Quills, usually by saying or typing a short message and maybe including a photo or brief video. Voting was easy by design, and votes were public but anonymized to the point where even a statistics whiz couldn’t tie one vote to a specific person—same as with major elections. The votes went directly to the City Core, which tracked, tabulated, produced reports, and offered solutions with the help of workers in the city government.  Trees voted too, thanks to sensors in their bark, and so did birds and squirrels that had eaten special birdseed that monitored their gut flora harmlessly. events.title: Can’t bear to say goodbye to your pet? Biotech’s got you covered.
events.summary: I don’t remember much about Peppy, my first and only pet cat. I can conjure the sensation of stroking her while she purred, recall how she used to get stuck in trees (just like in cartoons!), and chuckle about the time she pooed in my baby sister’s cot. That’s about it. What I do vividly remember, though, is the day she went missing. I was 10 years old, and I searched everywhere for her, scouting nearby fields and woods until sunset. I made posters. We never found her. I was devastated. There was no way to get more time with Peppy, but almost 30 years later, pet owners are being offered an ever-expanding set of options to potentially prolong their years with their furry companions. The possibilities include drugs, cloning, and even cryonics. But is that a good thing? There’s certainly a market for pet preservation. And a growing number of biotech companies have their sights set on pet longevity. Loyal, a company that is currently working on three potential longevity drugs for dogs, is trialing one designed to improve metabolic health in around 1,300 pet dogs across the US. Others are testing dog drugs that aim to combat both age-related diseases, including conditions like obesity and osteoarthritis , and aging itself. There’s even a company focused on longevity medicines for domesticated cats. I don’t know how or when Peppy died. But if there had been a drug that might have protected her from diabetes or arthritis, there’s no doubt I would have tried to get my hands on it. That’s about where my enthusiasm for pet life extension ends, though. I’m far less interested in cloning, a relatively new option for people mourning a pet and seeking a replacement. In most cases, this technology involves taking the DNA of a pet, putting it into an egg cell from another animal of the same species, and growing the resulting embryo in a surrogate animal. It worked for Dolly the sheep, who was born the year before Peppy went missing. It has since worked for other mammals, including cattle, horses, and ferrets—and cats and dogs. In the US, a company called Viagen Pets offers to clone cats and dogs for $50,000 a go. This doesn’t result in an exact replica of the animal but a genetic twin. Still, there are lots of reasons why a person might want to clone a pet. On its website, Viagen explicitly offers customers “a way to hold on.” Lori Kogan, a professor of clinical sciences at Colorado State University who has studied human-animal relationships for decades, doesn’t have a problem with the practice. She points out that while we have well-established rituals for coping with the loss of a person—such as funeral services, time off work, and memorial gifts—we don’t really have the same for pets. As a result, pet owners can experience what is sometimes called “disenfranchised grief,” she says. Having their feelings go unrecognized can feel isolating. If cloning a pet brings a person peace, she says, “who are we to judge?” Fair enough. But I can’t help thinking that pet loss in childhood might be different. It’s often the first time a child confronts death. Losing Peppy was a formative experience, and distressing though it was, I like to think it helped prepare me for losses I experienced in adulthood. I wouldn’t want my own children to think that death is not final, and that individuals can be replicated or replaced. Or, for that matter, revived, which is the promise behind pet cryonics. For a fee, a handful of companies offer to cool dead pets to extremely low temperatures and store them for long periods of time—even indefinitely. The idea is that at some point in the future, we’ll have invented incredible technologies that will not only bring your pet back to life but also cure whatever it died of. Alcor , a cryonics facility in Arizona, is currently storing the remains of hundreds of pets as well as people. It even recently announced it had cooled a small marsupial—its first pet sugar glider. With cryonics, the chances of being reunited with your pet are bordering on zero. Even those who work in the field acknowledge that the stored people and animals are unlikely to be reanimated. As things stand, there is no way to really and truly bring any animal “back.” I miss Peppy. But given the chance, would I stick her in a vat of liquid nitrogen? Or get another cat to give birth to a genetically identical animal? No, I would not. RIP to the one and only Peppy.

events.title: “Devoid of Any Factual Basis”: Again and Again, Judges Have Dismissed Trump’s Voter Data Lawsuits
events.summary: Since September 2025, the Department of Justice’s Civil Rights Division has sued 30 states and the District of Columbia to demand their unredacted voter rolls.  The rolls contain confidential information on millions of Americans and have historically been managed by states. Now these lists are a major focus of President Donald Trump’s push to take federal control over elections and prosecute alleged noncitizen voters. To date, there have been final rulings in 26 of the DOJ lawsuits. Four cases are yet to be decided, and one state settled.  Of the judges randomly assigned to the 26 cases, eight were Trump appointees, four were appointed by another Republican — George W. Bush — and 14 were appointed by Democrats. Tactic No. 1 The first seven lawsuits used the same opening, citing Trump’s March 2025 executive order on election integrity to claim the Justice Department needed states’ voter rolls to check that they were following federal election laws. “The United States’ championing of its claims under the [election laws], in both its briefing and its presentation at the hearing on this matter, can only be described as halfhearted. And for good reason, since neither statute gives the United States the power to compel Maine to produce its current [unredacted voter list].” —Maine federal Judge Lance E. Walker (Trump appointee) The judges ruled that there was no legal or factual basis for the government’s demand. They noted that the laws require states to keep accurate, up-to-date computerized voter lists that include confidential information. But the statutes give the federal government limited power to enforce those mandates. Several judges accused the administration of using the election laws as a pretext to suppress voting. “The foundation upon which American democracy has been built is the right to vote. … Now it seems the Executive Branch of the United States government wants to abridge the right of many Americans to cast their ballots. … The Court does not take lightly DOJ’s obfuscation of its true motives.” —California federal Judge David O. Carter (Bill Clinton appointee) “Public statements from government officials reveal its intentions: to create a nationwide voter-database, for potential weaponization in future elections; as a ‘fishing expedition,’ hoped to advance unsubstantiated claims of non citizen voting; and as a tool for immigration enforcement.”   —Pennsylvania federal Judge Cathy Bissoon (Barack Obama appointee) In an extraordinary rebuke ( echoed by other courts around the country ), the judge hearing the Oregon case wrote that the federal government’s actions undermined the judiciary’s longstanding trust in the Justice Department. He called them “chilling.” “The presumption of regularity that has been previously extended to Plaintiff that it could be taken at its word — with little doubt about its intentions and stated purposes — no longer holds.” —Oregon federal Judge Mustafa T. Kasubhai (Joe Biden appointee) All seven lawsuits using the first tactic were dismissed. Tactic No. 2 The next 19 lawsuits used a different strategy.  They made no mention of Trump’s executive order and didn’t depend on federal voting laws. Instead, they cited a provision of the Civil Rights Act of 1960 called Title III, which requires the preservation of state and local election records.  The government lawyers claimed that Title III gave the attorney general “sweeping power” to obtain these records to curb noncitizen voting. In reality, the law allowed the federal government to access such records to protect the right to vote, for example, by enabling investigations into practices that disenfranchised Black voters in the South.  Judges rejected the government’s arguments, ruling that Title III applies only to voter registration documents, not records that states generate themselves, like voter rolls. They noted the government had also failed to give an explanation of why it needed the records, as the statute requires.  “Clearly, this demand is devoid of any factual basis.” —West Virginia federal Judge Thomas E. Johnston (George W. Bush appointee) Several judges marveled at the audacity of the administration’s attempt to use an anti-discrimination law to keep people from voting and condemned the administration’s logic. “Title III was the Department of Justice’s answer to two years of resistance and obstruction by state election officials who destroyed, failed to retain, or simply refused to disclose the voting records … that would prove that black voters were victims of disparate treatment and had been unlawfully excluded from the rolls based on nothing more than their race.” —D.C. federal Judge Randolph D. Moss (Obama appointee) Judges also noted that there was a conflict between the DOJ’s claim to be enforcing election laws, which require voter lists to be continuously updated, and Title III, which bans any alteration of voter records. “The United States’s proposed interpretation of the CRA would therefore criminalize the same conduct that the [voting laws] require. This Court will not read [Title III] to produce such an absurd result.” —Maryland Judge Stephanie A. Gallagher (Trump appointee) The administration’s interpretation of Title III, wrote Bissoon, the Pennsylvania judge, “does violence” to the law’s meaning. To date, judges have dismissed 19 DOJ complaints that relied on the Civil Rights Act claim. In written opinions, every one of the 26 judges has rejected the Justice Department’s arguments and thrown out its lawsuits. Four cases are still ongoing.   The Trump administration has appealed most of its losses to federal appeals courts and has said it will consider taking its fight to the Supreme Court. A Justice Department spokesperson issued a statement in response to ProPublica’s questions: “Our attorneys are skilled, principled advocates who argue every case honestly and in good faith. Disagreement with the government’s position is not evidence of bad faith. We look forward to making our case on appeal.” The only appeal decided so far backed the district judge who threw out the Michigan case. “Back then, the government used this power to ensure that everyone who had the right to vote could freely exercise that right. But today, the government invokes Title III for an inverse purpose — to ensure that some people have not voted.” —Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals opinion On Oct. 9, a U.S. district judge ruled that the Justice Department’s national effort to acquire and share state voter rolls was an illegal abuse of its authority. A Justice Department spokesperson said the department is “reviewing the ruling.” Images of presidents were obtained from the Library of Congress. The post “Devoid of Any Factual Basis”: Again and Again, Judges Have Dismissed Trump’s Voter Data Lawsuits appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: Kalshi in no rush for Supreme Court ruling in fight with states
events.summary: The News Prediction market Kalshi is in no rush for the Supreme Court to wade into its battle with states. The company agrees with skeptics like the NFL that justices must eventually opine on whether states and tribes should regulate its sports event contracts as sports bets, a Supreme Court litigator working with Kalshi told Semafor. But it also believes that pending rehearing petitions and forthcoming Commodity Futures Trading Commission rules are currently muddying the waters, the litigator said. Kalshi, represented by the attorney who convinced justices to strike down Trump’s tariffs, recently requested a month-long extension from the court. That extension, coupled with Kalshi’s rehearing petitions, has led the gaming industry to believe the company lacks confidence in its case. “It’s fitting that as Halloween approaches, Kalshi seems spooked by the idea of the Supreme Court taking up the case next year,” American Gaming Association spokesperson Rob Lockwood told Semafor. “Because they don’t want to risk losing sports gambling — which is roughly 85% of their total volume!” The litigator disputed that characterization, calling the extension request a common move that was necessary for Kalshi to respond to the amicus briefs due the same day. Nevada, they noted, recently requested a similar extension in a related case. Know More The Supreme Court has until January to decide which cases it wants to hear in its current term, which began earlier this month. A clash between federal appeals courts has made the prediction markets litigation a likely pick: The Third Circuit has sided with Kalshi, while the Sixth and Ninth Circuits have sided with the states. Kalshi has filed rehearing petitions asking the Sixth and Ninth Circuits to review their latest rulings, citing the forthcoming CFTC rules. Nevada has already pushed back on the Ninth Circuit request, arguing that the pending regulation “would not change the outcome here.” CFTC Chair Mike Selig, who’s defended prediction markets in courts across the country, told Semafor earlier this year that he would “welcome” a Supreme Court ruling. That “would really settle the matter,” he said.

events.title: US-Ukraine rift not affecting weapons
events.summary: The US’ relationship with Ukraine has reached a new low — but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s current spat with Trump hasn’t affected the flow of US weapons to his country. The Pentagon has communicated to NATO members that a US procurement program that sends weapons to Ukraine via NATO is continuing uninterrupted, a European official told Semafor, echoing comments made by the US ambassador to NATO earlier this week. That doesn’t mean that European officials aren’t worried about the prospect of a lapse in weapons, as CNN reported ; Trump has reportedly considered suspending arms shipments along with intelligence-sharing, and the Starlink slowdown Ukrainians suffered earlier this week was the result of an order from the White House , Reuters reported. Zelenskyy’s decision to resume strikes on Russian refineries may further strain ties. US lawmakers, however, are still demonstrating bipartisan support for Ukraine’s fight. — Morgan Chalfant

events.title: Trump administration logs record foreign investment
events.summary: The Commerce Department’s SelectUSA program has secured more foreign direct investment under President Donald Trump than its previous dozen-plus years combined, officials told Semafor. That’s $280 billion from firms like Singapore’s Bitdeer, Australia’s Graphinex, Belgium’s UCB, South Korea’s Korea Zinc, and Japan’s Isuzu Motors, spread across more than 345 projects. The program, launched in 2011, had previously brought in a total of $255 billion. Assistant Commerce Secretary David Fogel attributed the bump to the Trump administration’s efforts to scrap regulations and lower taxes — and its blunt use of tariffs, which have at times strained its relationships with trading partners. “One of the elements of that [agenda] is using tariffs as a leverage tool to exact investment commitments from foreign countries,” Fogel told Semafor. With the midterms less than three weeks away, Fogel argued that’s a “promise [to voters] kept,” since Trump “definitely ran on a pro-worker agenda, and now we’re seeing the follow-through on that in terms of hitting these record numbers.”

events.title: Conservative AI safety group proposes export controls, visa restrictions
events.summary: Humans First, a conservative-led group advocating for stronger AI guardrails, is out with an “America First AI Policy” platform on Friday, according to a memo shared first with Semafor. Key parts of the framework include tightening export controls against China and other adversaries; mandating independent testing for large AI companies; prohibiting the development of advanced AI practices like recursive self-improvement; banning federal use of cameras like Flock; requiring public reporting of AI incidents; and ensuring that frontier AI developers can be held liable for reckless conduct. The group also wants strict rules for AI used by children and calls for a pause on H-1B visas. “An AI policy that truly puts America First is centered around the American people — not globalist corporations and not unaccountable bureaucrats,” said Russ Walker, the group’s executive director and an adviser to President Donald Trump’s 2020 campaign. “It is time for Congress to act and it is time for conservatives in particular to lead on this critical issue.” The group is chaired by Amy Kremer, a longtime Tea Party activist who argues Republicans are missing an opportunity to lead on AI policy that doesn’t cater to big companies. She’s been leading a bus tour across the country dubbed the “AI Data Center Revolt.” The framework’s priorities go beyond what some Republicans who are interested in regulating AI on Capitol Hill have proposed, and significantly further than the Trump administration’s current light touch on AI. Still, this vocal group may have more sway going forward if Republicans perform poorly in the midterms and AI anxiety is a factor.

events.title: Why Suntory’s CEO is still investing in a sobered-up spirits market
events.summary: The Signal Interview Nobuhiro “Nobu” Torii’s appointment as CEO of Suntory last September returned the leadership of the group behind Yamazaki whisky to its founding family, 126 years after his great-grandfather, Shinjiro Torii, set up shop as a wine importer in Osaka. But the younger Torii’s succession was an abrupt and unplanned one. Takeshi “Tak” Niinami , Suntory’s first non-family CEO, quit after police searched his home for suspected illegal supplements. They found none, and the high-profile executive denied having broken the law. But the board decided that Niinami’s resignation was necessary, and elevated Torii from his role as president, which he’d assumed just a few months earlier. It was a rare upset in a family business that prizes stability, and Torii’s message in his first interview with a Western news outlet since becoming CEO is that he brings a steady hand and a long-term focus. But he also displays an ambition to turn an increasingly tough market for the alcoholic drinks with which Suntory is synonymous to its advantage. Niinami was a dynamic, “hands-on” leader, integrating deals like the 2014 acquisition of Jim Beam bourbon while family chairman Nobutada Saji “kept our corporate culture,” Torii says. Torii’s own role combines those two imperatives, he implies: “I don’t have any aggressive strategy, but I really want to keep our corporate culture,” he says. “[The] culture is very important for the further growth of the company.” The onetime banker’s challenge is that he took the reins as the group’s growth had faltered, with operating income falling last year on almost flat revenues of about $22 billion. Most notably, spirits consumption in Suntory’s largest markets has been in decline after peaking during the pandemic. Companies across the industry have been idling facilities, with Suntory pausing production at one of Jim Beam’s three Kentucky distilleries to upgrade the site while demand is low. Torii’s task is to find growth in new countries and categories while showing that he can find opportunities again in the core liquor business. The group has predicted a rebound in its profits this year, and its new CEO is projecting optimism. His family’s willingness to think across generations will be central to Suntory’s ability to achieve its goal of becoming the world leader in whiskies and ready-to-drink spirits, he suggests. “It takes at least five to 10 years to have a good whisky, so the strategy must be long-term-oriented.” A private company looks for long-term opportunity Suntory’s history informs Torii’s reticence about making sudden strategic turns. The spirits industry is not a fast-moving consumer goods business but a slow-moving one, he says, recalling how the company misread demand for one of its brands more than 40 years ago. “We believed Suntory Old Whisky would continue to sell more, more, more, more, more, and that was a mistake,” he says. “Once we change the strategy in the whisky business, it will take many, many years to recover.” Torii’s group has a Tokyo-listed subsidiary, Suntory Beverage & Food, but the holding company itself is private, he notes, allowing it to take a longer-term view of the market. “We don’t have any stock price. So now it’s a good chance for us to strengthen our brands,” he says. Shares in publicly listed spirits companies such as Diageo and Pernod Ricard have been falling for several years, he notes, so “they have to control their stock price by cutting some costs.” “We are still investing in our brands while our competitors seem not to invest a lot,” he says, describing his rivals’ market behavior as “defensive.” Torii’s belief in private companies’ superior ability to invest through cyclical downturns echoes that of Sazerac, the US drinks company whose unsolicited bid for Brown-Forman was rejected by the Jack Daniel’s maker this year. But he suggests that Suntory is unlikely to be so ambitious about acquisitions. More than a decade on from the balance sheet-stretching Jim Beam purchase, Suntory’s financial capacity is “relatively strong,” Torii says, but he notes that interest rates have increased, which would make any purchase more expensive to finance. “Our first priority now is [to] invest in our brands,” he stresses. Asked whether he expects further consolidation in the liquor industry, Torii replies with a joke. “Well, it’s already consolidated, and if some spirits company [should have] an interest to acquire us, I would consider [it],” he laughs. But he quickly confirms that the family’s controlling stake would let it block any unwanted transaction. How demographics and diversification shape Suntory’s strategy Investors have grown concerned that young consumers are more abstemious than their parents were at the same age. In a speech in New York earlier this month, Torii said people were becoming “more intentional in their alcohol consumption” but also more focused on the quality of the drinks they chose, which he believes will favor his products. “At Suntory, quality is not a department; quality is a philosophy,” he told his audience. “The biggest difference between my generation and the younger generation is probably this one,” he says, gesturing to an iPhone. His point is not just that more people are socializing virtually rather than in bars and restaurants; it is that the high cost of their electronic devices has made them more selective about other spending. “We have to educate younger generations to understand the attractiveness of whiskies or other spirits,” Torii says. Still, he sees little evidence that recent inflation gains are making them sharply more cost-conscious about their drinking. Instead, he thinks that consumers may be acclimatizing to higher prices. Twice in the past six years, Japanese customers raced to stock up on Suntory’s products before the government raised liquor taxes, he says. The third such increase went into effect this month, but this time there was no such rush. The risk that alcohol consumption will recover slowly strengthens the case for diversification. Already, Suntory makes more than half of its revenues from soft drinks such as Boss coffee and Orangina, and it will explore wider global distribution of its soft drinks, Torii says. The group also has an eclectic portfolio of other businesses, including flowers, health supplements, and skincare brands, but he says every new venture must build off areas where it has historic strengths. For now, Torii’s most visible diversification bet is a geographic one. He sees “a huge opportunity” in India, he says, because its population of legal-age drinkers is growing by 20 million people annually. That’s equivalent to “one Australia per year,” he notes. Oaksmith, the whisky Suntory blended for the Indian market and launched in 2019, has been gaining market share, while Jim Beam is enjoying double-digit growth in India.
