events.title: The $22B startup co-founder working to make chatbots talk back
events.summary: The Signal Insight When Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni moved to trademark her voice last week, she highlighted growing fears about AI deepfakes sounding ever more convincingly like the people they impersonate, from politicians to CEOs. But she also shone a spotlight on the fast-developing business of helping prominent individuals secure rights to their voice likenesses — and on the companies that say “voice AI” will soon become how many people handle customer service and corporate sales calls or interact with devices from cars to robots. ElevenLabs established itself as one of the most highly valued of those startups this month with a $300 million employee tender, at a $22 billion price tag. The London-based company has worked with celebrities from Matthew McConaughey to Sir Michael Caine to trademark their voices, and created a custom voice for Yahoo based on its co-founder, Jerry Yang. It says it has developed comprehensive safeguards to detect and prevent unauthorized voice cloning or other abuses. Most of ElevenLabs’ revenues come from corporate customers like Deutsche Telekom and Revolut, and co-founder Mateusz “Mati” Staniszewski says businesses should prepare for a world in which customers increasingly expect to speak to AI agents rather than type with chatbots. “Voice will be one of the key interfaces in the future; for a lot of use cases, the primary interface,” he predicts. “Voice is easier, it conveys a lot more information than text would, and it allows the technology to be present but not overwhelming.” Andrew Edgecliffe-Johnson: Give us an example of the benefits you see in voice AI. Mati Staniszewski: We have an AI interviewer for [sales and development representative job candidates]. Usually you go to the website and fill in a form. We added [the option] to speak with an agent, and a lot of people started engaging through conversation, and two things happened. One, the ease of making it quicker for you to speak than to type resulted in us having a lot more people [applying]. Two, people started leaving a lot more information than they usually would. We’ve had more than 3,000 leads come through this so far, and more than 500 were qualified, so they were good leads. What should CEOs do to make sure their human employees are getting the most out of their AI agents? If you don’t get this right, the other parts won’t matter. Ultimately, for an agent to work, it needs the right knowledge. It needs the right set of steps and workflow. It needs to understand what it’s doing. Like a human, it needs a lot of coaching in the early phases to make sure it works. And it needs the right guardrails and safeguards, so it doesn’t go off-script. You don’t want competition between [humans and agents.] You want to find a way to bring people to manage the agents and be rewarded fairly for doing that well. And it’s not a one-and-done process. You keep improving, you keep iterating, and sometimes [you] need to jump in. You want to make sure that there is a loop: agent to human to agent. The key thing across all those efforts is that the AI agent needs to know when to bring in a human agent. Are you looking to go public anytime soon? We would love to go public one day. We would like to be ready — ready, but not necessarily go public — in the next 18-24 months. And then decide based on the wider side of triggers. What’s the advantage, do you think, of going public when there’s been plenty of capital to power your growth so far? We would love for [our users] to have the ability to be part of the journey, and the later you do it, the lower ability they will have. We see a lot of people building with ElevenLabs, and we’d love for them to have an ability to be part of that. There are other [advantages], but we are building a company to stand the test of time, and the companies we work with are looking for partners that are planning to be here in 50 years, in 100 years, and we want to be that company. Sir Michael Caine’s voice is a big part of his identity as an actor. Why did he decide to work with you rather than against you? We created, effectively, a marketplace where people can [record] their voice, we authenticate it, they can share it, and they earn compensation as a result. So we’re trying to bring the industry on board, and [people like Michael Caine] want to be part of that future too, assuming you find a way to respect their work and give them the ability to earn compensation [from it]. CEO impersonation scams seem to be very prevalent. Have you ever had that problem with your technology? With our technology, you always have transparency into how [an AI voice] was generated. You can take action. So, if somebody [was scammed], we could assist. I’m not familiar with any CEO that was impersonated, but we have guardrails. So if you try to ask about money, that gets either blocked or detected and flagged for human review, so we can proactively take action. And then, if you want to clone a voice to a high [quality], you need to go through an additional authentication mechanism. So you cannot just clone a voice that easily. Notable Staniszewski sees his company’s European roots — it was born in Poland and is based in London — as “a huge advantage.” London has plentiful talent which wants to “build something ambitious on a global scale,” he says. And because ElevenLabs focused from the start on the polyglot European marketplace, creating a model that could work equally well in many different languages “was never an afterthought.”

events.title: Lithium mine expansion could rival global leader
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts WA government welcomes Pilgangoora lithium mine expansion as EV demand increases There will be significant investment in the PLS Pilgangoora lithium mine. ( Supplied ) A lithium company in WA's Pilbara has announced a $1.2 billion expansion, saying it will deliver 1,500 new jobs. Once completed, it could rival Talison Lithium as the largest miner of spodumene in the world. The global price of lithium has fallen sharply since May, but demand remains high. A West Australian mining company will spend more than $1 billion on an expansion in the state's north-west despite falling prices for the commodity. In a statement to the Australian Stock Exchange (ASX), PLS Group Limited announced it would push ahead with plans to increase spodumene concentrate production to about 2 million tonnes per annum at its Pilgangoora lithium mine, 140 kilometres south-east of Port Hedland. The company is investing $1.9 billion in the project, which will include building a new processing facility named Jimmagunya by Nyamal elders, meaning spring country. The PLS Pilgangoora site in WA will expand. ( Supplied ) PLS managing director and CEO Dale Henderson said in the statement he was determined to ensure the company was competitive in the lithium market. "Pilgangoora has grown significantly over the past decade and as we look ahead, we are continuing to invest in the infrastructure needed to support the long-term potential of this world-class asset," he said. "These [changes] are expected to reduce operating costs, improve productivity, and strengthen the existing operation while also providing the infrastructure capacity required to support the increased scale of P2000." The company has also announced a $600 million infrastructure investment over three years. That includes upgrading access roads, co-funded by the state government, building a new 1,200-bed permanent workers' village and a mine services facility. Funding for both will be underpinned by the company's existing cash balance and operation cashflows from existing production. The statement said lithium had been a strong growth market over the past decade, with forecasts for it to grow by 8 per cent per annum until 2040. If the company's predictions are correct, the expansion would make the PLS mine rival Talison's Greenbushes mine in WA's South West as Australia's largest hard rock lithium mine. Talison Lithium operates the Greenbushes mine in the state's South West. ( ABC South West WA: Jon Daly ) PLS predicts Pilgangoora will produce 2 million tonnes per year of spodumene concentrate when it is fully operational in 2029. Mining analyst Peter Strachan said demand for lithium had been steadily growing, but costs were falling. "The market for lithium miners in Australia has been quite weak on the back of this falling commodity price." Lithium prices have now almost halved from their May highs of $US3,000 per tonne to $US1,505 per tonne for spodumene and about $US15,500 per tonne for lithium carbonate. Peter Strachan says demand for lithium is high due to EVs. ( Supplied: Peter Strachan ) "Mines which were closed two or three years ago when the price really fell are now coming back online," Mr Strachan said. "It's a supply issue that's been pushing down the price of lithium." Mr Strachan said Talison Lithium, which owns the Greenbushes mine, would likely rein in operations to reduce its own costs off the back of the announcement. "They will scale back, they'll choose to do the lowest cost operation," he said. The WA government has welcomed the news, saying the expansion would create 1,000 jobs during construction and a further 500 ongoing operational roles. "This is exactly the kind of investment that keeps Western Australians in work today and creates the jobs of tomorrow," Premier Roger Cook said. Pilbara Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson said the move was a vote of confidence in the region. Amber-Jade Sanderson says there will be more opportunities for Pilbara workers. ( ABC News: Benjamin Gubana ) "The creation of about 1,500 jobs will deliver real opportunities for Pilbara workers, local businesses, and communities while strengthening the region's position as a global critical minerals powerhouse," she said. WA's lithium industry sold almost 4 million tonnes of spodumene concentrate in 2025, the highest volume on record.

events.title: Ofgem could force energy suppliers to pay rivals if they lure customers with cheaper deals
events.summary: Regulator for Great Britain weighs up reintroducing market stabilisation charge to prevent firms going bust Energy suppliers could be forced to pay a charge to rivals if they lure customers with cheaper deals, as the industry regulator for Great Britain attempts to prevent suppliers going bust this winter. Ofgem has published a consultation on a proposal to reintroduce the market stabilisation charge (MSC), which aims to prevent suppliers failing if there is customer exodus, as it frets over the impact of sharp swings in energy prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East. The charge was last activated between April 2022 and March 2024, when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine sparked soaring wholesale prices that caused more than 30 energy companies to go bust. “We’re preparing for what is likely to be a difficult winter for many households,” said Neil Kenward, the interim director general of markets at Ofgem. “While the energy market is stronger than it was during the energy crisis, volatility remains and the market stabilisation charge helps to protect consumers from that volatility. “In volatile market conditions, it’s important that suppliers can continue to secure the energy their customers need without taking unsustainable risks.” Under the mechanism, the MSC would be triggered if wholesale prices fall more than 10%. At that point, suppliers who win customers by being able to then offer cheap deals would have to compensate rivals 85% of the drop in wholesale rates. “When wholesale prices fall sharply, suppliers that have bought energy in advance for customers on default tariffs can face losses if large numbers of customers switch to cheaper fixed deals,” Ofgem said. When Ofgem last activated the MSC in 2022 Martin Lewis, the founder of the consumer advice site MoneySavingExpert, swore at the regulator on a press call and said the mechanism sold consumers “down the river” because it would deter competition. He later posted an apology for his “emotional rant” on the social media platform X. Reacting to Ofgem’s consultation, Lewis said on Friday that consumers’ will not get as good deals if wholesale prices drop because the mechanism acts as a “switching penalty” . He added: “The new supplier can’t pass a chunk of the saving from lower wholesale rates on to you, because it has to hand much of it to your old supplier. The cheap fixes and switcher deals offered will be a lot more expensive, in order to protect energy firms’ profits. It ain’t good for consumers.” He questioned the need to reintroduce the mechanism, pointing out that many energy companies have made significant profits since last time it was triggered. “The supplier market is pretty stable, and I doubt we are at the domino risk of suppliers going bust in the way they did in the early 20s,” he said. “Protecting them over winter by effectively dampening competition … feels raw. I don’t like it.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Ofgem said that reactivating the MSC would not “automatically create charges or increase customer bills”. The consultation is seeking views on how the mechanism should operate, including trigger levels, notice periods and deactivation arrangements. “The MSC supports responsible energy purchasing and helps reduce the risk of instability in the market during periods of significant price volatility,” Kenward said. “By acting now, we can help maintain a stable and resilient energy market and protect consumers from the costs and disruption that can arise when markets become unstable.” Households are facing the highest energy charges in three years this winter after rising market wholesale prices pushed up the government’s price cap from this month. About 22m homes are paying the equivalent of £1,723 a year for typical gas and electricity usage between October and December, up from £1,663 for the July to September period. Ofgem’s quarterly energy price cap is forecast to climb by the equivalent of a further £149 a year in January, according to energy consultants at Cornwall Insight, which would put the average annual bill at £1,872. The chancellor, John Healey, is planning a major intervention to cut energy bills for poorer households in this month’s budget.

events.title: Bush pub that inspired Slim Dusty's 'Humpty Doo Waltz' hits the market
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts 'World famous' Humpty Doo Hotel up for sale after publican's 39-year run The Humpty Doo Hotel is on the market for the first time in 39 years. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish ) Once just a convenient place to pull in for a pint, the Humpty Doo Hotel has become a Northern Territory landmark. For more than 50 years thirsty travellers have stopped at the pub, about 40 kilometres south-east of Darwin, on their way to Kakadu National Park. Despite having what are claimed to be the largest buffalo horns in the Southern Hemisphere hanging behind the bar, it is not stereotypical Aussie pub charm that put the Humpty Doo Hotel on the map. Rod Parry has been behind the bar at the Humpty Doo Hotel for almost 40 years. ( ABC News: Courtney Barrett-Peters ) "It's the name," licensee Rod Parry says. "Where do you find another Humpty Doo Hotel? You'll find a Railway, a Commercial, a Royal, but you'll never find [another] Humpty Doo Hotel." Mr Parry has decided it's time to call last drinks and is putting the hotel up for sale after four decades of ownership. "I think it's time I had a rest, let someone else take over the reins," he says. "Thirty-nine years is half my lifetime." Horses, crocs and a beer-sculling bull Established in 1971, the pub survived Cyclone Tracy and is believed to be one of the Northern Territory's longest-licensed premises. The pub has been a Territory landmark for many years. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) Since Mr Parry purchased it in 1987 the venue has inspired bush ballads such as Slim Dusty's Humpty Doo Waltz and former NT administrator Ted Egan's The Man from Humpty Doo. Mr Parry has seen plenty of patrons come through the doors in his time, including those with four legs. "Horses stand at the bar with their riders, their riders have a couple of beers, and the horses stand there very quietly, maybe they watch the TV," he laughs. "We've had a pig in here. The other day the girls called me and said, 'There's a wallaby in the men's toilet' — and the crocodile, last wet season, out the front of the bottle shop. Perhaps most notably, the hotel's Darwin Stubby drinking competition in 1988 was won by Norman the Brahman bull, who sculled a 2.25-litre stubby in 47 seconds, according to an ABC report. Norman the imbibing Brahman at the 1988 Humpty Doo Hotel Darwin Stubby drinking contest. ( ABC News ) Norman reportedly proceeded to wash that down with "half a dozen tinnies and a meat pie". In 2016, a tiny donkey, a pony and a cow walked into the premises and police had to ask them to leave. But Mr Parry says the customers he will miss the most are those with two legs — the generations of Top End locals who have grown up in the venue. "A lot of those guys have passed away, but their children still drink here and their children's children come in," he says. "I will miss the locals and I'll miss my staff, because some of them have been here for so many years." Rod Parry says his staff have come to be like family. ( ABC News: Courtney Barrett-Peters ) General manager Alex Taylor says the feeling is mutual. "Working with him for 10 years, he has definitely become more of a family than anything else," she says. "I don't really see Rod as my boss. "He's helped me a lot through my career and my development and he's always been there just in general as well." Although the business was "devastated" by the COVID-19 pandemic, in the past year the Humpty Doo Hotel has recorded more than 50,000 visitors. It says staff turn around an average of 400 lunch meals every day during the dry season. The bar area has remained untouched under Rod Parry's ownership. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) But the hotel's success can no longer just be purely attributed to its food and beverage sales, with its name recognisable worldwide. "We send [shirts] to America, England, New Zealand, just in the mail. They buy them online," Mr Parry says. "My daughter, years ago, was at Mount Everest Base Camp and she had a Humpty Doo Hotel shirt on there and she passed a guy on the track and he said, 'I've been there, that's great pub.'" The apparel, emblazoned with buffalo horns, has also become a drawcard for Australian holiday-makers such as Perth road-tripper Mel Catchpole, who stopped in for a "nostalgic visit". Mel Catchpole and her husband Nathan grabbed some merch during their visit. ( ABC News: Courtney Barrett-Peters ) "As a child, my uncle lived in Humpty Doo and I was fortunate to travel up when I was very young — 11 — and then again at 18 years of age," she says. Her husband, Nathan Catchpole, is visiting for the first time and says it's "a bit sad" to hear the hotel is up for sale.

events.title: Mercedes-Benz and NVIDIA Expand Strategic Partnership to Advance Safe Highly Automated Driving in the Next Decade
events.summary: Mercedes-Benz and NVIDIA will extend their partnership to jointly develop the next generation of driver assistance and automated driving systems. The collaboration combines Mercedes-Benz automotive engineering and MB.OS with the NVIDIA Hyperion compute and sensor architecture, Alpamayo Stack software and Halos safety system to accelerate the development of automated vehicles. Mercedes-Benz and NVIDIA today announced that they will extend their strategic partnership to advance the next generation of automated driving systems. The collaboration brings together Mercedes-Benz’s automotive engineering and safety expertise and its MB.OS operating system with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and AI technologies. “NVIDIA is our most important strategic partner in automated driving. Together, we developed the first Mercedes-Benz assistance system for urban point-to-point driving for the western world,” Jörg Burzer, member of the board of management of Mercedes‑Benz Group AG and chief technology officer, development and procurement. “The expansion of our partnership marks a significant milestone and reflects the mutual trust we have built over the years. Together, we aim to bring further pioneering innovations to the road, offering our customers the best automated driving experience while upholding the high safety standards they expect from a Mercedes-Benz.” “Accelerated computing is giving vehicles the intelligence to understand the world and reason through complex driving situations,” said Ali Kani, vice president of automotive at NVIDIA. “Mercedes-Benz brings the engineering excellence and commitment to safety this transformation demands. Together, we’re building on NVIDIA Hyperion to bring that intelligence and full-stack safety to the road and make autonomous driving an everyday reality.” Mercedes-Benz’s MB.OS operating system supports new driving functions and over-the-air updates, working with NVIDIA Hyperion’s in-vehicle computing and sensor architecture. NVIDIA Alpamayo Stack provides full-stack driving software with AI reasoning capabilities, supporting point-to-point urban assistance, active safety and automated parking. NVIDIA Halos adds to the Mercedes-Benz safety foundation, including a parallel safety stack that adds redundancy and guardrails. Together, these technologies support advanced driver assistance and the development of future SAE-Level 4 applications, including robolimousines. Beyond automated driving, Mercedes-Benz also relies on NVIDIA technologies for vehicle engineering simulation and within MO360, its digital production ecosystem — from virtual planning to AI-based applications. The two partners are working to further enhance efficiency, flexibility and quality across the global production network. events.title: Kids are outsmarting social media bans. That’s not a problem we need to solve.
events.summary: Social media bans are stacking up. In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds. The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15. But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented. A study published earlier this year found that four in five teens under 16 made their way onto barred platforms. Teens have successfully explored many tactics for bypassing bans, from using a sibling’s face for ID to drawing fake facial hair.  Some proponents of bans have called for an increased focus on enforcement that blocks these workarounds. But circumvention is a signal, not a nuisance or something to be simply deterred. The fact that kids are actively looking for ways to outwit the bans highlights their limitations. Social media bans suppress kids’ access to information, including information that’s essential to their development, identity formation, and socialization, especially during adolescence. Worse, further restriction is likely to backfire. Closing loopholes in age gates could harm kids by pushing them toward less-moderated, higher-risk corners of the web. It also degrades privacy and security for everyone by forcing people to submit sensitive personal information to prove their age. In our work , we’ve found that parents and kids both want smarter, more nuanced policies that protect children, families, and their rights. That can take the form of mandating stronger limits on data collection by companies, or giving families flexible tools to control content and access on their own terms.  Age gates won’t bring about the desired change, nor will they simplify parenting in the digital world. At best, they will only raise thornier questions and postpone the conversation to a child’s 16th birthday. At worst, they’ll leave kids with no guidance as they make their way through the online world. A less safe internet for kids When young people circumvent restrictions, they are often doing what we want developing minds to do and what we celebrate in other contexts: lean into curiosity, problem-solve, and exercise independence. It’s important for kids to do this online, an arena where they often develop social skills and refine their identities . Bans sweep these motivations under the rug, taking a paternalistic approach that doesn’t consider young people’s needs or the realities of what they do online.  It also ignores what some parents want. When we examined social media safety interventions last year, parents told us that they often join their kids in lies that help them gain access to needed but gated services. This isn’t a new phenomenon; research all the way back in 2011 showed that parents taught their children how to evade Facebook age restrictions. Some may say these parents are oblivious to the harms posed by the web or just don’t care. But parents are not a monolithic group. Many simply see offering their children responsible access to social media as a way to help them connect with like-minded peers, find informational content, and learn digital safety skills early on. Many parents believe the benefits outweigh the risks.  When parents don’t help provide access and kids are not able to get into the platforms they desire, they will likely move toward alternative online spaces, often ones with fewer guardrails. Sometimes kids wind up on fairly innocuous, if unconventional , platforms, communicating with each other in Google Docs or podcast comment sections . Other times they move to more dangerous platforms that can leave them vulnerable to abuse and predation. In the aftermath of the Australian social media ban, preliminary research shows that kids’ screen time has not meaningfully decreased but has sometimes been redirected, with some young users going to spaces that are unmonitored and unknown to parents. Just as cities are sketchiest when they are not bustling, the most risky platforms for young people are those with the fewest eyes on the digital street . Outdated, dying, and under-resourced platforms tend to attract both vulnerable youth and those who prey on them. A less safe internet for all Age gates come with dangers of their own. Some platforms automatically track users’ online activities to confirm their age. In doing so, they profile users—collecting and analyzing their data to make inferences about them, which can increase the risk that data will be misused or leaked.  Companies may also ask for personal documents like driver’s licenses to verify age, which can lead to mishandling of sensitive documents or even identity theft. Data breaches happen: Last year, for example, Discord reported that one of its third-party services, 5CA, which is used to confirm age, had been compromised, exposing at least 70,000 images of users’ government IDs. It can take little effort to find ways to use that kind of information for malicious purposes by, say, connecting driver’s licenses to specific accounts and private online activity, which could reveal anything from users’ political opinions to their sexual preferences.  Efforts to make it harder for kids to get around age gates have also led policymakers to clamp down on kids’ access to VPNs. State age verification bills in Michigan and Utah have tried to interfere with the privacy protections offered by these tools (the Utah bill is now blocked by a federal court ), and Australia’s eSafety Commissioner is nudging social media platforms to detect and block their use. But requiring adult users to prove their age to gain access to a VPN fundamentally defeats the purpose of that privacy-focused technology. It can put many users, particularly journalists and human rights defenders working on sensitive issues, in danger of government surveillance and even retaliation. What could work instead? Rather than attempting to block young people from online services that allow them to access information and engage in age-essential communication, policymakers should focus on the incentives that drive companies to engage in behavior that creates risks for kids in the first place.  For example, platforms should decrease what experts call unhealthy engagement or addictive activity by limiting the collection and use of data that companies use to target content and features to all users, including children. Nearly all parents and teens we spoke with want policymakers to impose such restrictions, knowing full well that the companies’ use of data is at the core of features such as targeted advertisements. events.title: AI threatens democracy. But we are not powerless: here’s how to fight back | Carine Fouteau
events.summary: AI threatens democracy. But we are not powerless: here’s how to fight back Tech platforms pillage public-interest journalism for profit. But we have leverage as they sow the seeds of their own downfall Carine Fouteau is president and publishing director of the French investigative news outlet Mediapart B ig tech companies pose an immeasurable threat: socially, politically, militarily and ecologically. They are also causing a profound crisis of information. The tools they design now serve as weapons of mass destruction against democracy. There is so much at stake that an urgent and broad mobilisation is required. From the harvesting of personal data and the weaponisation of public opinion, to the destruction of jobs, the infringement of civil liberties and environmental damage, ordinary citizens are the main victims of this predatory economy – an economy with an agenda that aligns with the interests of the planet’s most authoritarian and reactionary states. The threats facing the information landscape affect us all. Journalists of my generation have witnessed four major digital revolutions: the internet, social media, smartphones, and now, artificial intelligence. What fundamentally changes with AI is our relationship with the truth. For big tech companies, the boundary between truth and falsehood has vanished. This makes it essential to reaffirm the role of public-interest journalism. Our mission is to publish information that is in the public interest by seeking the factual truth, standing against “fake news” and propaganda. Our mission is to help create a democratic public sphere that serves citizens. Yet AI companies are completely reshaping this space to their own advantage; their mission is not the public interest, but generating profits. Their methods include plundering news outlets without authorisation or compensation. By disseminating so-called summaries of our reporting , they siphon off our audiences and revenue, serving the private interests of a select few at the expense of the common good. The difference between AI-generated content and a real news article is journalism. AI-generated responses are not information. They are merely a logical assembly of words that all too often produces falsehoods, distorts facts and misinterprets information. A real news article is something else entirely. Quality journalism is the product of expertise guided by ethical standards: persuading sources to speak, painstakingly gathering eye-witness testimonies, cross-referencing, verifying and establishing facts. This process relies on reporting or investigative work – in other words, human effort in the field. Good journalism organises and prioritises information, providing context and nuance; AI, by contrast, levels everything down to the lowest common denominator and breeds confusion. Journalism uncovers facts that certain parties – particularly economic and political powers – would prefer to see hidden, ignored, or suppressed. Generative AI uncovers nothing, it merely regurgitates and condenses existing material. Quality journalism comes at a high price. Some of the costs can’t even be quantified. Journalists who report from war zones for example, risk their lives. Mediapart’s recent investigation into Jordan Bardella, the head of Marine Le Pen’s far-right party, has resulted in anonymous cyber-harassment and death threats against our editorial team. Ultimately, media outlets are accountable for the information they publish. They answer to the courts and to their readers. AI companies appear answerable only to their shareholders. They refuse to vouch for the reliability of their conversational agents to evade legal liability. If nothing is done to stop it, this pillaging will result in the destruction of journalism. This is dangerous not just for news publishers, but for all of us, because it signifies the demise of a public sphere defined by free, pluralistic and democratic discourse. Do we want a public sphere that guarantees access to reliable, independent information, or one governed by algorithms that amplify fake news, deepfakes and propaganda – fuelling fear, anger and division? Fortunately, the tech companies have sown the seeds of their own downfall. Since they are bleeding dry the very sources of information from which they derive their profits, they are courting their own failure; without quality information, they will produce nothing but AI slop. This is precisely where we find leverage. OpenAI has admitted that it would be impossible to train today’s leading AI models without using copyrighted material. A Microsoft vice-president acknowledged that training models on quality content significantly improves the quality of output. The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment The priority is to act collectively, pressuring these platforms by every available means – including legal action – to uphold the rights of the press and the public.

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Spirit of Tasmania I and II sale details unclear days before final Bass Strait voyages The Spirit of Tasmania I is set to sail its final journey between Devonport and Geelong at the end of next week. ( ABC News: Morgan Timms ) There are questions over where the Spirit of Tasmania I and II will be moored, and at what cost, after they are replaced. The Tasmanian government says talks to sell the vessels are "progressing well", but the state opposition has doubts. The ferries will be replaced by the new Spirit IV and V by the end of this month. Just one week out from their final voyage between Devonport and Geelong, it is still not known what exactly will be happening to the two current Spirit of Tasmania vessels. TT-Line, the state-owned company which runs the ferries, has said a sale process is underway for Spirit I and II, which were launched nearly 25 years ago. But it would not say where the ferries would be moored, and what this would cost if they were not sold by the time Spirit IV and V began operating. One of the newer, larger Spirit of Tasmania ships passes one of the old fleet in Devonport earlier this year. ( Supplied: TT-Line ) The two new ferries have been moored in Geelong, and the Tasmanian government has expressed confidence in a deal being secured to sell the soon-to-be decommissioned ships soon. Earlier this year, a parliamentary inquiry heard the total cost of the new ferries was more than $700 million above forecast , which did not include the cost of berthing them in Scotland and Victoria while a new Devonport deeper water berth was constructed. 'No berths' in Tasmania for old ships TT-Line chief executive Chris Carbone confirmed Spirit I and II would stop sailing from October 24 and said a sale process has been underway for some time, with "interest in the ships". He ruled out the vessels being moored in the state. "Depending on when the ships are sold will determine where they are stored — there are no berths in Tasmania," Mr Carbone said. Chris Carbone says there is "interest in the ships". ( ABC News ) Labor infrastructure spokesperson Anita Dow expressed doubt that a sale was progressing. "They've said they've got interest from buyers in acquiring those old vessels, but they've gone quiet for some time now about whether there's actually been a successful follow-through," she said. "The government should be providing regular updates to the community about this process, about what these plans are for the old ships. Anita Dow is questioning why the Tasmanian government has "gone quiet" on the sale of the current ferries. ( ABC News ) During a public accounts committee earlier this year, TT-Line said the cost of mooring the new ships ranged from $600,000 a month in Scotland to $900,000 a month in Geelong, but the company did not provide the total cost incurred. The same committee heard the company was expected to remain in debt until 2052. "Every month that they're being stored [is] a cost endured by the company that's going to eventually eat into the price that's paid for these vessels into the future," Ms Dow said. Minister declines to answer 'hypotheticals' When asked where Spirit I and II would be docked when Spirit IV and V came into service at the end of the month, government minister Jo Palmer declined to answer. "I'm not going to be getting into hypotheticals," Ms Palmer said. "As I say, the process is underway. There's been a great response to that, and we look forward to making that announcement when that process has gone through." Kerry Vincent says the state government is "confident" the current ferries will be sold soon. ( ABC News: Jake Grant ) The state's infrastructure and transport minister, Kerry Vincent, said the sale talks were going well. "The Tasmanian government is confident TT-Line will secure a deal to sell Spirits I and II as soon as possible," Mr Vincent said. "TT-Line are working hard with their brokers and negotiations are progressing well. [They] have discussed the sale process and provided updates." The minister said due to negotiations being underway, he would not comment further.

events.title: Chip Industry Week In Review
events.summary: Manufacturing and process technology GlobalFoundries will operate two new fabs in Malta, New York , under a U.S.-Japan initiative involving up to $21B in investment. The first fab is expected to come online in 2029. GF also unveiled an FD-SOI roadmap for physical AI. Applied Materials unveiled its $5B EPIC Center , a 600,000-s.f. semiconductor process and equipment R&D facility in Silicon Valley. Infineon and Wolfspeed inked a new multi-year supply agreement for 200mm SiC wafers . Nikon introduced a new lithography system for advanced packaging, offering 1.5 µm line-and-space resolution and 40% higher throughput than its predecessor, at 72 panels per hour. The maskless system supports large substrates and RDL patterning, with availability planned for April 2027. Packaging and test FormFactor and Teradyne will co-develop semiconductor test technologies for HBM, advanced packaging, silicon photonics, and HPC. Teradyne also agreed to invest $300M in FormFactor. Teradyne also introduced a semiconductor test platform for edge-AI chips. ASE expanded its PowerSiP platform with a vertically integrated 3D packaging solution that places voltage regulation closer to AI processors, reducing parasitic routing losses by 50% or more to improve power efficiency in data centers and HPC systems. China narrows the gap CXMT reportedly plans to introduce a DDR5 server RDIMM using 4F² DRAM cells by year-end, potentially improving density and manufacturing costs. The development could help narrow China’s memory gap, although CXMT has not disclosed production yields, manufacturing volumes or evidence of cost competitiveness. China-based Langdao Silex unveiled a prototype EUV light source with 90% localized components, reports SCMP. TrendForce says the source exceeds 15W output but remains far below commercial EUV power levels, with mass production still estimated to be three to five years away. Nvidia ’s AI-accelerator shipments in China fell 44% year over year in the first half of 2026, leaving it with 34% of the data-center AI-accelerator market by units shipped, compared with Huawei’s 28%, according to IDC data reported by Reuters. Around the Valley This week’s SEMICON West conference: Synopsys CEO Sassine Ghazi said in a keynote address that autonomous chip design can already take some customer specifications to verified RTL, while physical implementation, verification and final sign-off still require human involvement. Nvidia expanded its AI tools for semiconductor manufacturing , including the new cuPotential CUDA-X library for atomic-scale simulation. Lam Research plans to integrate Nvidia NanoVDB into SEMulator3D, which is expected to speed select wafer-etch modeling by up to 30x. Siemens and Nvidia integrated cuLitho with Calibre to speed computational lithography , saying it’s up to 12x faster for full-chip OPC workloads. It supports High-NA EUV and curvilinear inverse lithography. Fig. 1: Synopsys President/CEO Sassine Ghazi and Semiconductor Engineering’s Ed Sperling at SEMICON West this week. Source: G. Haley/Semiconductor Engineering The OCP Global Summit was also held this week in San Jose. Find all the highlights in our New Technologies section below. Earnings season heating up TSMC reported Q3 revenue of roughly US$46.7B , up 41.2% year over year in U.S. dollar terms, with 2nm accounting for 8% of wafer revenue. CEO C.C. Wei said the company has seen “no sign of slowdown” in AI demand. But rising prices and macroeconomic uncertainty are weighing on consumer and other price-sensitive markets, prompting more cautious planning for 2027. TSMC also said it has discussed participating in Musk’s Terafab, but any fab collaboration would need to be operated by TSMC. ASML reported record Q3 sales of €11.7B, up about 55% from a year earlier, and said planned supply for the next two years will not fully meet customer demand. The company is evaluating additional capacity beyond its previously planned expansion. Market and investment More than $8.5B in Q3 chip industry startup funding was tracked across 80 companies, with AI inference, memory alternatives, photonics, networking, and other data-movement technologies drawing some of the quarter’s biggest rounds. SEMI projects global 300mm front-end fab equipment spending will rise 31% to $149B in 2026 and reach $227B by 2029, driven by AI, HPC, and leading-edge semiconductor demand. Equipment investment in the Americas is expected to more than double from $18.1B in 2026 to $40.6B in 2029. Fig. 2: SEMI 300mm Fab Outlook, Q326 update. Big hauls Salience Labs raised $125M to accelerate deployment of its optical circuit switching technology for AI infrastructure. Mueon raised $65M to scale up its stackable, modular 3D platform that integrates compute, memory, interconnect, power delivery, and thermal management. events.title: Revealed: VW, Ford and Tesla batteries linked to destructive deforestation of indigenous lands
events.summary: Mines in supply chains of western carmakers linked to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by Tolaki people in Indonesia Volkswagen, Ford and Tesla are among the electric carmakers whose batteries may contain nickel mined in indigenous woodlands plagued by deforestation, an analysis has found, highlighting the struggle to make vehicles that are free from environmental destruction. Corporate disclosures and trade flows from the last two years show mines in the battery supply chains of automotive giants are linked to the loss of trees in Sulawesi, a wildlife hotspot in Indonesia that houses the world’s largest nickel deposits. The metal is widely used in cathodes in car batteries because it boosts energy density and increases range. Ore from the Cahaya and Hengjaya mines was traced through regional smelters and Chinese processing plants run by Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt, a cathode manufacturer that supplies CATL, the world’s largest battery maker. Huayou’s corporate reports list US and European carmakers as end-users, while additional corporate files and trade data show a separate route from Huayou to LG, a South Korean group that also supplies battery products to leading carmakers, via Poland. Satellite analysis shows the mines have led to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by the indigenous Tolaki people. “We used to ask the forest for protection in return for our offerings,” said Wadimula, a Tolaki elder whose home sits on the edge of the 21,000-hectare Cahaya mining concession. “Destroying it means destroying our own life.” Electric vehicles are less environmentally harmful than fossil fuel-burning engines, which spew gases that foul the air and heat the planet, but western carmakers have struggled to clean up supply chains for batteries built with critical minerals from Africa, Asia and South America. Environmental groups warn that a failure to curb the boom of material-hungry SUVs is exacerbating the destruction by increasing the quantity mined. Ore from the two mining concessions is sent to a nickel smelter in an industrial complex in Morowali, on Indonesia’s eastern coast, operated by Huayou’s local subsidiary, where limonite is refined into mixed hydroxide precipitate, the primary raw material used to make battery cathodes. In 2024, $606m worth of mixed hydroxide precipitate was shipped from the Morowali plant to ports in China, followed by further shipments worth $470m in 2025. The processed ore was transported overland to Huayou cathode manufacturing sites in Quzhou, near Shanghai, and Yulin, near the border with Vietnam. Public filings do not disclose specific volumes or timings of sales from Huayou to CATL, which would be needed to directly connect specific ore shipments to car batteries, but Huayou confirmed group-level supplies to CATL in response to a regulatory inquiry by the Shanghai Stock Exchange in 2024. Chengdu B&M, a downstream subsidiary of Huayou, has also confirmed the supply of “large quantities” to CATL. The investigation, published in partnership with Voxeurop and other European media partners, traced shipments from mines and refineries in Sulawesi to China, and then again from Huayou cathode and CATL battery factories to the assembly lines of carmakers in the US and Europe. Volkswagen’s facility in Braunschweig, for instance, received a shipment in October 2024 of 24 tonnes of cell modules worth about $390,000, according to data from Volza, a trade platform. The shift to a carbon-free economy is pushing up demand for critical minerals in countries with weak environmental safeguards, though experts have argued the mining boom can be tempered without slowing the shift away from dirty fuels. In 2023, a report found lithium demand in the US transport sector could be reduced by 18% to 66% compared with a business-as-usual scenario, by improving public transport, walking and cycling more, and buying smaller cars. Better recycling could bring demand reductions as high as 92%, the report found. Global demand for nickel is set to double to 5.5m tonnes by 2040, according to the International Energy Agency, much of it mined in Indonesia and then refined in China. The loss of trees in mining concessions means the carbon footprint of nickel from the worst mines may be up to 500 times greater than previously reported, a study in Nature Communications found last year. The Cahaya and Hengjaya mines are located in woodlands designated as “production forest”, which are intended for forestry rather than industrial activities. However, successive Indonesian governments have weakened safeguards and carved out exemptions for miners as demand for nickel has soared. Nickel mining may be responsible for two-thirds of the forest loss recorded since 2001 within the area encompassed by the Cahaya concession, and over half of the loss in the Hengjaya concession, spatial analysis conducted by geospatial firm The TreeMap suggests.

events.title: From Dallaglio’s medals to Cantona’s shorts, sporting memorabilia is big business | Emma John
events.summary: From Dallaglio’s medals to Cantona’s shorts, sporting memorabilia is big business Like transfer fees and ticket prices, mementoes are one more marker of sport’s rampant self-inflation T he auctioneer cradled his gavel in his palm like a pipe, the handle pointing towards him. It gave his patter the air of a Victorian gentleman holding forth by the mantelpiece in a period drama. “Are you bidding, Wilf? You’re waving at me.” Under the hammer was a Barclays Manager of the Month trophy, complete with travel case, but no indication of which Premier League luminary once owned it. It outstripped its estimate and sold for £700. An hour and a half into what Budds auction house dubbed its “Octoberfest” of sporting memorabilia, David Convery at the podium showed no sign of fatigue, save the occasional swig from a water bottle. There were 332 lots in total; Convery regularly manages sales with twice as many. In his three decades as an auctioneer he’s even secured some world-record prices, from the oldest surviving FA Cup to Pelé’s 1970 World Cup final shirt. But sporting collectibles have never been bigger business than now. This week a jersey worn by Michael Jordan in the second game of the 1998 NBA finals – his “Last Dance” season for the Chicago Bulls – sold for over £10m , the kind of sum that might otherwise buy you a Mayfair townhouse. It was unprecedented in basketball but only just – two weeks previously, the jersey Jordan wore in game three had gone for £9.3m. And that had broken the record set by – you better believe it – Jordan’s game one jersey, which Sotheby’s sold in 2022. Last week’s Budds catalogue was never going to reach those heights but it still contained some star items. Almost all were the property of Lawrence Dallaglio, the former England rugby union captain, declared bankrupt a year ago and now treading the well-worn path of sportspeople forced to sell their mementoes of the glory days. Seven years ago Boris Becker raised nearly £700,000 by selling trophies he had amassed, including a replica of the US Open trophy he won against Ivan Lendl in 1989. Unfortunately in his case it wasn’t enough to prevent further trouble with the taxman. Running an auction is like writing a set list – you can’t just start with your biggest numbers, you have to warm up the audience, build to the good stuff. Diane Modahl’s leotard from the 1998 Commonwealth Games proved, somewhat ironically, a false start; no takers, even at £50 and with the 800m runner’s spikes and signature thrown in. A £5 note autographed by Jack Nicklaus did considerably better, and gradually the ephemera – signed prints, photos and programmes – gave way to more substantial stuff, like cricket caps and blazers from the days when England still wore the MCC’s colours and crest overseas. Admittedly, those postwar names are out of vogue now: still, it was a surprise to discover you could pick up one of Trevor Bailey’s touring blazers for less than you’d pay for a decent new one at John Lewis. Or that Paul Stirling’s Ireland T20 shirt is worth more than a pair of Godfrey Evans’s wicketkeeping gloves. A new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisis Dallaglio’s collection, when it arrived, was one for the bigger spenders. A set of tankards sold for £1,600 – perhaps to a rugby fan who knows he can never emulate the former England captain on the pitch but likes the idea of matching him at the bar. His 2003 World Cup winner’s medal was the prize item. It went for £54,000, near the bottom of its estimate, yet even more poignant was the rapacious flurry of bids on his England and Lions caps, with their old-fashioned gold braid and tassel, and individual numbers stitched on the peak. As Convery himself said, it’s rare for such items to make it to market. Still, no time for sentiment at an auction. The lots marched on, relentlessly, from the sublime to the ridiculous: Harry Kane shirts, Eric Cantona’s shorts, and the coffee table Des Lynam presided over in the BBC television studio at the 1998 Fifa World Cup. Whether Robbie Williams, its previous owner, was a careful one was not disclosed, but the added stardust fuelled a transatlantic contest between the UK and the US, with Blighty ultimately triumphing for £800. The US has always valued both on- and off-field artefacts – witness its trading card tradition, or the brawls in the bleachers when a baseball is hit straight into the stands. The jersey that Babe Ruth wore when he hit his “called shot” against the Chicago Cubs in the 1932 World Series – arguably the most legendary moment in his storied career – remains the most expensive item of sports memorabilia ever, having sold for over £18m in 2024 . But globalisation – and, needless to say, the internet – has transformed the market in the past two decades.

events.title: UBS exploring options abroad in case Swiss rules prove intolerable, sources say
events.summary: Switzerland is crafting new regulation for banks in response to the 2023 collapse of Credit Suisse. UBS is weighing overseas options, including moving its headquarters or merging, if Swiss banking rules become too strict after the Credit Suisse collapse. The bank is studying possible US bank purchases and even a takeover of UBS, but sources say there are no active talks. Swiss plans could force UBS to hold up to 100% CET1 capital for foreign units, which UBS says would trap more than US$20 billion and hurt competitiveness. ZURICH – UBS is working on possible scenarios including shifting its headquarters, or a merger with another bank , if Switzerland introduces new banking rules it deems excessively strict, according to three sources familiar with the matter. Switzerland is crafting new regulation for banks in response to the 2023 collapse of Credit Suisse , and a Lower House committee will later in October begin debating rules passed in September by the Upper House that UBS hinted were intolerable. A group inside the bank is considering the various options, which include drawing up a list of smaller banks in the United States that UBS could potentially buy, and the prospect of the bank being taken over itself, according to the sources. There are no active talks under way, the sources said. UBS, which is closely following how events play out in Parliament, said: “We don’t comment on speculation or views expressed on such matters.” The British government and UBS discussed in 2026 the possibility of a move to London if the bank were to redomicile, the Financial Times said on Oct 16. The city emerged as one of the best options in the bank’s 2025 contingency planning, a source told Reuters at the time. In March, UBS obtained a US banking licence and is eager to expand its business in the United States. But the rules drafted by the Swiss government are partly designed to reduce the risk taxpayers could face if the bank suffered losses in the United States. Sources familiar with the bank’s thinking say US investment bank Morgan Stanley would be the best theoretical match for UBS. The Swiss bank has repeatedly stated that it is not planning to move and sees great value in its Swiss base. There are notable ties between the leadership of the two banks, as UBS chairman Colm Kelleher spent many years at Morgan Stanley, eventually rising to one of the top jobs there. Kelleher said in September that UBS might need to consider its future in Switzerland if the incoming rules were too harsh. Under its overhaul, the Swiss government wants ⁠UBS to back its foreign units with 100% Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital, which could tie up in excess of US$20 billion (S$25.6 billion). UBS views this as excessive and harmful to its international competitiveness. The Upper House in September trimmed that requirement to 90% CET1 capital, but UBS also regards that as excessively high. At present, the bank needs to 60% capitalise its foreign units, but that can be partly met with cheaper capital. Since 2025, speculation has swirled around the possibility that UBS could move its base abroad to avoid the tougher regulation, and sources familiar with the bank’s thinking say it has a duty to shareholders to consider all options. Swiss Finance Minister Karin Keller-Sutter, who has led the charge to introduce tougher banking rules, said in September she felt it was unlikely that UBS would leave its homeland, arguing this would be costly and legally complicated. events.title: Warsh boosts market expectations of Fed rate hold in October
events.summary: At the IMF’s annual meetings in Bangkok, US Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh reiterated that the Fed will deliver price stability. Warsh did not signal any policy change, which lifted bets that the Fed will hold rates at its Oct 27-28 meeting. Market odds of a hike fell from about 27% to below 15%. He repeated that the Fed will deliver “price stability” and said he does not “prejudge meetings”. Stocks rose and the US dollar slipped after his remarks, said Derek Tang of Monetary Policy Analytics. Warsh also backed artificial intelligence as a major innovation, but warned it is boosting demand now and could overheat the economy. His AI task force will hold a field hearing in San Francisco Bay Area on Nov 16. US Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh did nothing to dispel market expectations that the US central bank will hold interest rates steady when it meets at the end of October . In a moderated discussion on Oct 16 morning in Bangkok at the International Monetary Fund’s annual meetings, he made no remarks on monetary policy or his outlook for the US economy, apart from reiterating that the Fed will deliver price stability. “We made very clear that we would deliver price stability, and we removed a dose of accommodation about a month ago,” Warsh said. “I don’t prejudge meetings. I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year.” Investors pared their bets for a rate hike at the US central bank’s Oct 27-28 policy gathering. The odds, which were hovering around 27% before Warsh spoke, dropped below 15% following his remarks. Stocks extended gains and the US dollar edged lower, with futures for the S&P 500 Index erasing losses of as much as 0.6% to climb 0.2%. “It was clear that he wasn’t going to deliver anything that the market could latch on to as hawkish,” Derek Tang, an economist at Monetary Policy Analytics, wrote in a note to clients. The Fed raised interest rates by a quarter percentage point in September , the first hike since 2023. It was backed by all 19 policymakers, and a majority also saw another increase as likely in 2026 . A few key officials in recent weeks reiterated that additional rate hikes may be needed, but emphasised they have time to gather economic data before acting again. Warsh repeated his bullish views on artificial intelligence, calling it the most important innovation in the global economy during his lifetime. But he also warned that it may be driving demand in the near term. The Fed chief said that as a central banker, he is taking the new technology seriously but also “soberly, responsibly”. “It’s obviously hitting the demand side of the economy before it’s going to hit the supply side of the economy,” Warsh said. “If you’re a central banker, you’re in the business of trying to ensure stable prices and full employment, you’ve got to recognise this as a shock.” While it is a positive supply shock in the medium term, Warsh argued, it is driving increases in aggregate demand now and the impact on employment is uncertain. Some of Warsh’s colleagues have expressed similar concerns, even questioning whether the surge in investment that is buoying the AI build-out could lead to an overheating of the economy. Warsh also announced that his task force on productivity and jobs – which is grappling with the implications of AI – will hold a field hearing in the San Francisco Bay Area on Nov 16. It is one of five task forces he convened that will present recommendations to the Federal Open Market Committee in late 2026 or early in 2027. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Stocks, futures rise as Fed bets ease after Warsh: Markets wrap
events.summary: Stock markets were already rising on Oct 16 before US Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh’s comments as a selloff in chip stocks eased. Stocks rose after Fed chairman Kevin Warsh gave no signal of urgency for more rate hikes, and traders cut October hike bets to 15%. Asian shares gained as chip stocks recovered, with Samsung and SK Hynix up more than 4%, while South Korea’s Kospi rebounded 4%. Indonesia’s stocks fell sharply after MSCI removed its emerging-market status, and investors warned the rally may stay fragile if gains remain focused on AI shares. Stocks extended gains as traders pared bets on an interest-rate hike after United States Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh refrained from signalling greater urgency to tighten policy despite this week’s hotter-than-expected inflation data. The dollar edged lower. MSCI’s Asia Pacific equities gauge climbed 1.4% , while US equity-index futures climbed 0.2%. European shares were set to gain 0.8% at the open. The modest uptick in sentiment – stocks were already higher as a rout in chip stocks eased – came after Warsh’s comments about the benefits of artificial intelligence (AI) to the US economy. He made no remarks on monetary policy or his outlook for the US economy, save for reiterating that the Fed will deliver price stability. “Warsh’s refusal to commit to another rate hike is resulting in some Fed-rate-hike bets being unwound,” said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo Markets. “His comment that ‘I don’t prejudge meetings’ after strong inflation prints is not helping the dollar.” Traders reduced bets on a Fed rate hike in October to 15% after Warsh’s speech, from more than 25% on Oct 15. A Bloomberg gauge of the dollar fell 0.1%, after dropping 0.3% the prior session, which was the biggest decline in more than a month. Gold was little changed at US$4,172 an ounce . Treasuries stayed lower on the day as Warsh spoke, after rallying across the curve in US trading. Global crude oil benchmark Brent dropped 0.7% to US$105.20 a barrel. Investors looked to Warsh’s speech in Bangkok for clearer signals on the policy path after the fastest US inflation in five months boosted expectations for further Fed tightening . US inflation has remained stubborn, fuelled by elevated oil prices since the Middle East war broke out. “We made very clear that we would deliver price stability, and we removed a dose of accommodation about a month ago,” Warsh said in Bangkok. “I don’t prejudge meetings. I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year.” The Fed raised rates by a quarter percentage point in September, the first hike since 2023. It was backed by all 19 policymakers, and a majority also saw another increase as likely in 2026. A few key officials in recent weeks reiterated that additional rate hikes may be needed, but emphasised they have time to gather economic data before acting again. “Markets are reassured to hear Warsh reiterating his belief that AI will uplift productivity in the medium term, which could help moderate inflation expectations and temper fears of back-to-back Fed rate hikes,” said Chang Wei Liang, a macro strategist at DBS Bank. Stock markets were already rising on Oct 16 before Warsh’s comments as a selloff in chip stocks eased. In Asia, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix both advanced more than 4%. That helped South Korea’s Kospi Index rise 4% rebounding from the slump on Oct 15 that sent the gauge to its lowest close since April. Indonesian stocks slumped as much as 11%, the most since January 1998, after MSCI said the country no longer merits emerging-market status. The rupiah also edged lower. The durability of the equity rebound may depend on whether gains spread beyond the technology heavyweights that have driven much of the advance in 2026. Broader participation across sectors would help reduce the market’s reliance on AI-linked stocks after this week’s volatility exposed the risks of that concentration. “It seems like we are seeing a technical rebound, with the overall market settling down somewhat,” said Ryuta Otsuka, a strategist at Toyo Securities. Volatility could remain relatively high next week as traders monitor earnings “while searching for a bottom”, he said.

events.title: Keeping the haze out: Malls shut automated doors, suspend outdoor activities
events.summary: A sign at VivoCity on Oct 16 stating that an automated door is closed to keep the haze out. Singapore malls are closing automated doors and outdoor areas to protect shoppers and staff as haze stays unhealthy for a 12th day. Lendlease, Far East Organization and CapitaLand Investment are cleaning filters, checking air systems and giving N95 masks to workers with outdoor exposure. Malls are following NEA advice and may change access or suspend events; past haze cost Singapore $1.83 billion in 2015, according to NTU researchers. SINGAPORE – As Singapore entered the 12th consecutive day of unhealthy air on Oct 16, major retail landlords told The Straits Times they were taking steps to reduce haze exposure for shoppers, tenants and staff. Lendlease, Far East Organization and CapitaLand Investment have stepped up air filter cleaning and monitoring for their air-conditioning and mechanical ventilation (ACMV) systems. To protect people indoors, they are keeping automated mall entrances shut, with landlords such as Lendlease and CapitaLand Investment distributing N95 masks to employees and contractors facing prolonged outdoor exposure. At noon on Oct 16, the hourly PM2.5 readings across the island hit the “high” range, which is above 150, while the 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) in western, central and eastern Singapore remained in the “very unhealthy” range above 200. Singapore’s PSI has five bands – good (0-50), moderate (51-100), unhealthy (101-200), very unhealthy (201-300) and hazardous (more than 300). A CapitaLand Investment spokesman said management may reduce outdoor airflow at its malls – including Ion Orchard, Plaza Singapura, Tampines Mall, Junction 8, Funan and Kallang Wave Wall – by closing windows and automatic sliding doors where possible and directing shoppers to alternative entrances. Outdoor facilities at the malls may also be closed when air quality reaches unhealthy levels, the spokesperson added. A sign on the sliding entrance doors at Junction 8 stated that they were disabled to maintain indoor air quality as pollutant levels hit the unhealthy range , directing shoppers to use the side entrances instead. Deborah Tan, director for operations and marketing at Far East Organization’s commercial group, said mall tenants with exterior exits have also been advised to keep their entrances closed. Far East Organization’s portfolio of malls includes Orchard Central, Clarke Quay Central, Square 2 and One Holland Village. Tenants at One Holland Village, which has a more open layout, have been advised to keep their shop doors closed where suitable, while outdoor events have been rescheduled to November. Tan added that they are monitoring updates from the National Environment Agency (NEA) closely and will adjust their safety approach as conditions develop. Jenny Khoo, head of retail and workspace management at Lendlease, said staff are encouraged to prioritise their well-being and discuss any concerns with their supervisors, and that flexible work arrangements “may be considered where appropriate”. She added that under normal conditions, the malls’ ACMV air filters are cleaned and replaced on a stringent maintenance schedule. When haze conditions worsen, management steps up active monitoring of indoor air quality and filter performance, and carries out additional replacements. Khoo added that management has also enhanced the malls’ air quality with bi-polar ionisation systems, which release positive and negative ions to eliminate dust, odours and pathogens such as bacteria and viruses. Retail malls in Lendlease’s portfolio include Parkway Parade, 313@somerset, Jem and PLQ Mall. Khoo said outdoor play areas at Lendlease malls, such as Jem, may close temporarily when the 24-hour PSI reading exceeds 200. “Lendlease takes precautionary measures guided by prevailing NEA advisories, including suspending outdoor facilities and activities,” she added. Mapletree Pan Asia Commercial Trust, which manages VivoCity, declined to comment, although one of its entrances featured a sign stating it was closed to keep the haze out. VivoCity’s level-three rooftop features an open, shallow wading pool, while level two has free-to-access outdoor playgrounds alongside children’s ride operator ZooMoov. A spokesperson for City Square Mall said its outdoor playgrounds have been temporarily closed, while mall personnel’s non-essential outdoor duties have been reduced. “Non-essential” auto-doors have also been closed to limit outdoor pollutants entering the mall. The mall will also give away 100 complimentary honey lemon drinks, while stocks last, at the mall’s customer service counter at B2 from Oct 19 to Nov 1, from 10am to 10pm daily. The Singapore Institute of International Affairs had in June issued a rare “red” warning in its Haze Outlook 2026 report, and said there was a high risk of severe transboundary haze affecting Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore.

events.title: Drone strikes in the Black Sea raise fears of Russian escalation to test NATO
events.summary: Drone attacks on cargo ships in the Black Sea this month have raised concerns among NATO members SOFIA, Bulgaria -- A string of drone attacks on at least seven cargo vessels in the Black Sea this month, off the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria, has some members of the alliance wondering if Russian President Vladimir Putin is seeking escalation to test their support for Ukraine in its war against Moscow's full-scale invasion. The attacks in the two countries' exclusive economic zones threaten a global shipping route and have left two people dead, with at least 25 still missing. They also run the risk of drawing other countries directly into the war for Ukraine. Throughout the war, Russia has repeatedly bombarded Ukraine’s Black Sea and Danube river ports, leaving Kyiv increasingly reliant on alternative routes to get its grain exports to markets in Africa and the Middle East. Russian drones have repeatedly violated Romanian airspace near some of Ukraine's Danube ports. In the latest incidents, fires broke out on two ships struck by drones Wednesday and Thursday, one in Romania's territorial waters. Romanian President Nicusor Dan said Thursday in Brussels that “two drones” had hit the vessels but did not say whose drones they were. “There will be a reaction from the Romanian state,” he warned. Increasingly, the suspicion falls on Russia. “There is no logic in Ukraine attacking its own ships and crews, given that the outcome of all these attacks favors Russia — and indeed, the logic points in that direction,” Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told his country’s Parliament. “The problem is that we cannot prove it.” The San Marino-flagged Wine Trader , a chemical tanker traveling from Tunisia to Romania, was struck by a drone Thursday and caught fire. Five crew members were rescued but another seven are missing. On Wednesday, a drone strike and fire were reported on the Comoros-flagged Yara J, a chemical and oil tanker traveling from Turkey to Romania. Romania’s acting Defense Minister Radu Miruta said an investigation was underway. On Tuesday, two ships were struck by drones off Bulgaria's coast. Rescuers evacuated all 15 crew members from the Ukraine-operated Chelsea 3, sailing under a Maltese flag, but 11 crew from the Guinea-Bissau-flagged HS Dignity are still missing . The crew of the Chelsea 3 reported the ship’s deck and hull were hit by three aerial drones. Earlier this month, sea and aerial drones attacked two other commercial vessels in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. A Togo-flagged ship sank with no sign of the 12 sailors reported on board, while a Bulgarian ferry evacuated 18 crew members from a Palau-flagged vessel that was damaged. A day earlier, a Turkish-owned cargo ship carrying corn caught fire following a drone attack and later sank off the coast of Romania. Two people died and 11 crew members were rescued. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the attack as “a horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel” in neutral waters. Russia's ambassador in Sofia, Bulgaria, said she didn't have any information from the Russian defense ministry. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said on X on Thursday that he met Radev and Dan to discuss security in the Black Sea and “the latest attacks on commercial shipping.” “NATO has strengthened our posture along the eastern flank including with increasing counter-drone capabilities,” he said. “NATO will continue to work closely with our Allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defense posture as needed.” Article 5 of the NATO charter has a mutual defense guarantee — an attack on one is an attack on all — but Romanian defense analyst Radu Tudor said it was uncertain as to whether it covers many of the Black Sea drone strikes because they occurred in the alliance members’ exclusive economic zones. Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Fort Hood survivors speak out on Pentagon's decision to livestream Hasan's execution Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded “It’s a matter of discussion whether the exclusive economic zone is included in the Article 5-type reaction or not,” he said. “And it seems that until now, it isn’t — which raised a lot of questions.” NATO has been too slow to respond in the Black Sea, he argued. “Tens of incidents are happening and Russia is getting closer to NATO borders. … Words are not enough,” Tudor said. The Black Sea drone incidents in October are just the latest in a long string of drone airspace incursions to rock Romania and other NATO members since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. While most have come from Russia, Ukrainian drones have also crossed borders.
