events.title: World Bank sets fivefold minerals goal as Fed chairman Warsh flags financial stability risks
events.summary: The World Bank aims to increase its critical minerals business fivefold over the next five years, while US Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh expressed surprise at the resilience of major economies amid geopolitical shocks and tighter monetary policy. "In critical minerals, we ⁠plan to quintuple our business in five years … this ​week, ⁠we launched our ‌first country compacts with MDB partners, to build local industries and keep ​more jobs and value at home," World Bank president Ajay Banga said at the 2026 IMF -World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Friday, as the multilateral lender seeks to support mining, processing and local industries. He also outlined plans to expand partnerships with countries developing critical minerals industries. The World Bank's new metals and minerals implementation plan is aimed at securing $19 billion in critical minerals financing over the 2026-2030 fiscal period, up from $3.6 billion in the 2021-2025 fiscal period. The lender has identified 20 countries with which it could partner on critical minerals development projects. It also launched its first country compacts with its partners this week, aiming to build local industries and retain more jobs and economic value in producing countries. Mr Banga also laid out a vision on Friday for how the World Bank should operate, focusing primarily on creating jobs, expanding economic opportunity and connecting private capital to developing nations that need investment. Addressing the plenary session at the annual meetings, Mr Banga said the current economic climate of tightening fiscal space, rising debt and global conflicts had made the work challenging – but not impossible. “Those are the twin challenges we have been working to address: making scarce resources go further, while helping countries create jobs at scale. They must be addressed together,” he said in prepared remarks. “The future of development will depend on bringing public finance , private investment, philanthropy and technology together around what each country needs. The partnership – and mix – should evolve as countries do.” He also spoke of the World Bank’s new initiative to focus on “small AI” – bespoke artificial intelligence-enabled applications that do not rely on the most advanced and expensive version of the technology, but can provide solutions for people in the developing world. “Practical, or ‘small’, AI can help a farmer improve yields, a teacher tailor instruction, a health worker make better-informed decisions, or an entrepreneur reach new customers,” Mr Banga added. Separately, Mr Warsh said the Fed needed to consider financial stability risks as it assesses the outlook for the US economy , while declining to offer indications about its next interest-rate decision. ⁠Speaking at the annual meetings, heh said he did not “prejudge” policy decisions before the Fed’s meetings from October 27 to 28, when markets expect interest rates to remain unchanged. The Fed raised rates in September and made it clear that it intended to deliver price stability and withdraw some monetary policy accommodation, he said. “I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year,” Mr Warsh said. He said ⁠the Fed must ​continually bolster its credibility to get ⁠monetary policy right, adding that that includes the supervision and operations side ⁠of the central bank. He also expressed optimism about AI and its potential to transform the real economy, although he said the technology’s near-term impact on employment remained uncertain. Mr Warsh also said he was surprised by the global resilience and how many G20 member ⁠states are “hanging in there” amid the geopolitical shocks of recent months, ​as ⁠most ‌central banks tightened monetary ​policy to deal with inflation. “We're seeing common things and we're taking action and I view that as a positive development,” Mr Warsh said. “I believe, optimistically, ​you ‌might think ⁠naively, at least ​in the US, we're ​going ‌to come out of ⁠this stronger with a ⁠more durable economy, more capable of leading the world on economic growth.” With reporting from Reuters and AFP

events.title: Commercial goods are no longer entering Gaza, raising fears
events.summary: No commercial goods are entering the Gaza Strip, Israeli authorities said, attributing the suspension to local vendors they said are fed up with Hamas raising taxes on them JERUSALEM -- No commercial goods have entered the Gaza Strip for two days, Israeli authorities said Thursday, blaming the suspension on merchants angered by taxes imposed by Hamas — a claim that Palestinian importers deny. The halt to commercial shipments, including fruit and winter clothing, cuts off a key source of food and other critical supplies as fears grow about procuring supplies needed to get through winter in the territory. The move stands to immediately reduce Gaza's supplies, because the closed-off territory is completely reliant on whatever goods Israel allows in through border crossings. Aid groups generally bring in staples such as flour, while merchants import more perishable foods like fruits and meat, according to data released earlier this year by COGAT, the Israeli military body that oversees humanitarian affairs in Gaza. The suspension is raising fears about affordability, with humanitarian workers saying a combination of aid and a robust commercial market is needed to keep prices under control. “The humanitarian sector on its own cannot meet the needs of all the people,” said Shaina Low, a spokesperson for the Norwegian Refugee Council, an aid group. “The markets need to be functioning.” COGAT announced the suspension of commercial shipments Wednesday. Its deputy spokesperson, Lt. Daniel Kantorovich, said the agency was acting on a decision made by Palestinian merchants a day earlier and could reverse it at their behest. “We were prepared to coordinate the entry of their trucks as usual, but the vendors informed us that they were cancelling the coordination due to Hamas’s taxation mechanism and threats against them,” Kantorovich said. “The merchants don’t want to bring goods into Gaza.” The world’s leading authority on food insecurity reported earlier this year that conditions in Gaza had improved since famine was declared in the territory in August 2025, but were still at crisis levels. Most families in the war-battered enclave weren’t getting nearly enough to eat, said the report, adding that “even small disruptions to humanitarian access could rapidly reverse recent gains.” Merchants in Gaza coordinate directly with vendors outside the territory, whose shipments are examined by Israel's military before entering Gaza. In announcing the measure, COGAT claimed to be communicating a decision made by local merchants in Gaza who had grown tired of Hamas taxing their trucks and threatening them. Israel has long accused the militant group of levying fees on imports to fund its operations. COGAT said no private-sector vendors had attempted to import goods to Gaza since the merchants alerted Israel on Tuesday. Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Fort Hood survivors speak out on Pentagon's decision to livestream Hasan's execution Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded But the head of Gaza’s private truckers union, Nahed Sheheiber, disputed Israel's account, saying they were the ones who had made the decision. “The merchants are not the ones who stopped the shipments,” he said. “The Israeli coordinator is claiming that Gaza’s merchants are responsible, but the truth is that the Israelis are the ones who imposed the restrictions.” Following COGAT's announcement, Sheheiber's union met with Gaza's Ministry of Economy to express concern and say Israel was citing fees levied by the ministry as a pretext to cut off commercial goods. The ministry had been asking merchants to pay 10,000 shekels (about $3,226) per truck entering Gaza, Sheheiber said. At the meeting, ministry Undersecretary Khaled Al-Raqab told the union that the amount was not a tax, but rather a donation sought by the ministry to help pay civil servants in the strip. It was not clear from the COGAT announcement if aid agencies would be allowed to increase shipments into Gaza to compensate for the loss in commercial goods. The agency claimed that Gaza's population — of roughly 2 million people — required approximately 250 truckloads of goods each day. That's far below the minimum of 600 trucks a day stipulated by a ceasefire brokered by the U.S. a year ago. The war started when Hamas-led militants killed some 1,200 people on Oct. 7, 2023, and took 251 hostages . Israel responded with a massive bombardment and a ground invasion that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to the Gaza Health Ministry. That includes over 1,400 Palestinians killed since the ceasefire took effect, the ministry says. Sporadic attacks have killed five Israeli soldiers in Gaza in the same period. The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, maintains detailed records and is seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts.

events.title: Yields on S’pore Government Securities climb higher: Should investors buy in or stick to stocks?
events.summary: The interest rate on the one-year T-bill rose to its 2026 high of 1.92% on Oct 15. T-bill yields in Singapore have risen to about 1.9%, and experts expect more gains as US Federal Reserve hikes push up short-term rates. Nov's Singapore Savings Bonds hit a 2026 peak of 2.45%, though early redemption cuts year-one yields to 1.67% Some investors still prefer dividend stocks, as their yields can beat T-bills and SSBs, while keeping more cash ready for market opportunities. SINGAPORE – The returns that retail investors are getting for Treasury bills (T-bills), a type of short-term Singapore Government Securities, are climbing after dipping to around 1.3% to 1.4% in 2025 and the first half of 2026. With yields now hovering near 1.9%, fixed-income experts believe there is more upside in the coming months. Another form of Singapore Government Securities, Singapore Savings Bonds (SSBs), will pay the highest rates so far in 2026 for its November issue. If investors hold the SSBs for the full duration of 10 years, they will earn an average return of 2.45% a year. T-bills are short-term securities with maturities of either six months or a year. Investors buy the bills at a discount upfront and receive the full face value at maturity, earning the difference as interest. In contrast, SSBs are longer-term instruments that can be held for up to 10 years, though investors have the flexibility to exit their investment in any given month without penalty. Both T-bills and SSBs are deemed risk-free investments backed by Singapore’s triple-A credit rating. The appeal of T-bills grew in 2022 as yields climbed steadily from sub-1% levels. The six-month T-bill subsequently hit a peak of 4.4% on Dec 8, 2022, and the one-year T-bill went as high as 3.87% on Jan 26, 2023. Drawn by their safe nature and rising yields, investors from all walks of life piled in. Senior lab technician Dallas Goh was one of them. He accumulated as much as $100,000 in T-bills at one point. Interest in these short-term government securities waned in 2024 as equity markets became more attractive. Investors – including Goh, who stopped buying T-bills in the middle of 2024 – looked elsewhere for higher returns. However, the yields on T-bills are climbing again. The interest rate on the one-year T-bill rose to its 2026 high of 1.92% on Oct 15, from 1.68% on July 23. There will be no more one-year T-bill auctions in 2026. Meanwhile, the cut-off yield for the six-month T-bill dipped slightly to 1.9% on Oct 8, remaining just shy of its Sept 24 peak of 1.92%. There are five more six-month T-bill auctions – on Oct 22, Nov 4, Nov 19, Dec 3 and Dec 17. Goh said the yields are “still too low” and that he will wait until they cross 2.5% before he considers investing in T-bills again. His wish may just come true. Market watchers anticipate higher yields in the upcoming auctions as the US Federal Reserve is expected to raise interest rates at least once by December 2026 and a total of twice within the next six months. Eugene Leow, head of fixed-income research at DBS Bank, said: “As long as Fed hike bets are in play, we would reasonably expect six-month T-bill rates to continue climbing.” He noted that the interest rates on a six-month T-bill reflect where investors expect the Fed to move rates over the next half a year. “We think the six-month and one-year T-Bill rates would still grind higher in the coming months as Fed hikes get delivered,” he added. Wesley Hoon, research analyst with the global fixed-income team at digital wealth platform FSM Global, noted that the Monetary Authority of Singapore manages the economy through the exchange rate rather than by setting interest rates. As a result, Singapore’s short-term rates largely take their cue from US interest rates. To illustrate his point, Hoon noted that following the Federal Reserve’s rate hike on Sept 16, the cut-off yield for the six-month T-bill auction on Sept 24 climbed from 1.7% to 1.92%. “If the Fed pauses in October and hikes in December, as markets expect, that adds upward pressure into year-end, though some of it is already reflected in today’s yields,” he said. Hoon expects six-month yields to keep climbing over the remaining auctions in 2026. FSM Global is also positive on the one-year T-bills. However, since there are no more one-year bills in 2026, investors must wait until January 2027 to participate. To avoid sitting on idle cash, Hoon suggested that investors consider building a T-bill ladder with staggered maturity dates by spreading their cash across multiple upcoming auctions. Because six-month bills are auctioned every two weeks, investors can allocate a portion into each of the next few issues, making January 2027’s one-year T-bill just another rung in their ladder rather than the final destination, he added. “With a ladder, you don’t have to call the peak to earn a decent yield,” Hoon said. “Part of your money matures every couple of weeks.

events.title: Fuel costs squeezing margins for some businesses
events.summary: Diesel prices in Jersey have reached more than £2 per litre in recent weeks Some businesses in Jersey have expressed concern about the impact of rising global fuel prices. Locally, and in the UK, diesel prices recently topped £2 a litre , and global leaders have since made efforts to ease the strain on supply. The Government of Jersey has proposed to freeze fuel duty in 2027 in a bid to "help ease cost-of-living pressures". A&A Scaffolding Solutions said it welcomed that move, but said it would provide "limited relief if global prices continue to rise". Listen to the latest news for Jersey Fuel duty was frozen in Jersey from 2023-2025, before rising in line with inflation in 2026. In the proposed budget for 2027 , external , the government has suggested freezing it once again. It said "maintaining fuel duty at its current rate will help avoid additional costs for households and businesses that rely on transport, providing continued support at a time when many islanders remain under financial pressure". However, some businesses on the island worry that it will not be enough to offset global prices. Which war is having the biggest impact on diesel prices - Iran or Ukraine? Published 4 days ago Kelly Keating, from A&A Scaffolding Solutions, said "rising diesel prices are a real concern for us, particularly when they come on top of so many other costs that seem to be increasing across Jersey". "Construction is taking a hard hit. We rely on diesel for machinery, vehicles and deliveries, so increases put direct pressure on the cost of carrying out work. "Alongside rising material, freight and operating costs, this is squeezing margins and making it harder to price projects with confidence". "A freeze in fuel duty would be welcome, but our concern is that it would offer limited relief if global fuel prices continue to rise. "The wider issue is the cumulative impact. Businesses can only absorb so many increases before they affect investment, project viability and ultimately the prices customers pay". Businesses said it was becoming more difficult to absorb price rises Fuel costs are also having a "noticeable impact" for tree surgeons, Jonathan Le Maistre Ltd. Darren Hopkins, from the firm, said "we depend on our vans, trucks, chippers, stump grinders, and other machinery that consume significant amounts of fuel". "Increased diesel prices will raise our operating costs, reducing margins on jobs and making it more difficult to absorb costs without passing some of them on to our customers". Hopkins said continued increases would be a "concern for their business, and the wider industry". However, some businesses are managing through the disruption. Jeremy Phillips, from Barette Plant Hire, said it "hasn't been too much of an issue so far, but that fuel surcharges are being added to hourly rates". However, he said that "if the prices keep going up, customers aren't going to be carrying on with their projects". Treasury Minister Alan Maclean said support was being targeted directly at consumers rather than expecting businesses to absorb costs In the run-up to the unveiling of the 2027 budget, Deputy Lucy Stephenson called for a reduction in fuel duty , but those plans were withdrawn following assurances from ministers that support was coming. Speaking at the time, Treasury Minister Alan Maclean said the government "didn't like the idea of reducing fuel duty because it wasn't targeted". Instead, ministers opted for a freeze on duty for 2027, prioritising targeted support for families and those "struggling the most". Responding to the fresh concerns from businesses, Maclean said: "Rather than expecting businesses to absorb increased costs such as higher fuel prices, the budget provides support directly to consumers to help them manage those pressures and spend in the local economy". "Fuel prices are largely driven by global markets and geopolitical events outside Jersey's control. "What the government can do is avoid adding further pressure where it can. "The proposed freeze in fuel duty will help mitigate the impact of prices rises by reducing the level of duty in real terms". events.title: Even Benchmark thinks AI is eroding the venture pact against backing rivals
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. For decades, the unwritten rule of venture capital was that a firm doesn’t back two companies that compete head-on. But speaking at TechCrunch Disrupt earlier this week, the partners of Benchmark readily acknowledged that the AI boom is straining that rule. It’s been on the verge of snapping for some time. The towering AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic share dozens of the same investors at this point. Then, at the end of September, Factory, a startup that builds an AI agent to write software, said it was firing board observer and adviser Chris Degnan for “unethical conduct involving Cognition,” its direct rival and the maker of the Devin coding agent. Factory’s CEO alleged Degnan had discussed a job at Cognition while privy to Factory’s board-level discussions. Degnan said he had already resigned and denied sharing anything confidential. Soon after, he announced he was joining Cognition as chief revenue officer. Powerhouse investor Vinod Khosla sided with Degnan on X, blasting Factory’s CEO and calling the company “a struggling second tier competitor.” Khosla Ventures backs both companies. Even Benchmark, a firm whose reputation rests on 10- to 15-year partnerships with founders at the earliest stage, said the old rule can no longer be counted on. Asked at Disrupt whether the pact against backing rivals still holds as portfolio companies expand into each other’s territory, its partners described the conflicts as a matter of necessity, not preference. “The harsh reality of this world is every company is evolving very quickly,” said Eric Vishria. Companies pivot and change, he said, and “you are going to get conflicts, and that’s just the reality of the current dynamic.” Vishria said Benchmark stays committed to each founder and keeps what it learns confidential, and he downplayed how much a VC could pass along anyway: “We are not product or technology experts.” Seemingly referring to the Factory-Cognition dispute, he said Benchmark has been fortunate not to land in “that type of insane direct conflict.” Exclusivity, he said, remains “really important” at the very early stage Benchmark favors. “But things are evolving. There’s no doubt about that.” Chetan Puttagunta said AI is accelerating the problem. As the cost of building software “effectively goes to zero,” he said, founders are “incredibly ambitious.” Because they now see a “surface area” and want to claim all of it, he continued, “[i]t’s probably going to happen more, where you start to run into each other.” He drew a line between a direct competitor at the outset, which he called “an easy answer,” and a portfolio company that expands into another’s turf over time. “That happens,” he said. Peter Fenton called the issue “kryptonite” and the firm’s toughest problem. He described a spectrum of how investors relate to their companies. At one end is the co-founder, who would never work on a competing company. At the other is the public-market stock picker, who can own several rivals because he is merely allocating capital, not shaping any of them. Benchmark sits nearer the co-founder end, Fenton said, and treats transparency as a golden rule. “There shouldn’t be the surprise after the fact.” If a conflict does emerge, a founder should never feel shortchanged, he added. Benchmark isn’t declaring the pact dead. At the same time, when a firm that built its name on loyalty says conflicts are coming, founders might rightly wonder who else will be this candid. events.title: 'TV and cheap booze' blamed for landlord quitting
events.summary: Landlord Patrick Hughes says fewer people are going to the pub Former pub landlord Patrick Hughes is blunt when explaining why he has called time on his tenure behind the bar. "I thought there was a gap in the market but there was no market for the gap", he said. The 66-year-old took over The Royal Mail Cart pub in Spalding, in August 2025, hoping to attract customers with live music nights and "a sense of community". Just over a year on he is packing boxes and looking around the empty rooms after he quit his tenancy with the pub's owner, Stonegate Group. The government said it was supporting pubs with business rates discounts. Patrick has given up his tenancy of The Royal Mail Cart in Spalding Patrick told BBC Politics North that he blames a perfect storm of rising utility and wage prices, people's changing habits and major roadworks directly outside the pub, which began in the summer. "These days people are used to staying at home, watching TV, having cheap drink from the supermarket or off licence and getting food deliveries," he said. "To make a pub like this work you need to turn over £12,000 a week, some weeks we were doing quite well, around £8,000, but once the road works began outside that went down quite dramatically." Figures from the Office for National Statistics , external show that 27% of pubs and bars in Lincolnshire closed between 2009 and 2025. That is a drop from 710 to 515. In South Holland, of which Spalding is a part, the rate is almost double that, at 53%, a drop from 75 to 35. That is also way above the England average of 19%. "The government needs to look at the low cost of alcohol in supermarkets primarily," said Patrick. "Certainly the taxation in supermarkets needs to be looked at to bring about some kind of equilibrium." Duty paid on draught alcohol in pubs and bars is up to 11 pence cheaper than that sold in supermarkets. But other costs associated with running a business still makes supermarket alcohol cheaper overall. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced a 20% cut in business rates for qualifying pubs, social clubs and live music venues in England, effective from April 2027. Emma McClarkin OBE, chief executive of the British Beer and Pub Association, says they want that to be made permanent at the Budget this month, "alongside a freeze in beer duty and a widening of the draft discount". "We're set to lose one pub a day by the end of the year and 295 have closed already," she said. "When a pub does close, it's not just the front door that's closing, it's the heritage, the culture, the economic contribution to society and the social value." Mark Newlands believes that people still want to visit their local pub Just outside Spalding, The Ship Inn pub stands by the River Welland in the small hamlet of Surfleet Seas End. "There used to be tables and chairs with people eating food and drinking by the river," said Mark Newlands, who lives a few doors down. The pub closed last year but now some locals, led by Mark, have formed The Shipmates group to try to raise £600,000 to buy and run it. So far they have managed to get the pub listed as An Asset of Community Value under the Localism Act 2011. That gives them the right to bid for the property, if it goes up for sale. "People have become fed up of the Covid way of living and they want to see their pub open," said Mark. "The indications from smaller and larger investors is that it's worth doing and we've proven to our own satisfaction that it is a viable business." An HM Treasury spokesperson said: "The Chancellor prioritised support for the hospitality industry in his first week in the job when he cut business rates by 20% for pubs, social clubs and live music venues - saving thousands of locals over £1,000 a year." Stonegate has been approached by the BBC for comment. Listen to highlights from Lincolnshire on BBC Sounds , watch the latest episode of Look North .

events.summary: The prime minister has a once-in-a-generation chance to reintroduce fairness to the system. He has to seize the moment Back in 2009, months before the coalition government unleashed sweeping austerity, the then Conservative backbencher Iain Duncan Smith produced a study that would go on to lay the foundations for the rollout of universal credit. Now, nearly two decades later, Duncan Smith and his thinktank, the Centre for Social Justice (CSJ), has published State of Dependency: a landmark report promising to expose “the full scale of Britain’s worklessness crisis”. The study paints a picture of mass benefits reliance: it identifies 3,400 local areas where more than half the working-age population are on out-of-work benefits, or “economic opiates”, as the authors call them. They’ve even provided an interactive map (in the yellow and black colours of a road hazard sign, no less) so members of the public can type in their postcode to see if their neighbourhood is “a welfare hotspot”. events.title: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow
events.summary: The number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz has hit a record high, BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows. Twelve vessels were attacked between 5 and 11 October - the largest number of weekly strikes reported to the UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency since the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The previous week saw 10 ships reporting attacks. Six of the vessels were struck last Sunday, according to the UKMTO - a one-day high. So far this week, there have been four reported attacks. As the number of strikes has risen, the recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen last month has slowed, industry data suggests. BBC Verify collated incident reports published by the UKMTO on its website and created a timeline based on the first date cited in each report. This is approximate because some incidents use the date of the attack and some the date on which it was reported. Experts say Tehran has been attacking ships in an effort to assert greater control over the waterway as the US military has increased the number of tankers it is shepherding through the south of the strait to evade Iranian strikes. Iran is also carrying out more attacks on vessels further away from the Strait of Hormuz, according to experts. The US military's Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, posted on social media that despite the attacks "commercial traffic continues to flow through the Strait of Hormuz with co-ordinated protection from US forces and regional partners". Two crew missing after one of Sunday's attacks The aftermath of one of Sunday's six reported attacks was captured in verified footage showing the Nicaragua-flagged tanker Petro Dolphin on fire, as filmed by the crew on a smaller boat nearby. The vessel was struck by a drone close to the Sohar Anchorage, Oman, more than 250km (150 miles) from the strait, according to the maritime intelligence firm Vanguard. Eleven Indian seafarers were rescued but two are still missing, the Forward Seamen's Union of India said. Attacks have continued this week with the container ship GFS Pride sinking after a strike by an unknown projectile in the strait on Tuesday. Twenty-one crew were safely evacuated. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) published footage of what appeared to be the same ship sinking. It said the vessel was carrying "2,500 containers of contraband" and had taken an "unauthorised route". Middle East oil exports have slowed as the number of ship strikes has risen. About 12.6 million barrels per day went through the strait on 13 October, below the 15 million reported at the end of September, data from trade intelligence firm Kpler shows. This compares with a pre-war baseline of some 17 million barrels per day. The recent increase in attacks comes as US Navy data indicates the number of vessels given assistance to navigate the Strait of Hormuz during the first 10 days of October was up 85% compared with the same period in August. Most of the oil being shipped from Gulf Arab states recently has been carried using a "shuttle" system where a fleet of tankers load up and sail through the strait before transferring their cargo to larger tankers in the Gulf of Oman. These shuttle ships use a route close to Oman's coastline. Iran says this is "unauthorised" and insist vessels take an alternative route closer to its own shore. So-called assisted transits were a key factor in helping drive oil flows from the Middle East back towards pre-war levels in September. This does not include Iranian exports which have completely stalled as a result of the US blockade of Iranian ports and ships. Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, said Iran has "evolved its strategy" in response to this loosening of its control over the strait and has been carrying out "near daily or multiple attacks every single day". "The aim here is to stop the ships going through and to deter others," he added. The IRGC's navy has said strikes would not be "limited to the Strait of Hormuz" and later announced a "new deployment formation" across the region, according to state media. Martin Kelly told BBC Verify that Iran is widening its attacks and targeting ships near the coast of Gulf Arab states and in the Gulf of Oman. A tanker was struck by multiple projectiles north of Qatar on Thursday 8 October, more than 500km (310 miles) from the strait, resulting in multiple reported casualties, according to Vanguard. Another tanker was attacked close to the UAE town of Al-Jazirah al-Hamra on Friday 9 October, Vanguard said. Verified footage shows crew members running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rises over the ship. events.title: ASEAN companies keen on AI for business benefits, despite its energy costs
events.summary: Firms should assess not just the token prices before building an AI application, but also its carbon footprint, says an expert. SINGAPORE – Almost four in five South-east Asian businesses expect the benefits from artificial intelligence to outweigh its energy burden – even as they brace themselves for rising costs and infrastructure pressure. Out of 514 regional business leaders polled by The Business Times and market research firm Kantar, 78% see AI’s benefits outweighing its energy requirements. Released on Oct 12, The Business Times Insights: Powering ASEAN’s Future 2026 – the second regional survey by BT and Kantar – showed Singapore, Vietnam and Thailand as having the highest levels of optimism. This comes as AI adoption is accelerating across South-east Asia – 62% of respondents have increased their investments in AI or data-driven technologies over the past 12 months. Growth is particularly pronounced in Indonesia, where 85% of businesses reported moderate-to-significant increases in AI investment over the last year. The regional optimism around AI is “no surprise” to Sunil Veetil, whose Singapore advisory Perdura helps companies with green finance and the energy transition. He noted that AI returns materialise quickly when applied to the right use cases. For instance, it can enable multilingual customer service, providing distinct advantages in a region as diverse as ASEAN. In addition, said Manik Bhandari, ASEAN data and AI leader at EY, energy costs are currently “a very small fraction” of the overall AI token pricing, and thus “quite minimal” when building AI applications in an enterprise setting. Bracing for costs, infrastructure pressure That said, there is awareness of energy pressures – 41% of ASEAN businesses expect a moderate increase in energy demand as AI adoption scales, while another 40% are bracing themselves for a significant increase. Businesses expect energy demand to manifest in operational challenges: Rising electricity or operating costs, as cited by 46% of respondents; Pressure to upgrade existing infrastructure (39%); and Increased competition for energy resources (37%). While businesses may not currently be bearing the energy costs of AI, Veetil noted that this “changes when AI becomes captive or domestic, when companies run their own models or countries build sovereign (models) on local power”. “Then, the energy bill lands on the business.” Some markets are less optimistic about AI. In the Philippines, just 64% of respondents see AI’s benefits outweighing energy requirements, below the regional average. One explanation could be that “the trade-off looks different in markets where electricity costs, grid reliability and energy security are already significant business concerns”, said Zayana Zaikariah from the Institute of Strategic and International Studies in Malaysia. Climate exposure may be another reason. “In countries facing frequent typhoons, flooding and other disruptions, businesses may place a higher premium on the resilience of electricity and digital infrastructure before adding new sources of demand,” she said. It is thus critical for businesses to use AI judiciously. Lawrence Loh from the National University of Singapore said FOMO – the “fear of missing out” – is leading many businesses to step up AI adoption, and that their staff and management “may be experiencing severe AI fatigue now”. “The wrong metric for business is how much AI is being used,” said Loh, who is director of the university’s Centre for Governance and Sustainability. “The right one should be how much measurable economic and other benefits are being derived.” EY’s Bhandari said that before building an AI application, companies should assess not only the token prices, but also the application’s carbon footprint. Businesses can use smaller, task-specific models that reduce memory usage and can be run on standard hardware or edge devices, with a vastly reduced carbon footprint. “Not only is it cheaper for me as an enterprise, it’s also better for the environment,” he said. Zayana echoed that businesses should “match the level of compute to the value of the task”. A compute-intensive AI system “should not be the default if a smaller, task-specific model can achieve the same business outcome”, she said. AI-driven hunger for energy has implications not just for businesses, but also for countries’ energy resilience and decarbonisation goals. If not managed well, greater energy demand from AI could translate to more dependence on fossil fuels, said Dinita Setyawati, external affairs and strategic impact lead for Asia at energy think-tank Ember. Conversely, AI facilities “can actually become part of the solution if they help mobilise investment in renewable energy, storage and the grid infrastructure needed to support that demand”, she noted.

events.title: Proposed Dalby data centre to harvest rainwater from roof
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Proposed Dalby data centre to 'air-cool' operations and harvest rainwater from roof The concept model of a large-scale data centre project that has been proposed for the Western Downs. ( Supplied: Urbis ) The proposed Western Downs Digital Park says it will air-cool operations and not draw from bores or town water. Its developer says artificial intelligence customers would be responsible for paying for the power supply. The development application remains in its early stages and public consultation is ongoing. The international developer that has proposed Australia's largest data centre says it would be able to operate during even the worst droughts. The proposed $32 billion Western Downs Digital Park in regional Queensland would consist of four data centres, the first of which has been leased by Anthropic for use as early as 2027. Zerra DC is holding community consultation session in Dalby on the Western Downs. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) Planning documents by Singapore-based developer Zerra DC said each of the four buildings planned for the Western Downs Digital Park would require 21,000 litres of water a day, equivalent to the water usage of a small shopping centre. The company's chief data centre officer Matt Ward said modelling showed that even in 2019, when Dalby received less than 200 millimetres of rain, it would catch enough rainwater to operate. Matt Ward says the developer is committed to being a "good neighbour". ( Supplied: Zerra DC ) Mr Ward said the buildings housing the data centres were "large sheds" with "35,000-odd square metres of roof space" and the facility would be entirely air-cooled and would not draw from bores or town water. Mr Ward said supplying new power to the grid would be the responsibility of its artificial intelligence customers such as Anthropic, which the company has signed an agreement with. He said Zerra DC would act like the "landlord of any commercial building", where the tenant, Anthropic, would be responsible for paying for power supply. The data centre is proposed on the site of a feedlot outside of Dalby. ( ABC News: Nathan Morris ) It comes as the federal government works to establish a framework that would require data centres to bring as much power into the electricity grid as they take. Australia's largest proposed data centre could draw a quarter of Queensland's energy use The proposed $30 billion data centre in Queensland has a peak capacity comparable to the average power requirements of 1.5 million households. But who pays for that power production was a dilemma, according to Climate Energy Finance director Tim Buckley. He said both sides needed to be "collectively held to account" to commit to new renewable energy generation. "If they aren't held to account in substance over the life of the project, we will inevitably see higher power prices for everyone across Queensland as a result," Mr Buckley said. Some in the Western Downs have questioned how the region would benefit from the multi-billion-dollar investment. Zerra DC began community consultation sessions during the day last week, but recently announced the "drop-in" sessions would run in the afternoons from midday to 8pm. Robyn Sheehan attended an information session in Dalby about the proposed data centre. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) Dalby resident Robyn Sheehan said she took part in a session because she felt tired of big industries making "empty promises" in the area. Zerra DC has committed to 1,500 jobs per year during construction and 1,400 ongoing operational jobs at full capacity, which would transform the local economy. "To keep this thing running, we'll need a team of skilled people across mechanical, electrical, security, engineering at a 24-7 basis," Mr Ward said.

( AAP Image: Dan Himbrechts ) RBA governor Michele Bullock received total remuneration of $1.22 million in 2025-26. RBA workers are demanding an 11 per cent pay increase over three years, but the RBA is offering 9.5 per cent. The latest data show Australia's unemployment rate is 4.7 per cent, but economists say the RBA may not have finished lifting rates. The Reserve Bank's senior officials are among the highest paid people in Australia. RBA governor Michele Bullock received total remuneration of $1.22 million in 2025-26, with a base salary of $1.01 million. Deputy governor Andrew Hauser received total remuneration of $955,033, with a base salary of $903,217. Half of young adults living with parents Half of all young Australians are still living with their parents, up from 39 per cent in 2001, a survey reveals. The RBA's four assistant governors received total remuneration between $743,000 and $868,000 each, and its chief operating officer received total remuneration of $905,543. The figures can be found in the RBA's 2026 annual report , which was released on Thursday afternoon. The median annual earnings for all employees in Australia is $74,672 . In March this year, Ms Bullock received unwanted media attention when she and her husband bought a $2 million home in Yamba, in northern NSW, on the same day that the RBA lifted interest rates on February 3. It was her third investment property. Her property purchase was recorded in her declaration of material personal interests on the RBA's website. Michele Bullock says she sympathises with the plight of Australian workers. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) The RBA governor's pay is slightly above most federal departmental or agency heads, which are mostly clustered around $900,000-$1,000,000. However, the chief executives of some publicly owned corporations are paid far more. Ellie Sweeney, the NBN Co chief executive, received $3.4 million in total remuneration in 2025-26, up from $1.9 million a year earlier, making her Australia's highest-paid public servant . Paul Graham, the chief executive of Australia Post, received $3.3 million in 2024-25. Dennis Barns, the chief executive of Snowy Hydro Limited, received $2.1 million in 2024-25. RBA workers don't want a real wage cut The RBA is currently arguing with junior RBA staff about pay and conditions. Lower-ranked RBA staff have been asking for a pay increase of 11 per cent over three years and an inflation-protection mechanism that triggers additional pay rises if inflation outpaces wages, to avoid real wage cuts in coming years. Workers' pay not keeping pace with productivity growth Workers' pay not keeping pace with productivity growth, research suggests But last month, hours after the RBA lifted rates for the fourth time this year, Ms Bullock emailed RBA staff and asked them to vote for a pay offer of 9.5 per cent over three years. A majority of RBA staff had rejected a similar proposal in July. The Finance Sector Union says enterprise agreement negotiations have been dragging on since late last year and the RBA has refused to move on its original pay offer. The latest round of voting for the RBA's proposed enterprise agreement will close on Monday at 5pm . After lifting interest rates last month, Ms Bullock said she sympathised with the plight of Australian workers. But she said the only way workers could keep receiving sustainable increases in real wages was from productivity growth, and Australia's economy was struggling to deliver it. "People are feeling, quite rightly, very annoyed and very upset about the fact that the costs of everything are rising, that their wages are not keeping pace with that, they’re seeing real wage cuts," she said . "If we don't get productivity growth, there's not going to be real wage rises coming down the pipeline." According to the RBA's annual report, the bank has 2,201 employees, equating to 2,082 full-time equivalent employees. It has 76 senior executives, and another 222 highly paid staff. The RBA's workforce has increased by 8 per cent over the past 12 months. The RBA says that reflects the additional resources it needs to implement its transformation and change agendas. The additional staff are concentrated in technology and corporate support functions. RBA staff numbers increased by 8 per cent in the past year. ( Source: RBA annual report 2026 ) Higher unemployment will help to control inflation Australia's unemployment rate is 4.7 per cent, in seasonally adjusted terms.

events.title: Malaysia’s growth tops forecasts as AI boom drives export surge
events.summary: The government expects Malaysia’s economy to grow at 4.2% to 5.2% in 2027, supported by sustained domestic demand investment activity. Malaysia’s GDP rose 5.3% in the third quarter, beating the 5.1% forecast, but growth slowed from 6% as mining fell and most sectors still stayed positive. AI demand lifted exports, especially electronics, while strong domestic spending and household support kept the trade-dependent economy resilient. The government expects about 5% growth in 2026 and 4.2% to 5.2% in 2027, with full third-quarter GDP details due on Nov 18. KUALA LUMPUR – Malaysia’s economic growth slowed but still exceeded expectations as the artificial intelligence boom continued to bolster exports and domestic demand remained resilient. Gross domestic product (GDP) rose 5.3% in the three months through September from a year earlier, according to advance estimates from the Department of Statistics Malaysia on Oct 16, beating the 5.1% median prediction in a Bloomberg survey. Third-quarter growth, however, slowed from the 6% expansion in the previous three-month period. Third-quarter growth was underpinned by positive performance across most economic sectors, the department said in a statement. Only the mining and quarrying sector contracted, it added. The better-than-expected reading underscores the resilience of Malaysia’s economy, even as growth moderates from a strong first half. Robust domestic consumption and demand for electronics used in AI have helped cushion the trade-dependent economy from disruptions caused by the US war against Iran . “The out-turn is broadly in line with our forecast and suggests the growth momentum remains robust, albeit moderating from strong growth in the first half of 2026,” said Lavanya Venkateswaran, economist at OCBC Bank. “This very much leaves the door open for Bank Negara Malaysia to normalise its policy rate by 25 basis points. Our baseline for the adjustment is in January but it is a close call for the November meeting.” The ringgit was steady at 4.08 to the US dollar after the GDP print, while local stocks held losses. The services sector rose 5.4%, bolstered by wholesale and retail trade, information and communication as well as finance, the statistics department said. Manufacturing strengthened by 7.5%, backed in part by export-oriented industries, particularly electrical and electronic products. Bank Negara Malaysia governor Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour said in an interview this week that the economy is likely to grow about 5% in 2026, with the nation’s diverse sources of growth helping to cushion it against any slowdown in the AI boom. Malaysia’s economy grew 5.5% during the first three quarters of 2026, the department said, above the government’s revised growth forecast of 4.8% to 5.3% for the year. The government in October raised the forecast from 4% to 5%. Household spending remains firm as fuel subsidies helped shield consumers from elevated energy costs. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim earlier in October also announced more cash aid and a higher minimum wage for 2027 to ease cost-of-living pressures. The Malaysian government expects the economy to grow at 4.2% to 5.2% in 2027, supported by sustained domestic demand investment activity. Preliminary GDP data, which will provide a detailed analysis of the third quarter, will be released on Nov 18. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Palm oil stocks slide after Singapore begins looking into which firms responsible for haze
events.summary: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said that where warranted, Singapore will take action under its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act. Singapore is investigating which firms may be behind haze-causing fires, and may act under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, PM Lawrence Wong said. Palm oil shares fell after a report named First Resources and Bumitama Agri in areas with haze source points; First Resources blamed outside fires and a severe El Nino drought. Singapore’s air quality worsened sharply, with the central PSI at 227 and “very unhealthy”; Indonesia blamed peatland damage and said it will restore its peat ecosystem. SINGAPORE – Shares of palm oil producers fell on Oct 16, a day after Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said that Singapore is looking into which companies may be responsible for haze-causing fires. Where warranted, Singapore will take action under its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, and also explore joint action with other countries, said PM Wong in a Facebook post on Oct 15 . Bumitama Agri retreated 7.5% to an intraday low of $1.73, then rebounded somewhat to close 4.8% lower at $1.78. Golden Agri-Resources shares dropped one cent to 28 cents. A report by The Straits Times on Oct 15 cited a recent Greenpeace investigation which named First Resources and Bumitama Agri among entities with concession areas registering haze source points. First Resources on Oct 15 defended itself, stating that fires detected within its Indonesian palm oil concessions were largely caused by external blazes spreading across its boundaries. The company attributed the elevated fire risk in West Kalimantan to a “severe” El Nino-induced drought. Indonesia on Oct 15 blamed peatland degradation by past food estates for its worst wildfire season in 11 years, and said it will work to restore its peat ecosystem. Air quality deteriorated across all areas of Singapore overnight. The 24-hour PSI reading for the central region hit the “very unhealthy” level at midnight on Oct 16 and stood at 227 at 9am – a new high for 2026. Readings for the rest of the country were at the “unhealthy” level. On whether Singapore will take action against errant companies under the Act, Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu said on Oct 14 that the country was “keeping its options open”. That followed a National Environment Agency spokesperson stating that the agency “has been closely monitoring the haze situation, gathering information on fire hot spots, their sources and impact on Singapore’s air quality”. events.title: Nationals say Liberals oppose EU trade deal, Liberals beg to differ
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Liberals insist EU free trade position not settled, despite Canavan's assertion Some Liberals are frustrated by Matt Canavan's suggestion that both Liberals and Nationals oppose the free trade deal with the EU. ( ABC News: Callum Flinn ) Liberals insist they have not agreed to oppose the proposed Australia-EU trade deal, despite Nationals leader Matt Canavan claiming both parties are against it. Some Liberals believe Trade Minister Don Farrell could renegotiate aspects of the deal, an idea strongly rebuffed by those on both sides of the negotiations. A joint parliamentary committee is expected to scrutinise the deal early next year. Nationals leader Matt Canavan's claim that both Nationals and Liberals are against a slated European Union trade deal has angered some Liberals who privately insist the issue has not been settled. In an opinion piece published in The Australian today, Senator Canavan said the deal landed by Trade Minister Don Farrell would "weaken Australia's sovereignty on climate change policy" and was bad for the steel industry and some farmers. He said the deal, which parliament must approve, was opposed by both Coalition parties. That assertion was backed by his colleague, Bridget McKenzie. "Don Farrell can try all he likes to find a Coalition senator willing to vote for it. He won't because we are absolutely united," she told ABC Radio National today. But two Liberal senators subsequently told the ABC the proposed deal was better than the status quo and should be adopted. One cited the diplomatic importance of the deal at a time when the US was waging trade wars. "As long as it's not a really bad free trade agreement, and I don't think it is, we should support it," the senator said. "It goes to what the Liberal Party stands for. "There is a lot of internal disquiet about this." 'Opposed … subject to proper process' Multiple senior Liberals told the ABC the matter had not been considered by shadow cabinet or discussed in the Coalition party room, and that could only happen after scrutiny by the parliament's joint standing committee on trade. Farmers rubbish 'worst ever' EU free trade agreement The National Farmers' Federation says the deal will leave farmers without meaningful access to the EU market. "You can't short-circuit that by [writing] an op-ed," one said, framing Senator Canavan's intervention as a clear attempt to strongarm Liberals, reigniting tensions between the parties that plagued the leadership of Angus Taylor's predecessor, Sussan Ley. The joint standing committee process is still some time away. While the deal's text was agreed between leaders this year, it will not be signed until Australia and each EU member country complete the requisite legal checks, most likely early next year. Some Liberals believe this leaves time to renegotiate aspects of the deal. Two Liberals seeking to downplay any disagreement said the agreed position was "opposed to the deal as it stands, subject to the proper parliamentary and Coalition process". Senator Canavan used more cautious language in a press conference today, saying the opposition was "opposed to the deal in its current form". Farrell says veto would be 'vandalism' The government has rubbished the idea that renegotiation would be possible. "There is no room … the deal is done," Senator Farrell said today. The minister has projected confidence that the Senate, where the government does not have the numbers in its own right, will not stand in the way of the deal, telling the ABC on Wednesday he believed "enough senators … understand how important this is". One interpretation of that comment is that Senator Farrell believes enough Liberals might cross the floor to vote for the deal, although none of those who spoke to the ABC suggested they would. Don Farrell (right) led negotiations with the European Union and says the deal is no longer up for negotiation. ( Supplied: Supplied: Minister for Trade and Tourism ) Another is that Senator Farrell is confident that the Coalition – or at least the Liberals – will eventually land in favour of the deal, a view shared among some European diplomats, who have directly lobbied Mr Taylor and other Liberals in recent weeks. One diplomat from an EU nation told the ABC it would be "very damaging" if Australia did not ratify the deal and echoed Senator Farrell's comments: "There is no appetite [in Europe] to revisit this … the deal is done." The deal broadens access to the European market for Australian beef and sheep meat exporters, although not by as much as those industries had hoped.

events.title: Indonesia gets a ‘wake-up call’ as MSCI prepares to remove it from global indexes
events.summary: MSCI said on Oct 16 it would put Indonesia on a path to “standalone” status. MSCI said Indonesia is no longer fit for ‘emerging market’ status and plans to move it to ‘standalone’ status, which could force major fund outflows and cut it from global indexes. The announcement shocked investors, sent Jakarta shares down 11.57% in their worst fall since 1998, and pushed the rupiah to its weakest since late July. Indonesia rejected the move, said it has improved transparency, and the regulator fined market participants over alleged manipulation in three listed firms; MSCI will consult until April 2027. JAKARTA – Indonesia’s stock market is no longer worthy of “emerging market” status, MSCI said on Oct 16 , laying out a plan to expel it from a suite of indexes tracked by funds, a shock move that sparked the steepest one-day drop in Jakarta shares since 1998. Coming a month ahead of a scheduled review, MSCI’s change of tack stunned investors and irked Jakarta officials, with the Indonesian regulator unveiling sanctions against those linked to alleged trading manipulation in shares of three firms. The benchmark stock index, already the world’s worst performers in 2026, closed down 11.57%, in its biggest single-day drop since January 1998 . The rupiah currency slid as much as 0.8% to 18,070 per US dollar, its weakest since late July, but recovered some ground . Equities in South-east Asia’s biggest economy have struggled since January, when MSCI froze Indonesia in its indexes and threatened a downgrade to “frontier” status because of opacity in ownership and trading behaviour. The market has lost more than US$350 billion (S$447.77 billion) in capitalisation since, with about US$60 billion wiped out on Oct 16 alone. MSCI cited insufficient reforms to tackle the problems and said even a downgrade to “frontier” status would not reflect the severity of the issues, but proposed instead to move further beyond that, to “standalone” status. “Significant concerns remain around market dysfunction,” MSCI said in a statement on Oct 16. “Accordingly, MSCI considers Indonesia’s continued classification as an emerging market no longer appropriate.” The lower “standalone” status it proposed would exclude Indonesian stocks from global indexes tracked by billions of dollars in passive investment, forcing funds that follow, or are ranked against, the indexes, to sell. UBS estimated a removal by MSCI could trigger about US$4 billion of passive outflows from Indonesia, with active investors potentially adding a further US$15 billion in outflow. Foreign investors have already net sold US$4.7 billion worth of Indonesian stocks in 2026. Indonesia’s senior economic minister Airlangga Hartarto said there was “a big question mark” over why MSCI did not discuss downgrading the country to “standalone” status during a meeting this week in Bangkok. He made the comment ahead of a meeting of the country’s top officials, including the finance minister, the governor of the central bank and other related officials to discuss MSCI’s announcement. The Indonesia Stock Exchange said it has taken concrete steps to enhance transparency and integrity in the country’s capital market, and chief executive Jeffrey Hendrik said in a statement he would request further clarification on the basis for the announcement. Angus Mackintosh, an ASEAN specialist at Aletheia Capital in Singapore, said the move does not reflect the health of the vast majority of listed companies or indeed the Indonesian economy, and “grouping Indonesia with Lebanon, Palestine and Argentina does not make sense”. “This is a wake-up call for Indonesia,” he said. Indonesia would be the largest economy in the group if it was downgraded to “standalone” status. MSCI scrutiny raises more questions MSCI’s announcement piles pressure on the government under President Prabowo Subianto. It is the latest of a series of setbacks in 2026, with Moody’s and Fitch cutting their sovereign rating outlooks to negative, citing reduced policymaking credibility. “The proposal highlights MSCI’s dissatisfaction with the pace of reforms and raises further questions about the investability of the market,” said Tan Altundag, investment manager for emerging equities at Pictet Asset Management. “ The investment implications could be significant,” said Altundag, who has no holdings in Indonesia. The office of Finance Minister Suahasil Nazara, who chairs the country’s financial stability board, did not reply to a request for comment. In a sign of investor anxiety over the index provider’s move, there was a rush for the exits when the market opened, triggering a 30-minute trading halt on the Jakarta exchange. “It’s the first time this has ever happened in my 20 years in the stock market,” said Liza Camelia Suryanata, head of research at stockbroker Kiwoom Sekuritas Indonesia.

events.title: 3M lays out 'attack' on Commonwealth's $2 billion PFAS lawsuit
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts 3M sheds light on defence to Commonwealth lawsuit over PFAS contamination 3M is being sued by the Australian government for PFAS contamination. ( ABC News: Simon Amery ) The Australian government is suing 3M, the manufacturer of a firefighting foam it claims contaminated 28 Defence Force bases across the nation. The US chemical giant has detailed its planned defence to the $2 billion lawsuit. 3M must file its defence by December 11. US chemical giant 3M has shed light on its planned "attack" on the federal government's $2 billion lawsuit, which alleges the company withheld evidence that its firefighting products were toxic to humans and the environment. The Commonwealth is seeking damages arising from per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) contamination at 28 Defence Force bases across Australia and the areas surrounding them. The largest-ever court claim brought by the Australian government alleges the company continued to make and sell aqueous film-forming foam (AFFF) until 2003, despite knowing the dangers of its chemical make-up since 1979. The 1,600-page statement of claim says the use of 3M's AFFF "resulted in significant contamination" of land and water, including drinking water, that posed risks to human and animal health and the environment. Citing 310 internal company documents, the federal government's lawyers allege 3M falsely made assurances the product was safe despite having studies that proved variants of PFAS were toxic to animals, could cause birth defects and harmed the environment. During a case management hearing in the Federal Court today, King's Counsel for 3M Phillip Solomon outlined what the defence's case would entail when it was filed to the court on December 11. Mr Solomon KC said a "large team is working hard" and that it would "attack" the case. He told the court that there were three courses of action it would plead to; public nuisance, a Victorian Environment Protection Authority claim, and a misleading and deceptive conduct claim. Mr Solomon said the latter would need to be "delineated" between the overseas manufacturer and the local distributor of 3M products. In its statement of claim, the Commonwealth alleges the company caused a public nuisance by interfering with the use and enjoyment of the environment and by hindering access to contaminant-free water. Justice Catherine Button was told by the defence that the issue of public nuisance was not available in the matter. "We will plead and ultimately contend that it doesn't contend a nuisance claim," Mr Solomon said. "The allegation [is] that we had the means to abate the nuisance, that we caused the nuisance, that we were responsible for the special loss associated with the nuisance … and broadly had the ability to control the nuisance." Williamtown residents in NSW have been exposed to PFAS chemicals from firefighting foam used at the RAAF base. ( Four Corners ) The 28 bases have been split into three categories, including steady state, expanding, and in exceedence of Australian Drinking Water Guidelines and Australian Recreational Guidelines. The Commonwealth has proposed that 3M plead to six "representative bases" that have features across those categories, including Wagga (NSW), Tindal (NT), Townsville (Qld), Oakey (Qld), Edinburgh (SA) and East Sale (Vic). Mr Solomon told Justice Button the defence would be seeking to focus on one of the 28 bases in question, rather than six. In reply, counsel for the Commonwealth Fiona McLeod AO SC said the Crown was "seeking representative bases" that covered issues such as cross-contamination, topography and soil type. Questions over liability and toxicity 3M's AFFF firefighting foam was used by the Australian Defence Force for training and operational activities. ( Supplied: CRC CARE, file ) The Commonwealth is seeking $2 billion to cover "substantial costs" incurred from contaminated land and water. That includes $214 million for investigations, remediation and ongoing monitoring, and $367 million in settlements from five class actions brought against the government. Mr Solomon told the court the case raised questions about allegations of toxicity and whether there was subsequent liability, particularly in instances where remediation had been carried out. The court also heard discussion about the definition of the term "potentially toxic". "[The phrase] "potentially toxic" isn't a legal concept," Mr Solomon told the court. "If [the Crown] mean to tell us that their reliance isn't really on a collection of words but a particular concentration [or] type, they can tell us.

events.title: Prime Minister Mark Carney says US is trying to break Canada as Alberta votes on separation path
events.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has campaigned for national unity as advance voting is underway in oil-rich Alberta in a referendum that could set the province on a path toward a future vote on separation from Canada CALGARY, Alberta -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney warned Thursday that the United States is trying to break Canada so it can “own us” as he urged oil-rich Alberta not to begin a process toward separation in Monday’s referendum. The vote is not a direct referendum on independence. Alberta, which has the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves, will decide whether to remain a province or instruct the government to begin the legal process toward a future referendum on separation. “This referendum comes at the worst possible time,” Carney told a large pro-Canada rally in Calgary. “The world has become more dangerous and divided. Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us.” He did not directly mention the U.S. or its President Donald Trump in that passage, but has done so in similar past speeches. Carney’s warning came as U.S. President Donald Trump wages a trade war with Canada and after his repeated threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state. Carney has argued that Canada needs to become more economically resilient and less dependent on the United States. Carney urged Albertans not to use the vote simply to send Ottawa a message, saying a decisive result could settle the separation question. “Don’t be fooled by the idea you can ‘send a message’ with your vote,” Carney said. “This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep division and great uncertainty.” Carney, who grew up in Alberta, spent Thursday campaigning in Calgary before addressing the Forever Canadian rally at the BMO Centre. His office estimated about 5,000 people attended, with some waiting more than two hours to get through security. Organizers were also holding a second rally with Carney in Edmonton on Friday. Earlier Thursday, he pointed to the many Albertans who were born or educated elsewhere in Canada and to firefighters who come from across the country to help Alberta during wildfires as examples of the ties binding the province to the rest of Canada. At the rally, Carney also acknowledged the grievances that have fueled alienation in Alberta. “The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real,” he said. Carney said that while growing up, Ottawa made Albertans feel “like our resources weren’t our own” and that more recently the province was made to feel its energy contributions were “against the tides of history.” The setting is striking for a Liberal prime minister. Alberta has spent decades feuding with Liberal governments in Ottawa, particularly over energy and federal power. But Carney has broken with some of the policies associated with his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, fast-tracked a proposed new oil pipeline to the Pacific and called Canada an energy superpower. Carney pointed to the Pacific Link pipeline as evidence of a changed relationship, saying it would create more than 140,000 jobs and generate revenue for social programs. His biggest cheer came when he said the pipeline would reduce Canada’s dependence on the United States. “Careful, they might think that’s election interference. A little touchy,” Carney joked, drawing laughter. He was referring to U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra’s warning to Canadian politicians not to interfere in the U.S. midterm elections. Tanya Clemens, co-chair of the pro-independence group Let Alberta Decide, acknowledged Carney presents a challenge. “He’s formidable for sure,” Clemens told The Associated Press. Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Fort Hood survivors speak out on Pentagon's decision to livestream Hasan's execution Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded Clemens argued, however, that Carney’s agreements with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith amount to “pinky promises” that do not resolve long-standing grievances with Ottawa. Keith Wilson, another leader of Let Alberta Decide, rejected Carney’s argument that global instability made this the wrong time for the vote. “The worst timing for this, why? I don’t understand what’s the logic,” Wilson said. “Then it’s the best time for him to get back to Ottawa.” Wilson said Carney should ask Parliament to repeal federal measures that separatists say have hurt Alberta, including authority he says could be used to tax oil exports in retaliation against the United States. He predicted Carney would eventually impose such a tax despite Carney saying he sees no value in using Canadian energy exports as leverage against the U.S. “It’s one cabinet meeting away,” Wilson said. “He’s gonna do it. He has to do it.” Smith, who called the vote but supports remaining in Canada, cast her ballot Wednesday and said she voted for Alberta to remain in Canada.

events.title: Fund managers quit to trade their own money in Taiwan stock boom
events.summary: Limits on trading on personal accounts are more onerous in Taiwan, and stringent checks at work for fund managers have overwhelmed the benefits of those jobs for some. Taiwan’s stock boom is luring fund managers and analysts away from traditional firms. They want to trade their own money and keep more of their gains. Strict personal-trading rules, low pay and heavy checks at asset managers are pushing talent to private investment shops and offshore hedge funds. This is making hiring harder. Regulators may review the rules, but they want to protect investors and stop conflicts of interest. The talent drain is reshaping Taiwan’s asset-management industry. TAIPEI – The world’s biggest equity rally is creating an unusual bout of FOMO (fear of missing out) among Taiwan’s professional stock pickers. Barred by local regulations from owning individual stocks in their personal accounts, fund managers and equity analysts are ditching prestigious finance jobs so they can bet their own money on shares they have spent years analysing. Fewer than half of the 20 largest local equity mutual funds have retained the same portfolio manager for more than three years, according to fund-data website MoneyDJ. The temptation is clear: Taiwan’s benchmark stock index soared 62% in 2026 to become the world’s best-performing major equity gauge, adding about US$1.8 trillion (S$2.31 trillion) in market capitalisation. Some stocks buoyed by the artificial intelligence trade such as memory and circuit makers Nanya Technology and Macronix International have more than doubled in 2026. While personal trading restrictions are common across global finance, they bite harder for Taiwan’s money managers. Limits on trading on personal accounts are also more onerous in Taiwan, and stringent checks at work for fund managers have overwhelmed the benefits of those jobs for some. As seasoned professionals leave traditional money managers, they are often ending up at less-regulated trading firms that allow more freedom for employees to trade their personal accounts. That is coinciding with the allure of faster career progression where junior staffers spend less time early on doing more mundane work and, crucially, a chance to earn large bonuses in a profit-sharing model. “The trend is impossible to ignore,” said Huang Wen-ching, chief strategy officer at Taishin Securities Investment Advisory. “Private investment firms are springing up everywhere, and the pools of capital they command are getting bigger and bigger.” Institutional money managers, for years the destination of choice for the island’s top finance talent, face an increasingly difficult hunt for personnel, according to people familiar with the recruitment process. That is forcing them to accept less skilled hires due to the dwindling pool of potential recruits, they said, asking not to be identified discussing private information. Mutual fund managers in Taiwan typically start out earning about half what their Hong Kong counterparts make, and the gap persists as pay rises with experience in subsequent years, according to industry veterans and headhunters who spoke with Bloomberg and data from recruitment firm Robert Walters. Taiwan’s portfolio managers receive the equivalent of around US$124,354 to US$310,884 annually, depending on performance and seniority, compared with base salaries in the range of US$229,372 to US$637,144 in Hong Kong. The concerns over missing out are becoming more acute due to the breadth of Taiwan’s stock-market surge. Around 10% of Taiex shares have more than doubled in 2026, compared with just 2% of South Korea’s main index and around 5% of Japan’s Nikkei 225 index. Even as global stocks sold off recently, the island’s equity benchmark outperformed all major peers, extending the resilience it has shown throughout 2026. For Ken Tsai, one winning bet still stings. In 2024, while at one of Taiwan’s biggest asset managers, the 40-year-old fund manager made a Taiwanese supplier of components that transfer data between AI servers his fund’s biggest holding. The stock surged more than fivefold the following year – then another sixfold in 2026. Bound by rules, Tsai did not own a single share in his personal accounts. Tired of seeing his calls enrich the fund – but not himself – he departed in July for a Taipei-based private investment firm that provides a more attractive revenue sharing model and grants bigger room for personal investments. Tsai declined to name the firm. “It left me with a strong sense of relative deprivation.” he said, “People who were free to buy the stock ended up making more money than I did.” Cases like Tsai’s are creating fresh challenges for asset managers trying to retain senior talent and recruit younger ones.
