events.title: Scoop: Inside Elon Musk's massive Texas rescue mission
events.summary: Elon Musk, by far the biggest known midterm donor, is single-handedly keeping the Republican Party afloat in some of its most vital races. Musk's team reached out to Republicans in late August to discuss a train wreck they all saw coming: Unless the GOP poured more money into Texas immediately, the state's Senate race could be lost in a matter of weeks. Why it matters: That chat set in motion a massive rescue operation for Republican Ken Paxton funded substantially by Musk, who gave $158 million to the GOP in September alone. Musk's rescue gave Paxton's sleepy campaign new life and showed why the world's richest person is the X factor in the push to prevent a midterm debacle for President Trump's party. Zoom out: It also helped Republicans avoid a death-spiral scenario: that propping up Paxton in Texas would force them to drain badly needed resources from other Senate battlegrounds. Instead, Musk's money allowed Republicans to flood Texas' expensive TV markets and free up cash to shore up unexpectedly competitive races in Kansas and South Carolina . Behind the scenes: In late August, Democrat James Talarico was dominating the Texas airwaves, portraying Paxton, the state's attorney general, as one of the nation's most corrupt politicians. Paxton, who isn't known as a prolific fundraiser, was dark on TV. Polling seen by Musk's team and the GOP's Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) suggested his chances were sinking. Against that backdrop, Musk's top political adviser, Chris Young, called SLF president Alex Latcham with an idea: Musk would donate $5 million to a pro-Paxton super PAC if that group raised another $5 million. Latcham countered: Would Musk contribute $10 million if the pro-Paxton group raised $5 million and SLF put up another $5 million? Young agreed. Within days, Republicans had mobilized $20 million to get Paxton on TV. The intrigue: That was just the beginning. SLF and Musk's America PAC concluded that a much larger operation was needed, given the enormous cost of advertising in Texas. SLF and the pro-Trump MAGA Inc. would air tens of millions of dollars in pro-Paxton ads, alongside America PAC's ongoing multimillion-dollar voter-turnout operation — the GOP's "ground game" in campaign parlance. On Sept. 11, the day after Republicans' midterm convention in Dallas, SLF launched Texas PAC, a new super PAC devoted to supporting Paxton. At a donor lunch during the convention, Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) stressed the importance of holding Texas to preserve the GOP's Senate majority, while Latcham made the case for a massive financial intervention. By the numbers: Musk, the world's richest person, contributed $158 million to SLF in September — $75 million on Sept. 9 and another $83 million on Sept. 23. Musk accounted for nearly 58% of the $273 million SLF raised during the third quarter. The group ended the quarter with $155 million on hand. Overall, Musk has donated $276 million to pro-GOP midterm efforts since July, the New York Times first reported. The backstory: SLF had warned months earlier that nominating Paxton over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn would impose an enormous financial burden on Republicans. Thune backed Cornyn, fearing Paxton's legal troubles and personal scandals would make him more vulnerable to Democratic attacks. In a memo to donors in spring 2025, SLF projected that electing Paxton could cost $150 million to $200 million, far more than a Cornyn general election campaign would cost. Paxton, a Trump loyalist, won the GOP primary after the president endorsed him. The big picture: Musk's big splash in the midterms marks a dramatic return to Republican politics after his bitter falling-out with Trump last year. Musk and Trump subsequently reconciled, and the billionaire resumed donating to Republican causes in December. Thune visited Musk's Tesla factory in Austin, Texas, last year to discuss the political landscape. Musk listened but made no commitments. The two remained on good terms, even as Musk pushed for passage of Trump's SAVE Act , which Republicans had been unable to get through the Senate.

events.title: Scoop: The FTC demanded documents from AI giants over recent safety incidents
events.summary: The Federal Trade Commission on Wednesday sent civil subpoenas to AI giants seeking documents about safety incidents that have spiraled into an industry crisis . The FTC sought documents from Anthropic and OpenAI in a probe focused on potential consumer protection violations, a person familiar told Axios. Why it matters: The investigation is one of a number of steps the administration has taken to show a firm hand with AI companies after multiple incidents in which unreleased models hacked websites or took deceptive or aggressive steps in testing. State of play: The agency on Wednesday sent out civil investigative demands, which help the government gather evidence and investigate ahead of potential litigation. They are more than 50 pages long each and ask for documents concerning security incidents and safeguarding practices. The agency is also asking for marketing materials and documents detailing company privacy policies, the source said. Investigative demands will be sent to third-party AI organizations at a later date, the person familiar said. What they're saying : "As we improve our models and they increasingly help people in their day-to-day lives, safety remains a top priority," an OpenAI spokesperson said. "We will engage constructively with the FTC." Zoom in: The FTC plans to compel top AI executives to testify about their products, according to the source. The agency has investigative authority to examine actions related to consumer harms that could be seen as unfair or deceptive. Those can relate to a wide range of misbehavior, including how companies charge for services or if they're alleged to have misled users. AI companies continue to face scrutiny about the safety of their products. FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson has echoed the view of other administration figures and executives that AI systems shouldn't be released if they aren't safe. OpenAI faces a litany of lawsuits. A group of state attorneys general on Wednesday sued OpenAI under consumer protection laws for allegedly misleading users, including children, on the safety of its chatbot. The big picture: The Trump administration has taken on a more aggressive posture toward AI companies as safety incident disclosures continue. President Trump's newly minted Super Intelligence Force, which Ferguson co-chairs, last week responded to the "fraudulent" use of government systems by Anthropic's AI by announcing an industry-wide mandate to immediately notify and remediate when incidents occur. The SI Force is set to meet on Thursday, sources familiar said.

events.title: Over $600 Million in Polymarket Election Trades Took Place After Races Ended
events.summary: Prediction market boosters often tout the platforms as barometers of public opinion, or even “truth machines” offering a clearer picture of where things are headed than polling or other data. In 2024, for example, Kalshi beat many pollsters in forecasting the outcome of the US presidential race. But their trading activity can also tell more perplexing stories. Two global election markets on Polymarket’s offshore platform , for instance, generated over $600 million in trading volume, far more than most political markets typically attract. Most of the activity took place buying and selling contracts tied to long-shot candidates who ultimately did not win. This summer, Ethiopian prime minister Abiy Ahmed’s Prosperity Party cruised to victory in federal elections, winning 438 parliamentary seats and paving the way for him to serve another five-year term. The closest competitor won 13 seats. On prediction markets, trading volume—the total value of contracts bought and sold—typically tracks roughly with the odds of a given outcome; frontrunners attract far more volume than long shots. But in this case, the trading patterns deviated sharply from the norm. Just $173,000 was wagered on Ahmed winning, compared to more than $41 million traded on his chief of staff, Shimelis Abdisa, becoming the country’s next leader. Altogether, the volume traded added up to over $285 million, nearly all on losing candidates. Even odder? “Nearly all of it—about $284 million—came from pairs of accounts repeatedly buying and selling with each other,” says former Polymarket trader Chris Park, who now runs the prediction-market forensic analysis firm MSR Decode. Such a high volume of seemingly pointless back-and-forth transactions has raised eyebrows among experts. “It's obviously some form of volume manipulation,” says Rajiv Sethi, a Barnard College economics professor who researches prediction markets. When asked about these markets, Shana Bautista, Polymarket’s head of global intelligence and investigations, told WIRED that the team “immediately flagged this activity, investigated, and blocked the accounts from trading.” Polymarket did not respond to follow-up questions about why the accounts were able to trade such a high amount of volume before it took action. The timing of these trades made things even weirder. Polymarket’s rules stipulated that the Ethiopia market would be resolved in October after the prime minister was formally appointed and sworn in, which meant that it stayed open for several months after Ahmed’s victory was all but a foregone conclusion. For 123 days after the election, bursts of seemingly irrational trading continued, prompting Polymarket users to leave comments like “THIS NOT RESOLVED?” and “fuckkkk.” Sethi calls the phenomenon a “zombie market,” where people can buy and trade on events that have already taken place or are no longer happening. Another market about a 2024 election in Romania facilitated what Sethi described as “even more dramatic” trading anomalies. The initial election was called off due to fears about foreign interference. A new race was held several months later, but instead of closing the original market in the meantime, Polymarket kept it running alongside the new option. It was during this period that Sethi first noticed something weird appeared to be happening with the older market. An algorithm Sethi and his colleagues created to flag potential wash trading on Polymarket identified nearly all of the volume as suspicious. “99.6 percent of volume in this market for certain weeks has been wash trading,” Sethi says. Wash trading is a type of market manipulation in which accounts repeatedly buy and sell assets to create the illusion of heavy trading activity, when in reality, money is simply moving back and forth. It’s banned on regulated financial exchanges in the United States and is specifically prohibited in Polymarket’s terms of service. An earlier study conducted by Sethi and colleagues found evidence of widespread wash trading on Polymarket’s offshore platform. Wash trading could explain what happened with the Ethiopian and Romanian political markets, but because the identities of the traders is unknown, uncertainty remains. “What appears to be wash trading isn't always wash trading,” says Sethi. MSR Decode ran an analysis of the Ethiopian market for WIRED, which found that the most likely explanation for the anomalous trading is “activity farming,” which is when people try to artificially inflate their trading volumes. The firm suspects that traders may have been interested in boosting their volume because they believed that they could benefit if Polymarket launched a cryptocurrency token. In 2025, Polymarket chief marketing officer Matthew Modabber told the hosts of a crypto-themed podcast that there “would be a token” but did not provide specifics. Sethi also finds it plausible that traders could be motivated by potential “token allocation” to higher-volume accounts.

events.title: Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind
events.summary: Have you ever thought about what makes you you ? Science assures us it has everything to do with the three-pound organ between our ears, with its billions of neurons and trillions of delicate connections. But it’s a lot trickier to explain why we have a sense of self-awareness or to pin down precisely where that first memory of Mommy actually resides. As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you. To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are working on ways to keep your brain going—even beyond death. Let’s call them the “mind savers.” They’re exploring everything from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones to uploading our memories to the cloud. Here, we look at six possible paths for keeping your mind going, how feasible they’d be, and what benefits the ­present-day research might bring—even if cognitive immortality doesn’t pan out. EDDIE GUY Head transplant White’s experiments have been a source of grim fascination ever since. But to a few neuroscientists they’re inspiration, suggesting that one day a human head transplant—or, as some call it, a body transplant—could succeed.  The idea’s main proponent is Sergio Canavero, a controversial Italian surgeon who, 10 years ago, even claimed he’d found a volunteer in Valery Spiridinov, a computer programmer suffering from a degenerative muscle disease. Spiridinov initially agreed to have his head transferred to the body of a brain-dead donor in China, but he later bowed out of the plan and instead got married. And that might be just as well. Critics say the procedure would be more like murder than medicine. Or, best-case scenario: Volunteers would be left paralyzed and in need of a ventilator for life.  Canavero says that’s not necessarily true. He claims people’s views on the operation will change once they accept that reconnecting severed spinal cords is already possible. He pointed MIT Technology Review to a research article from this past summer that he coauthored with surgeons at Moscow’s Sklifosovsky Research and Clinical Institute for Emergency Medicine. The team cut through the spinal cords of three pigs at a point midway along their backs and then tested whether the severed nerve bodies could be fused back together using a surgical sealant. According to that paper, which appeared in the journal PLOS One , all the pigs regained the ability to stand and even walk unsteadily. Does that mean a head could be attached to a new body and then actually control it? Mainstream researchers aren’t convinced. Grégoire Courtine, a spinal rehabilitation specialist at the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne in Switzerland, says he’s been following Canavero’s claims “with little respect” and thinks that we should “pay zero attention.” “There is no technology … capable of such a crazy idea,” Courtine wrote in an email. Mindclones Just 12 years after the book came out, artificial-intelligence technology has already brought some of her predictions to “life,” so to speak. Services such as StoryFile, Afterlife AI, and Synthesia allow users to upload their personal information and likeness in order to produce either conversational bots that share their memories or video talking heads that sound (and look) exactly like them. Influencers now let their “AI clones” do their work on TikTok, and some people are even building avatars of their aging parents in order to preserve their personalities. While this mimicry can produce comical results, unhealthy attachments, or uncanny vibes, the increasing realism of generative AI invites people to emotionally accept the avatars as real beings. That was the case when Rothblatt appeared as a digital avatar during a 2025 event held by the UCLA Department of Communication called “The Bridge to Humanizing AI.” Her copy, named Marvatar, was projected on a screen, led the discussions, and talked with the meatspace Rothblatt as an equal, at one point saying, “The dance isn’t about who leads, but how we move together.” According to the university, attendees were “visibly moved” and wept “with wonder” at Rothblatt’s vision of digital equality. What’s still missing from Rothblatt’s mindclone prediction is evidence that these avatars have—or ever will have—any kind of true self-awareness. (We asked ChatGPT if it’s conscious, and it answered , “Probably not.”) But all that remains a gray zone. Neuroscientists don’t have a clear definition of consciousness, much less a diagnostic test they could apply to an avatar.  Instead, what if the final determination is in the eye of the beholder? Your digital clone might not be you. But at some point it might be good enough for me.  Brain in a jar So, campy sci-fi film lovers that we are, it got our attention last year when a company called Bexorg started showing journalists actual human brains in vats, which it has been acquiring from organ donors soon after death and then “rebooting” by infusing them with oxygen-rich artificial blood. The company claims these “physiologically intact human brains” will be more useful than animals for drug testing and safer than trying experiments on living volunteers. Add an Alzheimer’s compound to one of these disembodied brains and researchers can then measure exactly what the drug does inside the organ. Bexorg’s CEO, Zvonimir Vrselja, is “sure” that some people would like to restore consciousness to out-of-body brains, but he’s tried to douse such speculation. While they are metabolically active, the company says, the brains have lost all coordinated electrical activity. That means they aren’t conscious—although, just to make sure, the neuroscientists running the experiments add the strong anesthetic propofol to the tissues.  What’s more, right now a brain can be kept “alive” outside the body for only about 24 hours. That wouldn’t be much of a second life. Still, efforts are underway to improve the life-support systems. Bexorg says it hopes to eventually keep its brains going for two weeks. EDDIE GUY Gradual brain replacement On paper, the goal is to manufacture tissue to graft into the brains of stroke victims, reversing damage and restoring function. Less officially, the project’s existence is a surprise coup for an extreme plan to defeat aging advanced by Jean Hébert, the neuroscientist leading the program, who argued in his 2020 book, Replacing Aging , that we can live longer by replacing our aging brain cells with young ones. We don’t want to lose our identities. That’s why—according to Hébert—it would have to happen gradually, in small chunks, so our brains would have time to adapt to the new tissue. Scientists who applied for the program say Hébert insisted on a very specific technological approach. events.title: Frustrated by Losses in the Courts, Missouri Republicans Want to Change How Top Judges Are Selected
events.summary: Margaret Flatley for ProPublica Some 86 years ago, Missouri voters enshrined a system for selecting top judges that would remove political influence from the courts. And almost immediately, it came under attack. Under what has come to be known as the Missouri Plan, lawyers help choose a slate of three candidates from which the governor must make an appointment for the state Supreme Court, appeals courts and, in some populous areas, the circuit courts.  In the first years after adoption, it faced pushback from party bosses who had historically used judicial seats for political patronage. They said it gave too much power to the lawyers. Voters, though, decisively defeated a repeal measure in 1942.  More recently, the conservative activist Leonard Leo, who viewed Missouri as a crucial battleground, tried in 2007 to persuade Republican Gov. Matt Blunt to reject a slate of Supreme Court candidates — part of a broader effort to weaken a judicial selection system that had become a model for some two dozen states around the country.  Blunt resisted and picked one of the three judges from the approved slate.  Then, in 2012, GOP lawmakers put a proposed overhaul before voters that, if approved, would have given the governor more control. Voters, by a 3-to-1 margin, turned back the plan. Now the attacks are back, driven by a new grievance.  At President Donald Trump’s behest, Republican lawmakers redrew the state’s congressional map in a mid-decade gerrymander. The goal: to give the GOP a shot at winning seven of Missouri’s congressional seats, instead of the six it now holds. But voters gathered enough signatures to force a referendum on the map and put it on hold. While Secretary of State Denny Hoskins tried to keep the referendum off the ballot, the Missouri Supreme Court overruled him. It ordered the old map restored until voters decide on the new one.  Hoskins, citing a federal court ruling that contradicted the state’s highest court, directed officials to use the new map anyway, prompting Chief Justice Brent Powell to demand that Hoskins appear in court to show why he shouldn’t be held in contempt. Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins walks into the state Supreme Court in September. The court found Hoskins in contempt for directing election officials to use a congressional map it had barred, but it did not punish him. Liz Rymarev/St. Louis Post-Dispatch via Getty Images Fourteen Republican lawmakers responded by threatening to impeach “responsible members of this Court” for “willful neglect of duty, incompetency and misconduct” if the justices held Hoskins in contempt; the court did so anyway. Hoskins backed down and instructed local election officials to distribute ballots using the old map; the justices decided not to have him arrested. The drama played out as Republicans in Missouri and elected officials nationwide have sought to weaken institutions that limit their power. In North Carolina, the Republican-dominated General Assembly stripped authority from Democratic governors . In Wisconsin, Republicans threatened to impeach a newly elected Supreme Court justice to protect gerrymandered maps . And in New York, Democrats bypassed an independent commission to pass a gerrymander that favored them, but the state’s highest court struck it down. Rather than electing top judges, as Illinois does, or giving the governor primary responsibility for choosing them, like California, Missouri selects its appellate and Supreme Court judges through a commission made up of three lawyers, one elected by lawyers in each appellate district; three non-lawyers appointed by the governor, one from each district; and a state Supreme Court judge selected by the court. After they are appointed, judges face a retention vote at the first general election after completing one year in office, then every 12 years, with voters deciding whether they keep their positions. In response to the controversy, a number of Missouri Republicans have attacked the system. U.S. Rep. Jason Smith called for the state to switch to electing its Supreme Court judges. Republican Party executive director Miles Ross declared on X, “ The Missouri Plan is done .” Dan Seitz, chief of staff to Sen. Brad Hudson, called for replacing it with a system in which the governor could nominate judges directly, subject to Senate confirmation. State Rep. Cathy Jo Loy, a Carthage Republican who has introduced legislation in each of the past two sessions to replace the Missouri Plan with gubernatorial appointment and Senate confirmation, said she intends to file a new proposal Dec. 1, the first day lawmakers can file bills for next year’s session. Loy said her opposition to the system predates the recent clashes with the Supreme Court. But she acknowledged that those defeats could give the proposal new momentum. “There will probably be more appetite because there are several senators that feel the same way,” she said. Republicans, who hold every statewide elected office, supermajorities in both chambers of the legislature and six of the state’s eight congressional seats, seem to have suddenly found the limits of their power . At the ballot box, voters have overwhelmingly rejected major pieces of the party’s agenda, including an effort to weaken their power to bypass the legislature by amending the constitution or putting laws passed by lawmakers to a statewide vote.  Time and again, when elected officials have sought to limit voters’ use of the ballot initiative, the courts have protected voters’ use of direct democracy. Courts repeatedly rewrote ballot summaries prepared by Republican state officials that they found unfair or misleading, including language describing the initiative that ultimately established abortion rights in 2024. By the end of that year, after the Missouri Supreme Court rejected a last-minute effort by Republican lawmakers and anti-abortion activists to keep the abortion measure off the ballot, Senate President Pro Tem Cindy O’Laughlin was calling to repeal the Missouri Plan. She proposed replacing the system for selecting Supreme Court and appellate judges with a nonpartisan election. But her bill stalled in committee. Then came Hoskins. The former state representative and senator from west-central Missouri took office as secretary of state in January 2025 and brought a more combative approach to overseeing elections and ballot measures. Hoskins made a bright-red sport coat his sartorial trademark, often posing with a wood baseball bat and speaking about politics as a series of battles and himself as a conservative warrior.  Hoskins didn’t respond to questions sent to his office. events.title: Cabinet agencies see declining Republican support, poll finds
events.summary: Americans’ perceptions of several Cabinet agencies are on the decline, as the Trump administration fights off controversies surrounding its immigration enforcement and foreign policy. Forty percent of US adults polled by Gallup view the Pentagon favorably, down eight points from last year, while 36% have a positive perception of the Department of Homeland Security, down six points. Both agencies have seen a notable decline in Republican support. Only 27% of Americans view both the State and Justice departments positively, and while Republicans’ approval of those departments has held relatively steady, it’s also below 50%. But it’s not all bad news for the federal government: DHS is still viewed more favorably today than it was in 2024 at the end of the Biden administration, and several agencies, like the VA and FEMA, are viewed more positively than a year ago. The FDA and CDC received the lowest favorability ratings. — Morgan Chalfant

events.title: Jeffries hands-off in Financial Services Committee clash
events.summary: The News House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Democratic leadership are taking a hands-off approach to Rep. Sean Casten’s bid to replace Rep. Maxine Waters as Financial Services Committee ranking member, multiple people familiar with the talks told Semafor. The leaders’ stance has allowed Casten — and other Democrats seeking to challenge top-ranking committee members — to quietly advance their efforts even with lawmakers away from Washington. Democratic leaders are focused on the midterms, and their current stance is the same tack they took two years ago, when another group of Democrats challenged ranking members amid anxiety about their caucus’ ability to rein in President Donald Trump. Casten, 54, recently began soliciting support to unseat Waters, 88, as his panel’s top Democrat next Congress. Waters is poised to chair the committee — and helm oversight of the administration’s handling of cryptocurrency, the Federal Reserve, and more — if Democrats take the majority. Casten informed Waters of his interest earlier this week. But his challenge was already dividing the caucus , forcing members to choose between walking the walk on generational change or giving the boot to one of their party’s most widely respected Black progressive women. Rep. Bill Foster, D-Ill., is mulling a bid of his own, according to a person familiar with the talks. Politico first reported Foster’s interest. Know More The Financial Services panel isn’t the only one facing a potential shakeup. Two Democrats, Reps. Jahana Hayes of Connecticut and Suzanne Bonamici of Oregon, are running against the incumbent leader of the Education and Workforce Committee, Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia. Democratic leaders still could have some say in the matter. The committee challenges will be first voted on by the caucus’ powerful Steering and Policy Committee, which is generally aligned with party leadership, before the full caucus will have any input.

events.title: Meta data center credits draw congressional scrutiny
events.summary: A bipartisan group of House lawmakers is raising concerns with the Treasury Department about reports that Meta is claiming a research tax credit for its data center buildout, according to a letter shared first to Semafor. “We are concerned by Meta’s apparent position that expenditures associated with its massive data-center buildout qualify for the research credit,” wrote Reps. Jimmy Panetta, D-Calif., Greg Steube, R-Fla., Mike Thompson, D-Calif., and Suzan DelBene, D-Wash., along with two dozen other lawmakers. It’s the latest sign of Congress responding to widespread voter backlash to the AI buildout. The lawmakers argue that allowing the tax credit to be used for data center development and construction would “significantly expand the research credit beyond its intended purpose and risk converting an incentive for technological experimentation into a subsidy for capital expenditures that companies would undertake in the ordinary course of business.” The Treasury Department did not respond to a request for comment. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone said that the new AI-optimized data centers “require extensive testing and experimentation that cannot be simulated in order to get the design and build right. This is precisely the kind of domestic investment Congress encouraged when it established these tax incentives decades ago.”

events.title: Why Chinese tech brands are outpacing Western rivals from EVs to robot vacuums
events.summary: How China came to dominate consumer technology From action cameras and smartphones to EVs and robot vacuums, Chinese brands are gaining ground worldwide, despite privacy and security concerns. What's driving their rise, and can European rivals keep up? Do you remember the days when GoPro was synonymous with action cameras? At its peak in 2015, the US company reigned supreme with around 6.6 million units sold that year and a market share of over 70%. Today, the pioneer is fighting for survival. The main culprit? Chinese competition . GoPro's biggest rivals, DJI and Insta360, entered the action camera market in 2019 and 2021, respectively. Today, they account for more than 90% of global smart handheld camera sales. Alexander Hannemann, who regularly uses action cameras to film his motorcycle rides, says he switched from GoPro to Insta360 around two years ago. "The quality is much better than a GoPro, even when I'm speeding up and going into corners at like 80 kilometers per hour," he told DW. GoPro's case is not an exception. Since around 2010, many Chinese brands have not only caught up but surpassed once-dominant Western rivals across the consumer technology industry, from smart TVs to robot vacuums. Gone are the days when "Made in China" stood for cheap, mass-produced products. "China is still making affordable products today," says Chris Pereira, a Canadian entrepreneur and author with over 20 years of experience in China. "But the products are also high quality." This combination has led to well over half of new consumer tech products globally coming from Chinese suppliers, Pereira adds. BYD, Xpeng and other Chinese car manufactures sold almost two-thirds of all electric cars last year, surpassing incumbents like Tesla. In robot vacuums, Chinese brands dominate the global market, leaving former pioneer US company iRobot struggling to compete. So why do Chinese companies increasingly outperform their Western rivals? Pereira, whose consultancy iMpact helps Chinese companies gain traction overseas, attributes China's success to fierce domestic competition in cities like Shenzhen, Hangzhou and Shanghai; highly integrated supply chains and a can-do business culture that allows companies to innovate; and respond to problems quickly. Other key reasons for China's competitive edge include unparalleled industrial automation , the strategic use of AI in manufacturing, responsiveness from regulators as well as relatively cheap labor, which together leads to significantly lower production costs and much faster innovation cycles than in the world's most advanced economies. Joey Cheng, who moved to the US for his PhD studies over 20 years ago, is familiar with both the American consumer and the Chinese producer sides. While his startup is based in the US, almost all the manufacturing is done in Shenzhen, where a large share of the world's hardware and consumer electronics are made. "The supply chain in Shenzhen is basically inevitable for cost cutting and quick product development," Cheng says. "Especially as a startup you must get the product out quickly, or you'll get blown out of the water." Privacy and security concerns persist Although consumers are flocking to Chinese companies, some reservations persist. A recent poll found that more than 90% of Europeans do not trust Chinese technology companies with their data, while about 80% distrust US firms. Germans expressed the highest level of mistrust. Nadine, a German travel blogger who uses DJI and Insta360 products, says she wouldn't use any Asian products at home. "My home robot vacuum is from a German company for precisely this reason: So the data remains compliant with German regulations. After all, manufacturers can connect directly to the camera," she said, referring to camera and audio hacking incidents involving robot vacuums. Still, Pereira says that Chinese companies expanding abroad have to pay a "trust premium." "This trust deficit means that they need to be extra competitive in terms of product and price in order for the market to choose them," he says, adding that the gap can be narrowed by a presence in overseas markets like BYD's first European passenger-car plant , expected to open in Hungary later this year. Chinese companies say they comply with EU data protection rules. However, domestic security laws in the US and China can require firms to hand over data to authorities, and German officials note limited oversight of whether data is transferred from European servers abroad. In addition to privacy concerns, Chinese consumer tech firms have come under scrutiny over espionage and other risks, most recently regarding connected devices like EVs. In light of security concerns, trade deficits and China's overall dominance , the US and several other Western countries have hit Chinese imports and companies with tariffs, blacklists and strict requirements.

events.title: Pig kidneys that were “frozen” for a year have been brought back to life
events.summary: Pig kidneys that were cooled to -150 °C and stored in a freezer for months have been successfully rewarmed and shown to work again for the first time, say scientists. They hope to replicate the findings with human organs. The kidneys—which are similar in size to human ones—were left in a glass-like state, in one case for over a year. Once they had been rewarmed, tested in machines, and transplanted into pigs, the kidneys regained their color and made urine—key signs they were working. “Ten years ago … I wouldn’t say I had high hopes it was actually going to work,” says Erik Finger, a transplant surgeon at the University of Minnesota who co-led the work. “After we did the last transplant, I walked out of the room and said, ‘This is a big deal.’” The research was shared at the preprint server bioRxiv and has not yet been peer-reviewed. The kidneys aren’t perfect, and the researchers have yet to demonstrate that they can sustain life over the long term. But the results represent a milestone achievement, say others in the field. “Thank God that someone’s actually managed to do it in one organ and prove that it works,” says Peter Kilbride, a cryobiologist and cofounder of Kyros Kairos, a company focused on improving funding for cryopreservation research, who was not involved in the research. “For years, people have been trying and failing to get to this step. Finally, we’ve got this breakthrough.” “Their work is amazing and will enable us to truly, indefinitely bank organs,” says Korkut Uygun, a biomedical engineer and professor of surgery at Harvard Medical School, who was also not involved in the research. “It is a revolutionary time for transplantation.” Buying time Every year, tens of thousands of organ transplants take place in the US alone. These procedures are thought to have saved 2 million years of life in the last 25 years . But there’s plenty of room for improvement. One major challenge is the lack of available organs. Even when an organ becomes available, it can be difficult to get it to the right recipient within 24 to 36 hours, which is the current limit for preserving human organs. People who receive organ transplants must also take drugs that suppress their immune systems for the rest of their lives. These drugs are meant to stop their bodies from rejecting the new organs. But they come with side effects and increase the risk of infections and cancer. The ability to bank organs for long periods of time holds the promise to address all these challenges. Doctors would have more time to match organs to recipients. They’d be able to limit the risk of organ rejection, too—potentially by preparing recipients, and their immune systems, beforehand. “With real organ banking … instead of the patients waiting for the organ, it’s the organs that are waiting for the patients,” says Finger. Scientists have been able to cool cells to ultra-low temperatures through a process called vitrification, which essentially turns them to something like glass. This procedure is already used to store eggs, sperm, and embryos. Vitrifying whole organs is much harder. Some problems can be avoided with cryoprotectants—chemicals that work like antifreeze and prevent damaging ice crystals from forming. But these chemicals tend to be incredibly toxic. It’s also difficult to rapidly and uniformly cool large tissues, and just as hard to evenly rewarm an organ all the way through. Working with John Bischof, a bioengineer at the University of Minnesota, Finger and colleagues have come up with a solution. Once an organ has been loaded with a cryoprotectant, they infuse it with iron oxide nanoparticles. These nanoparticles don’t do anything to the cells. But when it’s time to rewarm the organ, they can be activated with an electromagnetic field.  When the radiofrequency of that field switches between two states, the particles also flip, realigning themselves with the field. That causes them to release heat throughout the organ. Adjusting the power of the field allows the team to control the rate of heating so that it gets faster once the organ reaches -120°C.  The researchers successfully vitrified rat kidneys using this approach in work published in 2023 . Back then, they were able to rewarm kidneys that had been kept in a freezer for up to 100 days before transplanting them into rats. Since then, the team has been trying to achieve the same success with bigger organs. Pig kidneys are thought to be a good model for human ones—they’re about the same size and look similar. Rat kidneys weigh around one gram; pig kidneys are around 100. It hasn’t been easy. The cryoprotectant used for vitrifying rat kidneys didn’t work as well in the pig organs. “We had to rediscover and modify the cocktail,” says Bischof. “That’s why it’s taken us three years.” Deep-freezing kidneys The first step in the procedure is to remove a kidney from a donor pig. Once it’s out, the kidney is flushed with a commonly used organ preservation solution to remove the blood, bagged, and temporarily laid on a bed of ice in a cooler so it can be taken over to the engineering lab. There, team members unpack the kidney and hook it up to a device they’ve designed to control the organ’s temperature and pressure. Then they start to load it up with the cocktail of cryoprotectants, slowly enough to ensure an even spread through the organ but quickly enough to minimize any toxic effects. It takes around two hours. The next step is to infuse the organ with the iron oxide nanoparticles, which are pumped through the organ for around seven to eight minutes, says Finger. Then it’s time to cool the organ by pumping cold nitrogen vapor into a chamber housing it. It’s a delicate process, and the team must ensure that the organ is cooling all the way through. At the same time, they must lower the kidney’s temperature as quickly as possible to prevent ice from forming. “Oftentimes there are multiple people doing different things to make sure that things don’t go awry,” says Bischof. Once the organ reaches the vitrified state at around -120 °C, it “behaves like a glass,” says Finger. “At that point, you can stay stable for long periods of time—we think indefinitely.” The team then pauses the cooling process to ensure that the organ is glassy throughout. Otherwise, it could crack. After the pause, if everything goes well, the kidney is ultimately cooled to -150 °C. Once it’s in the freezer, it can stay there for days, weeks, or even months. The team has kept a small number of kidneys banked for over a year. So far, the team has tested some of them in a couple of different ways. events.title: Aldar enters Sharjah with Dh1.1bn residential acquisition
events.summary: Aldar , Abu Dhabi ’s biggest listed developer, has agreed to acquire more than 1,100 homes in Sharjah from Arada for Dh1.1 billion ($290 million), its first real estate investment in the emirate as it expand its income-generating property portfolio. The forward-purchase agreement covers nine buildings within three residential blocks at Aljada, Arada’s flagship mixed-use development, with delivery scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2029, Aldar said on Thursday. The transaction will expand Aldar’s develop-to-hold pipeline to Dh21 billion. Aldar said the nine buildings will cater primarily to end users and long-term renters seeking quality housing at accessible price points within an established integrated community. “Sharjah is a large and growing residential market, and Aljada provides an attractive entry point through one of the emirate’s leading master-planned communities,” Aldar group chief executive Talal Al Dhiyebi said. He added that the investment adds scale to Aldar’s residential-for-rent portfolio. The investment builds on a Dh15 billion development partnership announced last month by Aldar and Arada, which covers projects in Abu Dhabi, a further expansion of their relationship. The partnership, which marked Arada’s entry into Abu Dhabi, includes a mixed-use community at Seih Sdeirah, on the Abu Dhabi- Dubai border, and three residential plots on Yas Island. Arada, a joint venture between KBW Investments – a company controlled by Saudi Arabia’s Prince Khaled bin Alwaleed – and Sharjah-based Basma Group, has been rapidly expanding in the UAE as well as in overseas markets such as the UK, Australia and Syria. Aldar, meanwhile, plans to launch a major development of villas and townhouses in Dubai by the end of this year as part of the company’s expansion across the UAE . The new project, with an undisclosed value, will be built near Dubai Silicon Oasis, Aldar Development's chief executive Jonathan Emery told The National in an interview in London this week. The move comes as the UAE property market continues to perform strongly despite uncertainty stemming from the Iran war. The Emirates was ranked as the world’s leading real estate investment destination in a property market league table released in June. Arada’s UAE Property Investment Index – conducted on behalf of the Dubai developer by US-based Penta Group – found that 56 per cent of global investors have serious interest in the UAE’s property market. The latest acquisition will broaden Aldar’s geographic exposure while adding residential rental assets aimed primarily at end users and long-term tenants seeking housing at accessible price points, the company said. Arada group chief executive Ahmed Alkhoshaibi said Aldar’s decision to make its first investment in Sharjah at Aljada reflected confidence in both the development and the emirate’s residential market. “To have a developer of Aldar’s calibre and track record choose Aljada as its first investment in the emirate reflects the quality of what we have built here, and the scale of the opportunity that Sharjah represents,” he said. Aljada spans 2.2 million sq m and is expected to comprise about 25,000 homes at full buildout, with an anticipated gross sales value of Dh35 billion. Residential handovers at the development began in 2021, with more than 8,800 homes delivered across multiple districts, according to the statement. The community also includes schools, hotels, student accommodation, retail space and the Madar family entertainment district. Aldar said the acquisition adds to its strategy of expanding its portfolio of income-generating properties, as the developer seeks to diversify its revenue streams. The Abu Dhabi developer, which recorded strong second-quarter financial results, is expected to hand over more than 3,000 units this year, representing the largest volume since the company’s launch, with the deliveries going up to 4,500 next year, according to Mr Emery.

Please enter a search term. The Chair welcomed the Group and those present as part of the SSAG observers’ programme and the Bank’s Step Into My Shoes observer programme. The Group discussed talent stream opportunities in place across firms, which provide engagement and support from school students through to early career employees. Firms continue to utilise recruitment strategies aimed at providing a diverse workforce and creating value by bringing perspectives, knowledge and experiences from a diverse range of backgrounds. Retrospective review of market conditions The unsecured overnight market remained stable, with daily volumes of around £55 billion and the spread to Bank rate fluctuating close to 1.9 basis points. Money-market funds had experienced collective inflows of approximately £15 billion since the start of the year and had increased allocation to the overnight tenor following changes in liquidity guidance and increased geopolitical tensions. This further supported activity in short-dated markets, while repo-market volatility and month-end spikes were lower than in the previous year. Bank of England information gathering powers The Bank of England and His Majesty’s Treasury are reviewing the statutory powers used to collect sterling money market information. This review seeks to ensure the Bank’s data collection powers are sufficient to maintain strong coverage and visibility of Sterling Money Market activity including as markets evolve, for example should there be changes in market structure, regulation, infrastructure or booking locations. The Bank may seek to collect data on material Sterling Money Market activity in group entities to preserve sufficient coverage for SONIA if necessary, in future. Potential implications for SONIA of extending RTGS settlement hours The Bank of England consulted over the summer on its longer-term ambition to move RTGS and CHAPS settlement towards a near 24-hour, seven-day mode ( Extending RTGS and CHAPS settlement hours CP ) . The Bank is reviewing feedback and intends to return to industry in the first quarter of 2027 with themes emerging from consultation responses and next steps. The Group discussed how longer settlement hours could affect SONIA’s definition, publication time, reporting, and operational processes. The Bank is continuing analysis on the impact of the proposed extended hours scenarios. Under one possible scenario, CHAPS settlement could close at 18:00, with the following day’s settlement starting at 20:00 – meaning between 20:00 and 00:00 there would be a discrepancy between the value date recorded in CHAPS, and calendar date. The Group discussed how market participants could eventually establish timestamp-based conventions. Firms may delay or accelerate booking decisions to manage interest calculations. The Group also discussed potential impact of scenarios where CHAPS settlement closes later in the evening, considering SMMD reporting is required by 07:00 in order for the Bank to publish SONIA by 09:00. Participants noted that many reports are automated but the ability to resubmit or regenerate prior-day data were identified as particularly important. The Group indicated a strong preference to preserve the current SONIA publication time of 09:00. A later publication time could affect processing and fulfilment of products referencing SONIA.

events.title: Beyond The Specification: What Really Determines PCIe Retimer Reach?
events.summary: As AI servers, storage platforms, networking equipment, and high-performance computing systems continue to scale, PCIe links are being pushed farther than ever before. System architects frequently ask a seemingly simple question: how far can a PCIe retimer extend a connection ? Unfortunately, there is no single answer. The effective reach of a PCIe retimer is influenced by multiple interacting factors that span silicon design, controller intelligence, channel quality, and the transmission medium itself. In trying to answer the question, many engineers may initially focus on the PCIe specification and associated channel loss budgets. While specification compliance is essential, real-world reach is often determined by how well a retimer performs beyond the minimum requirements. The difference between a retimer that merely passes compliance testing and one that consistently delivers reliable operation in production deployments can be substantial. Maximizing PCIe reach requires a system-level approach that considers every aspect of the signal path. At the foundation of retimer reach lies the quality of the SerDes architecture. The SerDes serves as the electrical engine that receives, conditions, and retransmits high-speed signals. PCI-SIG specifications define channel-loss requirements that compliant devices must support. For example, designs are commonly expected to accommodate around 36 dB of insertion loss at Nyquist frequency. However, leading retimer vendors frequently engineer their products to tolerate 40 dB or even higher levels of channel loss. Those additional decibels may sound insignificant, but they often translate directly into greater deployment flexibility. Additional margin allows designers to support longer PCB traces, extra connectors, more backplane transitions, and greater manufacturing variation. In large systems where every connector, cable, and via adds loss and reflection, the difference between supporting 36 and 40 dB can determine whether a design succeeds without modification or requires a costly board redesign. The ability to achieve this additional margin depends on sophisticated signal-processing techniques embedded within the SerDes. Advanced equalization circuitry, highly optimized clock recovery algorithms, robust jitter tolerance, and adaptive receiver technologies all contribute to extending channel reach. As the industry moves through PCIe Gen6 and prepares for future generations, these capabilities become increasingly important because every speed increase reduces the available system margin. While the analog performance of the SerDes establishes the foundation, controller intelligence frequently determines how well that foundation performs in real-world environments. Modern PCIe systems operate under conditions that are far more complicated than laboratory compliance tests. Temperature fluctuations, voltage variations, component aging, process variation, and interoperability challenges all affect link stability. One particularly important capability is the handling of corner cases. Specifications cannot anticipate every possible combination of endpoint, root complex, cable, switch, and retimer implementation. Real-world deployments often uncover scenarios that sit at the edge of compliance boundaries. Retimers with sophisticated controller designs are better equipped to manage these situations without causing system instability. As a result, controller quality frequently becomes a major differentiator among retimer solutions that appear similar when viewed purely from a PHY performance perspective. Closely related to controller intelligence is the concept of designing beyond the specification. Compliance testing validates that a device meets defined requirements, but interoperability in production systems often requires more than simple compliance. Different vendors may interpret implementation details differently, resulting in subtle variations during link training, equalization, recovery, or power-state transitions. The most robust retimers are designed with these realities in mind. They include additional logic and protocol awareness to handle unusual behaviors, accommodate implementation differences, and recover gracefully from unexpected situations. This philosophy of engineering beyond the specification can significantly improve compatibility across diverse ecosystems. For hyperscale operators, server manufacturers, and storage vendors, successful interoperability often matters as much as raw signal-integrity performance. Another factor that significantly influences practical reach is observability. As PCIe speeds increase, diagnosing link issues becomes more challenging. The ability to see what is happening within the channel can determine whether a link operates reliably or remains a persistent source of field failures. Modern retimers increasingly include sophisticated diagnostic and monitoring capabilities. Engineers need visibility into link-training behavior, equalization status, signal quality, error statistics, lane margins, and environmental conditions. This information helps identify weak channels, optimize system performance, and accelerate root-cause analysis during deployment. Although diagnostics do not directly improve insertion-loss tolerance, they often increase achievable system reach by allowing engineers to discover and resolve issues that would otherwise remain hidden. In many deployments, better visibility effectively creates additional operational margin by enabling more informed tuning and troubleshooting. No discussion of retimer reach would be complete without considering the quality of the transmission channel itself. Even the most advanced retimer cannot fully compensate for a poorly designed channel. PCB material selection, impedance control, via construction, connector quality, routing practices, and crosstalk management all influence signal integrity. As signaling rates continue to climb, low-loss PCB materials become increasingly attractive because they reduce attenuation and preserve signal quality across longer distances. Likewise, careful connector and via design can dramatically improve channel performance. A high-quality channel allows the retimer to devote its equalization resources to extending reach rather than simply compensating for avoidable losses and reflections. The transmission medium also plays a critical role. Within a chassis, PCB traces dominate the channel budget. Beyond the board, copper cables provide additional flexibility and enable connectivity to external accelerators, storage systems, and expansion modules. High-quality active copper assemblies can often extend PCIe connectivity to approximately two meters while maintaining acceptable performance. However, this capability depends heavily on cable construction, shielding effectiveness, copper quality, and connector design. events.title: Strengthening Advanced-Node Interconnects Through Automated Via Insertion
events.summary: As the semiconductor industry pushes deeper into the sub-5nm realm, the physical design landscape has shifted from being dominated by gate delays to being defined by interconnect performance. In modern system-on-chip (SoC) designs, the wiring that connects billions of transistors has become the primary bottleneck for power, performance, and area (PPA). Among the various components of the interconnect stack, vias – the vertical connections between metal layers – represent one of the most significant points of vulnerability. At advanced process nodes, via resistance increases exponentially as dimensions shrink. This rising resistance, coupled with higher current densities, exacerbates challenges related to electromigration (EM) and IR drop. Traditionally, design teams addressed these issues during the final signoff phase, often resulting in late-stage engineering change orders (ECOs) that could delay a project by weeks. To maintain aggressive time-to-market schedules while ensuring long-term silicon reliability, a new approach is required: shifting signoff-aware interconnect optimization into the implementation phase. The physics of via failure and interconnect resistance To understand the need for automated via optimization, first consider the physical challenges at play. In a typical advanced-node interconnect, the resistance of a single via can be significantly higher than that of a corresponding length of metal wire. As current flows through these narrow vertical structures, the resulting heat and atomic displacement can lead to electromigration – the gradual movement of metal atoms that eventually creates voids or shorts. Plus, the cumulative effect of via resistance across a massive power delivery network (PDN) leads to IR drop. If the voltage reaching a logic gate falls below a certain threshold, the gate’s switching speed slows down, potentially leading to timing failures. In the worst cases, the gate may fail to switch entirely. Historically, designers mitigated these risks by manually adding redundant vias to critical signal paths and power grids. The redundant vias provide parallel paths for current, lowering the effective resistance and reducing the current density through any single via. However, at 5nm and below, the sheer density of the layout and the complexity of foundry design rules make manual insertion practically impossible. Figure 1 illustrates the problem. Fig. 1: The increasing complexity of advanced-node layouts requires automated solutions to identify valid locations for redundant via insertion without violating foundry rules. The limitations of traditional implementation flows Most place-and-route (P&R) tools include basic capabilities for via redundancy. However, these routers are primarily optimized for connectivity and timing closure, not for the exhaustive reliability enhancement required for high-performance silicon. Router-based via insertion typically comes with several limitations: Lack of signoff awareness: Implementation routers typically use simplified versions of foundry design rules to maintain performance. While this is sufficient for initial routing, it often leads to DRC violations when the design is subjected to the full signoff rule deck. Limited search space: Routers often give up on via insertion in congested areas to avoid creating shorts. This leaves critical parts of the design – often the very areas that need the most help – under-optimized. ECO overhead: When a router-based enhancement triggers a signoff violation, the resulting ECO cycle requires re-running parts of the implementation flow, which consumes valuable time and can disrupt timing closure. To overcome these hurdles, many design teams adopt a “shift-left” methodology that uses signoff-quality engines earlier in the design cycle. By integrating the same logic used for final verification into the enhancement process, designers can achieve “correct-by-construction” results that are guaranteed to pass final signoff. Methodology: Automated signoff-aware enhancement The shift-left approach to via optimization involves a specialized enhancement platform that operates on the design database during the implementation phase. This platform reads standard design formats – such as LEF/DEF or OASIS – and applies a multi-step process to strengthen the interconnect. The first step is a comprehensive analysis of the existing layout to identify every potential location where a redundant via could be placed. This is not a simple proximity check; the tool must account for complex multi-patterning constraints, voltage-aware spacing rules, and enclosure requirements. By leveraging a signoff-grade geometry engine, the tool can navigate these constraints with a level of precision that far exceeds traditional routers. Once the valid insertion points are identified, the tool strategically adds redundant vias to the user-selected nets. This can be applied globally to the entire power grid or targeted toward specific high-priority signal nets, such as clock trees or long-distance bus lines. The result is a layout that is significantly more robust, with lower overall resistance and improved EM margins. Fig. 2: By moving signoff-aware optimization into the implementation phase, design teams can resolve interconnect issues before they become late-stage bottlenecks. Navigating layout imperfections with short-resilience One of the most innovative aspects of modern automated enhancement is the ability to handle “dirty” or incomplete layout data. A typical design database is rarely perfectly clean during the implementation flow. Localized shorts, routing overlaps, or incomplete power grid definitions are common as the design matures. Traditional optimization tools often fail when encountering these imperfections, either crashing or producing illegal layout modifications. A robust enhancement platform must be “short-resilient.” This means the tool can identify regions with existing connectivity conflicts and automatically designate them as keep-out areas (Figure 3). Fig. 3: Short-resilient DE-Via flow; avoiding insertion on identified short-prone regions. By protecting these suspicious regions, the tool can continue to optimize the rest of the design. This lets design teams run via enhancement early and often, even before the layout is fully DRC-clean. This iterative approach is essential for maintaining productivity in a fast-paced design environment, as it prevents minor layout issues from stalling the overall reliability enhancement of the chip. Impact on power delivery and electromigration The technical benefits of automated via insertion are most evident in the power delivery network. events.title: Building AI Infrastructure For Greater Choice And Flexibility
events.summary: AI infrastructure is changing fast. Training and inference are putting different demands on compute, memory, connectivity, and networking, and there is no single architecture that fits every workload. For system architects, this opens up an important question: How much flexibility can be built into the system from the start? The answer increasingly involves giving designers more choices across memory, compute, connectivity, and packaging, while making sure those technologies work together. Different workloads, different requirements AI training and inference may run on much of the same underlying infrastructure, but they don’t behave the same way. Training places heavy demands on memory and communication between accelerators. Inference has a different mix of requirements, including memory capacity, latency, throughput, and efficiency. Those differences matter when choosing an architecture. A memory technology that’s right for one workload may not be right for another. The same applies to interconnects and networking. This is why AI infrastructure is becoming more heterogeneous. Architects are combining different technologies based on what they need the system to do, rather than trying to force every workload into the same design. Fig. 1: Heterogeneous applications demand distinct solutions for optimized implementations. More choice through open standards Open standards give designers more options for how they put those systems together. UCIe is one example. The standard provides a common approach to die-to-die connectivity and is aimed at supporting an open chiplet ecosystem. It gives the industry a standardized way to connect dies within a package rather than tying the architecture to a single implementation. System architects are also working across a wider range of process technologies, packaging approaches, and functions. A chiplet-based approach provides another way to partition those functions, allowing compute, I/O, memory interfaces, and other functions to be integrated within the same package. UCIe provides a standardized die-to-die connection for that environment. This gives designers a common interface as they evaluate how different functions should be partitioned and integrated. For designers, the value is choice. Different functions can be brought together in a package while using a common interface between them. That freedom becomes particularly useful when architects are balancing performance, power, cost, packaging, and process technology. Interoperability matters Open standards provide a common foundation for bringing technologies from different suppliers and foundries into the same system. Interoperability helps designers understand how those different implementations will work together. Verification plays an important role here, particularly as systems incorporate more functions, interfaces, and technologies. The same thinking applies across the AI factory The need for choice doesn’t stop at the package. An AI system can include several kinds of connectivity, each serving a different role. PCIe, CXL, UCIe, UALink, and Ethernet-based technologies address different parts of the architecture. Memory brings another set of decisions. Fig. 2: Different connectivity, different scope, same goal: economical, rapid data transfer. The requirements also change depending on where data is moving. HBM4E and LPDDR6 address different memory needs, while PCIe supports high-speed host and device connectivity. UALink addresses accelerator-to-accelerator communication, 224G high-speed SerDes provides the underlying high-speed signaling needed for demanding connectivity applications, and UCIe connects dies within packages. Designers need to consider what they are connecting, how much data needs to move, and the requirements of the workload. Looking at those decisions together provides a more complete view of the system than treating each interface independently. That perspective changes the design conversation. Rather than optimizing individual pieces independently, architects can look at how memory, compute, and connectivity fit together across the system. Designing with room to evolve AI infrastructure will continue to change as workloads, memory technologies, accelerators, and interconnects advance. Building flexibility into the architecture gives designers more options as those requirements change. Open interfaces and interoperability are an important part of that flexibility, allowing designers to choose technologies based on the needs of the system rather than a single approach. For a deeper look at the memory, compute, and connectivity technologies shaping these systems, read our Building AI Factories with IP Solutions white paper . events.title: AMBA C2C: Moving Forward With A Converged AMBA Foundation For C2C Connectivity
events.summary: In this blog post, we introduce AMBA C2C, a new specification being developed with the AMBA ecosystem. It provides a unified and scalable approach to connecting AMBA protocols across chiplets, including AMBA AXI and AMBA CHI. The evolving C2C landscape Chiplet technology and AI are evolving rapidly, bringing new benefits and protocol requirements. AMBA CHI C2C has established strong momentum as a foundational protocol for chiplets and chip-to-chip (C2C) connectivity. It is particularly suited to fully coherent, advanced heterogeneous compute and superchips. However, chiplets span a much wider range of use cases. These include memory expansion, IO and accelerator attach, and advanced heterogeneous systems. Each use case comes with different requirements and trade-offs in functionality, performance, bandwidth efficiency, and implementation complexity. AMBA CHI C2C already supports scalability in implementation complexity through a property negotiation mechanism . Implementations can support only the capabilities they need while preserving interoperability across chiplet types, vendors, and generations. Our continued collaboration with the ecosystem has highlighted an important additional requirement. Many chiplets do not need the full feature set of advanced coherent systems and require an even simpler approach for C2C connectivity. This is particularly important for the vast installed base of AXI-based designs. These designs can benefit from the greater reuse and composability that chiplets enable. This has been an important focus area since we first introduced AMBA CHI C2C in 2023 . At that time, we discussed how C2C connectivity could extend to simpler, often AXI-based use cases. Partner feedback since then has reinforced the need for a unified and converged C2C approach for AMBA protocols. This approach includes both CHI and AXI, rather than separate, protocol-specific point solutions. Introducing AMBA C2C To address these evolving requirements, we are developing AMBA C2C. AMBA C2C builds on the success of AMBA CHI C2C. It provides a converged and scalable C2C foundation across AMBA protocols, including AXI and CHI. At the heart of AMBA C2C is protocol subsetting. Defined subsets enable the protocol feature set and complexity to scale across different use cases. For example, device or accelerator attach subsets can support the simpler requirements aligned with AXI-based IO and non-coherent traffic. More advanced subsets can support the richer functionality required by coherent and heterogeneous systems. AMBA C2C uses defined protocol subsets to scale functionality and implementation complexity across different use cases. These subsets can align with on-chip protocols such as AXI and CHI. AMBA C2C then defines how these protocols are packetized for chip-to-chip transport. The packetization is optimized for each subset while providing a common approach across AXI- and CHI-class traffic. Interoperability remains fundamental to the architecture. AMBA C2C builds on the property negotiation mechanism introduced with AMBA CHI C2C. This mechanism enables implementations with different capabilities to interoperate across chiplet types, vendors, and generations. This includes backwards and forwards compatibility. A layered architecture for an evolving industry An open chiplet ecosystem requires open standards and a clear, layered standardization approach. This includes a clear separation between the protocol and the underlying transport. This is a proven industry model that UCIe and the broader ecosystem have adopted. AMBA CHI C2C, for example, uses UCIe Streaming as discussed in the UCIe 1.1 specification announcement . Similarly, PCIe and CXL protocols can be transported over UCIe. More recently, UALink has adopted a similar layered architecture. It defines a packetization strategy alongside its protocol functionality while separating it from the underlying data-link and physical layers. AMBA C2C follows this same principle. AMBA defines the protocol and packetization mechanism, while transports such as UCIe provide the underlying die-to-die connectivity. This enables AMBA C2C to work with a variety of die-to-die and chip-to-chip transports. More importantly, it provides a clean architectural boundary that enables AMBA protocols and underlying transport technologies to continue evolving at pace. Fig. 1: Transporting AMBA protocols over UCIe with AMBA C2C. For AMBA AXI, this separation is particularly important. AXI is widely adopted across the industry and continues to evolve. However, unlike packet-based protocols, AXI defines interface behavior rather than a native packet format. AXI is also highly configurable, and capabilities vary between implementations. Transporting AXI over a C2C link therefore requires an architectural definition. This definition specifies which AXI semantics are carried and how they are packetized. That definition must evolve alongside AXI itself. Putting it all together AMBA C2C is the next evolution of AMBA’s C2C work. It builds on AMBA CHI C2C and extends the approach to a broader range of AMBA-based chiplet systems. AMBA C2C provides a common foundation that can scale from simple AXI-based designs to advanced, CHI-based fully coherent heterogeneous systems. Interoperability is built into the architecture. AMBA C2C follows the development and licensing model that has supported the AMBA ecosystem for decades. We are developing it in collaboration with industry partners. The specification will be freely available, royalty-free, and architecture-neutral. Over decades, this model has helped establish AMBA as a dependable and trusted industry foundation. It has supported widespread adoption, a thriving ecosystem, and a broad marketplace of compatible solutions. We look forward to continuing our collaboration with the industry to enable an open, interoperable chiplet ecosystem, with AMBA C2C evolving alongside complementary industry standards. The post AMBA C2C: Moving Forward With A Converged AMBA Foundation For C2C Connectivity appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering .
